The verse, therefore, is not only a statement of belief but an existential commitment: to orient one's identity, actions, and worldview entirely toward the one necessary Creator, in a posture of sincere submission (*islām*) that admits no rivals in lordship, worship, or allegiance.

translation: And his people argued with him. He said, 'Do you argue with me concerning Allah while He has guided me? And I do not fear what you associate with Him unless my Lord wills something. My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge. Will you not then take heed?'
interpretation: This verse from Surah Al-An'am (6:80) portrays Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) firmly confronting the objections of his people regarding his rejection of their idols and exclusive devotion to Allah. The phrase 'أتحاجوني في الله' (Do you argue with me concerning Allah) shows his astonishment and firm resolve against disputing the fundamental truth of monotheism once divine guidance ('هدان') has been received. Ibrahim clarifies that he does not fear the false deities they associate with Allah ('ما تشركون به') because they possess no power to harm or benefit, except to the extent that Allah Himself allows ('إلا أن يشاء ربي شيئا'). This phrase is sometimes understood as a conditional clause meaning he fears nothing from these false gods whatsoever, *unless* it is in accordance with Allah's permissive will—affirming that all occurrences ultimately fall under divine decree. The mention that 'وسع ربي كل شيء علما' (My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge) emphasizes Allah's absolute omniscience and comprehensive control over creation. Ibrahim concludes by urging his people to reflect ('أفلا تتذكرون') on the reality of their beliefs and the clear guidance he has been granted, inviting them to heed the truth rather than persist in polytheistic error. The verse ultimately illustrates Ibrahim's unwavering faith, theological clarity, and reliance upon Allah's knowledge and will over all creation.

translation: And how should I fear what you associate [with Him] when you do not fear that you have associated with Allah something for which He has not sent down to you any authority? So which of the two parties has more right to security, if you should know?
interpretation: This verse from Surah Al-An'am (6:81) draws a stark contrast between true faith and idolatry to reveal which is more reasonable. The speaker, a servant of Allah, questions how he should fear powerless false gods that humans themselves have carved, while the idolaters feel no fear despite committing the audacious act of inventing partners for Allah without any divine justification. The rhetorical question at the end—

translation: Those who believe and do not mix their faith with wrongdoing—those will have security, and they are [rightly] guided.
interpretation: This verse defines true security and guidance as contingent upon keeping faith untainted by zulm (wrongdoing/injustice/idolatry). In the Qur'anic worldview, the greatest zulm is shirk (associating partners with God), and 'mixing faith with wrongdoing' implies allowing any form of spiritual, moral, or social injustice to coexist with belief. The verse assures that genuine safety from fear and misguidance comes not merely from professing faith, but from purifying that faith from all forms of transgression—ensuring that belief remains pure, consistent, and undefiled by actions that contradict it.

translation: And that was Our argument which We gave Abraham against his people. We raise by degrees whom We will. Indeed, your Lord is Wise, Knowing.
interpretation: This verse highlights that the reasoning and proof (hujjah) Abraham used against his people, particularly in refuting idolatry and affirming monotheism, was divinely given to him by Allah as a means of guidance. It indicates that Allah grants wisdom, understanding, and spiritual insight to whomever He chooses, elevating certain individuals in rank and knowledge for purposes known only to His wisdom. The closing statement affirms that Allah's decisions are rooted in perfect wisdom and complete knowledge, meaning that His selection of prophets and His manner of revealing truth are never arbitrary but always purposeful and just. This verse serves as a reminder that faith must be accompanied by sound reasoning, and that spiritual rank is bestowed by Allah, not earned through worldly status.

translation: And We gave him [Abraham] Isaac and Jacob – both did We guide. And Noah We guided before, and from his descendants, David, Solomon, Job, Joseph, Moses, and Aaron – and thus do We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the continuity of divine guidance through a chosen lineage of prophets, illustrating that God's favor and direction are not limited to one individual or generation but are extended to a righteous heritage. By mentioning Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Noah first, the verse establishes that guidance was granted to those who submitted sincerely to God. The subsequent listing of David, Solomon, Job, Joseph, Moses, and Aaron demonstrates that prophethood and moral responsibility were distributed across various roles—kings, workers, sufferers, and lawgivers—each called to fulfill a distinct mission. The concluding statement, 'thus do We reward the doers of good,' frames prophethood not as an arbitrary selection but as a divine reward for righteousness, suggesting that those who embody virtue and sincerity are entrusted with carrying forward God's message. The verse also subtly reinforces the idea that the Qur'anic prophetic tradition is plural and continuous, countering any notion that God's care is confined to a single people or moment in history.

translation: And Zakariya, and Yahya, and Isa, and Ilyas—and each [of them] was among the righteous.
interpretation: This verse groups these four prophets together to affirm a theological principle: righteousness is not confined to one nation, lineage, or period. Zakariya, Yahya, Isa, and Ilyas span different generations and contexts, yet the Qur'an deliberately unites them under a single descriptor—*al-salihin* (the righteous). This serves as a subtle rebuke to any exclusivist claim that God's favor rests with one particular people. True righteousness, in the Qur'anic framework, is determined by sincere devotion and moral conduct, not by bloodline or religious identity. The verse also subtly responds to those who elevated certain figures beyond their prophetic station; by placing Isa among other prophets without distinction, it reinforces that prophethood, however exalted, remains within the human realm of servanthood to God.

translation: And [mention] Ishmael and Elisha and Jonah and Lot - and all [of them] We preferred over the worlds.
interpretation: This verse groups together several prophets—Ishmael, Elisha, Jonah, and Lot—affirming that each of them was granted a distinguished rank by God over all other people of their respective eras. By mentioning them collectively after other prophets, the verse underscores a central Qur'anic theme: prophethood is a divine gift bestowed upon chosen servants, and God elevates those He wills above the rest of creation in wisdom, mercy, and purpose. The specific mention of these figures, who came from different backgrounds and faced different trials, highlights that divine favor is not limited to one people or lineage but extends to whoever God chooses to honor with the responsibility of revelation.

translation: And [We chose some] from their fathers, their offspring, and their brothers, and We selected them and guided them to a straight path.
interpretation: This verse highlights Allah's continuous mercy and guidance across generations. It emphasizes that divine election and guidance are not limited to a specific era or community but extend to the righteous descendants, offspring, and brethren of those who were initially chosen. The verse underscores the concept of spiritual inheritance and the perpetuation of faith within families, suggesting that sincerity and devotion can pave the way for successive generations to be guided. The mention of 'a straight path' reinforces the idea of unwavering adherence to divine principles, free from deviation or misguidance. This reflects the broader Qur'anic theme that Allah's favor and guidance are linked to righteousness, not merely lineage, and that communities bound by faith and moral integrity are continuously supported by divine wisdom.

translation: That is the guidance of Allah, with which He guides whom He wills of His servants. But if they had associated others with Allah, then worthless for them would be whatever they were doing.
interpretation: The divine guidance described in the preceding verses—particularly the laws governing lawful and unlawful foods, the sabbath, and the covenant with the Children of Israel—is presented as Allah's gift to lead His servants toward righteousness. Yet divine guidance is not imposed universally; Allah directs it toward those among His servants whom He chooses, based on His wisdom and justice. This implies that acceptance of guidance requires inner receptivity and sincere submission. The verse then issues a stark warning: if the recipients of this guidance were to commit the ultimate spiritual error of associating partners with Allah (shirk), all their righteous deeds would be rendered void. translation: Those are the ones to whom We gave the Scripture, authority, and prophethood. But if these [people] disbelieve in it, We have already entrusted it to a people who are not disbelievers in it.
interpretation:
This verse speaks to the divine plan regarding the preservation and transmission of truth. The 'those' at the beginning refers to the prophets and righteous figures from earlier nations—such as Abraham, Moses, and David—who were given scripture, wise judgment, and the station of prophethood. They bore the weight of revelation and were responsible for guiding their communities.

However, the verse acknowledges a painful reality: not all who receive divine gifts remain faithful to them. The 'these' who may disbelieve refers to communities that were given these blessings but turned away from them despite the clarity of the truth.

In response to this potential failure, God declares that He has already entrusted the message to another group—a people who are not among the disbelievers. Many scholars understand this to refer to the Muslim ummah (community), as mentioned in Surah Al-Baqarah (2:143), where God says He made the Muslim community a 'just nation' to bear witness over mankind. This does not mean Muslims are inherently superior, but rather that they accepted the responsibility of upholding the final revelation and passing it to all of humanity.

The verse carries a deep lesson: divine guidance is never left without a bearer. Even when some abandon the truth, God's plan ensures that others will carry it forward. It also serves as a warning to the Muslim community that they have been entrusted with this responsibility, and they must remain steadfast, lest they also fall into the ranks of those who disbelieve.

translation: Those are the ones whom Allah has guided, so follow their guidance. Say, 'I do not ask you for it any payment. It is only a reminder for the worlds.'
interpretation: This verse establishes a profound principle of prophetic pedagogy and universal mercy. By directing the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ to follow the guidance of those previously guided—namely the earlier prophets and righteous servants of God—the Qur'an links him to an unbroken chain of divine instruction, emphasizing that his message is not an innovation but a continuation and fulfillment of the same truth revealed to all nations. The instruction 'follow their guidance' elevates him not above his predecessors but alongside them as a fellow seeker of the same light. Simultaneously, the declaration that he asks no payment for conveying the Qur'an strips the message of any taint of personal ambition, transaction, or ulterior motive. By describing the Qur'an as a 'reminder for the worlds'—addressing all of creation, human and jinn—this verse universalizes the scope of the revelation, framing it not as a tribal or ethnic possession but as a mercy and admonition intended for every being capable of heeding it.

translation: They have not appraised Allah with true appraisal when they said, 'Allah has not sent down anything to any human being.' Say, 'Then who sent down the Book that Moses brought as a light and guidance for the people, which you make into separate pages, revealing some while concealing much? And you were taught that which you did not know, neither you nor your fathers.' Say, 'Allah.' Then leave them amusing themselves in their wandering.
interpretation: This verse addresses those who deny divine revelation by asserting that Allah has not communicated with humanity. By challenging the deniers to identify the source of the Torah—given its profound guidance and knowledge beyond human capacity—the verse establishes that revelation is a self-evident reality, not merely a claim. The selective disclosure and concealment of scripture by its handlers exposes human manipulation of divine guidance, while the reference to knowledge previously unknown underscores that true insight comes only through Allah's grace. The concluding directive to leave such people to their delusions acknowledges that deliberate rejection of clear truth is a choice from which argumentation cannot retrieve them; it rests with Allah alone to judge those who prefer speculation over submission.

translation: And this is a Book which We have sent down, blessed, confirming what came before it, so that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around it. And those who believe in the Hereafter believe in it, and they are mindful of their prayers.
interpretation: This verse presents the Qur'an as a divinely revealed, blessed scripture that affirms the truth of earlier revelations, carrying a universal warning directed first to Makkah—the center of the world in Islamic geography—and extending outward to all humanity. The certainty of its message is such that sincere belief in the Hereafter naturally leads to faith in the Qur'an, because true acknowledgment of ultimate accountability compels one to accept the guidance that prepares the soul for it. Moreover, such faith is not merely intellectual assent but is demonstrated through consistent, disciplined devotion to prayer, linking sound belief with righteous conduct as inseparable dimensions of genuine faith.

translation: And who is more wrong than he who invents a lie against Allah or says, 'It has been revealed to me,' while nothing was revealed to him, or says, 'I will reveal the like of what Allah has revealed'? If only you could see when the wrongdoers are in the throes of death, and the angels stretch out their hands, saying, 'Deliver your souls! Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation for what you used to say against Allah other than the truth, and you used to be arrogant toward His signs.'
interpretation: This verse establishes the gravity of three distinct yet related sins against divine authority: (1) fabricating lies and attributing them to God, (2) falsely claiming prophetic revelation, and (3) arrogating God's prerogative by attempting to produce revelations comparable to His. The verse does not merely condemn these acts but vividly portrays their ultimate consequence through a dramatic eschatological scene. The angels 'stretching out their hands' represents the violent extraction of the soul from the body, while the command to 'deliver your souls' (ukhruju anfusakum) is deeply ironic—the very souls they cherished and considered their own must now be forcibly surrendered. The 'punishment of humiliation' (adhāb al-hūn) signifies a disgrace that encompasses both the body and the soul, reversing the dignity the wrongdoers falsely claimed in their earthly lives. The verse connects the theological crime (speaking falsehood about God) with the spiritual crime (arrogance toward His signs), showing that the root of all false claims is a fundamental refusal to submit to divine sovereignty. The conditional 'if only you could see' (law tarā) suggests that the reality of this moment transcends human comprehension in its severity.

translation: And you have certainly come to Us alone, just as We created you the first time, and you have left whatever We bestowed upon you behind you. And We do not see with you your 'intercessors' which you claimed that among you they were [Your] partners. It has [all] been severed between you, and lost from you is what you used to claim.
interpretation: This verse depicts the state of absolute accountability on the Day of Judgment, where every individual will stand before Allah in complete isolation, stripped of all worldly attachments and false supports. The imagery of being created 'the first time' underscores human vulnerability and powerlessness without divine sustenance, while the reference to leaving behind 'what We bestowed upon you' highlights the futility of hoarding wealth, status, or relationships, as none of these can accompany a person into the afterlife. The denial of 'intercessors' or 'partners' directly confronts the spiritual delusion of associating intermediaries with Allah—whether through idols, saints, wealth, or false ideologies—clarifying that such fabricated connections will disintegrate entirely. The phrase 'severed between you' signifies the total collapse of the illusions, alliances, and ideologies that once bound people together in worldly life, leaving them utterly estranged from the very things they believed would save them. Ultimately, the verse serves as a profound warning against spiritual complacency, urging believers to recognize that true security lies solely in a sincere relationship with Allah, independent of any worldly or fabricated reliance.

translation: Indeed, Allah is the splitter of the seed and the date stone; He brings forth the living from the dead and brings forth the dead from the living. That is Allah — so how are you deluded away from the truth?
interpretation: This verse presents the concept of biological genesis and transformation as a fundamental proof of divine power and creative will. By pointing to the splitting of seeds and date stones—where dormant potential is broken open to produce new life—Allah is presented as the initiator of life from within inert matter. The Quranic logic then extends this observable natural phenomenon into a metaphysical principle: He brings forth the living from the dead (such as a bird from an egg, or a sprouting plant from a buried seed) and the dead from the living (such as a sperm or an egg produced by a living organism, or the return of the dead to life on the Day of Resurrection). The pairing of these opposites underscores a central theological claim: life and death are not absolute or random categories but are under the sovereign control of a single divine agent who transcends both. The concluding rhetorical question—'so how are you deluded away from the truth?'—is a challenge to those who acknowledge the natural cycles of life yet deny the resurrection or assign divine creative power to other entities. The verse ultimately argues that recognizing Allah as the source of these continuous natural transformations logically compels recognition of His power over the ultimate transformation from death to life after death.

translation: He breaks the dawn (from the darkness of night) and has made the night for rest, and the sun and the moon for reckoning. This is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: The verse underscores Allah's sovereignty over the cosmos and His purposeful design within creation. The image of

translation: And it is He who placed for you the stars, so that you may be guided by them in the darknesses of the land and the sea.
interpretation: This verse highlights a profound sign of God’s care and mercy toward humanity: the creation of the stars as a means of navigation. By calling human attention to the use of stars for guidance through darkness—whether in deserts or oceans—the verse points to the fact that the natural world is not accidental but purposefully designed to serve human needs. It also reflects the broader Qur'anic theme that the universe contains signs for those who reflect and seek knowledge, inviting believers to recognize divine wisdom in even the most ordinary aspects of creation.

translation: And He is the One who originated you from a single soul, and there is [for each of you] a place of settlement and a place of deposit. We have detailed the signs for a people who understand.
interpretation: This verse affirms God's creative power by tracing all of humanity back to a single origin, emphasizing the unity and equality of the human race despite the diversity of languages, ethnicities, and cultures that subsequently emerged. The pairing of mustaqarr (a fixed place of settling, often understood as the womb or the world) and mustawda' (a place of temporary deposit, such as the loins of ancestors or the grave) frames human existence as a series of ordained stages within a divine plan, reminding believers that their journey from conception through life to death and beyond lies entirely within God's knowledge and decree. By stating that the signs have been clearly elaborated for those who reflect, the verse invites sincere contemplation of these realities as a path to deepening faith and recognizing the purposeful design underlying human creation and existence.

translation: And it is He who sends down from the sky rain, and We produce thereby every kind of growth, and We produce thereby the green growth from which We bring forth clustered grain, and from the palm trees, from its fruiting clusters, hanging dates low and near, and gardens of grapevines, olives, and pomegranates, similar and not similar. Look at their fruits when they yield and ripen. Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.
interpretation: The verse underscores Allah's power and mercy as the sole source of life and sustenance. The rain from the sky is not merely a physical phenomenon but an act of divine will through which all vegetation is brought forth, illustrating that behind natural processes lies purposeful creation. The detailed mention of grains, dates, olives, and pomegranates—each described as both similar and distinct—highlights the balance between unity in origin and diversity in form, reflecting a designed order that invites reflection rather than passive observation. The command to look at the fruits when they appear and ripen is an invitation to contemplate transformation, growth, and the careful timing embedded in nature, all of which point to a Creator. The closing remark that these signs are for those who believe emphasizes that recognition of divine wisdom is not merely an intellectual exercise but a matter of faith; meaningful insight into creation is reserved for those who approach it with sincere belief.

translation: And they have made equal to Allah the jinn as associates, though He created them, and they have fabricated for Him sons and daughters without any knowledge. Exalted is He and high above what they describe.
interpretation: This verse condemns the grave error of associating partners with Allah, specifically the audacious claim that jinn share in divinity alongside Him, despite the fact that jinn themselves are Allah's creation and wholly dependent on Him. It further denounces the unfounded and baseless attribution of offspring to Allah—assigning to Him sons and daughters invented by human imagination and cultural tradition—without any authentic knowledge or revelation to support such claims. The verse concludes with a declaration of Allah's absolute transcendence (subhanahu) and exaltation (ta'ala) above all the false descriptions, attributions, and associations that people fabricate about Him. The underlying message is a critique of anthropomorphic and polytheistic tendencies in human belief systems, emphasizing that true recognition of Allah requires acknowledging His oneness, His sole creative power, and rejecting all forms of speculative theology that arise from ignorance rather than revelation. It serves as a reminder that human reasoning, when divorced from divine guidance, inevitably leads to distortions of the nature of the Divine.

translation: Originator of the heavens and the earth—how could He have a son when there was never any consort belonging to Him, and He created all things, and He has full knowledge of all things.
interpretation: The verse highlights God's absolute uniqueness and self-sufficiency by stating that He created the heavens and the earth from nothing, without precedent or model. It rhetorically asks how He could have a child when He has no partner or companion, thereby rejecting the notion of divine offspring or familial relationships within God's nature. The verse further emphasizes His sovereignty by affirming that He is the creator of everything and possesses complete and intimate knowledge of all His creation, reinforcing that human concepts of lineage and association do not apply to the Divine.

translation: That is Allah, your Lord—there is no deity except Him, the Creator of all things, so worship Him. And He is, over all things, the Disposer of affairs.
interpretation: This verse defines the nature of God by what He is not (there is no deity besides Him) and what He is (Creator of all things). The statement

translation: No vision grasps Him, but He grasps all vision, and He is the Subtle, the All-Aware.
interpretation: This verse affirms God's absolute transcendence over all created perception: nothing in the realm of sight, imagination, or intellect can encompass or contain Him, for He is utterly beyond the limits of any created faculty. Yet the flow of the verse reverses direction in a profound reversal of expectation—while all vision fails to grasp Him, He Himself perceives and encompasses every act of seeing. The mention of sight in particular, rather than hearing or other senses, addresses the most immediate and concrete mode of human perception, emphasizing that even the most direct form of encountering the world cannot reach the Divine. The pairing of His names at the end, al-Latif and al-Khabir, deepens this meaning: He is Subtle, meaning His knowledge and action penetrate the finest, most hidden, and most delicate realities of existence, beyond the reach of any coarse or external perception; and He is All-Aware, meaning nothing escapes His consciousness, not even the inner workings of sight itself. Together, these attributes reveal that the inability of vision to grasp God is not due to His distance, but to His overwhelming subtlety and intimacy—He is closer to creation than their own faculty of sight, yet remains utterly beyond its capacity to capture. This invites the believer into a mode of knowing God that transcends sensory limitation: recognizing Him through His traces, His signs, and the signs within oneself, rather than seeking to encompass Him through any image or form.

translation: There has come to you clear proofs from your Lord. Whoever sees [the truth], it is for [the benefit of] his soul; and whoever remains blind, it is only to his detriment. And I am not a guardian over you.
interpretation: The verse affirms that God has sent clear signs and guidance to humanity, placing the responsibility of recognizing truth squarely on the individual. Sight and blindness are used metaphorically here: the one who 'sees' exercises faith, reason, and moral awareness, thereby benefiting their own soul, while the one who 'chooses blindness'—deliberately rejecting or ignoring these proofs—bears the consequences of that choice alone. The closing statement, 'And I am not a guardian over you,' is a profound declaration that the Prophet Muhammad's role is not to compel belief or monitor hearts, but solely to convey the message. This underscores the Qur'anic principle of free will: divine guidance has been provided, but human beings retain the autonomy to accept or reject it, with each person fully accountable for the spiritual outcome of their own decision.

translation: And thus do We diversify the verses so that they may say, 'You have studied,' and so that We may make it clear to a people who know.
interpretation: This verse highlights a profound divine principle regarding the method of Quranic revelation and communication. Allah states that He presents the truths of faith in multiple, varied expressions and styles—using parables, commands, prohibitions, warnings, and glad tidings—so that the message resonates with every type of human disposition. This diversity is also a test: those who are hostile to the truth will accuse the Prophet ﷺ of having learned these accounts from others or from previous scriptures, rather than acknowledging their divine origin. Yet, the ultimate purpose behind this varied and comprehensive presentation is to establish clear, undeniable guidance for those who are sincere in their pursuit of knowledge and reflection. It underscores that true understanding is a gift from Allah, granted only to hearts that are genuinely open to His wisdom.

translation: Follow what has been revealed to you from your Lord—there is no god except Him—and turn away from the polytheists.
interpretation: This verse establishes the foundational stance of the Prophet Muhammad: unwavering adherence to divine revelation as the sole source of guidance, coupled with disengagement from those who associate partners with God. The command 'follow' implies continuous action, not merely initial acceptance—it demands that every aspect of life be aligned with what God has revealed. The declaration of God's absolute oneness serves as the criterion by which revelation is recognized and by which all other claimants to divinity or authority are rejected. Turning away from the polytheists does not necessarily mean physical avoidance in all contexts, but rather a principled separation from their creed and practices. This verse also reflects a spiritual reality: one cannot truly follow divine guidance while remaining attached to systems of belief or loyalty that compete with or contradict it. The believer must prioritize revelation over social conformity, ancestral tradition, or political alliance. It is a call to intellectual and spiritual independence grounded in divine truth, trusting that God's guidance is sufficient regardless of how many oppose it. The verse thus sets the Prophet apart as a model of total reliance on God—neither seeking validation from the disbelievers nor compromising his message to appease them, because his authority and direction come from a source beyond human approval.

translation: And if Allah had willed, they would not have associated [anything with Him]. And We have not made you a guardian over them, nor are you over them a manager.
interpretation: The verse establishes that polytheism and disbelief occur not by compulsion from Allah, but by His leave within the scope of human free will; had He willed to coerce faith, He could have, but His wisdom chose to test humanity through choice. The Prophet ﷺ is being consoled and instructed that he is neither a custodian responsible for forcing their guidance nor a guardian accountable for their choices—his duty is solely to convey the message, while the affair of hearts and ultimate accountability rests entirely with Allah. This relieves the Prophet ﷺ of grief over those who reject faith and clarifies that responsibility for deviation lies with the individuals themselves, not with the bearer of the message.

translation: And do not insult those they invoke besides Allah, lest they insult Allah in enmity without knowledge. Thus We have made pleasing to every nation their deeds; then to their Lord is their return, and He will inform them of what they used to do.
interpretation: This verse establishes a profound principle of religious coexistence and ethical conduct in the face of theological disagreement. It prohibits Muslims from verbally disparaging the deities or sacred figures worshipped by polytheists, even though those deities are false. The reasoning is strategic and moral: if Muslims insult the idols and gods of others, those others may retaliate by insulting Allah out of ignorance and hostility, which would result in harm to the sacred. This demonstrates that the defense of truth requires wisdom and restraint, not provocation, and that the honor of God should not be placed in jeopardy through careless speech. The verse then broadens to a theological observation: every community finds its own deeds pleasing because Allah has allowed humans the freedom to follow their inclinations as a test. Ultimately, judgment belongs to God alone, who will reveal the true nature of every action on the Day of Return, reminding believers that human perception of righteousness is limited and that divine justice will ultimately clarify the value of all deeds.

translation: And they swore by Allah their most binding oaths that if a sign came to them, they would surely believe in it. Say, 'The signs are only with Allah.' And how do you know that, even if it came to them, they would not believe?
interpretation: This verse exposes the dishonesty and stubbornness of those who demand miraculous proofs as a precondition for faith, suggesting that their insistence is not a genuine pursuit of truth but a pretext for continued denial. The divine response clarifies that miracles are within God's exclusive domain and will not be produced at the behest of skeptics. More profoundly, the verse reveals a psychological and spiritual reality: when hearts are already sealed against guidance, even undeniable signs would fail to penetrate their resistance. This indicates that faith is ultimately a matter of inner disposition and divine grace, not merely empirical evidence, and that those who reject truth often construct their denial so deeply that no external proof can overcome it.

translation: And We would turn their hearts and their sights [away] as they had not believed the first time, and We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly.
interpretation: This verse speaks to a profound spiritual reality: when a person persistently rejects truth after it has been made clear to them, their capacity to perceive and accept that truth becomes increasingly impaired. The turning of hearts and sights here is not arbitrary punishment but rather the natural consequence of repeated rejection—when the inner eye and the heart are continually turned away from faith, they gradually lose the ability to recognize truth even when it stands before them. This is why the verse connects their state to their initial unwillingness to believe: they had chosen not to recognize truth when it first came, and that same willful blindness now defines their condition. Being left to wander in transgression means being abandoned to the logical outcome of their own choices—confusion, disorientation, and inability to distinguish guidance from misguidance. The verse carries a sobering warning that rejection of truth is not a neutral act; it shapes the soul and progressively darkens understanding, ultimately leaving the person stranded in a state of self-imposed blindness from which they cannot easily return.

translation: And even if We had sent down to them the angels, and the dead spoke to them, and We gathered all things before them, they would not believe unless Allah should will. But most of them are ignorant.
interpretation: This verse highlights the concept of divine predestination in matters of faith, emphasizing that belief ultimately depends on Allah's will. It suggests that even the most extraordinary signs or miracles would not compel people to believe if Allah has not decreed faith for them. This underscores the idea that guidance is a divine gift, and human hearts can only be opened by Allah's grace. The verse also critiques the ignorance of those who demand signs as a precondition for belief, pointing out that their obstinacy stems not from a lack of evidence but from a deeper spiritual blindness. It serves as a reminder that faith is not merely a rational conclusion but a matter of the heart, which only Allah can soften and illuminate.

translation: And thus have We made for every prophet an enemy - devils from mankind and jinn, inspiring to one another decorative speech in delusion. And if your Lord had willed, they would not have done so. So leave them and that which they fabricate.
interpretation:
This verse establishes a fundamental theological reality about the nature of prophethood and opposition to it: every prophet sent by Allah inevitably faces adversaries, and these adversaries come from both human and jinn sources. The term شياطين (devils) here is not limited to the jinn alone but includes humans who actively oppose divine guidance, indicating that opposition to truth is not random but a structural feature of the prophetic struggle.

The phrase يوحي بعضهم إلى بعض زخرف القول غرورا (inspiring to one another decorative speech in delusion) reveals the methodology of these adversaries: they engage in mutual reinforcement through embellished rhetoric and persuasive falsehoods. This suggests that error is not merely a passive state but an active project requiring collaboration, where falsehood is dressed in attractive forms to deceive others. The word غرور (delusion) implies that both the propagators and victims of such speech are ensnared, highlighting the self-deceptive nature of opposing truth.

The conditional statement ولو شاء ربك ما فعلوه (And if your Lord had willed, they would not have done so) asserts divine sovereignty over all events, including human rebellion. This removes any deterministic excuse for wrongdoing while emphasizing that opposition occurs within Allah's permissive will. The directive فذرهم وما يفترون (So leave them and that which they fabricate) instructs the Prophet to disengage from disputation with those who persist in fabrication, trusting that truth will prevail through divine wisdom rather than through endless argumentation.

The verse thus combines three elements: a realistic acknowledgment of persistent opposition, an explanation of how falsehood operates through beautified speech, and a command for disengagement rooted in trust in divine sovereignty. It provides a framework for understanding that the struggle between truth and falsehood is expected, that falsehood relies on rhetorical manipulation, and that the believer's response involves steadfastness rather than retaliation.

translation: So that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline towards it, and that they may be pleased with it, and that they may commit what they are committing.
interpretation: This verse is part of the broader Qur'anic critique of how corrupt speech and alluring falsehood can seduce those whose spiritual orientation is already misaligned. It speaks to a moral and psychological dynamic: people who have turned away from belief in ultimate accountability are predisposed to find appealing that which confirms their existing inclinations. The verse does not claim that the listener is forced or deceived against their nature; rather, it describes an internal receptivity in which the heart, already inclined toward denial of the Hereafter, finds the false discourse pleasing and consonant with its desires. Their 'acceptance' and 'satisfaction' are not rational convictions but affective affinities—they like what flatters their worldview. Consequently, they persist in the very sins and moral compromises ('what they are committing') that such speech encourages. The verse thus exposes a self-reinforcing cycle: worldly temptation shapes hearts already closed to accountability, and those hearts, in turn, welcome more of what deepens their estrangement from truth. It is a sober warning about the complicity between desire and deception, and about how spiritual heedlessness makes one vulnerable to narratives that promise pleasure while confirming one's own avoidance of moral reckoning.

translation: Should I seek other than God as judge, when it is He who revealed to you the Book, detailed? And those to whom We gave the Book know it was sent down from your Lord in truth; so be not of those who doubt.
interpretation: This verse establishes the absolute sufficiency and supreme authority of the Qur'an as the criterion for judgment and truth, declaring that no other source can stand alongside or above God's revelation. The detailed nature of the Book signifies that it contains all necessary guidance, leaving no need for external arbitration. The mention of those given prior scriptures who recognize the truth of the Qur'an serves as an external validation from earlier communities who possessed authentic knowledge, indicating that divine revelation forms a continuous and consistent testimony to the message. The concluding command forbids doubt, not as an injunction against critical thought, but as a prohibition of the kind of wavering that stems from spiritual weakness or unwillingness to commit to truth once it has been established through evidence and witness.

translation: And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and in justice. None can alter His words, and He is the Hearing, the Knowing.
interpretation: This verse affirms the perfection and immutability of God's decree, emphasizing that His promises and commands are both truthful in their content and just in their application. It highlights that no created being can change or override what God has established, underscoring His absolute authority. At the same time, the closing attributes—'the Hearing, the Knowing'—serve as a reminder that God is fully aware of all human actions and intentions, meaning that His unchangeable word is not arbitrary but rooted in perfect knowledge and responsiveness to what He hears and understands of His creation. This combination reassures the faithful of the reliability of divine guidance while warning that accountability remains intact, since nothing escapes God's perception.

translation: And if you were to obey most of those upon the earth, they would mislead you from the way of Allah. They follow nothing but assumption, and they are not but guessing.
interpretation: This verse establishes a foundational epistemological principle: the truth of any matter is not determined by its popularity or the consensus of the majority. Human beings, by their very nature, are limited in their perception and are prone to error. The verse identifies the root cause of this misguidation as 'assumption' (الظن) and 'conjecture' (يخرصون), indicating that when people lack certain knowledge or divine guidance, they substitute it with speculation, personal desires, and inherited traditions. Consequently, the believer is called to ground their certainty and direction not in the fluctuating, often misguided, opinions of the masses, but solely in divine revelation and clear knowledge from Allah. True guidance transcends human whim; adhering to it may require standing against the majority when the majority strays.

translation: Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of the [rightly] guided.
interpretation: This verse affirms that Allah's knowledge encompasses all human conduct and spiritual orientation. He perfectly discerns those who deviate from the truth of Islam and those who follow it, meaning that divine wisdom—not human judgment—determines who is misguided and who is rightly guided. This establishes that guidance is ultimately in Allah's hands, and believers should rely on His knowledge rather than their own assessments of others, while remaining committed to following the clear guidance of the Qur'an and the Sunnah of the Prophet (peace be upon him).

translation: So eat of that [meat] upon which the name of Allah has been mentioned, if you are believers in His verses.
interpretation: This verse establishes a principle of reliance on divine guidance in matters of lawful sustenance, calling believers to consume only what has been properly dedicated to Allah's name and to abandon practices rooted in ignorance or blind tradition, reflecting a faith that is lived out in daily choices.

translation: And why should you not eat of that upon which Allah's name has been mentioned while He has explained in detail to you what He has forbidden you, excepting that to which you are compelled. And indeed many, by their own desires, lead astray without knowledge. Indeed, your Lord knows best who transgresses.
interpretation: This verse teaches that believers should not abstain from eating lawful meat slaughtered in the name of Allah based on mere suspicion or blind adherence to unverified prohibitions, since Allah has already clarified what is truly forbidden (such as carrion, blood, pork, and what is slaughtered for other than Allah). The only exception is when one is forced by extreme necessity, such as starvation, in which case eating the prohibited becomes permissible. The verse also warns against those who, driven by personal whims and desires rather than divine knowledge, mislead others into forbidding what Allah has made lawful. It affirms that Allah alone knows the true condition of those who overstep His limits, whether by inventing false prohibitions or by misguiding others, emphasizing that human judgment must yield to divine guidance.

translation: And abandon the outward sin and the inward one. Indeed, those who commit sin will be recompensed for what they used to earn.
interpretation: This verse calls upon believers to refrain from sin in all its forms—both the open, publicly visible sins and the hidden, secret sins committed privately. It emphasizes the comprehensive nature of moral accountability in Islam, where no sin escapes divine notice simply because it is concealed from human eyes. The term "إثم" (ithm) refers to acts of disobedience and transgression, and the instruction to leave both its "ظاهر" (zahir, outward) and "باطنه" (batin, inward) aspects indicates that true righteousness involves not merely the avoidance of conspicuous wrongdoing but also the purification of the heart and conscience from subtle, private sins such as greed, envy, lustful thoughts, and hypocrisy. The closing statement, promising that those who earn sin will be fully recompensed according to their deeds, serves as a solemn warning that divine justice will inevitably address every transgression, regardless of whether it was performed openly or in secret, reinforcing the believer's duty to maintain consistent integrity in both public conduct and private character.

translation: And do not eat of that upon which the name of Allah has not been mentioned, for indeed, it is grave disobedience. And indeed, the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you, and if you were to obey them, you would indeed be of those who associate others with Allah.
interpretation: This verse establishes a clear principle of mindful consumption and intentionality in one's relationship with the divine. The prohibition against eating meat not consecrated by the mention of God's name is not merely a dietary restriction but a spiritual discipline—it calls upon believers to infuse even their most basic, everyday actions with conscious awareness of God. Eating becomes a sacred act rather than a mere biological necessity. The verse then addresses a deeper spiritual danger: the influence of negative forces that seek to distort religious understanding through argumentation and doubt. These forces do not attack faith head-on but rather through subtle reasoning and debate that can lead believers away from clarity into confusion. The warning about being rendered polytheists through obedience to such influences highlights that polytheism (shirk) is not limited to the explicit worship of multiple deities but extends to any form of divided loyalty—any situation where a person follows competing authorities besides God. When believers prioritize human opinions, cultural pressures, or intellectual rationalizations over divine guidance, they effectively elevate those alternatives to a status of authority that rivals God. Thus, the verse connects the physical (food) with the spiritual (faith), teaching that wholehearted devotion to God must extend into all aspects of life, including what one consumes, what one believes, and whom one ultimately obeys.

translation: Is one who was dead and We revived him and gave him a light by which he walks among people like one who is in darkness from which he cannot emerge? Thus the disbelievers have been made to consider their deeds as appealing.
interpretation: This verse presents a powerful metaphorical contrast to illustrate the transformative impact of faith and guidance. The 'dead' person represents one engulfed in the darkness of disbelief, ignorance, and spiritual heedlessness, devoid of purpose and true life. God revives this person through faith, illuminating their heart with divine guidance, represented by the 'light' which allows them to navigate the complexities of human existence with clarity, moral discernment, and purpose. Conversely, the person enveloped in 'darkness' symbolizes the state of the persistent disbeliever, who is trapped in confusion, misguidance, and spiritual blindness, unable to find an exit or true direction. The concluding statement reveals a profound spiritual reality: misguidance is not merely a passive state but often a self-perpetuating delusion. Through the subtle workings of the lower self and external temptations, evil deeds and false beliefs are 'made to appear appealing' (زين) to those who reject faith, creating a deceptive veneer of satisfaction that reinforces their estrangement from truth. The verse thus calls for reflection on one's inner state, urging an appreciation for the priceless value of divine guidance that brings one out of the darkness of the soul into the light of meaning and truth.}

translation: And thus We have placed within every city its greatest sinners to conspire therein, yet they conspire only against themselves, and they do not perceive.
interpretation: This verse reveals that God's law of balance and consequences operates in every community. The greatest criminals and conspirators are given prominence and influence in their societies as part of a divine pattern, yet their scheming ultimately rebounds upon themselves. It highlights a profound truth about evil: its architects become its first victims. Those who plot darkness for others are often blinded by their own ambition and arrogance, failing to recognize that the harm they intend for others will ultimately consume them. This serves as a warning that injustice, despite appearing to flourish temporarily, is inherently self-destructive, and that the perpetrators of corruption, regardless of their apparent power, cannot escape the natural moral consequences of their actions.

translation: And when a clear sign comes to them, they say, 'We will not believe until we are given the same as what was given to the messengers of Allah.' Allah knows best where to place His message. Those who commit crimes will soon be subjected to humiliating punishment from Allah and a severe torment for what they used to devise.
interpretation: This verse addresses the arrogant rejection of prophethood based on envy and a demand for equality with the chosen messengers. The disbelievers, rather than submitting to the divine selection, insist on receiving the same status or tangible proof as the prophets, revealing that their objection is not intellectual but rooted in pride and resentment of human chosenness. The declaration that 'Allah knows best where to place His message' affirms that prophethood is a divine trust placed exactly where it belongs according to perfect wisdom, not a position to be claimed, competed for, or redistributed. The warning of 'humiliating punishment' and 'severe torment' indicates that those who scheme against Allah's choice through denial, ridicule, and conspiracy will be abased both in this world and the Hereafter, because their crime is not merely disbelief but the deliberate plotting to obstruct and demean what Allah has honored. The verse thus distinguishes between honest seekers of truth and those who oppose revelation out of egotism, promising that divine wisdom ultimately exposes and disgraces those who reject it with arrogance.

translation: And whoever Allah wills to guide, He opens his breast to Islam; and whoever He wills to lead astray, He makes his breast narrow and constricted as though he were climbing up into the sky. Thus does Allah place defilement upon those who do not believe.
interpretation: This verse teaches that genuine acceptance of Islam is ultimately a matter of divine grace; God expands the heart of the one He chooses to guide so that faith becomes natural and easy, while the heart of the one He chooses to leave astray becomes choked with resistance, so that even the most obvious truth feels unbearable—like a soul trying to ascend into the heavens without wings. The verse does not portray divine will as arbitrary or unjust, because it is linked to a person's inner disposition and willingness to receive truth: when a soul turns away from sincere reflection, attachment to truth, and the remembrance of God, it gradually loses the capacity to absorb faith, and that hardening is the natural consequence of its own choices. The phrase "defilement" (rijs) upon disbelievers refers to this inner darkness and spiritual impurity—a covering over the heart that prevents recognition of God's signs, distorts moral reasoning, and leaves the person trapped in confusion and spiritual suffocation. Ultimately, the verse calls the reader to seek the expansion of the heart through sincere remembrance of God, humility, and reliance on His guidance, knowing that spiritual ease in faith is itself a gift from God that must be continually sought and preserved.

translation: And this is the straight path of your Lord. We have detailed the verses for a people who take heed.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the guidance revealed through the Qur'an constitutes the singular, upright path leading to Allah, leaving no room for deviation or alternative routes to truth. The act of 'detailing the signs' reflects divine mercy, as the clarity of the message removes any excuse for ignorance. However, this clarity is framed as a conditional gift—its transformative power is actualized only within hearts that possess 'dhikr' (remembrance and mindful awareness). This implies that mere intellectual exposure to the verses is insufficient; true benefit requires a receptive, contemplative inner state. Thus, the verse distinguishes between passive hearing and active remembrance, emphasizing that spiritual understanding emerges from the synergy of divine clarity and human attentiveness.

translation: For them is the Home of Peace with their Lord, and He will be their protector because of what they used to do.
interpretation: This verse describes the ultimate reward awaiting the righteous believers in the afterlife: a dwelling characterized by peace, safety, and tranquility in the presence of Allah. The phrase 'Home of Peace' (Dar al-Salam) signifies a state of absolute security, free from fear, sorrow, or any form of harm, where believers find rest from the trials of worldly life. The mention that Allah Himself becomes their protector and companion reflects the profound intimacy and honor granted to them, as divine guardianship replaces all earthly dependencies. Importantly, this reward is not unconditional mercy but is tied to their righteous deeds ('because of what they used to do'), emphasizing the causal relationship between faithful obedience and ethical conduct in this world and the attainment of salvation in the next. The verse thus serves as both a consolation for the struggles of the righteous and a motivation to persevere in faith and good works.

translation: And [mention] the Day when He will gather them all together, [saying], 'O company of jinn, you have greatly misled the humans,' and their allies among the humans will say, 'Our Lord, we enjoyed one another through each other, and we have reached the term which You appointed for us.' He will say, 'The Fire is your dwelling, wherein you will abide eternally, except for what Allah wills. Indeed, your Lord is Wise and Knowing.'
interpretation: This verse depicts a profound moment of ultimate accountability, revealing the deeply intertwined nature of the trial between humans and jinn in the worldly life. The statement that the jinn 'greatly misled' or 'took in great numbers from among the humans' highlights that the deception was not merely incidental but a massive, calculated effort by the jinn to lead humanity astray. The response of the human allies—admitting they 'enjoyed one another'—exposes the raw reality of that relationship: it was one of mutual exploitation masquerading as companionship. Humans gained worldly desires, power, or false comfort through the jinn, while the jinn gained worship, obedience, or amusement through the humans. Both parties used each other as instruments for fleeting gratification. When the appointed term arrives, this corrupt alliance collapses, and the so-called friends become accusers of one another. However, the verse also contains a terrifying divine prerogative: the declaration that the Fire is their eternal abode 'except for what Allah wills.' This exception is not a guarantee of escape but an assertion of God's absolute sovereignty over mercy and punishment. No creature's fate is sealed outside of His will, reminding that even in judgment, divine wisdom ('Hakeem') and perfect knowledge ('Aleem') prevail, and what appears to be unending torment remains subject to a decision that only the All-Wise can make. It is a sobering reminder that all worldly bonds cut off from Allah are ultimately hollow, and true enjoyment is only that which is rooted in His pleasure.

translation: And thus We let some of the wrongdoers have authority over others because of what they used to earn.
interpretation: This verse reveals a profound divine law regarding the consequences of collective human behavior. It indicates that the granting of power or dominance by God to certain groups over others is not arbitrary but is directly linked to the moral and spiritual state of the people involved. When a society collectively engages in wrongdoing, corruption, and injustice, God may allow tyrannical or oppressive individuals or groups to rise to power over them as a form of consequence for their own actions. This suggests a reciprocal relationship between a people's deeds and the nature of the leadership or circumstances they experience. The verse implicitly carries a warning: the character of those who rule or dominate is often a reflection of the moral condition of those over whom they hold sway, urging individuals and communities toward righteousness lest they become deserving of such a fate due to their own misdeeds.

translation: O company of jinn and men, did there not come to you messengers from among yourselves who related to you My verses and warned you of the meeting of this your Day? They will say, 'We bear witness against ourselves.' And the worldly life had deceived them, and they will bear witness against themselves that they were disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse portrays a scene on the Day of Judgment where humanity and the jinn are collectively addressed and asked whether divine guidance was sent to them through messengers of their own kind. The acknowledgment 'we bear witness against ourselves' reflects a profound realization where denial becomes impossible, as the evidence of having received clear signs and warnings is undeniable. The phrase 'the worldly life deceived them' points to the illusion of material existence as the primary cause of their heedlessness and ultimate spiritual loss. The verse ultimately underscores the universal nature of prophetic guidance, the self-incriminating nature of rejection, and the consequences of prioritizing transient worldly pursuits over eternal truth.

translation: That is because your Lord would not destroy the towns [unjustly] while their people were unaware [of wrongdoing].
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that Allah's justice is rooted in knowledge and awareness; He does not punish a community for transgression unless they have been given clear guidance and have consciously chosen to turn away from it. The mention of 'ignorance' here does not excuse wrongdoing but highlights that divine punishment follows a warning, making people accountable only after the message has reached them. It reflects a core principle of Islamic theology: divine mercy precedes divine wrath, and accountability is tied to awareness.

translation: And for all are degrees [or ranks] according to what they have done, and your Lord is not unaware of what they do.
interpretation: This verse establishes the Islamic principle of spiritual hierarchy based on deeds and inner intention. Every soul occupies a specific station in the sight of Allah determined not by wealth, lineage, or worldly status, but by the sincerity, effort, and righteousness of their actions. The concluding statement that Allah is never heedless of human deeds serves as both a warning against complacency and a source of comfort for the oppressed, affirming that no deed—no matter how hidden—is lost, forgotten, or without consequence in the divine order.

translation: And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient, the Possessor of Mercy. If He wills, He can remove you and replace you with whom He wills, just as He produced you from the descendants of other peoples.
interpretation: This verse highlights two complementary divine attributes: absolute self-sufficiency (الغنى) and boundless mercy (الرحمة). Allah is in no need of His creation; His sustaining of humanity is a manifestation of His mercy, not any necessity. Because of this self-sufficiency, He is free to remove any generation that disobeys Him and to bring forth a new one in its place, just as He once brought forth the Arabs from the lineage of earlier nations, such as those of Noah or Abraham. The verse carries a stern warning: communities are not permanent fixtures in the earth, and security from divine replacement is not guaranteed by lineage or worldly power. It depends instead on conscious submission to God. The phrase 'كما أنشأكم من ذرية قوم آخرين' also underscores the cyclical nature of divine creation—humanity is continuously raised and raised again from successive peoples—pointing to the fact that worldly dominance is transient and that accountability before God remains constant across all generations.

translation: Indeed, what you are promised is bound to come, and you cannot escape [it].
interpretation: This verse is a divine assertion of the certainty of accountability and the inevitability of the promised consequences—whether reward or punishment—that await every soul. The Arabic phrase 'lati' (آت) conveys an emphatic, inescapable arrival, denying any possibility of evasion or escape ('ma antim bi-mu'jizin'). It serves as a profound spiritual reminder that worldly distractions, procrastination, and denial cannot shield one from the ultimate reckoning. For the believer, this instills a sense of urgency and mindfulness, encouraging conscious living, ethical responsibility, and sincere preparation for the eternal life beyond the transient world. The verse essentially bridges divine promise with human accountability, reinforcing that moral choices in this life carry definitive, non-negotiable outcomes in the next.

translation: Say, 'O my people, work according to your position; indeed, I am working. Soon you will know who will have the final abode. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed.'
interpretation: This verse presents a profound principle of divine wisdom regarding human accountability and the certainty of ultimate justice. The Prophet is commanded to address his people with a statement of detachment and resolve, essentially saying: 'Persist in your path as you see fit, while I remain steadfast upon mine.' This is not merely a declaration of separation, but an invitation to reflect upon the consequences of one's choices. The phrase 'work according to your position' implies that each individual bears responsibility for their own conduct and will reap what they sow. The assurance 'soon you will know who will have the final abode' points to the inevitability of a reckoning, whether in this world or the Hereafter, where the transient successes of the unjust will be revealed as hollow and doomed. The concluding statement, 'indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed,' establishes an immutable spiritual law: those who transgress the bounds of justice, whether through oppression, disbelief, or corruption of the soul, cannot attain true flourishing or ultimate victory. Success, in the Qur'anic sense, belongs to those aligned with truth and righteousness, while the 'flourishing' of the wrongdoer is an illusion that shatters against the reality of divine order. Thus, the verse calls for patience in the face of opposition and trust in the eventual triumph of righteousness over wrongdoing.

translation: And they assign to Allah a share of what He has created of crops and livestock, and they say, 'This is for Allah,' so they claim, 'and this is for our partners [i.e., the idols].' But what is for their partners does not reach Allah, while what is for Allah does reach their partners. Evil is that which they rule.
interpretation: This verse condemns the practice of the pre-Islamic Arabs who divided their agricultural produce and livestock between Allah and their idols, but gave the better portions to the idols while reserving the inferior portions for Allah. It exposes the irrationality of polytheism: if they believed Allah was the supreme deity, why would they shortchange Him and give the best to lesser beings? The verse asserts that whatever is dedicated to false deities remains with those deities and never benefits Allah, while whatever is genuinely meant for Allah in truth cannot be diverted to idols, since Allah is self-sufficient and above need. The concluding judgment—'Evil is that which they rule'—delivers a sharp moral verdict, declaring such distorted allocations as corrupt and unjust, both rationally and spiritually.

translation: And thus the polytheists' associates (devils) have made the killing of their children appear fair to many of them, that they may destroy them and confound for them their religion. And if Allah had so willed, they would not have done it. So leave them and their fabrications.
interpretation: This verse addresses the phenomenon where polytheists were influenced by their false deities or evil companions to commit acts like killing their children. The verse clarifies that these satanic influences made such heinous acts seem appealing to them, leading them to deviate from the true path and mix up their beliefs. It also emphasizes that such actions only occur because Allah allows them as a test for humanity, and if He had willed, He could have prevented them entirely. The verse concludes with a command to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) to disregard their false claims and leave them to their delusions.

translation: And they say, 'These animals and crops are forbidden; no one may eat them except whom we will,' by their claim, and there are animals whose backs they forbid, and there are animals over which they do not mention the name of Allah; [all this is] a fabrication against Him. He will recompense them for what they used to fabricate.
interpretation: The verse condemns the arbitrary superstitions and ritual restrictions imposed by the pre-Islamic Arabs upon Allah's creation. It exposes how they declared certain animals and produce to be forbidden for certain people while allowing it for others, banned riding on specific beasts, and dedicated other animals to their idols without invoking Allah's name. By labeling these man-made rules as sacred laws, they committed the sin of attributing falsehood to Allah. The verse warns that such lies about divine law will not go unpunished, as Allah will hold them accountable for the fabrications they invented against His authority.

translation: And they say, 'That which is in the wombs of these animals is exclusively for our males and forbidden to our wives. But if it be stillborn, then they [all] share in it.' He will surely recompense them for their description [i.e., attribution]. Indeed, He is Wise and Knowing.
interpretation: This verse condemns the superstitious and arbitrary practices of the pre-Islamic Arabs regarding livestock dedicated to their idols. They would designate the viable offspring of specific she-camneys, sheep, and goats as exclusively for the males of the tribe to eat, while declaring it forbidden to their wives. However, if the animal was born dead or stillborn, they would share it among everyone, including the women. This demonstrates the irrationality and injustice of their man-made religious rulings, which had no basis in divine revelation. The verse declares that Allah will hold them accountable for these false attributions and oppressive rules, emphasizing that such arbitrary discrimination is rejected by God, whose wisdom and knowledge encompass the truth behind all things.

translation: Indeed, those who killed their children foolishly, without knowledge, and forbade what Allah had provided them, inventing falsehood against Allah—those have certainly gone astray and were not guided.
interpretation: This verse condemns those who destroy their offspring through senseless violence born of ignorance, and who simultaneously restrict the lawful provisions Allah has placed at their disposal, fabricating religious prohibitions they attribute to the divine will. Such people are described as having utterly lost their way—their actions represent a compound error: the taking of innocent life and the invention of divine law through deception. The verse establishes that true misguidance lies not merely in straying from the path, but in actively constructing falsehood and sanctifying it with God's name. Their deviation is total because it combines moral corruption with intellectual arrogance, as they presume to dictate what is sacred and what is forbidden despite possessing no genuine knowledge. The statement that they 'were not guided'—using a past tense—suggests that their condition of being astray is so entrenched that it defines their very state of being, rather than being a temporary lapse from which they might recover.

translation: And He it is who produces gardens [both] trellised and untrellised, and palm trees and crops of different kinds, and olives and pomegranates, similar and unlike. Eat of its fruit when it yields and give its due [zakah] on the day of its harvest, and do not be wasteful. Indeed, He does not love the wasteful.

translation: And of the livestock, some are for carrying burdens and some are for [providing] fur and wool. Eat from what Allah has provided for you and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.
interpretation: This verse distinguishes between types of domesticated animals—those used for labor and transportation versus smaller animals like sheep and goats raised for wool, milk, and meat. It highlights that the practical, lawful benefits Allah has placed in these animals are meant to be enjoyed, while obedience to Allah is the guiding principle that distinguishes lawful consumption from prohibited excess. The prohibition on 'following the footsteps of Satan' serves as a caution against corrupting these pure blessings by altering Allah's creation, exploiting animals contrary to their nature, or adopting rituals of sacrifice associated with pagan traditions. Satan's enmity is made explicit here because he seeks to distort the natural order by leading humans to either forbid what Allah has made lawful or engage in practices that cause harm to themselves or the creatures under their care.

translation: Eight mates: two of sheep, two of goats. Say, 'Is it the two males He has forbidden or the two females? Or what is in the wombs of the two females? Inform me with knowledge, if you are truthful.'
interpretation: This verse is a direct challenge to the pre-Islamic Arab practice of prohibiting certain animals based on arbitrary categories, and it exposes the illogical nature of such prohibitions. The rhetorical questions demand that those who invent these restrictions provide actual knowledge to justify them, rather than relying on superstition or tradition. The emphasis on being informed 'with knowledge' highlights that religious rulings regarding what is lawful or unlawful must be grounded in divine wisdom, not human whim or baseless customs passed down without understanding.

translation: And of the camels two, and of the cattle two. Say, 'Is it the two males that He has forbidden, or the two females, or what is contained in the wombs of the two females? Were you witnesses when Allah commanded you to do this?' So who is more unjust than he who invents a lie against Allah to mislead people without knowledge? Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: The verse confronts those who invent baseless religious restrictions, exposing the absurdity of arbitrary prohibitions by demanding that those who forbid certain animals provide evidence for their claims. The rhetorical questions challenge them to specify exactly which part of the animal creation—males, females, or offspring—they declare unlawful, since they cannot justify their fabricated rules with any genuine divine command. The verse condemns such fabrication as a grave injustice, warning that inventing falsehoods against Allah to mislead others without any legitimate knowledge is among the most corrupt of actions. The closing statement affirms that those who deliberately persist in this wrongdoing have removed themselves from divine guidance, as Allah does not lead astray the unjust, but rather abandons them to the consequences of their own deceit.

translation: Say, 'I do not find within what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who eats it, except that it be a dead animal, or blood poured forth, or the flesh of swine—for it is indeed impure—or it be [the meat of] that which has been dedicated to other than Allah. But whoever is compelled by necessity, neither desiring [it] nor transgressing [its limits], then indeed your Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.'
interpretation: This verse establishes that Islam does not impose ascetic restrictions on lawful food, emphasizing that the prohibitions are specific and limited rather than pervasive. The prohibited categories are symbolic: carrion represents decay and neglect of what sustains life; poured blood signifies violence and the taking of life without purpose; swine flesh is declared impure, likely reflecting its dual nature as both harmful and unworthy of ritual consumption; and food dedicated to other than Allah represents turning away from divine recognition in daily sustenance. The concluding exception reveals a profound principle of Islamic law: necessity overrides prohibition, provided the person does not act out of greed or rebellion. This framework balances divine command with human welfare, portraying mercy as integral to God's governance. The pairing of divine forgiveness with mercy at the end underscores that strict adherence is not expected when survival is at stake, while willful transgression remains excluded from divine clemency.

translation: And to those who are Jews We have forbidden every animal with claws, and of cattle and sheep We have forbidden to them their fat except what is carried on their backs or what the entrails contain or what is mixed with bone. That is what We repaid them for their transgression; and indeed, We are truthful.
interpretation: This verse outlines specific prohibitions imposed upon the Jewish people, including animals with claws and the fat of cattle and sheep, with certain exceptions such as the fat that adheres to their backs, is found within their entrails, or is mixed with their bones. The verse explicitly states that these restrictions are a consequence of their own wrongdoing and transgression, emphasizing that divine commandments are not arbitrary but rather a just response to human misdeeds. The affirmation 'وَإِنَّا لَصَادِقُونَ' ('and indeed, We are truthful') underscores the absolute certainty and reliability of Allah's pronouncements, leaving no room for doubt regarding the divine origin of these prohibitions and the rationale behind them. This serves as a reminder that divine law is purposeful and that accountability is an integral aspect of the relationship between the Creator and creation.

translation: But if they deny you, [O Muhammad], then say, 'Your Lord is the possessor of vast mercy; however, His punishment will not be turned back from the criminal people.'
interpretation: This verse consoles the Prophet ﷺ and, by extension, every bearer of truth in the face of rejection: the failure of people to accept the message does not invalidate the message nor exhaust the mercy of God, for divine mercy is immense and precedes the call. Yet that same mercy does not negate divine justice; those who deliberately persist in wrongdoing (al-mujrimūn) are not shielded from the consequences of their choices. The verse thus establishes a vital balance—mercy is not weakness or permissiveness, and punishment is not cruelty or arbitrariness. Believers are therefore called to remain patient and steadfast in conveying truth without coercion, trusting that God's vast mercy encompasses sincere seekers, while His inescapable justice will ultimately hold those who choose crime and corruption accountable. The address implicitly teaches that rejection of truth is itself a form of transgression, since people are capable of recognizing it when they are sincere, and God will not deflect His decisive response from such wrongdoers.

translation: Those who associate others with Allah will say, 'If Allah had willed, we would not have associated [anything] with Him, nor would our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything.' In the same way, those before them denied until they tasted Our punishment. Say, 'Do you have any knowledge that you can produce for us? You follow not except assumption, and you are not but guessing.'
interpretation: This verse exposes the hypocrisy of those who commit shirk (associating partners with Allah) or make unlawful what He permitted, yet attempt to justify their actions by falsely attributing them to divine will. They claim, 'If Allah did not want us to do this, He would have prevented it,' using predestination as a convenient excuse to evade personal accountability and moral responsibility. The Qur'an refutes this by pointing to the fate of previous nations who similarly fabricated lies against Allah until they faced His严厉 punishment. The verse then challenges the polytheists to present any genuine knowledge or divine authority for their practices, exposing that their beliefs are based on nothing more than conjecture, wishful thinking, and blind adherence to ancestral traditions.
