translation: Except those who are patient and do righteous deeds; those will have forgiveness and a great reward.
interpretation: Patience (sabr) is a central theme of the Qur'an. By placing it alongside righteous deeds as the distinguishing feature of those who are exempted from divine displeasure, the verse does not equate the two but rather identifies those whose inner fortitude becomes visible in outward ethical action. The negation in the preceding verses establishes a broad warning or consequence for humanity at large; the exception operates as a divine guarantee for any soul that commits to perseverance in faith and moral conduct, especially under hardship, persecution, or trial. The mention of sabr is not merely passive endurance but active steadfastness that restrains the self from despair, retaliation, and disobedience; this inward restraint then issues forth in outward deeds that conform to divine command. The promise of *maghfirah* (forgiveness) is comprehensive: it covers sins, failures, and spiritual shortcomings, restoring the soul's relationship with God and clearing it of guilt. *Ajr kabir* (a great reward) indicates something so vast that human language cannot accurately describe it, suggesting that what awaits the patient and righteous believer far exceeds any sacrifice endured in worldly life. The sequence patient-then-deeds reflects a profound ethical logic: no truly righteous deed can be performed consistently without patience, since trials, opposition, or the pull of desire test every act of goodness. Similarly, patience without righteous action risks becoming hollow or even self-destructive. Thus, the verse presents an integrated picture of the God-fearing believer whose perseverance and moral effort together qualify them for divine mercy and an everlasting recompense that cannot be measured in earthly terms.

translation: Perhaps you [O Muhammad] are abandoning some of what is revealed to you, and your chest is tight because they say, 'Why has there not been sent down to him a treasure or come with him an angel?' You are only a warner, and Allah is Disposer of all things.
interpretation: This verse addresses a subtle psychological pressure that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ may have felt while delivering the Message. The disbelievers' demands for miraculous proof—a treasure or an accompanying angel—reflect their refusal to accept faith based purely on the divine wisdom and eloquence of the revelation itself. Some scholars note that the phrase 'perhaps you are abandoning' may carry a tone of divine reproach: the Prophet is being reminded not to withhold any part of the revelation, even if parts of it seem difficult for people to accept, or even if he feels personal distress at the opposition it provokes. The command 'You are only a warner' serves to define the limits of his prophetic mission—his role is to deliver the warning with clarity and integrity, not to satisfy the material or sensory expectations of his audience. The closing affirmation, 'Allah is Disposer of all things' (Wakeel), is the theological anchor: ultimate authority, protection, and the outcome of the message rest entirely with Allah, freeing the Prophet from the burden of proving his message through extraordinary worldly means.

translation: Or do they say, 'He has invented it'? Say, 'Then bring ten surahs like it, invented [by yourselves], and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you should be truthful.'
interpretation: This verse represents a profound challenge from the Qur'an to those who denied its divine origin by accusing Prophet Muhammad of fabricating it. The challenge is not merely to produce similar content, but specifically to invent ten complete surahs that match the Qur'an in its unmatched qualities—its linguistic inimitability, rhetorical beauty, profound wisdom, spiritual guidance, and comprehensive scope. The mention of calling upon 'whomever you can besides Allah' indicates that the challenge is open to human effort alone, without divine assistance, emphasizing that the Qur'an's excellence is beyond human capability to replicate. This serves as evidence that the Qur'an could only be from God, since despite the literary genius of the Arabic language and the numerous attempts made throughout history, no one has been able to produce anything comparable to it. The verse also demonstrates Islam's confidence in the truth of its message, inviting sincere investigation rather than demanding blind belief, and it establishes a criterion for evaluating the Qur'an based on objective challenges that can be tested and verified.

translation: , if they do not respond to you, then know that it has been sent down only with the knowledge of Allah, and that there is no deity except Him. So will you submit [to Him]?
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the ultimate sovereignty of divine revelation as a matter of certain divine knowledge, independent of human acceptance or rejection, and calls for a conscious, willing submission to the singular reality of God, regardless of worldly opposition.

Interpretation of the verse from Surah Hud (11:16):

This verse addresses a fundamental spiritual reality about human motivations and divine justice. It describes those who prioritize worldly life and its adornments over higher spiritual goals. The phrase "نوف إليهم أعمالهم فيها" (We will pay them in full for their deeds within it) indicates that Allah will compensate such individuals materially in this world—they will receive the fruits of their efforts. The phrase "وهم فيها لا يبخسون" (and they will not be diminished therein) assures that this worldly compensation is complete and just; they will not be cheated of their material rewards.

However, the broader context of the Qur'an reveals that this is not purely favorable. Receiving full recompense in this world for worldly deeds implies that their share in the afterlife may be diminished or nonexistent. This serves as a subtle warning: those who exhaust their spiritual capital pursuing temporal pleasures will find that their worldly success is their only reward, while the eternal rewards of the hereafter are reserved for those who seek them.

The verse underscores a profound spiritual principle: there is a dichotomy between those oriented toward worldly success and those oriented toward divine pleasure. It neither condemns worldly life entirely nor endorses its pursuit as an ultimate goal. Instead, it establishes that Allah is just and fulfills His promises—if one chooses worldly rewards, they will receive them fully, but this comes at the cost of the greater, everlasting rewards. It invites reflection on what one truly values and what one is willing to sacrifice for it.

translation: Those are the ones who will have nothing in the Hereafter except the Fire, and futile will be whatever they did there, and void whatever they used to do.
interpretation: This verse describes the ultimate futility of the efforts of those who reject faith and pursue worldly gains at the expense of their spiritual accountability. Their actions, even if seemingly successful or impressive in this life, carry no weight in the eternal realm because they were devoid of sincere belief and righteous intention. The word 'حبط' (ḥabiṭa) conveys the idea that their deeds are rendered null and void, as if they never existed, because they were not grounded in truth or directed toward God. Similarly, 'باطل' (bāṭil) emphasizes that their works are fundamentally empty and misdirected. This serves as a stark warning that worldly accomplishments, when separated from faith and moral purpose, hold no value in the sight of God and cannot save one from the consequences of one's choices in the eternal life to come.

translation: Then is one who stands upon a clear proof from his Lord like [one who is blind]? A witness from Him recites it (the proof), and before it was the Book of Moses as an imam and mercy. Those [believers] believe in it. But whoever disbelieves in it from the [various] factions - the Fire will be his promised destination. So be not in doubt about it. Indeed, it is the truth from your Lord, but most of the people do not believe.
interpretation: This verse establishes a profound contrast between those grounded in divine certainty and those who wander in spiritual blindness. The 'clear proof from his Lord' refers to the Qur'an itself, which is presented as an unmistakable guidance that stands in stark opposition to mere conjecture or inherited tradition. The phrase 'a witness from Him recites it' points to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, whose role is to convey this revelation authentically, while the reference to 'the Book of Moses' as 'an imam and mercy' emphasizes the continuity of divine guidance through scripture, showing that the Qur'an is not an isolated teaching but part of an unbroken tradition of monotheistic revelation beginning with the Torah. The verse then issues a clear warning: those who reject this guidance from the various factions and alliances of disbelievers are destined for the Fire, leaving no room for complacency or doubt about its reality. The concluding command to the Prophet - 'be not in doubt about it' - serves as both reassurance and a call to unwavering conviction, reminding that while the truth may be rejected by the majority, its authenticity is guaranteed by its divine origin. The verse ultimately teaches that certainty in faith is not a matter of popular consensus but of standing firmly upon transcendent proof, and that true belief requires recognizing the harmony between successive revelations while remaining steadfast against the doubts raised by worldly alliances and majority opinion.

translation: ,And who is more unjust than he who invents a lie against Allah? Those (whom Allah described) will be brought before their Lord, and the witnesses will say, "These are the ones who lied against their Lord." Unquestionably, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse establishes a fundamental principle of accountability in the Hereafter: those who deliberately attribute falsehoods to God—whether by fabricating beliefs, laws, or revelations not from Him—will stand exposed before their Lord. The presence of 'witnesses' (الشُّهَدَاء), understood by many classical scholars as the prophets, angels, or the prophets' own communities bearing testimony, underscores that no lie against God will remain hidden or unchallenged. The condemnation is absolute (لعنة الله على الظالمين), indicating that the root of such fabrication is not merely intellectual error but a profound moral transgression (ظلم)—the act of transgressing against truth itself by placing human invention in the position of divine authority. This serves as a severe warning to anyone who would knowingly distort religious truth for worldly gain, influence, or pride.

translation: Those who turn away from the path of Allah and seek to make it crooked, while they themselves are disbelievers in the Hereafter.
interpretation: This verse describes those who actively obstruct people from following the straight path of Allah, attempting to distort or misrepresent it. Their defiance is rooted in a deeper rejection of accountability, as they deny the reality of the Hereafter. This combination of leading others astray while disbelieving in ultimate divine justice highlights the depth of their spiritual corruption and moral responsibility, for they not only deviate themselves but also hinder others from guidance, sealing their fate through conscious rejection of truth.

translation: Those [disbelievers] were not unable to overcome [the Prophet] on earth, nor did they have any protectors besides Allah. But the punishment is doubled for them; they were unable to hear, and they were unable to see.
interpretation: This verse addresses the defiant rejectors of faith, clarifying a profound spiritual reality: their failure to grasp the truth was not because they lacked intellectual capacity to understand worldly matters, nor because they were invincible opponents who could frustrate divine purpose. Rather, their condition stems from a willful, habitual rejection that has spiritually deadened their faculties. The doubling of punishment reflects the compounding nature of misguidance when one persists in denial despite clear signs—each layer of stubbornness adding to their reckoning. Their inability to hear and see is metaphorical, describing hearts so sealed by arrogance that the Quran's guidance passes by them without effect. The mention of having no protectors besides Allah is a warning that worldly alliances, power, and status cannot shield them from divine consequence; true victory and refuge belong only to Allah. Ultimately, the verse calls the listener to reflect: spiritual blindness is chosen, and its consequences are severe, while sincere submission to Allah remains the only path to safety. It also serves as a caution that refusal to listen with humility leads not only to missed guidance in this life but to multiplied accountability in the hereafter, emphasizing both divine justice and the personal responsibility each individual bears for how they engage with truth.

These verses describe those who claimed to have partners with Allah (whether idols, false deities, or fabricated beliefs). On the Day of Judgment, they will be the ultimate losers—they wasted their very selves because their souls were deprived of the true purpose of existence, which is to worship and know Allah. Moreover, all the falsehoods they invented—be it idols, superstitions, or lies about Allah—will vanish entirely, leaving them with no one to worship, no protection, and no intercession. It serves as a stern warning that any deviation from the truth of tawhid (monotheism) leads to spiritual bankruptcy; the things people fabricate to replace Allah are merely illusions that will desert them when they need them most, while the believers who relied on the truth will find their reward with their Lord.

translation: Assuredly, it is they who will be the greatest losers in the Hereafter.
interpretation: This verse serves as a definitive warning from Allah regarding the eternal fate of those who persist in ingratitude, disobedience, and rejection of divine guidance. It employs the emphatic expression "la jarama" (لا جرم) to underscore an undeniable truth, asserting with certainty that the ultimate losers on the Day of Judgment will not be those who suffered poverty, illness, or worldly hardship, but rather those who traded their eternal souls for transient worldly gains. The verse inverts human perceptions of success and failure: while the disbelievers and wrongdoers may appear prosperous and victorious in the fleeting life of this world, their bargain is fundamentally bankrupt. They exchanged the everlasting rewards of Allah's mercy and paradise for fleeting pleasures, and as a result, they will emerge from the Day of Judgment as the most profound losers, having forfeited their souls, their destinies, and any hope of redemption or recompense.

translation: ,Indeed, those who believe, do righteous deeds, and humble themselves before their Lord—they are the people of Paradise, and they will abide therein eternally.
interpretation: This verse establishes a clear connection between three qualities and ultimate salvation: faith (iman), righteous action (amal salih), and humble submission to God (khushu'). The word 'akhbatū' (أخبتوا), often translated as 'humbled themselves' or 'turned in repentance,' carries the meaning of returning to God with a serene and tranquil heart, free from arrogance and pretense. It signifies a state of inward humility that complements outward deeds, suggesting that true righteousness is not merely performative but rooted in genuine reverence and surrender to the divine. By placing this internal spiritual state alongside belief and action, the verse emphasizes that authentic religion integrates belief, ethics, and a humble orientation toward the Divine. The promise of eternal paradise ('khālidūn' - خالدون, 'abiding forever') underscores the permanence of the outcome, suggesting that these qualities are not transient but define the very nature of those who attain God's favor. The verse can be read as a culmination of a thematic section, summarizing the qualities of those whom God guides to success, contrasting with other groups mentioned elsewhere who possess belief or action alone but lack the essential quality of humble devotion.

translation: The example of the two parties is like the blind and deaf, and the seeing and hearing. Are they equal in example? Will you not then take heed?
interpretation:
The verse draws a clear and decisive analogy to highlight the moral and spiritual chasm between two groups: those who reject faith and those who embrace it. The first group, characterized by disbelief, is likened to a person who is both blind and deaf—unable to perceive the truth or hear the guidance that surrounds them. Their inability is not merely physical but reflects a deeper, voluntary closure of the heart and mind to divine signs. As a result, they wander in confusion and darkness, disconnected from the reality that faith illuminates.

In stark contrast, the second group—those who believe—is compared to a person who can see and hear. They possess spiritual sight to recognize the truth and spiritual hearing to accept divine guidance. Their faculties are open and responsive, allowing them to engage with the world meaningfully and to navigate life with clarity and purpose.

The rhetorical question, "Are they equal in example?" underscores the absurdity of treating these two groups as comparable. It challenges the listener or reader to recognize the profound difference in their conditions and outcomes. The verse then issues a gentle but firm call: "Will you not then take heed?" This invitation is directed at those who may be wavering or indifferent, urging them to reflect on the consequences of their choices and to recognize the value of faith before it is too late.

The verse also serves as a subtle critique of those who might claim that both paths lead to similar ends, or that moral and spiritual distinctions are irrelevant. By using the analogy of physical faculties, it makes the abstract concept of spiritual guidance tangible and relatable. Just as no rational person would consider a blind and deaf individual equal to one who can see and hear, no thoughtful person should consider the believer and the disbeliever as equivalent in their understanding, purpose, or ultimate destiny.

Ultimately, this verse calls for a moment of sincere introspection. It asks whether one is willing to remain in a state of willful blindness and deafness, or whether one will open oneself to the light of faith. The choice presented is not merely between two beliefs but between two fundamentally different ways of existing—one marked by confusion, loss, and spiritual poverty, and the other by clarity, purpose, and richness. The verse does not coerce but invites, trusting that reflection will lead to awakening. It is a reminder that the faculties of the heart, like those of the body, must be intentionally engaged if one is to perceive the truth and live a life of meaning.

translation: And We certainly sent Noah to his people, [saying], 'Indeed, I am to you a clear warner.'
interpretation: This verse establishes the prophetic principle that divine guidance reaches humanity through chosen messengers who deliver explicit warnings. Noah's mission to his own community demonstrates that prophets are not sent from outside the human realm but emerge from within the people they address, giving them intimate knowledge of their audience's condition while possessing a transcendent authority. The self-identification as a 'clear warner' (نذير مبين) indicates that the prophetic function centers on making consequences unmistakably visible—warning is not vague prophecy but a lucid articulation of the danger awaiting those who persist in wrongdoing, coupled with an implicit promise of deliverance for those who respond. The phrase 'to his people' (إلى قومه) emphasizes accountability within specific social and historical contexts, suggesting that each community receives tailored guidance addressing its particular circumstances, yet the core message remains universal. This opening of Noah's narrative also serves a meta-function in the Qur'an: by recounting the pattern of past prophets who faced rejection despite clear warning, it consoles Muhammad and warns his contemporaries that opposition to prophetic truth is the historical norm, not an anomaly, while simultaneously affirming that divine patience eventually manifests in both salvation for the righteous and accountability for those who deliberately choose denial.

translation: "That you worship none but Allah. Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a painful Day."
interpretation: This verse captures the essence of Noah's (Nuh's) prophetic mission as presented in the Qur'an, delivering a dual message of divine guidance and moral urgency. The opening phrase, 'that you worship none but Allah,' establishes the core principle of tawhid—the absolute oneness of God—stripped of any intermediaries or rivals. It is not merely a theological correction but a radical reorientation of human loyalty, requiring total devotion to the singular Creator. The second clause, 'indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a painful Day,' reveals the emotional dimension of prophetic responsibility. Noah does not warn out of malice or self-interest but from genuine compassion, burdened by the knowledge of what awaits those who reject truth. This fear is not weakness; it is the anguish of a messenger who understands the gravity of eternal consequences while his people remain indifferent. Together, these statements frame the prophetic role: to call humanity toward exclusive devotion to God while urgently warning of accountability beyond worldly life. The verse thereby balances hope (through clear guidance) with warning (through honest warning), illustrating that true compassion involves speaking difficult truths rather than offering comfortable silence.

translation: He said, “O my people, have you considered: if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord and He has given me mercy from Himself, but it was hidden from you, shall we force it upon you while you are averse to it?
interpretation:
This verse captures a profound moment of prophetic protest and moral persuasion. The speaker—Prophet Noah, though unnamed here—addresses his people not with coercion but with a deeply rational and ethical appeal. He begins by establishing his own position: he stands upon clear evidence (بينة) from his Lord and has received divine mercy (رحمة). This combination signifies authentic prophethood—certainty of knowledge coupled with a grace that empowers and validates the mission. By describing this mercy as having been "hidden from you" (فعميت عليكم), he acknowledges a painful reality: divine guidance is not always perceptibly accessible to everyone, and its absence in their experience does not negate its reality.

The rhetorical question that follows is particularly striking. He asks whether he should "force" (نلزمكموها) this truth upon them while they are averse. This is a powerful affirmation of the Qur'anic principle that there is no compulsion in matters of faith. The verse enshrines the ethics of prophetic da'wah: truth may be proclaimed with clarity and conviction, but it cannot be imposed upon those who reject it. The word "كارهون" (averse) is crucial—it highlights that guidance, by its very nature, must be received willingly to be transformative.

On a deeper level, the verse also speaks to the limitations of human responsibility. The prophet is not accountable for the acceptance or rejection of his message; his duty is to deliver it with sincerity and clarity. The people's aversion is their own choice, and the consequences will follow accordingly. This distinguishes authentic prophetic witness from manipulative or coercive movements—true guidance respects human autonomy even when that autonomy is exercised in rejection.

Finally, the verse implicitly critiques those who demand tangible, sensory proof before believing. The prophet's clear evidence and divine mercy were real, but not always empirically visible to those who refused to see. This points to a spiritual reality: some truths are self-validating to the open-hearted, but remain "hidden" from those whose hearts are closed—not because the truth has failed, but because the capacity to perceive it has atrophied. The prophet's gentle rebuke here is also an invitation: to reconsider, to open the heart before the window of mercy closes.

translation: And O my people, I do not ask you for wealth in return for it; my reward is only from Allah. And I am not going to drive away those who have believed. They will surely meet their Lord. But I see that you are a people behaving ignorantly.
interpretation: The speaker is distancing themselves from any hint of worldly self-interest in their prophetic mission, which builds relational trust with the audience; at the same time, they refuse to marginalize sincere believers out of fear of the influential, because authentic faith is an ultimate matter between the servant and God that no social pressure can override; and, finally, the speaker diagnoses the audience's mistake not as a lack of information but as a willful misuse of reason and status — a moral arrogance that allows them to dismiss truth in favor of preserving their position.

translation: And O my people, who will protect me from [the punishment of] Allah if I drove them away? Then will you not remember?
interpretation: The verse presents the defensive and pleading plea of a faithful warner (as embodied in Shu'ayb or another prophet) confronting his people. He poses a rhetorical question that reveals the deep tension between obedience to God and social conformity. By asking who would defend him against divine punishment if he expelled the believers, he underscores two fundamental truths: first, that no human power, alliance, or societal pressure can shield one from God's judgment; second, that expelling those who believe in Allah is not an act of strength or tribal loyalty, but a grave error that invites divine retribution. The phrase "afala tadhakkarun" (then will you not remember?) serves as an emotional and intellectual appeal, urging the audience to pause, reflect on the consequences of their stubbornness, and recognize the foolishness of valuing worldly allegiance over spiritual truth. The verse critiques blind adherence to tradition or communal pressure, suggesting that true wisdom lies in recognizing God's authority as supreme and in protecting, rather than persecuting, those who uphold faith. It also implicitly condemns any system—whether familial, tribal, or societal—that demands the marginalization of the righteous as a prerequisite for belonging. Ultimately, the verse invites introspection, calling listeners to awaken to the reality that human support is transient, while divine justice is inevitable, and that remembering this is the first step toward righteousness.

translation: And I do not tell you that I have the depositories of Allah or that I know the unseen, nor do I tell you that I am an angel. Nor do I say about those whom your eyes look down upon, 'Never will Allah give them any good.' Allah is most knowing of what is within their hearts. Indeed, I would then be among the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the Prophet Noah (or a similar prophetic figure) to his people, outlines a profound theological and ethical stance rejecting false claims of divinity or exclusive knowledge. The speaker is preemptively denying four arrogant assertions: first, having control over Allah's treasures (a denial of divine power); second, possessing knowledge of the unseen (a denial of omniscience, which belongs to Allah alone); third, being an angel (a denial of a superhuman nature, affirming ordinary humanity under prophetic mission). Finally, and most tellingly, the speaker refuses to pass negative judgment on the poor or weak whom the elite disdain, stating that only Allah knows the true state of their hearts. This last point is crucial, as it prevents the prophet from usurping Allah's role as the ultimate judge of human worth, which is often based on inner piety rather than outward social status. By making this declaration, the speaker establishes that true prophethood involves complete humility and absolute reliance on divine knowledge and judgment; to claim otherwise would be an act of injustice (ẓulm) against Allah's exclusive rights and against the people themselves. Thus, the verse teaches that genuine spiritual leadership is marked by the rejection of self-divinization and the delegation of all ultimate knowledge and judgment to Allah.

translation: They said, 'O Noah, you have disputed with us and have prolonged the dispute. So bring upon us what you promise us, if you are among the truthful.'
interpretation: This verse presents the defiant and mocking response of Noah's people to his persistent warnings. Their statement reflects a hardened attitude of rejection, as they accuse him of excessive argumentation rather than genuinely engaging with his message. By challenging him to hasten the promised punishment, they reveal both their disbelief and their attempt to belittle his prophethood, treating his call to repentance as mere idle talk. This response illustrates a recurring pattern in the Qur'an where disbelievers, when confronted with clear evidence, retreat into stubbornness and mockery rather than sincere reflection, ultimately sealing their own fate.

translation: He [Prophet Saleh] said, 'You will only be brought it by Allah, if He wills. And you are not able to escape [Him].'
interpretation: The verse expresses the Prophet's complete reliance on divine will, acknowledging that all outcomes are subject to God's decree, while simultaneously warning the disbelievers of their inability to evade or overpower God's plan. The phrase إن شاء (if He wills) reflects tawakkul (trust in God) and humility, affirming that even the destruction threatened against the people would only come through God's permission, not by the Prophet's own power. The closing statement وما أنتم بمعجزين (and you are not able to escape) functions as a stern admonition that human resistance to divine will is futile, reinforcing the themes of divine sovereignty and human weakness that permeate the stories of the prophets in confronting their communities.

translation: And my advice will not benefit you, even if I wish to advise you, if Allah should intend to misguide you. He is your Lord, and to Him you will be returned.
interpretation: This verse addresses the limits of human persuasion in matters of faith and the ultimate sovereignty of the divine will. It conveys that sincere counsel or well-intentioned guidance cannot change what Allah has decreed for individuals; if He has willed that certain people remain in error or deviation, no external advice can reverse that divine determination. The verse emphasizes tawhid (the oneness of God) by declaring Allah as the sole Lord and the ultimate destination of all creation, reminding that accountability lies entirely with Him. It serves as a profound warning about the futility of resisting divine purpose and underscores human dependence on God's mercy and guidance.

translation: Or do they say, 'He has fabricated it'? Say, 'If I have fabricated it, then upon me is my crime, and I am free of what you commit.'
interpretation: This verse presents a decisive and logical response to the accusations of the disbelievers who claimed that the Prophet Muhammad fabricated the Qur'an himself. The divine instruction to the Prophet is to deliver a powerful challenge: if the message truly came from his own devising, he alone would bear the full consequence of that falsehood, but he is entirely absolved of the persistent crimes (disbelief, rejection, and opposition) that the accusers themselves commit. The deeper meaning lies in establishing a separation of moral responsibility and asserting the truthfulness of the revelation. By framing it this way, the verse highlights that the Prophet's conscience and record are clear of their false claims, while emphasizing that their own rejection constitutes a far greater offense against divine truth.

translation: And construct the ship under Our eyes and Our revelation, and do not address Me concerning those who have wronged; indeed, they are to be drowned.
interpretation: This verse, directed at Prophet Nuh (Noah), conveys a profound lesson in divine wisdom and human limits. On the surface, it instructs him to build the Ark under God's watchful guidance and revelation, signifying that even acts of obedience require divine inspiration and oversight. More deeply, the phrase 'do not address Me concerning those who have wronged' carries a heavy spiritual weight: it is a divine command to cease intercession or argument on behalf of those who persist in wrongdoing and reject truth. The concluding assertion, 'indeed, they are to be drowned,' is not merely a physical description of punishment but a metaphor for the inevitable consequence of persistent injustice and denial of divine signs. Theologically, the verse teaches that divine mercy has its limits; while God remains patient and gives ample opportunity for repentance, there comes a point when the decree becomes unalterable. It also illustrates the principle of divine sovereignty—God's decisions are not subject to human bargaining or emotional appeals. For believers, this serves as a warning about the consequences of habitual wrongdoing and a reminder that prophetic duty is to deliver the message, not to force its acceptance. The imagery of the Ark itself symbolizes salvation through faith and obedience, while the drowning represents the destruction that comes from rejecting divine guidance, reinforcing the Qur'anic theme that worldly success or longevity does not protect those who turn away from truth.

translation: And he constructed the ship, and whenever a company of his people passed by, they would ridicule him. He said, 'If you ridicule us, then we will ridicule you just as you ridicule [us].
interpretation: This verse highlights Prophet Noah's unwavering perseverance and resilience in the face of constant mockery from his people while he was building the ark in obedience to God's command. The verse teaches that those who follow divine guidance must often endure ridicule and opposition from those entrenched in disbelief, and that patience, steadfastness, and reliance on God are essential, trusting that the ultimate outcome will favor the righteous, just as the flood would later overtake those who mocked him.

translation: Soon you will know who will be overtaken by a disgracing punishment, and upon whom an enduring punishment will descend.
interpretation: This verse delivers a stern warning of inevitable accountability, emphasizing that the mocking attitude of disbelievers toward divine warnings will be answered with a punishment that humiliates them publicly and torments them eternally. The repetition of 'you will know' underscores certainty—doubt is removed and the outcome is fixed, serving as both a caution to heed truth before consequences arrive and a declaration that falsehood cannot escape eventual exposure and reckoning.

translation: Until when Our command came and the oven boiled over, We said, 'Load into it [the ark] a pair from every [species] and your family, except those against whom the word has already gone forth, and those who believe.' And none believed with him except a few.
interpretation: This verse marks the climactic moment of Noah's narrative, where the command to build the ark transitions into the command to board it. The image of the oven boiling over (fār al-tannūr) signals the beginning of divine judgment upon the earth and the onset of the cataclysm. The instruction to carry pairs (zawjayn) of every species reflects a divine preservation of creation through the flood, while the exclusion of those already decreed for punishment shows that salvation is not automatic but determined by prior divine judgment. The lament that only a few believed highlights a recurring Qur'anic theme: the rarity of genuine faith even when warning is clear, and the majority's persistence in denial despite prolonged prophetic appeal.

translation: And He said, 'Board it; in the name of Allah is its course and its anchorage. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.'
interpretation: This verse, revealed in the context of the story of Prophet Noah and the great flood, reveals a profound theological truth about the relationship between divine sovereignty and human effort. When Allah commands Noah and his followers to board the ark, He reminds them that even their action of boarding and the subsequent movement of the vessel are not independent events but occur under Allah's sanction and control—'in the name of Allah is its course and its anchorage.' This signifies that every departure and every arrival, every beginning and every end, is under divine authority. The concluding declaration, 'Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful,' delivered by Noah after enduring decades of rejection and persecution from his people, demonstrates that the prophetic mission is rooted in hope and compassion rather than vengeance. Despite the destruction that befalls those who reject truth, the prophetic message remains anchored in divine mercy, emphasizing that Allah's forgiveness remains available even to those who have turned away, and that His mercy precedes and accompanies His judgment. The verse thus teaches that human salvation requires both active obedience (boarding the ark) and trust in divine governance (recognizing Allah's control over outcomes), while the prophetic attitude toward even adversaries remains one that calls to God's mercy rather than His wrath.

translation: And it sailed with them through waves like mountains. And Noah called out to his son, who was in a distant place, 'O my son, come aboard with us and do not be with the disbelievers.'
interpretation: This verse depicts a moment of profound human tragedy within the narrative of the great flood. The imagery of the vessel moving through massive, mountain-like waves conveys the overwhelming power of the divine decree and the terrifying vulnerability of those aboard. Noah's plea to his son, who had separated himself from the believers, underscores a universal spiritual lesson: sincere admonition and invitation to faith are obligations that must be fulfilled, even when directed toward one's own family, regardless of the outcome. The son's choice to remain in a place of separation—both physically distant and spiritually apart—illustrates how disbelief can create a barrier that even a prophet's compassion cannot breach if the individual persists in rejection. The verse affirms that salvation is tied to conscious acceptance and trust in God, not merely to lineage or kinship with the righteous.

translation: He said, 'I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water.' [Allah] said, 'There is no protector today from the decree of Allah, except for whom He has mercy.' And the waves came between them, and he was among the drowned.
interpretation: This verse from Surah Hud describes the moment of the great flood when the disbelieving son of Noah, who had refused to board the ark, attempted to climb a mountain to escape the divine punishment. His statement reflects a purely materialistic worldview, seeking safety from physical elements rather than recognizing the spiritual reality of divine authority. The divine response establishes a fundamental theological principle: when Allah's decree comes to pass, no earthly structure, human effort, or natural barrier can provide salvation, for His command overrides all created causes. The exception 'except whom He has mercy' indicates that safety in the face of divine punishment is only granted through Allah's grace and mercy, not through human scheming or self-reliance. The phrase 'the waves came between them' signifies both a physical barrier separating the son from Noah and, more importantly, a spiritual separation that had already occurred due to the son's rejection of faith. Despite being the biological son of a prophet, he was not of those whom Allah saved, indicating that blood relations and proximity to righteousness do not guarantee salvation. This passage serves as a powerful warning against relying on worldly means when confronting divine decree, and emphasizes that salvation is contingent upon divine mercy granted through faith and righteous submission.

translation: And it was said, 'O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, withhold [your rain],' and the water subsided, and the matter was decided, and it rested upon [Mount] Judi, and it was said, 'Away with the wrongdoing people.'
interpretation: This verse describes the conclusion of the great flood narrative, emphasizing divine sovereignty over creation, as the cosmos itself obeys Allah's command to end the catastrophe. The mention of Mount Judi, where the ark came to rest, symbolizes a new beginning and a place of safety after divine punishment, while the declaration 'Away with the wrongdoing people' underscores the ultimate separation between the righteous, who are saved through faith and obedience, and the unjust, who are destroyed by their own corruption and rebellion.

translation: And Noah called upon his Lord and said, 'My Lord, indeed my son is of my family, and indeed Your promise is true, and You are the best of judges.'
interpretation: This verse captures a moment of profound human vulnerability and divine wisdom in the story of Prophet Noah (Nuh). After the flood, Noah addresses Allah regarding his son who refused to board the ark and was swept away by the floodwaters, despite Noah's earnest pleas. Noah's plea rests on two grounds: first, a natural claim based on kinship ('my son is of my family'), appealing to Allah's promise to save his family; and second, an acknowledgment of Allah's perfect wisdom and sovereignty ('You are the best of judges'). The deeper meaning reveals a tension between human intuition shaped by familial bonds and divine decree that operates beyond human logic. Noah, in his love for his son, momentarily intercedes on behalf of one who had consciously rejected faith and aligned himself with the disbelievers. The verse illustrates that spiritual kinship and salvation in Allah's sight are not determined by blood relations alone, but by faith and righteousness. It also teaches the prophets—and believers by extension—that while they may plead with heartfelt sincerity, they must ultimately submit to Allah's perfect judgment, recognizing that His decisions, though sometimes painful to human hearts, are rooted in absolute wisdom and justice. Noah's acceptance of Allah's will, despite the personal grief, becomes a model of tawhid (absolute monotheistic trust) and submission, demonstrating that divine mercy operates within the framework of divine wisdom, not merely human desire.

translation: He [Noah] said, 'O Noah, indeed he is not of your family; indeed, he is [a person whose] work was other than righteous, so do not ask Me [something] about which you have no knowledge. Indeed, I advise you, lest you be among the ignorant.'
interpretation: This divine address clarifies the boundaries of intercession and lineage in the sight of God. It conveys that biological or familial ties do not guarantee salvation unless accompanied by true faith and righteous deeds. Noah's request to intercede for his son, who rejected the message and chose disbelief, reveals a moment of human limitation in the Prophet's understanding, prompting God's gentle yet firm correction. The verse emphasizes that spiritual kinship, defined by belief and obedience to God, supersedes blood relations. Additionally, it serves as a profound lesson on the acceptance of divine wisdom: believers are exhorted not to plead for outcomes beyond their comprehension or to challenge God's perfect judgment, lest such insistence place them among those who act without knowledge. Ultimately, it reaffirms God's absolute sovereignty in decreeing matters of faith and destiny.

translation: He said, 'My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You about that of which I have no knowledge. And unless You forgive me and have mercy upon me, I will be among the losers.'
interpretation: This verse captures a moment of profound humility and spiritual awakening from Prophet Noah (as), following his dialogue with his son during the flood. After being rebuffed by his son who chose to seek refuge on a mountain rather than trust in divine promise, Noah does not react with anger or insistence; instead, he turns inward in humble supplication. His plea is twofold: first, a confession of the limits of human knowledge, acknowledging that only God comprehends the full reality of who will be saved and who will be destroyed. This is not merely about a single decision but a lifelong principle—recognizing that divine wisdom transcends human understanding, especially regarding matters of faith and destiny. Second, he seeks divine forgiveness and mercy, recognizing that his own salvation is not guaranteed by his prophetic status or his tireless efforts in calling his people. Noah, a man who preached for centuries and was described elsewhere as a ‘grateful servant,’ still felt the need to ask for forgiveness, teaching that no amount of good deeds makes one immune to human error and that reliance on God’s grace is continuous. Thus, the verse transforms Noah’s personal moment of weakness into an enduring lesson: true faith combines intellectual humility—knowing what we do not know—with constant dependence on God’s mercy for our ultimate success.

translation: It was said, 'O Noah, descend [from the Ark] with peace from Us and blessings upon you and upon nations [descending] from those with you. But there will be other nations to whom We will give enjoyment; then they will be touched from Us a painful punishment.'
interpretation: This verse marks the conclusion of the great flood narrative and the beginning of a new chapter for humanity. The command to Noah to 'descend with peace' signifies divine approval and protection; the storm of judgment is over, and a covenant of tranquility is established between God and Noah. The blessings mentioned are not merely material but encompass the honor of prophethood, the preservation of his lineage, and the spiritual guidance entrusted to him and his descendants. The mention of nations springing from those who sailed with him acknowledges that humanity will multiply and diversify, carrying both the potential for faith and the tendency toward misguidance. The warning regarding other nations whom God will allow temporary enjoyment before a painful punishment serves as a sober reminder that worldly prosperity is not a sign of divine favor, and that those who reject truth after being granted respite will ultimately face the consequences of their choices. The verse thus balances mercy with justice, portraying God as both the protector of the righteous and the just judge of the rebellious.

translation: These are from the reports of the unseen, which We reveal to you. You did not know them before, neither you nor your people. So be patient; indeed, the outcome is for the righteous.
interpretation: This verse establishes the divine source of the Qur'anic narratives concerning past nations and unseen realities, emphasizing that such knowledge is not acquired through human experience or cultural transmission but through direct revelation from God. The Prophet Muhammad is reminded that neither he nor his community possessed prior knowledge of these accounts, underscoring the miraculous nature of his prophethood and the sincerity of his message. The subsequent command to be patient is not merely an instruction to endure hardship but a directive to remain steadfast in conveying the truth despite opposition, knowing that ultimate success belongs to those who are conscious of God and adhere to His guidance. This verse thus links the reception of divine knowledge with the moral responsibility of perseverance, suggesting that true triumph in both this world and the hereafter is contingent upon righteousness rather than immediate worldly victory.

translation: And to 'Aad [We sent] their brother Hud. He said, 'O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. You are not but inventors of falsehood.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the prophetic methodology of inviting people to monotheism by presenting the message in its simplest and most direct form: affirming that there is no god worthy of worship except Allah alone. Hud's call to his people, the ancient tribe of 'Aad, was not based on complex theological arguments but on a clear declaration of the truth and a rejection of any partners associated with Allah. The phrase 'you are not but inventors of falsehood' is a strong condemnation of polytheism and the fabrication of deities, indicating that any worship directed toward other than Allah is a lie and an invention with no basis in reality. This reflects Islam's emphasis on the oneness of God (Tawhid) as the fundamental pillar of faith and the basis upon which all prophets built their message.

translation: ,لا تعقلون
interpretation: The verse is addressed to the people of the Prophet (or a previous messenger) who are being called upon to accept the message. It clarifies that the messenger seeks no reward from them for delivering the message; his reward comes only from God, who created him. The verse then rhetorically asks if they will not use their reason to understand the sincerity of the messenger and the truth of the call. It underscores the principle that prophetic guidance is a divine trust offered freely, and human beings are called upon to reflect rationally on the nature of the message and the one delivering it. The phrase

translation: And O my people, ask forgiveness of your Lord and then repent to Him; He will send [rain from] the sky upon you in showers and will add strength to your strength, and do not turn away as criminals.
interpretation:
This verse, addressed to Prophet Hud's people (the 'Ad), conveys a profound message about divine mercy and the direct correlation between repentance, faith, and worldly sustenance. The command to 'ask forgiveness of your Lord' (استغفروا ربكم) and 'then repent to Him' (توبوا إليه) establishes a sequence: first, seeking forgiveness for past transgressions, and second, a sincere turning back to God with a committed heart. This dual action is not merely about erasing sin but about restoring a conscious, obedient relationship with the Creator.

The promised reward for this repentance is twofold, encompassing both spiritual and material blessings. 'He will send the sky upon you in showers' (يرسل السماء عليكم مدراراً) addresses a specific, tangible need of the 'Ad, who were known for their arrogance and reliance on their own strength, but whose land likely suffered from drought as a test or consequence of their waywardness. The rain in 'showers' (مدراراً) signifies abundant, continuous, and life-giving mercy, symbolizing how divine grace can transform barrenness into fertility when hearts are receptive.

The second promise, 'and will add strength to your strength' (ويزدكم قوة إلى قوتكم), is deeply meaningful. It implies that God would augment their existing power and capability. Their strength, which they perhaps attributed solely to their physical prowess, wealth, or social structures, would be multiplied by divine support. This teaches that all genuine strength and success ultimately originate from God; human effort is necessary, but it finds its true fulfillment only when blessed by the Divine.

Finally, the warning, 'and do not turn away as criminals' (ولا تتولوا مجرمين), serves as a stark caution. 'Turning away' (التولي) here means deliberately rejecting the truth and the call to repentance after it has been clearly presented. The term 'criminals' (مجرمين) is severe, indicating that such a conscious, persistent rejection is not merely a mistake but a criminal act against one's own soul and against divine guidance. It implies that the crime lies in the willful choice to remain in transgression despite knowing the path to forgiveness.

In essence, this verse is a timeless lesson: sincere repentance opens the doors to divine mercy, which manifests in both spiritual peace and tangible blessings. It also clarifies that strength, whether physical or material, is a divine gift that flourishes with gratitude and obedience, while arrogant self-reliance and rejection of God lead to ruin. The verse encapsulates the Islamic principle that turning to God is the beginning of both inner transformation and outer abundance.

translation: They said, 'O Hud, you have not brought us clear evidence, and we are not going to leave our gods for your word, nor are we believers in you.'
interpretation: This verse captures the defiant response of Hud's people to his prophetic call. It reveals several dimensions of their rejection: first, they demand tangible, miraculous proof as a precondition for faith, demonstrating a superficial, transactional approach to belief rather than a sincere openness to truth. Second, they cling rigidly to their ancestral idolatry, dismissing Hud's message as mere 'words' not worthy of disrupting entrenched traditions and social norms. Third, their declaration that they will not believe in him reflects deep-seated arrogance and willful obstinacy—faith is not merely unattainable for them but actively unwanted. This attitude exemplifies a pattern of resistance to divine guidance throughout the Quran, where communities demand signs not out of genuine seeking but as a means to justify their predetermined rejection. Their statement also illustrates the psychological barriers to faith: pride in inherited beliefs, skepticism toward the unseen, and a reluctance to submit to moral accountability. The verse implicitly contrasts this closed-mindedness with the humility and courage required for true faith, serving as a warning about the dangers of allowing tradition and ego to override spiritual discernment. Hud's community's response ultimately seals their fate, as persistent rejection of clear prophetic warning invites consequences rather than continued divine patience.

translation: They say nothing but that some of our gods have afflicted you with evil. He said, 'Indeed, I call upon Allah to witness, and you too bear witness, that I am disassociated from what you associate [with Him].'
interpretation: This verse records the moment when the Prophet Ibrāhīm confronts his people after they accuse him of being afflicted or harmed by their idols. He refuses their accusation and instead summons Allah as the ultimate witness to his innocence, while also inviting them themselves to witness his declaration of pure monotheism. The theological emphasis is on tawḥīd as an active, conscious disavowal of shirk, and on bearing witness as a moral and legal obligation that even the disbelievers will be held accountable for. The use of the dual address ('you too bear witness') indicates that Ibrāhīm will later hold them to this testimony before Allah on the Day of Judgment.

translation: Other than Him. So plot against me all together, then do not give me any respite.
interpretation: After establishing that only Allah has knowledge of the unseen and that He alone can reveal it, the verse challenges those who associate partners with Him or deny His power. By saying 'plot against me all together,' the speaker (Prophet Muhammad) is expressing absolute trust in Allah's protection, daring all disbelievers and their false gods to combine their efforts against him, knowing they are powerless to harm him without Allah's permission. The phrase 'do not give me any respite' intensifies the challenge, showing that even if given a full chance to scheme, they would still fail. This reflects the Quranic theme that truth from Allah is invincible, and any opposition to it is ultimately futile. The verse also highlights the courage and reliance on Allah of the Prophet, and serves as a warning that rejecting divine revelation leads only to misguidance, while sincere faith in Allah's oneness and omniscience brings true security.

translation: Indeed, I have relied upon Allah, my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature except that He holds it by its forelock. Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path.
interpretation: This verse expresses absolute trust (tawakkul) in Allah as the sole sustaincher and controller of all creation. The imagery of grasping the forelock signifies that every living being is entirely subject to Allah's will and power, leaving no room for independence from His dominion. The reference to Allah being on a 'straight path' indicates that His governance, decree, and guidance are perfectly just and unwavering, serving as the ultimate framework within which all events unfold. It reassures the faithful that reliance on Allah provides security, as His direction is infallible and His authority over all creatures is absolute.

translation: But if they turn away, then I have already conveyed to you what I was sent with to you. And my Lord will cause to succeed [you] a people other than you, and you will not harm Him at all. Indeed my Lord is, over everything, a Guardian.
interpretation: This verse from Surah Hud (11:57) speaks to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and, by extension, to all who carry the message of truth. It addresses a fundamental reality: the responsibility of the messenger is to convey, not to force acceptance. If a people reject the message, it does not diminish the truth delivered nor place the messenger at fault. The verse then shifts to a warning: should they persist in rejection, divine providence will not leave the earth without a believing community, for God will raise up another people—'a people other than you'—to carry the legacy of faith. This implies that divine favor is not bound to any single nation; communities that fail in their covenant are replaced by those who are willing to uphold it. The phrase 'you will not harm Him at all' is profound: rejection does not weaken God's authority. The mightiest empires and the most defiant peoples cannot diminish divine sovereignty even by an atom's weight. Finally, 'Indeed my Lord is, over everything, a Guardian'—God watches, preserves, records, and recompenses. Nothing escapes His observation, no consequence goes unaddressed, and no rejection is without eventual accountability. The verse therefore carries a message of both consolation for the bearer of truth and solemn warning for those who dismiss it.

translation: :And when Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him, by a mercy from Us, and We saved them from a severe punishment.
interpretation: This verse portrays divine salvation as an active response to human faith rather than a passive cosmic event—God's mercy operates through historical agency, lifting the righteous out of collective destruction. The 'severe punishment' (ʿadhāb ghalīẓ) implies not merely physical annihilation but a moral reckoning that overwhelms communities built on arrogance and denial. Hud and his companions escape not because of their own power but because their belief aligned them with a transcendent order that refuses to let corruption consume the faithful. The phrase 'by a mercy from Us' suggests that salvation is never earned but gifted, yet it is given to those who have already oriented themselves toward it—their faith becomes the receptive vessel for grace. There is also a quiet warning: God's command arrives at a fixed moment, and no amount of delay or negotiation can reverse it, emphasizing that divine justice operates within a temporal framework beyond human manipulation.
This refers to the tribe of 'Aad, who denied the signs of their Lord, disobeyed His messengers, and followed the command of every obstinate tyrant.

translation: And they pursued in this world [the curse of God] and [will be pursued] on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, the people of 'Aad denied their Lord. Unquestionably, the people of 'Aad, the people of Hud, were destroyed.
interpretation: This verse addresses the people of 'Aad, the ancient Arabian community to which the prophet Hud was sent. They rejected his message of monotheism and righteous conduct, choosing instead arrogance, idolatry, and rebellion against God. The verse indicates that their rejection brought them a curse in this worldly life, pointing to the severe punishment God sent upon them through a destructive wind, and that they will also face a recompense on the Day of Judgment. The repeated use of 'ala' (alas, woe) underscores the severity and finality of their deviation. The verse serves as a warning that denial of God and rejection of prophetic guidance leads to ruin in both this world and the hereafter, and that communities which persist in such defiance ultimately face eradication.

translation: And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih. He said, 'O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. He produced you from the earth and settled you in it, so ask forgiveness of Him and then repent to Him. Indeed, my Lord is near and responsive.'
interpretation: This verse presents the prophetic mission of Salih to the people of Thamud as a manifestation of divine mercy and a call to exclusive monotheism. The phrase 'He produced you from the earth' signifies that human origins are rooted in earthly creation, implying that life, sustenance, and growth are granted by Allah alone. The subsequent mention of being 'settled in it' points to the trust placed in humanity to inhabit, cultivate, and develop the earth—a stewardship that necessitates accountability before the Creator. The call to seek forgiveness and repent reflects the Qur'anic principle that human error and moral failing are inevitable, but the door to divine mercy remains perpetually open. The concluding attribute, 'Indeed, my Lord is near and responsive,' conveys that Allah's nearness is not spatial but relational; He is attentive to the sincere pleas of His servants and answers them in ways that may be immediate or deferred, yet never beyond reach. This verse thus encapsulates tawhid (divine oneness), human responsibility, and the boundless accessibility of divine mercy.

translation: They said, 'O Salih, you were among us a figure of good hope before this. Do you forbid us to worship what our fathers worshipped, and indeed we are in grave doubt, concerning that to which you invite us.'
interpretation: This verse records the rejection and skepticism of Salih's people (the Thamud) in response to his prophetic call. Their statement reveals several psychological and rhetorical dynamics central to Qur'anic discourse on disbelief: first, an appeal to prior respectability ('you were a figure of hope among us') used not as genuine praise but as a weapon to delegitimize his new role, suggesting that his former social standing should have precluded him from challenging inherited norms. Second, an invocation of ancestral tradition ('what our fathers worshipped'), highlighting the Qur'anic theme that shirk (associating partners with God) is rooted in taqlid (blind adherence to tradition) rather than reasoned conviction. Third, their confession of being 'in grave doubt' about Salih's message is not an invitation to dialogue but a hardened stance: they frame their own uncertainty as sufficient grounds for dismissal, while ironically this very doubt demonstrates the moral responsibility they bear for not seeking clarity. The verse illustrates how the Qur'an portrays the human tendency to deflect prophetic truth by weaponizing social expectations, clinging to ancestral custom, and recharacterizing sincere doubt as a shield against accountability.

translation: He said, 'O my people, have you considered: if I am upon a clear proof from my Lord and He has given me mercy from Himself, who would protect me from Allah if I disobeyed Him? So you would not increase me except in loss.'
interpretation: The verse is a statement of Noah addressing his people after they rejected his prophethood. He presents a logical argument to them regarding his own credibility and sincerity. He asserts two things: first, that he stands upon a clear proof (بينة) from his Lord, referring to divine revelation, miracles, and the knowledge granted to him; second, that he has been given mercy (رحمة) from Allah, which encompasses prophethood itself, the support of divine guidance, and the assurance of his mission's legitimacy. From these premises, he draws a rational conclusion: if he were to disobey Allah, he would have no protector against divine punishment, as no one can shield a person from Allah's wrath. The rhetorical question (who would protect me from Allah if I disobeyed Him?) is designed to demonstrate that his obedience is not motivated by personal gain or fear of his people, but solely by the recognition that disobeying Allah leads to certain destruction. Therefore, the conclusion is that his message can only benefit his people; rejecting it would bring them loss (تخسير), meaning decrease, harm, and ultimate ruin in both this world and the hereafter. The verse highlights the sincerity of prophets, whose adherence to divine commands stems from an awareness of divine sovereignty and the consequences of opposition, rather than from any worldly consideration. It also underscores that rejecting divine guidance inevitably leads to loss, as it cuts one off from the source of true benefit and mercy.

translation: And O my people, this is the she-camel of Allah, [sent] to you as a sign. So leave her to eat in Allah's earth, and do not touch her with harm, lest there seize you an imminent punishment.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the Prophet Salih to his people, the Thamud, establishes a profound test of their willingness to submit to divine authority and respect the boundaries set by God. The she-camel is not an ordinary animal; she is a miraculous sign, a tangible representation of Allah's power and a test of the people's faith. The command to leave her to graze freely in Allah's land is, on the surface, a practical instruction, but it also symbolizes a broader spiritual principle: the people are expected to recognize and uphold the sacred limits ordained by God, even when those limits challenge their desires for immediate material gain (such as using the camel's water or land for themselves). The prohibition against harming her serves as the ultimate trial. By commanding them to protect what they may perceive as a useless or troublesome creature—rather than destroy it for their own convenience—the verse reveals whether the Thamud are willing to prioritize obedience to the unseen Creator over their own perceived interests. The warning of an 'imminent punishment' (عَذَابٌ قَرِيبٌ) underscores a central theological reality: divine patience with transgression has a limit. Allah provides signs, grants time, and issues clear warnings, but accountability is inevitable for those who, despite clear evidence, choose arrogance and defiance. The camel thus becomes a symbol of the covenant between God and humanity: respect what He sanctifies, trust in His provision, and you will be safe; violate it knowingly, and you will face the consequences. Ultimately, the verse teaches that true faith is demonstrated not merely by belief in the abstract, but by tangible submission to God's commands, especially when they require restraint and reverence for what He has designated as sacred.

translation: So they hamstrung her, and He said, 'Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days. That is a promise not to be broken.'
interpretation: The verse refers to the people of Shu'ayb who rejected his call to righteousness and instead stubbornly killed the she-camel that Allah had sent as a sign and a test. Their act of "hamstringing" was an act of defiance and rejection of divine authority. Following this transgression, they were given a brief reprieve of three days, a period of respite and ease, before the promised divine punishment would descend. The phrase "that is a promise not to be broken" signifies that the warning of divine retribution is absolute and inevitable; it will certainly come to pass. This serves as a profound lesson about the consequences of knowingly rejecting truth after clear evidence has been presented, emphasizing that divine justice operates according to a set timeline that cannot be averted by human intervention or delay.

translation: So when Our command came, We saved Salih and those who believed with him by Our mercy, and from the disgrace of that Day. Indeed your Lord—the Strong, the Almighty.
interpretation: This verse is a continuation of the story of the people of Thamud and their prophet Salih, highlighting that divine salvation is not arbitrary but a direct consequence of faith, occurring precisely at the moment when judgment descends. The 'mercy' (rahma) mentioned here is not merely a general benevolent attribute of God but an active, saving force that intervenes to rescue the believers from inevitable destruction, demonstrating that faith provides a tangible shelter when worldly structures collapse. Furthermore, the specific mention of being saved from the 'disgrace of that Day' (khazi yawmidh) implies that ultimate disgrace on the Day of Judgment is reserved for those who rejected the truth, while the saved believers are shielded not only from physical annihilation but from existential humiliation before God. By concluding with the divine names 'the Strong' (al-Qawiyy) and 'the Almighty' (al-Aziz), the verse establishes a profound theological contrast: the same power that crushes the oppressors and wrongdoers is the very power that extends mercy to the faithful, showing that divine might operates within a framework of moral purpose rather than mere dominance.

translation: And the cry seized those who had wronged, so they became within their homes lying prone (dead),
interpretation: The verse describes the sudden, overwhelming divine punishment that befell a wrongdoing people—their dwellings became their graves, a vivid image of how injustice collapses upon its own people and how no worldly refuge can stand against God's decisive command.

translation: As if they had never lived [in] it. Indeed, the Thamūd denied their Lord; so away with Thamūd.
interpretation: This verse from Sūrah Hūd delivers a powerful moral lesson about the consequences of ingratitude and disbelief in God. It describes how the people of Thamūd, an ancient Arabian community known for their prosperity, were suddenly destroyed and vanished from the earth as if they had never existed at all—a sobering reminder that worldly power and material comfort are fleeting when divorced from faith and righteousness. The repetition of the word 'indeed' (ألا) underscores the certainty and gravity of their fate, while the phrase 'away with Thamūd' (بعدا لثمود) serves as a curse and a distancing, meaning they are cast out from God's mercy and favor. The verse also functions as a warning to later generations, including the Qur'an's immediate audience, that rejecting divine guidance and becoming arrogant in worldly life leads not merely to decline but to utter obliteration, leaving no legacy behind.

translation: And Our messengers certainly came to Abraham with good tidings. They said, 'Peace.' He said, 'Peace.' And he did not tarry in bringing a roasted calf.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the noble character of Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham), who is described in the Qur'an as a model of hospitality, humility, and devotion to Allah. When the divine messengers—often understood to be angels—came to him bearing the glad tidings of a son despite his and his wife's advanced age, he responded to their greeting of 'Peace' with an equally gracious 'Peace,' demonstrating his gentle and respectful nature. His immediate action of preparing a roasted calf, without hesitation or delay, reflects the prophetic tradition of honoring guests and treating them with the utmost generosity, even when the guests are unknown or unexpected. This act also symbolizes the perfect balance between spiritual receptivity to divine messages and active, practical service to others, showing that true faith is expressed both in worship and in kindness to fellow beings. The verse further emphasizes that Ibrahim was a man of deep trust in Allah, quick to act in obedience, and endowed with a heart that was always oriented toward hospitality and goodness.

translation: When he saw their hands not reaching toward it (the food), he found them strange and felt fear within himself. They said, 'Do not fear; indeed, we have been sent to the people of Lot.'
interpretation: This verse describes a profound moment in the story of Prophet Abraham (Ibrahim) hosting his angelic guests. When the guests—disguised as ordinary travelers—declined to eat the roasted calf Abraham had prepared, he sensed something unusual about them. In his culture, refusing hospitality was deeply suspicious and unsettling, so Abraham experienced a natural sense of alarm. The angels quickly revealed their true identity, assuring him there was no danger and announcing their actual mission. The verse reveals several layers of meaning. First, it shows the humanity of even the prophets: Abraham experienced fear, reminding the reader that prophets are not immune to human emotions. Second, it highlights the prophetic instinct and spiritual discernment that God grants His messengers—they are able to perceive what others miss. Third, it illustrates the contrast between human limitations and divine purpose: Abraham's fear stemmed from not knowing his guests' true nature, while the angels operated with full knowledge of their divine mission. Finally, the verse sets up the transition from Abraham's story to that of Lot, reminding the reader of the interconnected nature of prophetic narratives and the continuity of divine warning to humanity.

translation: And his wife was standing [there] and she laughed (or smiled); then We gave her the glad tidings of Isaac, and after Isaac, of Jacob.
interpretation: This verse refers to the reaction of Abraham's wife Sarah (in some readings) or, according to another widely accepted view, the wife of Lot, though the majority of classical commentators identify her as Sarah. Her laughter is interpreted as an expression of astonishment at the extraordinary news that she would bear a child in her old age, after the age of childbearing had seemingly passed. The subsequent glad tidings of Isaac, and beyond him Jacob, signify the continuation of a blessed lineage and the fulfillment of God's covenant with Abraham, emphasizing that divine will operates beyond natural limitations and that God's promise of numerous progeny and enduring legacy will be realized across generations.

translation: She said, 'Woe to me! Shall I bear a child while I am an old woman, and this my husband is an old man? Indeed, this is an extraordinary thing.'
interpretation: This verse portrays the astonishment of Sarah, the wife of Abraham, upon receiving the angelic announcement that she would bear a son in her old age. Her exclamation reflects a natural human reaction of disbelief at the seemingly impossible nature of the news, emphasizing that such a miraculous event defies ordinary human experience and biological expectation, thereby highlighting the extraordinary power of the divine will.

translation: They said, 'Do you marvel at the decree of Allah? May the mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house. Indeed, He is Praiseworthy, Glorious.'
interpretation: This verse, situated within the narrative of the angels' announcement to Abraham and Sarah of the birth of Isaac and Jacob, addresses a profound human reaction to divine will. When Sarah, advanced in age, laughed in astonishment upon hearing she would bear a son, the angels gently chided her wonder, affirming that Allah's commands are absolute and beyond human expectation. The phrase 'May the mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house' elevates Abraham's family, recognizing them as recipients of divine favor and exemplars of faith. The concluding attributes 'Praiseworthy' (Hamid) and 'Glorious' (Majid) remind believers that Allah's plans, even when seemingly impossible, are worthy of praise and reflect His infinite majesty and perfection. Thus, the verse teaches that trust in Allah's decree should replace astonishment at His wisdom, while affirming the special status of righteous households chosen to bear His covenant.

translation: When the fear left Abraham and the glad tidings came to him, he began to argue with Us concerning the people of Lot.
interpretation: This verse portrays a profound moment of transition for Prophet Abraham (Ibrahim). After experiencing initial fear or apprehension ('الروع' - which can also be understood as a state of shock, awe, or the recoil of dread upon receiving news from angels), he is reassured with glad tidings—likely the promise of a son (Isaac) and the preceding removal of the terror from his heart. Once calm and reassured, Abraham, moved by his characteristic compassion and sense of justice, begins to intercede or argue with the divine messengers ('يجادلنا' - arguing/disputing with Us, a rhetorical device indicating the angels' arrival) on behalf of the doomed people of Lot. This reflects Abraham's deep sense of mercy and his understanding that the people of Lot, despite their transgressions, still had time for repentance, highlighting his role as a compassionate intercessor before the divine decree of punishment is finalized.

translation: Indeed, Abraham was gentle, tender-hearted, and inclined [to turn] toward Allah (in repentance and devotion).
interpretation: This verse praises Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) for three qualities: *haleem* (forbearing, patient, gentle), *awaah* (soft-hearted, compassionate, frequently invoking Allah), and *munib* (one who constantly turns back to Allah in repentance and devotion). The verse presents Ibrahim as the exemplary model of a believer whose gentle nature, tender compassion, and sincere returning to Allah define true faith. It serves as a reminder that strength of character is demonstrated not through harshness or rigidity, but through patience, humility, and an ongoing relationship with the Divine, inviting believers to embody these same virtues in their own lives.

translation: .O Abraham, turn away from this; indeed, the decree of your Lord has come, and they will inevitably be visited by a punishment that cannot be turned back
interpretation: The Qur'an here narrates a moment in the story of Prophet Abraham (Ibrahim) when he pleaded with his people not to worship idols, yet they refused and threatened him. The verse records a divine instruction addressed to Abraham to disengage from the confrontation, signaling that the matter has been settled by God's decree and that the impending punishment upon the disbelievers is inevitable and irreversible. The verse conveys the idea that God's plan operates beyond human resistance: once divine judgment is issued, no force can avert it.
