Abraham is advised to withdraw from the dispute not out of defeat but as submission to divine wisdom, leaving the consequence to God. This reflects a theological principle in the Qur'an: that prophets are called to deliver the message sincerely, but the outcome of rejection is in God's hands alone. It also reassures the faithful that injustice and idolatry will not prevail, for God's justice is certain and unalterable.

translation: And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed and felt straitened for them, and said, 'This is a distressful day.'
interpretation: This verse from Surah Hud (11:77) captures the moment when the angels disguised as handsome young men visited the prophet Lot (Lot). Lot's distress and feeling of being overwhelmed arise from his awareness of his community's immoral inclinations; he feared they might attempt to violate his guests, given the prevalence of this grave sin in Sodom. His lamentation, "This is a distressful day," reflects his anxiety over the potential moral and physical danger his guests faced, highlighting the immense burden borne by prophets who lived among wicked peoples. This narrative underscores the isolation and trials faced by those who call to righteousness in environments steeped in depravity, while also setting the stage for the subsequent divine intervention and punishment.

translation: And his people came rushing toward him, and before [that] they had been doing evil deeds. He said, 'O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you. So fear Allah and do not disgrace me concerning my guests. Is there not among you a man of sound reason?'
interpretation: The verse describes a prophet's confrontation with his community, who approach him in a state of aggressive urgency, driven by their persistent habit of committing wrongdoing. The prophet offers a redirective solution: he presents his own daughters as a lawful alternative, emphasizing their purity in contrast to the shameful act his people intend, while invoking fear of God as the proper moral framework. His appeal for protection of his guests reflects the sacred duty of hospitality in his tradition, and his final question—asking whether any among them possesses sound judgment—serves as both a plea and a reproach, highlighting the moral blindness of the community and the rarity of genuine righteousness among them.

translation: They said, 'You certainly know that we have no right to your daughters, and indeed, you know what we want.'
interpretation: This verse captures the defiant and deceitful response of Lot's people when he counseled them against their immoral behavior. Their statement is laden with sarcasm and insolence; they acknowledge that his daughters are not lawful to them, yet they brazenly declare that Lot already knows what they desire—homosexual relations with men. This reflects their utter rejection of moral约束 and their open defiance of divine guidance, while simultaneously exposing the hypocrisy of their claim to justice through their harsh treatment of travelers and strangers.

translation: He said, "If only I had power over you or could take refuge in a strong support."
interpretation: This phrase is spoken by Prophet Shu'ayb's son-in-law (or a member of his people, depending on the exegesis) in response to threats from the people of Madyan, expressing his frustration and powerlessness. It reflects the human experience of feeling defenseless against oppression and injustice. The phrase "قوة" (power) refers to physical or political strength to resist or punish the wrongdoers, while "ركن شديد" (a strong support) denotes seeking refuge in a powerful ally, a fortified place, or an undeniable authority that could provide protection. It conveys a sense of vulnerability and a desire for security in the face of overwhelming hostility. On a deeper level, it serves as a reminder that human power is limited, and that true refuge and strength are ultimately found in divine support. The verse also highlights the emotional burden borne by those who stand for truth against a hostile majority, acknowledging the very human wish to overcome the threat of persecution.

translation: They said, 'O Lot, indeed we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you. So set out with your family during the night, and let none of you turn back except your wife; indeed, what befalls them will befall her. Indeed, their appointed time is the morning. Is not the morning near?'
interpretation: Here the divine messengers, having come to warn Lot's people of imminent destruction, reveal their actual purpose to Lot himself: they have come to deliver him and his family from the calamity about to befall the city, while the divine decree of punishment remains irrevocably fixed. The instruction to depart at night reflects the practice of hastening to safety in times of peril, and it signals the suddenness and totality of the coming punishment. The prohibition against any of Lot's people looking back, coupled with the exception of his wife, identifies the single individual among those leaving who is aligned with the doomed city; the family is called to sever all ties of attachment to what is about to be destroyed. The phrase 'what befalls them will befall her' binds her fate to that of the sinners, so that even though she is physically leaving with them, her belonging lies with those whose punishment is approaching. The declaration 'their appointed time is the morning' fixes the moment of punishment at a known and inevitable instant, and the closing question 'is not the morning near?' underscores how short the interval is between warning and fulfillment, highlighting the certainty and the swiftness of the divine promise.

translation: And when Our command came, We made its uppermost its lowermost, and rained upon it stones of clay, stacked up.
interpretation: This verse describes the decisive moment of divine intervention in the destruction of the people of Lot. The sudden reversal of the land's structure, turning its high places low, signifies a total upheaval of the established order, showing that no worldly stability can resist God's decree. The raining of layered, hardened clay stones represents a punishment precisely measured and suited to the corruption of the people, demonstrating that divine retribution is neither arbitrary nor excessive, but corresponds to the gravity of the wrongdoing. The imagery conveys both the totality of destruction and the purposeful nature of divine justice.

translation: , marked [for punishment] with your Lord, and it is not far from the wrongdoers.
interpretation: The verse describes a dire warning regarding a severe punishment that is already designated, sealed, and waiting in the divine decree of God. The term 'musawwamah' (مسومة) refers to something marked, branded, or stamped, implying that this punishment is not a vague possibility but a confirmed fate, immutable and prepared. The phrase 'inda rabbika' (عند ربك) emphasizes that the authority and execution of this punishment belong entirely to God, highlighting His sovereignty and absolute power over the consequences of human actions. Furthermore, the statement 'wa ma hiya min al-zalimin bi-ba'id' (وما هي من الظالمين ببعيد) serves as a sobering caution that this punishment is not remote or distant from those who commit injustice; rather, it is ever-present, accessible, and ready to descend upon the wrongdoers whenever God wills. In essence, the verse warns that while divine punishment may appear delayed, it is firmly established in the realm of God's decree and is never beyond the reach of those who persist in wrongdoing and oppression. This serves as a call to self-reflection and repentance, urging individuals to recognize that accountability before God is inevitable and that injustice will ultimately meet its just recompense.

translation: And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb. He said, 'O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. And do not decrease the measure or the weight. Indeed, I see you in prosperity, but I fear for you the punishment of a surrounding Day.'
interpretation: This verse highlights Prophet Shu'ayb's mission to the people of Madyan, where he addresses two fundamental issues: theological monotheism and economic justice. By calling them to worship Allah alone, he dismantles the spiritual basis of their societal corruption, as idolatry often facilitates ethical decay by obscuring accountability to a higher moral authority. Simultaneously, his condemnation of tampering with weights and measures addresses the practical manifestation of that corruption—exploitative commerce that violates fairness and trust. The phrase 'I see you in prosperity' acknowledges their material abundance, while 'I fear for you the punishment of a surrounding Day' serves as a sobering warning that worldly success does not exempt one from divine consequence. The 'surrounding Day' metaphorically describes a punishment that encompasses the community completely, leaving no escape, reinforcing the Qur'anic principle that ethical conduct in both worship and worldly transactions is inseparable from true faith. Shu'ayb's approach demonstrates that prophetic guidance integrates spiritual rectification with social reform, showing that genuine belief in one God necessarily translates into just behavior among people.

translation: And O my people, give full measure and weight in justice and do not deprive the people of their due and do not go about upon the earth spreading corruption.
interpretation: This verse, addressed to Prophet Shu'ayb's people (though applicable universally), condemns dishonesty in trade and economic exploitation. It links unethical commerce—shortchanging people in measurement or value—with the broader sin of corruption on earth ("al-ʿithāʾ fī al-arḍ mufsidīn"), framing economic fraud not merely as a private wrong but as a communal harm that destabilizes society. The pairing of justice in transactions with the prohibition of corruption suggests a holistic moral vision: integrity in worldly dealings is inseparable from uprightness in one's relationship with the earth and its inhabitants. The verse thus warns that those who cheat others materially are simultaneously 'spreading corruption,' blurring the line between individual sin and collective disorder.

translation: The remainder [i.e., what remains of your wealth after giving obligatory charity] of Allah is best for you, if you are believers. And I am not a guardian over you.
interpretation: This verse establishes a profound principle of trust in divine providence and ethical stewardship. When individuals are willing to relinquish a portion of their wealth in righteousness, the sustenance that remains through God's permission carries greater blessing and lasting benefit than any material gain obtained through hoarding or exploitation. The verse assumes human accountability before God while denying any external coercive authority over people—it affirms that genuine faith cannot be compelled but must arise from conscious recognition that ultimate provision and judgment belong to God alone. The statement that the Prophet is not a

translation: They said, 'O Shuaib, does your prayer command us that we should leave what our fathers worship or that we should not do with our property what we wish? Indeed, you are the forbearing, the right-minded.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the response of Shuaib's people to his call to monotheism and ethical conduct in financial dealings. They mockingly question whether his act of prayer—which symbolizes his devotion and submission to God—has given him the authority to demand they abandon the idols and traditions of their ancestors, or to dictate how they manage their wealth. By sarcastically calling him 'the forbearing, the right-minded,' they are not truly complimenting him; rather, they are using irony to dismiss his prophetic counsel as irrational or overly cautious, implying that his patience and prudence are signs of weakness or foolishness. This reflects a broader pattern in the Qur'anic narrative where arrogant communities, attached to inherited customs and material interests, ridicule prophets as a means of deflecting moral accountability.

translation: He said, 'O my people, have you considered: if I am upon a clear proof from my Lord and He has provided me with a goodly provision from Him... And I do not intend to differ from you in that which I forbid you from; I only intend reform as much as I am able, and my success is only through Allah. Upon Him I have relied, and to Him I turn.'
interpretation: This verse presents a model of prophetic leadership and moral integrity, embodied in the figure of Shu'ayb (or a similar messenger) addressing his people. The verse emphasizes three foundational principles of genuine reform: first, the messenger's authority rests not on personal ambition but on divine knowledge ('clear proof from my Lord') and moral legitimacy ('goodly provision'); second, the reformer must embody consistency between word and deed, refusing to prohibit in others what he practices himself; and third, true reform acknowledges human limitation ('as much as I am able') while placing ultimate trust in divine guidance rather than personal power. This framework challenges those who call for change to examine whether their advocacy matches their conduct, whether they claim divine authority without accountability, and whether they recognize that sustainable transformation requires reliance on God rather than mere human effort. The verse thus critiques hypocrisy in reform movements and establishes that authentic guidance combines conviction, integrity, and humble dependence on the Divine.

translation: And O my people, let not your hostility toward me cause you to suffer a fate like that which befell the people of Noah, or the people of Hud, or the people of Salih; and the people of Lot are not far from you.
interpretation: The verse is a warning delivered by Shu'ayb (as) to his people, the Midianites, cautioning them not to let their opposition to his message and the enmity they harbor against him lead them to the same divine punishment that destroyed earlier nations who rejected their prophets. The mention of the people of Noah, Hud, Salih, and Lot serves as a reminder that these destroyed communities were geographically and historically close to the listeners, meaning the ruins of their punishment were still visible and accessible as tangible evidence of the consequences of defying divine guidance. The verse emphasizes that the distance between a community and divine retribution can be very short, and that stubbornness in rejecting truth brings about swift accountability.

translation: And ask forgiveness of your Lord and then turn in repentance to Him. Indeed, my Lord is Merciful and Loving.
interpretation: This verse is a divine call to believers to combine two essential spiritual actions: seeking forgiveness (istighfar) for past sins and shortcomings, followed by sincere repentance (tawbah) turning back to God with a renewed commitment to righteousness. It is not enough to merely ask for forgiveness while remaining in the same state of heedlessness; genuine repentance requires a heartfelt turning away from sin and toward obedience. The verse concludes by describing God's attributes as Merciful and Loving, offering profound hope and encouragement to the penitent. This pairing of divine mercy and love reassures believers that no matter how grave their errors, God's compassion awaits those who return to Him with sincerity, humility, and resolve. It transforms repentance from an act of fear into an act of hope, grounded in the certainty that the Lord who is addressed here responds to those who turn back with grace rather than rejection.

translation: They said, 'O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say, and indeed we consider you among us as weak. And were it not for your family, we would have stoned you, and you are not over us powerful.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the psychological tactics of those who reject divine truth: feigning ignorance ('we do not understand'), attempting to belittle the messenger's status ('we see you as weak'), and issuing veiled threats masked by a false justification ('were it not for your family'). The statement 'we do not understand' is not a confession of intellectual incapacity but a declaration of defiant refusal—the hearers willfully reject guidance because it conflicts with their entrenched interests. By calling Shu'ayb 'weak,' they seek to undermine his credibility, knowing that a marginalized individual has less power to challenge their authority. However, their admission that they would not have stoned him had he not had a family exposes their fear of social consequence rather than any respect for justice; their restraint is purely utilitarian, not moral. Finally, the assertion 'you are not powerful over us' is a psychological assertion of dominance, an attempt to reframe vulnerability as strength. In reality, the verse illustrates that rejection of prophecy is rarely about comprehension and almost always about power, pride, and the preservation of worldly advantage.

translation: He said, 'O my people, is my clan more esteemed by you than Allah, while you have put Him behind you, disregarded? Indeed, my Lord is encompassing of what you do.'
interpretation:
The verse is a direct confrontation by the Prophet Hud (peace be upon him) to his people, the people of Aad. The core meaning revolves around the inversion of values in human society: prioritizing tribal loyalty, blood relations, or social status over the divine command of Allah. The phrase "arhatee a'azzu 'alaykum min Allah" (is my clan more esteemed to you than Allah?) highlights that the people of Aad used Hud's kinship to them as an excuse to reject his message, implying that his prophethood was somehow invalidated or made arrogant because he was 'one of them,' or conversely, they clung to their own tribal structures and leaders, finding those loyalties more binding than their obedience to Allah.

The phrase "wa ittakhadhtumoohu waraa'a kum zuhuriyya" (while you have put Him behind your backs, disregarded) signifies active neglect and turning away. 'Zuhuriyya' implies that they have cast Allah behind their backs, completely ignoring His presence, His rights, and His sovereignty. This is not merely passive forgetting but an active choice to relegate God to irrelevance in their lives while focusing on worldly allegiances and idols.

Finally, "Inna Rabbee bima ta'maloona muheet" (Indeed, my Lord encompasses all that you do) serves as a divine warning. Despite their rejection and their false sense of security in their tribal unity and worldly power, nothing is hidden from Allah. Their deeds, intentions, and plots are all within His encompassing knowledge and power. This sets the stage for the inevitable accountability, emphasizing that no earthly alliance can shield one from the consequences of opposing the divine will. The verse thus critiques blind tribalism and the deliberate rejection of divine authority, warning of divine omniscience.

translation: And O my people, work according to your position; indeed, I am working. You will soon know who will be visited by a punishment that disgraces him and who is a liar. And watch; indeed, I am watching with you.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Prophet Hud to his people, conveys a profound message of detachment and resolute commitment to truth in the face of opposition. It does not represent resignation or despair, but rather a deliberate declaration of independence from the moral authority of a society that has rejected divine guidance. By urging them to 'work according to your position,' he acknowledges their freedom to persist in their rejection and transgression, while affirming his own unwavering dedication to his prophetic mission. This stance reflects a believer's responsibility to remain steadfast in their convictions without resorting to coercion or desperation when facing widespread disbelief. The subsequent warning, 'You will soon know who will be visited by a punishment that disgraces him and who is a liar,' places the ultimate judgment in the hands of God and the unfolding of history. Time itself becomes the arbiter that will vindicate truth and expose falsehood. The concluding call to 'watch' as he also 'watches' is not a threat but an invitation to witness the consequences of their choices. It embodies a profound spiritual patience, trusting that divine justice operates on its own timeline. From this perspective, the verse offers a timeless lesson for believers: maintain integrity and perseverance in upholding truth, entrust the outcome to God, and allow time to manifest the distinction between genuine faith and mere opposition.

translation: And when Our command came, We saved Shu'ayb and those who believed with him by Our mercy. And the blast seized those who wronged, and they became within their dwellings [corpses] fallen prone.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the principle of divine justice and mercy operating in tandem: the faithful are rescued through divine compassion not due to their own merit, but as a gift from God, while those who persist in wrongdoing and reject prophetic guidance face a sudden, decisive end that leaves them powerless in their very homes. The image of the wrongdoers lying face down in their dwellings signifies the totality of their defeat—their places of security and comfort become their tombs, demonstrating that worldly strength and entrenched positions offer no protection against divine decree. The contrast between being saved and being destroyed serves as a reminder that belief is not merely an intellectual assertion but a commitment that determines one's fate, and that God's mercy and judgment are not contradictory but operate according to a wisdom that distinguishes between those who turn toward truth and those who turn away from it.

translation: As if they had never lived there. Then away with Madyan as Thamud was taken away!
interpretation: This verse concludes the account of the people of Madyan, drawing a moral lesson by comparing their destruction to that of the Thamud. The phrase 'as if they had never lived there' emphasizes the total annihilation and the erasure of their existence and civilization, serving as a stark reminder of the consequences of rejecting divine guidance. The explicit condemnation 'away with Madyan as Thamud was taken away' connects the two communities as exemplars of communities that perished due to their corruption and rejection of their prophets. This statement invites reflection on the transient nature of worldly power and the enduring consequences of moral and spiritual failure. It also functions as a historical warning, suggesting that nations or individuals who engage in similar behaviors, such as dishonesty, oppression, or disbelief, face comparable fates. The use of the past tense and the finality in the condemnation 'away with' carries a tone of irrevocable divine judgment, emphasizing that the punishment is not merely a temporary setback but a complete dissolution of their presence.

translation: And We had certainly sent Moses with Our signs and a clear authority (to Pharaoh and his people).
interpretation: This verse affirms that Moses was sent with divine signs and a clear, evident proof to challenge the authority of Pharaoh and to call his people to the truth. The phrase 'clear authority' (سلطان مبين) emphasizes that Moses's mission was supported by undeniable, manifest power that left no room for doubt about its divine origin, yet the message shows that possessing undeniable proof does not guarantee acceptance—those who are entrenched in arrogance and power may still reject truth despite witnessing it firsthand. This serves as a timeless lesson that sincere faith requires the willing opening of the heart, not merely the presentation of evidence.

translation: To Pharaoh and his chiefs; but they followed the command of Pharaoh, and Pharaoh's command was not right-minded.
interpretation: This statement serves as a profound moral and theological critique of blind obedience to tyrannical authority. The verse emphasizes that the followers of Pharaoh (the 'malāʾihi' or chiefs/elites) did not simply adhere to his leadership out of political convenience but actively embraced his erroneous commands, internalizing them as their own framework for action. By describing Pharaoh's command as lacking 'rushd' (sound judgment, integrity, or true guidance), the verse asserts that secular or political power, when disconnected from divine moral principles, inherently produces corruption and foolishness. It implicitly warns believers against elevating human leaders or worldly systems to the status of ultimate arbiters of truth, suggesting that genuine authority must be rooted in wisdom and righteousness rather than coercion or social pressure. The repetition of 'Pharaoh' ('to Pharaoh... Pharaoh's command') highlights the central, consuming role he played in the moral failure of his court, indicating that authoritarianism corrupts both the ruler and those who submit to him willingly.

translation: He will lead his people on the Day of Resurrection and bring them to the Fire, and wretched is the place to which they are brought.
interpretation: This verse depicts a leader or figure of influence who, through misguidance and corruption, leads his followers astray in worldly life. On the Day of Judgment, he precedes them toward the reckoning and, by virtue of his leadership role, is responsible for guiding them into the punishment of Hellfire. The Quran uses the metaphor of "leading" and "watering" (from the image of a herder bringing animals to water) to emphasize the burden of leadership and the consequences of misguiding others. The phrase "wretched is the place to which they are brought" underscores the severity of Hell as a destination and serves as a warning about the eternal consequences of following false authorities who pull people away from faith and righteousness. This verse underscores the profound responsibility borne by leaders for the spiritual fate of those who follow them, whether they lead toward salvation or ruin.

translation: And they were followed in this [world] by a curse and on the Day of Judgment as well. And evil is the bounty which is bestowed (or refused).
interpretation: This verse addresses those who, despite witnessing the consequences of the cursed generation—the people of the Prophet Shuʿayb (peace be upon him)—still choose to follow their path of denial and corruption. The phrase 'followed in this by a curse' signifies that the rejection of truth and the persistence in wrongdoing have spiritual consequences that extend into this life as well as the Hereafter. The 'curse' here implies divine wrath, a state of being deprived of Allah's mercy and blessings, which manifests both as a detachment from faith and as a withdrawal of grace in worldly affairs. It is not merely a verbal condemnation but a spiritual reality that affects the heart and circumstances of the one who insists on disbelief. The mention of the Day of Judgment reinforces that the consequences are not limited to this transient life; the ultimate punishment awaits those who fail to heed the warnings. The verse then refers to the 'bounty which is bestowed (or refused),' meaning the grace or favor offered to them—whether it is the guidance, the signs, or the mercy of Allah—which they either reject or misuse, turning it into a source of arrogance and wrongdoing. Thus, what was intended as a blessing becomes, through their own corruption, a cause of their downfall. This serves as a profound reminder that the misuse of divine gifts leads to ruin, and that the persistence in rejecting truth invites both immediate and everlasting consequences.

translation: That is from the news of the towns which We relate to you; of them, some are standing, and some have been mowed down (or destroyed).
interpretation: This verse refers to the stories of past communities and their prophets—accounts of peoples such as the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, Abraham, Lot, and the dwellers of the Midian—whose dwellings and ruins serve as tangible evidence of the truth of the message conveyed through Muhammad. The phrase "some are standing" indicates towns whose ruins still remain visible, while "mowed down" or "destroyed" refers to those that have been utterly effaced, leaving no trace. The deeper meaning is that these historical narratives are not merely tales but are recounted as moral and spiritual lessons: every nation that rejected its prophet and clung to wrongdoing was ultimately overtaken by divine consequence. The verse thus calls the Quraysh—and all subsequent readers—to reflect upon the fate of those who defied divine guidance, recognizing that worldly power and established civilizations are impermanent when they stand in opposition to God's purpose. It also subtly warns the Prophet's contemporaries that their own prosperity and security are not guarantees against a similar end if they persist in rejecting the truth.

translation: And We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves. Their gods which they invoked besides Allah availed them nothing when the command of your Lord came. And they did not increase [the wrongdoers] except in ruin.
interpretation: The verse establishes that suffering is not an arbitrary injustice from God but a direct consequence of human choices that violate divine guidance. The 'gods' or attachments—whether wealth, status, ideologies, or relationships—that people prioritize over their covenant with God hold no protective power when divine judgment arrives. This indicates that misplaced reliance on false sources of security ultimately leads to compounding destruction rather than benefit, as these substitutes cannot withstand the test of ultimate reality.

translation: And thus is the seizure of your Lord when He seizes the towns while they are wrongdoers. Indeed, His seizure is painful and severe.
interpretation: This verse establishes a universal divine principle: when communities persist in injustice and oppression after warnings, divine retribution comes in a manner that is both intensely painful in its immediate consequences and severe in its thoroughness. The phrase 'His seizure' (akhdhuhu) is depicted as something inescapable, signaling that no worldly power or defense can withstand it. By placing the verse after accounts of destroyed nations, it reminds the reader that historical calamities befalling entire communities are not arbitrary but the inevitable result of entrenched wrongdoing, and that Allah's justice, though giving ample time and clear signs, is ultimately uncompromising and complete.

translation: Indeed in that is a sign for those who fear the punishment of the Hereafter. That is a Day on which all mankind will be gathered, and it is a Day witnessed.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the events described—whether the destruction of past nations, the signs of divine power in creation, or the warnings of messengers—serve as profound lessons specifically for those who hold the Hereafter in genuine awe. The fear of the afterlife's accountability is presented as the key that unlocks comprehension of divine signs, because only those who recognize the reality of ultimate return to God can truly perceive the warnings embedded in history and nature. The verse then highlights two attributes of the Day of Judgment: it is a day of universal gathering where all of humanity, from every era and place, will be assembled together, and it is a day that is witnessed and attested to, meaning its occurrence is established by the testimony of all creation including the angels, prophets, and the nations themselves, leaving no room for denial or dispute about its reality.

translation: And We do not delay it except for a specified term.
interpretation: This verse affirms that the Day of Judgment, or any divine decree that has been promised, will come to pass at a time already fixed by God's knowledge; its delay is not a sign of its abandonment but rather a mercy granting humanity the opportunity for repentance and growth before the appointed deadline expires.

translation: The day when it will come, no soul shall speak except by His permission. Then among them are wretched and glad.
interpretation: This verse from Sūrah Hūd (11:105) portrays the absolute sovereignty of God on the Day of Judgment, when all human beings—regardless of status, wealth, or worldly power—will be utterly silenced and powerless. No one will dare to speak, intercede, or advocate for themselves or others without divine permission, underscoring that authority and speech in that moment belong exclusively to God. Within this scene of cosmic stillness and awe, humanity is divided into two distinct groups: the *shaqī* (wretched), referring to those who are spiritually ruined because of their rejection of truth and persistence in sin, and the *saʿīd* (glad or blessed), referring to those who attain divine mercy, salvation, and lasting joy because of their faith and righteous deeds. The verse thus emphasizes both divine majesty and human accountability, reminding believers that the choices made in this life determine one's eternal state in the hereafter.

translation: And as for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire, for them therein is sighing and wailing.
interpretation: This verse draws a stark contrast between the eternal destinies of two groups: those who are 'wretched' (شقوا) due to their rejection of faith and righteous deeds, and those who are 'happy' (سعدوا) as mentioned in the preceding verse. The term 'wretched' implies a state of misery rooted in one's own choices and moral failings. The verse describes their abode as the 'Fire' (النار), a place of severe punishment. The specific descriptions of 'sighing' (زفير) and 'wailing' (شهيق) are powerful and visceral—zhiir refers to the deep, exhalation of breath expressing intense agony, while shahiq denotes the sharp inhalation of breath resulting from extreme suffering, akin to the sounds of someone in critical distress. These sounds reflect the constant, overwhelming distress and the unending nature of the torment, as opposed to the 'sound of chains' associated with the highest levels of Hell in another verse. Ultimately, the verse serves as a profound warning about the consequences of straying from divine guidance, emphasizing that the punishment is not only physical but also deeply psychological, characterized by perpetual anguish without relief or hope of an end.

translation: They will abide therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord may will. Indeed, your Lord is the doer of what He intends.
interpretation: This verse addresses the eternal nature of the inhabitants of Hellfire, indicating that their punishment is bound by the duration of the heavens and the earth, with the exception that Allah may extend or alter His decree according to His will and wisdom. The phrase 'إن ربك فعال لما يريد' (Indeed, your Lord is the doer of what He intends) serves as a profound reminder of Allah's absolute sovereignty and power to act in whatever manner He deems appropriate, unrestrained by any limitation. It highlights that divine will operates beyond human comprehension, and that Allah's decisions regarding mercy, punishment, and the ultimate fate of His creation are rooted in His perfect knowledge and justice. The mention of 'خالدين فيها' (abiding therein) emphasizes the permanence and severity of the consequence for those who reject faith and engage in wrongdoing, while the exception 'إلا ما شاء ربك' (except what your Lord may will) underscores the boundless authority of Allah, who is neither bound by time nor constrained by any created framework, including the heavens and the earth themselves.

translation: And as for those who are blessed, they will be in Paradise, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord may will—a gift, never to be cut off.
interpretation: This verse draws a profound distinction between the eternal nature of divine mercy and the bounded nature of the created cosmos. The people of happiness (as-Saʿidūn) are those who have attained divine favor through faith and righteous conduct, and their ultimate destination is Paradise. The phrase 'khālidīn fīhā mā dāmat al-samāwāt wa al-arḍ'—abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure—uses the duration of the cosmic order as a reference point, suggesting permanence that extends beyond human comprehension. The exception 'illā mā shā'a rabbuka'—except what your Lord may will—is not a limitation upon eternity but a profound theological acknowledgment of divine sovereignty; the Qur'an elsewhere affirms that the people of Paradise will never be expelled (cf. 11:108), so this exception underscores that their stay is contingent upon the will of a Lord whose generosity surpasses the temporal order itself. The final phrase, 'ʿaṭāʾan ghayr majdhūdh'—a gift, never cut off or interrupted—transforms the entire description from a reward earned into an unceasing bestowal. The word 'majdhūdh' means severed or cut off, implying that no sin, decree, or circumstance can revoke this blessing. Together, the verse paints Paradise not as a wage to be earned and then potentially lost, but as an ongoing, sovereign gift whose flow depends solely on the unalterable generosity of God. The use of 'saʿidū' (they were/they are happy) carries a sense of inherent blessedness—those who are happy in this world through faith are promised a happiness that transcends the duration of creation itself, anchored in the eternal will of the Divine.

translation: So do not be in doubt about what these [people] worship. They worship not except as their fathers worshipped before. And indeed, We will give them their share [of punishment] in full, with no deficiency.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad, reassuring him not to harbor any uncertainty or confusion regarding the misguided worship practices of the disbelievers (likely referring to the polytheists of Mecca who worshipped idols). The verse makes two profound points: First, their worship is not based on divine guidance or rational foundation, but merely on the inherited traditions and blind imitation of their ancestors. This highlights the human tendency toward taqlid (uncritical adherence to tradition) even when it leads away from truth. Second, it affirms divine justice—that while God grants them respite and their share of worldly provisions in this life, their accountability and ultimate punishment in the Hereafter will be given in full measure, with nothing diminished or overlooked. The verse subtly critiques the intellectual laziness of following ancestral customs without reflection, while simultaneously affirming that divine justice, though it may seem delayed, is certain and complete.

translation: And We had certainly given Moses the Scripture, but the people differed concerning it. And had it not been for a prior decree from your Lord, it would have been judged between them. And indeed they are in doubt concerning it, [and] disquieting.
interpretation: This verse acknowledges a recurring human tendency toward disagreement regarding divine guidance. Despite Moses receiving clear revelation, disputes arose among his people about its meaning or application. This highlights that receiving scripture does not guarantee uniform understanding or acceptance; differences in interpretation, bias, and worldly interests can lead to fragmentation. However, ultimate judgment is reserved for Allah, whose prior decree determines outcomes in His wisdom and timing. The mention of a "prior decree" reflects the divine plan unfolding according to Allah's knowledge, not human haste. The verse concludes by noting that some remain in troubling doubt about such matters, indicating that sincere certainty requires both intellectual and spiritual effort, and that lingering uncertainty can be a source of inner disturbance when one does not fully submit to the guidance received.

translation: And indeed, [O Muhammad], each [of the two groups]—your Lord will surely give them their full recompense for their deeds. He is fully aware of what they do.
interpretation: This verse affirms the principle of ultimate divine justice. It reassures the Prophet and believers that no one's actions will go unnoticed or unaccounted for, regardless of whether one belongs to the group that recognizes truth or the one that rejects it. The attribute of God being 'fully aware' (khabeer) emphasizes that divine judgment is not based on appearances or partial knowledge but on complete understanding of intentions, circumstances, and deeds. This serves as both a warning to wrongdoers and a comfort to those who are patient in the face of opposition, establishing that worldly outcomes are not the final measure of justice.

translation: , So remain steadfast as you have been commanded, you and those who have turned back [to Allah] with you, and do not transgress. Indeed, He is Seeing of what you do.
interpretation:
This verse establishes the foundational principle of tawḥīd (pure monotheism) by employing the preposition مع rather than simply stating 'you and those who turned back.' The grammatical structure wa-man tāba ma'aka does not merely mean 'whoever repents along with you' in the ordinary sense of abandoning sin; rather, it functions as a technical Qur'anic term designating those who direct their essence entirely toward God—those whose very being is defined by ṭalab al-waḥdāniyya (the quest for absolute Oneness). The term tāba literally means 'to return,' implying a fundamental ontological turning: the repenter abandons attachment to created realities and orients exclusively toward the divine reality. Thus the verse addresses the Prophet and a specific category of his followers whose state is characterized by this essential turning toward God, forming an inner community distinguished from nominal believers.

The imperative istaqīm (be steadfast, remain upright) is directed at two levels simultaneously: outwardly in following revealed law (sharīʿa) and inwardly in maintaining unwavering orientation toward the divine essence. This establishes that istiqāma is the central duty of this community—upholding the principle that nothing shares divinity with God, in speech, belief, and inner state. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ himself, despite being sinless, was enjoined to this same istiqāma because the command pertains to upholding truth, not to cleansing from sin.

The prohibition wa-lā taṭghaw (do not transgress, do not overstep bounds) immediately follows, serving as the necessary complement. In classical Arabic, ṭughyān denotes excess, tyranny, and crossing limits. In the context of tawḥīd, it warns against shirk (associating partners with God)—whether through attaching ultimate value to anything other than God, or through imposing one's desires upon revelation. Transgression here is the natural consequence of abandoning steadfastness: when the soul swerves from strict monotheism, it inevitably overreaches its proper station.

The verse concludes wa-lā taṭghaw innahu bimā taʿmalūna baṣīr, 'He is ever-Seeing of what you do.' This establishes God's uninterrupted surveillance over both actions and inner states. The divine attribute baṣīr (All-Seeing) is distinguished from samīʿ (All-Hearing) in this context: God perceives not only external deeds but also their hidden intentions, meanings, and spiritual dimensions. The human soul is transparent before God; nothing in the heart remains concealed. The verse thus forms a complete structure: command to steadfastness → prohibition against transgression → reminder of divine oversight. The hidden verb system reveals that this passage is not merely ethical instruction but a metaphysical charter, defining the inner constitution of the community of tawḥīd and establishing God's perpetual witness as the final guarantee of accountability.

translation: And do not incline toward those who do wrong, lest the Fire touch you, and you would then have no protectors besides Allah, nor would you be helped.
interpretation: This verse commands believers to refrain from showing any form of approval, reliance, or closeness toward those who engage in wrongdoing. The word 'ركن' (to incline) implies not only refraining from supporting injustice but also avoiding any form of dependence or emotional attachment to those who perpetrate it. The verse warns that such alignment leads to accountability and spiritual ruin, symbolized by the Fire. It also reminds believers that no worldly connections or alliances can rescue a person from divine consequence; salvation lies solely in Allah's mercy, attainable through steadfastness on righteousness and detachment from corrupt influences.

translation: ,And establish prayer at the two ends of the day and at the approach of the night. Indeed, good deeds remove bad deeds. That is a reminder for those who remember.

I will provide a concise interpretation focusing on the meaning and significance of the verse. I should not summarize the content but provide an actual interpretation (tafsir-like).

translation: And be patient; indeed, Allah does not waste the reward of those who do good.
interpretation: This verse is a divine command to the Prophet Muhammad and, by extension, to all believers, urging steadfastness in the face of trials, opposition, or delays in seeing the fruits of one's efforts. The term 'be patient' encompasses perseverance, self-restraint, and trust in Allah's wisdom and timing, rather than reacting with despair, frustration, or impatience when facing hardship or when good deeds do not yield immediate visible results. The latter part of the verse provides the foundational reason for this patience: a divine guarantee that no righteous action is ever lost, diminished, or forgotten by Allah. 'Those who do good' refers to individuals who perform virtuous deeds sincerely for Allah's sake, adhering to His commands and embodying moral excellence in their conduct. 'The reward' is comprehensive, encompassing both worldly blessings and, more significantly, eternal recompense in the Hereafter. This divine promise assures the believer that patience coupled with righteous action is a guaranteed investment; Allah's wisdom may ordain that rewards manifest in this life or be preserved in full for the eternal life to come, ensuring that sincere effort is always valued and ultimately compensated by the All-Knowing, All-Just Creator.

translation: So why were there not among the generations before you those possessing sound understanding who would prevent corruption on earth, except a few of those whom We saved among them? And those who wronged followed what they were given therein of luxuries, and they were criminals.
interpretation: The verse poses a rhetorical question to humanity, lamenting the absence of a sufficient number of wise and righteous individuals in past nations who would stand against moral and social decay. It suggests that in most previous communities, corruption spread largely unchallenged because people indulged in worldly comforts and privileges granted to them rather than upholding justice. The few whom God saved were those who recognized the truth and resisted wrongdoing. The verse thus condemns those who, given ease and abundance, chose to perpetuate injustice and sin rather than using their position to enjoin good and forbid evil.

translation: And your Lord would not have destroyed the cities unjustly while their people were reformers (righteously conducting themselves).
interpretation: This verse asserts that divine destruction or punishment of communities is never arbitrary or tyrannical; rather, it occurs only when a people persistently engage in wrongdoing after warnings have been made clear. The phrase 'while their people were reformers' implies that if a society is genuinely upholding justice, moral integrity, and righteous conduct, it will not be subject to annihilating punishment. Thus, the verse upholds divine justice as perfectly aligned with moral order: Allah does not punish the innocent or those striving for righteousness. The mention of 'your Lord' in the second person singular addresses the Prophet Muhammad, reminding him that Allah's wisdom and mercy precede His wrath, and that nations are granted opportunities to repent and reform before facing consequences. Implicitly, the verse also warns that the destruction of past civilizations like 'Ad, Thamud, and the people of Lot resulted from their corruption and injustice, not from divine cruelty. Believers are therefore called to remain steadfast in righteousness, trusting that a just society will not be abandoned to ruin, while a corrupt one will inevitably face the consequences of its choices.

translation: And if your Lord had willed, He could have made all people a single community, but they will not cease to differ.
interpretation: This verse affirms that human diversity in beliefs, worldviews, and ways of life is not accidental or contrary to divine wisdom, but is rather the result of God's deliberate will. Although God possesses the power to unify all humanity under one belief system or one way of life, He has chosen not to do so. This divine choice serves a higher purpose, as the existence of differing perspectives, schools of thought, and interpretations provides the essential framework for testing human beings. Through this natural divergence, each individual is presented with the choice to seek truth, exercise reason, and demonstrate commitment to the path they believe is correct. Ultimately, this verse reminds believers that pluralism and the existence of differing viewpoints are part of a divine plan aimed at fostering human accountability and moral responsibility before God.

translation: .Only those whom your Lord has shown mercy [will be saved from that fate], and for that [reason] He created them. And the word of your Lord is fulfilled: 'I will surely fill Hell with the jinn and mankind all together.'
interpretation: This verse highlights divine mercy and predestination, indicating that all beings were created within a framework where mercy plays a central role in distinguishing who is saved from who is condemned. The completion of God's word indicates that the ultimate outcome for those who reject faith will be confirmed and that evil will be fully gathered in Hell.

translation: And each [story] We relate to you from the news of the messengers is that which We strengthen your heart with. And there has come to you in this the truth and an admonition and a reminder for the believers.
interpretation:
This verse, from Sūrat Hūd, reveals a profound divine pedagogy: the stories of the prophets are not mere historical narratives but are precisely curated spiritual sustenance delivered to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ to fortify his inner being against the weight of his mission. The phrase "We strengthen your heart with" (نثبت به فؤادك) indicates that the recounting of prophetic struggles, persecutions, and ultimate divine victories serves as a form of psychological and spiritual resilience-building—preparing him to endure the opposition, grief, and trials he faced in transmitting the message. The word "fū'ād" refers to the innermost core of the heart, the seat of resolve and emotional stability, suggesting that divine revelation operates at the deepest level of human consciousness. 

The subsequent clause "there has come to you in this the truth" affirms that these narratives contain authentic, reality-based guidance, not fictional consolation. The threefold designation—"truth" (al-ḥaqq), "admonition" (mawʿiẓah), and "reminder" (dhikrā)—outlines the multidimensional function of the Qur'anic message: it establishes objective reality with certainty, it warns through lessons drawn from others' experiences, and it awakens dormant spiritual consciousness. 

Importantly, the restriction "for the believers" at the verse's end reflects a Qur'anic principle that guidance's transformative power depends on the receptive disposition of the audience. While the stories are universally presented, their full benefit is actualized only by those who approach them with faith—indicating that spiritual growth requires both divine grace and human readiness. The verse thus establishes a paradigm for the relationship between prophetic history, personal fortitude, and moral instruction.

translation: And say to those who do not believe, 'Act according to your position; indeed, we are acting.'
interpretation: This verse from Sura Hud (11:93) presents a profound paradigm of disengagement with graceful warning. The Arabic term 'مكانتكم' (makanatikum) encompasses 'your position,' 'your capability,' and 'your state,' suggesting that those who reject faith should proceed with whatever resources and convictions they possess. This is not merely a statement of indifference but a measured declaration with eschatological weight. Historically, this verse was revealed in a context where Prophet Muhammad was facing persistent rejection and ridicule from his people. Rather than responding with despair or anger, the divine instruction teaches a principled stance: continue your work while recognizing that the truth-taker and the truth-rejecter are on divergent paths. The subtle irony lies in the juxtaposition: while the disbelievers may feel empowered to act freely, their 'position' is actually one of spiritual limitation, whereas the believers' 'work' is anchored in divine purpose. The verse also carries a forward-looking dimension—the 'we are acting' (إنا عاملون) implies continuity and determination, suggesting that sincere effort in righteousness is its own reward, regardless of the immediate response. Psychologically, this teaches emotional resilience: one discharges one's duty without being paralyzed by the non-acceptance of others. It is a divine strategy for maintaining prophetic composure in the face of opposition, modeled by the Prophet himself who consistently demonstrated patience with his detractors. Ultimately, the verse establishes a principle of dignified disengagement coupled with unwavering commitment to one's mission.

translation: And wait; indeed, we are waiting.
interpretation: This verse serves as a stern warning to the disbelievers and sinners, declaring that they should continue in their state of denial and transgression while the believers and God await the inevitable outcome. The repetition of 'waiting' creates a sense of ominous anticipation, emphasizing that divine justice will surely come. It highlights a stark contrast: while the wicked persist in their misguidance, the righteous remain steadfast, trusting in God's promise of ultimate triumph. The verse underscores the transient nature of worldly life and the certainty of accountability in the Hereafter.

translation: To Allah belongs the unseen [aspects] of the heavens and the earth, and to Him will be returned the matter, all of it. So worship Him and rely upon Him. And your Lord is not unaware of what you do.
interpretation: This verse establishes the absolute sovereignty of Allah over all that is hidden and all that is manifest, emphasizing that every matter and outcome ultimately returns to Him for judgment. It calls for two complementary responses from the believer: sincere worship ('ibadah), which acknowledges His sole right to be served, and genuine reliance (tawakkul), which demonstrates trust in His wisdom and will. The concluding statement serves as a divine reminder that no action, however private or subtle, escapes Allah's awareness, thereby motivating conscious accountability and sincere devotion in all aspects of life.

translation: Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the clear Book.
interpretation: The opening two verses of Surah Yusuf present the disjoined letters (Alif, Lam, Ra) that appear at the beginning of several surahs, whose exact meaning Allah knows best and which are considered a challenge to anyone attempting to replicate the Qur'an. The phrase "the clear Book" affirms that the Qur'an is a self-evident scripture whose guidance, truth, and purpose are manifest. By placing this declaration immediately after the disconnected letters, the verse establishes a relationship between the miraculous phonetic nature of the Qur'an and the clarity of its meaning, suggesting that just as its letters are distinct and known, its message is equally lucid and unambiguous for those who reflect upon it. This clarity is not merely linguistic but also legal and doctrinal, indicating that the Book provides clear guidance on matters of faith, practice, and moral conduct, serving as a definitive standard that distinguishes truth from falsehood without obscurity or ambiguity.

translation: Surely We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an so that you may understand.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the Qur'an was revealed in the Arabic language specifically so that its intended audience, the Arabs, and all who engage with it could use their reason and intellect to grasp its meanings, rather than it being an incomprehensible or foreign text, highlighting that clarity of language serves the purpose of rational comprehension and reflection on its guidance.

translation: We narrate to you, [O Muhammad], the best of stories in what We have revealed to you of this Qur'an, although you were, before it, among the unaware.
interpretation: This verse affirms that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is receiving divine revelation containing the most excellent and beneficial narratives, despite his previous state of not knowing these accounts. It establishes the Qur'an as the ultimate source of true stories, particularly the story of Joseph (Yusuf) which follows, and emphasizes that his knowledge comes entirely from Allah's inspiration rather than from human learning or prior familiarity with these narratives.

translation: When Joseph said to his father, 'O my father, indeed I have seen [in a dream] eleven stars, the sun, and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me.'
interpretation: This verse presents a moment of profound spiritual significance, where young Joseph (Yusuf) shares with his father Jacob (Ya'qub) a vision that would foreshadow his future elevation. The dream of celestial bodies—the eleven stars representing his brothers, and the sun and moon symbolizing his parents—prostrating before him was not an expression of arrogance on Joseph's part, but rather a sincere disclosure of a divine revelation. Jacob's wisdom, as later verses reveal, enabled him to recognize the spiritual dimension of the dream, understanding that it indicated a future status wherein his son would be honored, though he wisely counseled Joseph not to share the vision with his brothers to prevent envy and discord. This narrative illustrates how dreams in the prophetic tradition can carry meaningful symbolism pointing to destiny and divine purpose, while also highlighting the importance of discernment in sharing such visions and the protective wisdom of parents in shielding their children from potential familial conflict.

translation: He said, 'O my son, do not relate your vision to your brothers, lest they devise against you a plan. Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy.'
interpretation: This verse reflects Prophet Jacob's wisdom and protective love for his son Joseph. After Joseph shared his dream of eleven stars, the sun, and the moon prostrating to him, Jacob immediately perceived the potential danger: such a revelation could incite envy and malice in his brothers' hearts, leading them to plot against Joseph. This teaches that disclosure of one's blessings or future potential can sometimes attract the envy of others, and a wise person exercises caution and discretion in sharing such matters. The verse also acknowledges the eternal enmity of Satan, who exploits human weaknesses such as envy and anger to sow discord and destruction within families and communities. Jacob's counsel to conceal the vision was a divinely inspired safeguard, demonstrating the prophetic understanding that spiritual insight must be paired with practical prudence, as the path to fulfilling God's purpose often requires protection from both human jealousy and satanic schemes.

translation: And thus your Lord will choose you and teach you the interpretation of narratives and complete His favor upon you and upon the family of Jacob, as He completed it upon your fathers before, Abraham and Isaac. Indeed, your Lord is Knowing, Wise.
interpretation: This verse describes Allah's selection of Prophet Joseph (Yusuf) and the gifts bestowed upon him: the ability to interpret events and dreams (ta'wil al-ahadith), and the completion of divine favor that had previously been granted to his forefathers Abraham and Isaac. It affirms that divine wisdom and knowledge govern the selection of prophets and the unfolding of blessings across generations.

translation: There were certainly in Joseph and his brothers signs for those who ask [i.e., who seek knowledge].
interpretation: This verse serves as a preface to the entire surah of Joseph (Surah Yusuf), which is the only chapter in the Qur'an that narrates a complete story from beginning to end. The Qur'an explicitly highlights that the account of Yusuf (Joseph) and his brothers contains profound 'signs' (ayat)—a term that, when used in the Qur'an, often denotes divine lessons, moral guidance, and evidences of God's wisdom and power, rather than mere miraculous events. These signs are presented specifically for 'those who ask' (al-sa'ileen), meaning those who earnestly seek understanding, reflect deeply, and inquire about the deeper meanings and purposes behind events. The verse thus invites the reader to approach the upcoming narrative not as a simple tale, but as a source of spiritual and moral instruction. The story of Yusuf is particularly rich with trials of patience, themes of trust in God amidst betrayal and hardship, the dangers of envy and pride, the power of forgiveness, and the ultimate fulfillment of divine plans despite human scheming. By declaring its instructive nature upfront, the Qur'an guides the audience to extract timeless wisdom from the complex interplay of familial conflict, personal suffering, moral testing, and eventual triumph that characterizes the story of Yusuf and his brothers.

translation: When they said, 'Joseph and his brother are more beloved to our father than we, while we are a group (strong in number). Indeed, our father is in clear error.'
interpretation: This verse exposes the psychology of resentment harbored by Joseph's brothers. Their objection was not merely over preferential treatment but revealed a deeper refusal to accept divine wisdom in allocation—'a group' implies they relied on numbers and strength as merit, contrasting with the father's recognition of Joseph's spiritual insight. Their accusation that their father was 'in clear error' shows how favoritism, or perceived favoritism, can fracture familial bonds, breeding arrogance and a sense of entitlement that blinds people to the actual worth of others.

translation: Kill Yūsuf, or cast him into a far land, so that your father's favor may belong to you alone, and after that you will be a righteous people.
interpretation: This verse captures the brothers of Yūsuf (Jacob) plotting against him out of jealousy over their father's affection. The phrase reflects a manipulative rationalization, where the brothers mask their cruelty with the promise of righteousness after the act. The word

translation: One of them said, 'Do not kill Joseph, but rather cast him into the bottom of a well, so that some travelers may pick him up, if you must do something.'
interpretation: This verse captures the moment of deliberation among Joseph's brothers as they plot against him. One among them, moved by conscience or familial attachment, attempts to mitigate the intended murder by proposing instead to abandon Joseph in the depths of a dark well. His suggestion reveals both an inner moral struggle and a pragmatic calculation: exile is offered as a compromise between absolute destruction and mere removal from the family. The phrase 'some travelers may pick him up' carries a veneer of plausible deniability, suggesting that the speaker seeks to reassure himself that abandoning Joseph does not necessarily mean his death, while simultaneously distancing himself from the direct act of killing. This voice of hesitation, though ultimately complicit in the cruelty, illustrates the Qur'anic theme that wrongdoing often begins with rationalization and partial resistance before collapsing into collective sin. The verse also prefigures Joseph's later trials of separation and betrayal, setting the stage for a narrative in which divine providence transforms human treachery into a means of elevation and eventual redemption.

translation: They said, 'O our father, why do you not trust us with Joseph, although indeed we are to him sincere counselors?'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the deceptive nature of the sons of Jacob (Israel), who outwardly expressed loyalty and concern for their brother Joseph while concealing their inner jealousy and intent to harm him. Their statement, despite its surface sincerity, is a manifestation of how those who intend wrongdoing often mask their malice with persuasive, caring words. The verse serves as a profound lesson about the danger of trusting appearances and the human tendency to use eloquence and affection as tools to achieve selfish or malicious ends.

translation: Send him with us tomorrow, that he may enjoy himself and play, and we shall surely guard him.
interpretation: This verse reflects a moment of persuasion and reassurance. The speakers (later identified as the brothers of a young child, referring to Yūsuf/Joseph) are asking permission to take their younger sibling along on a journey or outing. On the surface, their words convey care (

translation: He said, 'Indeed, it grieves me that you should take him, and I fear that a wolf would eat him while you are unaware of him.'
interpretation: This verse captures Prophet Jacob's (Ya'qub's) deep emotional conflict and paternal anxiety regarding the request by his older sons to take his youngest son, Benjamin (or Joseph's brother in some narrations), with them on a journey. While the verse presents Jacob's statement as a simple expression of grief and fear, it carries profound symbolic weight regarding the nature of parental love, the vulnerability of those under one's care, and the psychological burden of repeated loss. Jacob's grief is not merely fear of physical death, but represents an accumulation of trauma stemming from the prior loss of his beloved son Joseph. The phrase 'while you are unaware of him' points to a deep distrust of the sons' vigilance and attentiveness, suggesting that Jacob perceives them as neglectful or incapable of fulfilling the protective duty expected of them. This statement also reflects a profound theological tension: a prophet of God expressing intense human emotion, including fear and sorrow, demonstrating that faith does not negate genuine human attachment or concern. Furthermore, the excuse of the wolf serves as a test, both for the sincerity of the sons' intentions and as a divine mechanism unfolding within Jacob's life. The verse thus illustrates how sincere human emotion coexists with divine destiny, and how the protective instinct of a parent, even when based on incomplete information, reflects a natural responsibility that God honors and responds to, ultimately using the very circumstances feared to bring about reconciliation and deeper meaning.

translation: They said, 'If a wolf should devour him while we are a numerous band, then indeed we would be losers.'
interpretation: This statement reflects the brothers' feigned concern for Joseph (Yusuf) while masking their true intention to abandon him. The phrase acknowledges that losing one member from a large group would be a loss, yet ironically, their very act of conspiring to separate him from the family and leave him vulnerable was the real cause of loss—both for themselves and for their father. It also subtly reveals their awareness of their responsibility, making their subsequent lie to their father (claiming a wolf had eaten him) all the more culpable. The verse thus exposes the hypocrisy of claiming protection while planning harm, and serves as a reminder that mere verbal expressions of care do not absolve one from the consequences of deceitful actions.

translation: And when they went away with him and decided to throw him into a well of darkness, We revealed to him [Yusuf], 'You will surely inform them of this affair of theirs while they do not perceive.'
interpretation: This verse describes a pivotal moment in the story of Prophet Yusuf (Joseph), where his brothers carried out their plot to remove him from the family by casting him into a dark well. Despite their physical act of abandonment, the divine plan unfolds in the background. The phrase 'We revealed to him' indicates that even in the depths of despair and isolation, Yusuf received a direct communication from Allah. This serves as a profound reminder that divine guidance and reassurance are not contingent upon a person's external circumstances. The revelation that he would eventually inform them of their deed while they remain unaware ('while they do not perceive') alludes to a future reversal of fortunes, where the truth would be revealed and the perpetrators would be confronted by the very person they had wronged, without initially recognizing the connection. This encapsulates the Qur'anic theme of divine justice and the eventual triumph of the oppressed, assuring the believer that suffering is not the end of the narrative, but often a precursor to vindication and clarity, orchestrated by Allah's wisdom.

translation: And they came to their father at night, weeping.
interpretation: This verse describes a scene of deception and calculated emotional manipulation. The sons of Jacob return to him in the darkness of night, a time often associated with concealment, weeping as a performance of fabricated grief. The deliberate choice of the nighttime setting underscores their intent to veil the truth of what they have done to Joseph. Their tears are not born of genuine sorrow over a loss but are a rehearsed display meant to elicit their father's sympathy and cover their crime. This is a powerful illustration of how outward displays of emotion can be used as tools of deceit, and it stands in stark contrast to the honesty and patience that the Qur'an elsewhere extols.

translation: They said, 'O our father, we went racing [each other] and left Joseph with our belongings, and the wolf ate him. But you will not believe us, even though we are truthful.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the psychological tactics employed by the sons of Jacob (Ya'qub) as they attempt to deceive their father about the disappearance of Joseph (Yusuf). Their statement contains several layers of manipulation: they preemptively acknowledge that their father will doubt them ('you will not believe us, even though we are truthful'), which paradoxically functions as a guilt-reversal mechanism designed to make Jacob feel guilty for his suspicion rather than holding them accountable. The mention of specific details—racing and leaving him with their belongings—is designed to construct a plausible narrative. The phrase 'even though we are truthful' is particularly revealing, as it shows their awareness that their reputation as potential liars has preceded them, likely due to their own previous jealousies and ill-treatment of Joseph. From a Qur'anic perspective, this narrative illustrates how deceit corrodes relationships and how the guilty often project their own untrustworthiness onto others' perceptions of them.

translation: And they brought upon his shirt false blood. [Jacob] said, 'Rather, your souls have enticed you to something, so patience is most fitting. And Allah is the one sought for help against what you describe.'
interpretation: This verse is a powerful lesson in maintaining trust in God and exercising patience in the face of deceit and emotional manipulation. When Jacob's sons brought the bloodstained shirt of Joseph to deceive him into believing his son had been killed, Jacob's response demonstrates a profound spiritual principle: rather than giving in to despair or yielding to the emotional pressure of their fabricated story, he responded with composed patience (صبر جميل) and turned to God for help against the falsehood they were presenting. This teaches that when confronted with lies or manipulation designed to provoke an emotional reaction, the believer should remain calm, recognize the underlying deceptive intentions, and rely on God as the ultimate source of truth and support, knowing that time and truth will ultimately prevail over falsehood.

translation: And there came a caravan, and they sent their water-drawer, who let down his bucket. He said, 'Good news! This is a boy.' And they concealed him as [a piece of] merchandise, and Allah is Knowing of what they do.
interpretation: This verse refers to the episode in the story of Prophet Joseph (Yusuf), in which he was thrown into a well by his brothers. A passing caravan discovered him, and the one sent to draw water found him in the bucket. The travelers saw him as valuable goods to be sold, unaware of his true identity or prophethood, while God fully knew their intentions and actions regarding him.

translation: And they sold him for a paltry sum, a few silver coins, and they were of those who set no store by him.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Prophet Joseph (Yusuf), describing how his brothers sold him to passing travelers or merchants for a small, insignificant amount of money, far below the value of a free person, reflecting their utter disregard and lack of appreciation for him as a human being and a family member.

translation: And the one who bought him [Joseph] in Egypt said to his wife, 'Make his residence comfortable; perhaps he will benefit us, or we will adopt him as a son.' Thus We established Joseph in the land that We might teach him the interpretation of visions. And Allah has predominant control over His affair, but most of the people do not know.
interpretation: This verse highlights that Yusuf was placed by Allah under the care of a respectful Egyptian official. Through this man’s wife’s care, Yusuf grew up in comfort and was also given a formal role in the official’s household, eventually becoming like a son to them. This was not the action of the Egyptian alone, but part of Allah’s plan to prepare Yusuf for future leadership. By giving him comfort and stability, Allah created the conditions for Yusuf to learn the interpretation of dreams and visions, which would later be crucial in his rise to power. The verse emphasizes that even what may appear to be ordinary circumstances are under Allah’s divine orchestration, and He is always in control, guiding events toward His ultimate purpose. Most people, however, fail to recognize this divine hand at work in their lives, attributing events to chance or human effort alone.

translation: And when he reached maturity, We gave him wisdom and knowledge. Thus do We reward those who do good.
interpretation: This verse describes a stage of human development where physical and intellectual capacities reach their fullness. The divine gift of 'wisdom' (حكماً) and 'knowledge' (علماً) at this point is not automatic but contingent upon prior inner cultivation and moral readiness. The verse implies a divine pattern: those who strive to refine their character and act with integrity (المحسن) will be granted deeper understanding and discernment as a natural consequence of their efforts. It also suggests that wisdom and knowledge are not merely intellectual acquisitions but are bestowed as a reward for those who have already demonstrated excellence in conduct. The phrase 'وكذلك نجزي المحسنين' establishes a universal divine law connecting moral excellence with spiritual and intellectual growth.
