translation: Our Lord, forgive me and my parents and the believers on the Day the account is due.
interpretation:
This verse, drawn from the prayer of Prophet Abraham (Ibrahim) and his son, or possibly Prophet Noah, as referenced in surah Nuh and surah Ibrahim, embodies a powerful lesson on the importance of seeking forgiveness not only for oneself but also for one's parents and the broader community of believers. It highlights several key Islamic principles:

1. **Acknowledgment of Human Imperfection**: By asking for forgiveness, the supplicant demonstrates humility and recognition of one's own shortcomings before God. This is a vital aspect of faith, as it fosters a continuous state of self-awareness and reliance on God's mercy.

2. **Filial Piety and Respect for Parents**: The inclusion of parents in the prayer underscores the high status of parents in Islam. It encourages believers to honor, respect, and seek forgiveness for their parents, recognizing the immense debt owed to them for their nurturing and care. Even if parents were not believers, Islam teaches to maintain ties of kinship with them, though the specific mention of forgiveness for parents often assumes they were, or could potentially be, among those who accepted faith.

3. **Solidarity with the Community of Believers**: Asking forgiveness for "the believers" (al-mu'minun) emphasizes the concept of spiritual solidarity among the community of faith. This teaches that the well-being of the individual is deeply connected to the well-being of the community. Believers are encouraged to pray for and support one another, acknowledging that sin and the need for forgiveness are communal as well as individual realities.

4. **Eschatological Awareness**: The phrase "on the Day the account is due" (yawma yaqum al-hisab) introduces a clear eschatological dimension, reminding believers of the Day of Judgment. This serves as a powerful motivator for seeking forgiveness and striving for righteousness in this life. The Day of Judgment, when every soul will be held accountable for its deeds, underscores the urgency of turning to God in repentance.

5. **A Model Prayer for Believers**: This verse can be seen as a model prayer that Muslims are encouraged to recite and internalize. It provides a framework for supplication that balances personal humility, familial respect, and communal solidarity, all oriented towards the ultimate accountability before God.

Overall, this verse teaches the believer to cultivate a life marked by repentance, gratitude, compassion for family, and solidarity with the community of faith, all while keeping in mindful awareness of the ultimate accountability before God. It is a beautiful encapsulation of the believer's relationship with God, family, and community, framed within the sobering reality of the Day of Judgment.

translation: And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do. He only delays them until a Day when their gaze will stare fixedly [in horror].
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine reassurance that injustice, no matter how unchecked it may appear in worldly life, does not escape God's notice or judgment. The apparent delay in retribution should never be misconstrued as indifference, negligence, or weakness on God's part. Instead, the postponement carries purposeful wisdom: it grants the oppressors time that ultimately funnels toward a decisive moment of reckoning. The vivid image of eyes wide open and frozen in terror portrays the overwhelming magnitude of that Day, when the illusion of worldly power collapses and the truth of every deed stands exposed. It is simultaneously a warning to wrongdoers that their impunity is temporary, and a comfort to the oppressed who may feel abandoned, affirming that divine justice operates on a timescale and in a manner far beyond human perception, yet never fails to arrive.

translation: Rushing forward, with their heads uncovered, their gazes not returning to them, and their hearts being empty (of understanding)
interpretation: This verse depicts the state of those who are terrified and bewildered on the Day of Judgment, rushing towards the horrors they witness with uncovered heads, unable to look back or comprehend what is happening, their hearts devoid of any understanding or courage due to the overwhelming fear and shock of that day.

translation: And warn the people of a Day when the punishment will come to them, and those who wronged will say, 'Our Lord, delay us for a brief term; we will answer Your call and follow the messengers.' [But it will be said], 'Had you not sworn before that there would be no cessation for you?'
interpretation: This verse portrays a scene from the Day of Judgment, where those who engaged in wrongdoing and rejected the truth will, in their moment of realization, desperately plead with Allah for another chance to live, promising this time to respond to His call and follow the prophets. However, their plea will be rejected because they had previously, in their worldly lives, stubbornly sworn and believed that they would never face an end to their existence or any consequences for their actions. This highlights a fundamental aspect of human hypocrisy and denial: the tendency to make resolute declarations of disbelief and permanence in the world, only to panic and seek a reprieve when the ultimate reality confronts them. The verse underscores the finality of the afterlife and the regret that will be felt by those who wasted their opportunity for repentance and faith, emphasizing that the time for choice has irrevocably passed.

translation: And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves, and it was evident to you how We dealt with them, and We had given you examples.
interpretation: This verse serves as a historical and moral admonition, reminding the audience of the tangible consequences faced by past communities who engaged in wrongdoing. The mention of dwelling in their abandoned homes symbolizes inheriting the ruins of a destroyed civilization, indicating that the present generation lives amid the consequences of prior corruption, yet failed to learn from the visible evidence of divine punishment. The striking of parables emphasizes that these historical events and ruined landscapes are meant as didactic lessons, illustrating the inevitable end of those who persist in injustice and inviting the listeners to reflect upon their own moral and spiritual trajectory before they meet a similar fate.

translation: And they had planned their plan, but their plan was with Allah, even if their plan were such that the mountains should be moved thereby.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that while disbelievers or wrongdoers may plot and scheme, their cunning holds no power against the divine will of God; even the most formidable human stratagems, like attempts to uproot mountains, are ultimately rendered insignificant in the presence of God's sovereignty and predetermined decree.

translation: So do not think that Allah will fail in His promise to His messengers. Indeed, Allah is Exalted in Might and Owner of Retribution.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine reassurance that Allah's pledges to His messengers—particularly the promise of victory for the believers and the ultimate accountability of the disbelievers—will undoubtedly be fulfilled. By commanding 'do not think,' the Qur'an addresses a potential moment of doubt or impatience that believers might experience when facing prolonged trials or the apparent prosperity of the wicked. The description of Allah as 'Exalted in Might' (Aziz) affirms His absolute power to execute His will without any impediment, while 'Owner of Retribution' (Dhu Intiqam) underscores that His justice is not arbitrary or hasty, but perfectly measured and inevitable. Thus, the verse calls for steadfastness and trust in divine timing, reminding humanity that history unfolds according to a sovereign purpose and that no injustice, however prolonged, will escape ultimate rectification.

translation: The Day the earth will be changed to another earth, and the heavens as well; and they will come forth before Allah, the One, the Irresistible.
interpretation: This verse depicts the profound transformation of the entire cosmos on the Day of Judgment, when the present physical universe will be replaced by a new creation suited to the eternal realm. It emphasizes the absolute sovereignty of Allah, as all of creation will stand before Him alone, with no intermediaries, partners, or escape. The title 'Al-Wahid Al-Qahhar' highlights both His unique oneness and His irresistible, overwhelming power, under which every soul will be held accountable. The verse calls for deep reflection on the temporary nature of worldly existence and the ultimate reality of meeting Allah, urging believers to live with awareness of His unity and supreme authority.

translation: And you will see the criminals that Day bound together in shackles [chains/fetters],
interpretation: The verse depicts the state of the disbelievers and sinners on the Day of Resurrection, portraying them as being bound tightly together in chains and shackles. This vivid imagery conveys a powerful sense of their utter helplessness, humiliation, and the inescapable nature of their punishment. The bonds symbolize not only physical restraint but also the spiritual and moral captivity that resulted from their own evil deeds and alliances during worldly life. It serves as a stark warning that the consequences of sin are binding and that no one can escape divine justice. The mention of 'seeing' this scene emphasizes its certainty and visibility, urging the reader to reflect on the ultimate accountability that awaits those who persist in wrongdoing.

translation: Their garments will be of tar, and fire will cover their faces.
interpretation: The verse describes a severe state of punishment in the afterlife for the disbelievers and wicked. The 'garments of tar' (qitran) refer to a substance that is intensely hot, sticky, and clinging, representing a state where the punishment adheres to the body without any possibility of escape or relief. The image of fire covering their faces indicates an overwhelming, all-encompassing torment that directly targets the most sensitive and exposed parts of the body, sealing their sight and sense from anything but suffering. This serves as a powerful metaphor for the consequences of rejecting faith and righteousness, where the punishment is not only painful but inescapable and complete.

translation: That Allah may reward each soul according to what it has earned; indeed, Allah is swift in account.
interpretation: This verse affirms the principle of individual accountability before Allah, where every person will be recompensed in exact accordance with their deeds, whether good or evil, leaving no room for injustice or neglect; it also serves as a reminder that although worldly delays may make accountability seem distant, divine reckoning is swift and inevitable, urging the believer to remain conscious of their actions at all times.

translation: This is a proclamation for mankind, so that they may be warned by it, and so that they may know that there is only one deity, and so that those of understanding may take heed.
interpretation: This verse concludes Surah Ibrahim by emphasizing the universal and purposeful nature of the Qur'an. The Qur'an is presented as a divine communication meant to serve three interconnected goals: to warn humanity of the consequences of disbelief and sin, to establish the foundational truth of divine unity that monotheism is not merely a theological preference but the essential reality of existence, and to inspire reflective contemplation among those who possess sound intellect. The phrase 'وليذكر أولو الألباب' (so that those of understanding may take heed) highlights that mere awareness is insufficient; true benefit comes to those who actively reflect, remember, and internalize these truths. The verse also implicitly draws a contrast between those who heed the warning and those who, despite hearing it, remain heedless and will face the consequences described earlier in the surah.

translation: Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Book and a clear Qur'an.
interpretation: This opening of Surah Yusuf serves as a declaration of divine authorship and purpose: the Arabic letters (Alif, Lam, Ra) are considered by many scholars to be a sign of the Qur'an's miraculous inimitability, pointing to the divine source behind its composition, while the description of the scripture as 'the Book' affirms its comprehensive and preserved nature, and 'a clear Qur'an' emphasizes its function as an explicit guidance for humanity, whose meanings are accessible, unambiguous, and designed to illuminate the path of truth for those who reflect upon it.

translation: Perhaps those who disbelieve would wish they were Muslims (or submissive to God).
interpretation: This verse expresses a profound eschatological warning: the ultimate regret of those who rejected faith. It points to a future moment—likely the Day of Judgment—when the deniers of truth will desperately wish they had believed and surrendered to God, but such wishing will be too late. The word 'perhaps' (rubbamā) conveys both the divine hope that they might believe in this life and the certainty of their sorrow in the next. It serves as a powerful call to reflection, urging the listener to recognize that the freedom to choose faith is a temporary mercy, not a permanent condition.

translation: Leave them; let them eat and enjoy themselves and be diverted by [empty] hope, for they are going to know.
interpretation: This verse employs a tone of divine warning combined with foreboding patience. The command 'leave them' does not imply approval or indifference, but rather a relinquishing to the consequences of their own choices, allowing them the full weight of their misguidance to unfold. The mention of 'eating' and 'enjoying' highlights the material and sensory preoccupations that dominate the lives of those who turn away from truth—luxuries that are temporary and ultimately hollow. 'Being diverted by hope' refers to the deceptive nature of worldly expectations: aspirations, ambitions, and illusions of a future that never materialize in a meaningful way, or that distract the soul from reckoning with ultimate realities. The concluding declaration, 'for they are going to know,' carries a tone of inevitable disclosure. It signals that whatever veil of ignorance, comfort, or delusion currently shields them will be torn away. The 'knowing' here is not intellectual acquisition but experiential realization—often associated with the consequences of one's deeds becoming manifest. This could refer to punishment in the Hereafter, but it also functions as a broader spiritual principle: every soul eventually confronts the truth it has avoided. The verse thus serves as both a caution and a promise: a warning that prolonged heedlessness does not equate to safety, and an assurance that truth will ultimately prevail, regardless of how long it is delayed.

translation: And We did not destroy any town [i.e., any people] except that it had a decree determined.
interpretation: This verse asserts that divine punishment is never arbitrary or capricious; every destroyed community had a predetermined decree from Allah. This decree encompasses both the appointed time of their destruction and the prior warning given to them through prophets. Theologically, this refutes any notion of sudden or unjust divine retribution, emphasizing that Allah's knowledge encompasses all events before they occur, and that accountability is established through warning. It also implies that every nation had its allotted lifespan and opportunity, after which judgment inevitably arrived according to a fixed measure.

The verse expresses that every nation has a fixed term that cannot be hastened or delayed. This reflects the divine decree (qadar) in Islamic theology: that Allah has appointed a specific lifespan for each community and individual, beyond which neither advancement nor postponement is possible. The phrase carries a dual meaning—first addressing nations (ummahs) collectively, indicating their rise and fall according to divine wisdom, and second implying an individual dimension where personal lifespans are similarly predetermined. The use of the dual verbs "تسبق" (precede/anticipate) and "تستأخر" (delay/postpone) creates a comprehensive statement about the absolute nature of divine timing. This concept reinforces themes found elsewhere in the Qur'an about tawakkul (reliance on God) and the futility of trying to escape destiny, while simultaneously serving as a reminder of accountability—since each nation and individual will face their appointed end and subsequent judgment. The verse also indirectly consoles believers facing oppression or persecution, assuring them that while the oppressors may seem powerful, their time is also measured and limited by divine will.

translation: And they say, 'O you upon whom the Reminder has been sent down, you are indeed mad.'
interpretation: This verse highlights the dismissive and mocking attitude of disbelievers toward those who convey divine truth, showing how those who carry revelation are often labeled as irrational, while the reality is that faith comes from a source beyond worldly comprehension.

translation: }If you do not bring the angels to us, [you will not be believed], if you should be among the truthful.
interpretation: This is a sarcastic challenge from the disbelievers demanding tangible proof beyond the Prophet’s message itself; it reflects their stubborn refusal to accept faith on the basis of revelation and reason, placing arbitrary conditions that even messengers cannot meet when the demand comes from a heart already closed to guidance.

translation: We do not send down the angels except with truth, and they would not [then] be given any respite.
interpretation: This verse affirms that the angels are only sent down by God in matters of ultimate truth and decisive judgment, such as at death, the destruction of nations, or the Day of Resurrection. The angels are not sent arbitrarily or playfully; their descent always carries divine purpose and justice. The concluding phrase, 'and they would not [then] be given any respite,' serves as a stern warning to disbelievers who mock the prophetic message and demand angels to be sent down as proof. It means that when angels do descend with God's command, it is too late for the wicked to repent or seek delay; the judgment becomes immediate and inescapable. Thus, the verse emphasizes the gravity of God's timing, the seriousness of the angels' mission, and the futility of stalling when divine justice arrives.

translation: Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder (the Qur'an), and indeed, We will be its guardian/protector.
interpretation: The verse serves as a divine promise that God Himself will preserve the Qur'an from any alteration, distortion, or loss throughout human history, distinguishing it from all previous scriptures. It is often understood to refer specifically to the safeguarding of the text from corruption, ensuring that its words, meanings, and guidance remain accessible and intact for all generations until the Day of Judgment.

translation: And We did certainly send [messengers] before you among the sects of the former peoples.
interpretation: This verse affirms the historical continuity of divine revelation and the sending of prophets to every nation and community throughout human history. It emphasizes that the message brought by Muhammad is not new or unprecedented; rather, it follows the same pattern of guidance that Allah established with earlier peoples. The term 'shiyar' (sects or communities) indicates that every human grouping has been addressed with divine instruction through chosen messengers, highlighting Allah's universal mercy and His consistent guidance for all of humanity. This also serves to reassure the Prophet Muhammad and his followers that opposition to the truth is not unique to their situation, as previous prophets similarly faced rejection and persecution from their communities. The verse underscores the principle that revelation is an ongoing reality tied to human existence, with each prophet addressing the specific needs and circumstances of their respective communities while calling them to the same fundamental truth: the worship of Allah alone and adherence to righteous conduct.

translation: And there comes to them no messenger but that they used to ridicule him.
interpretation:
This verse describes a recurring pattern in human history: when Allah sends prophets and messengers to guide people, a segment of society—particularly the arrogant and dismissive—responds not with reflection or sincere inquiry, but with mockery and ridicule. The verse uses the past tense "كانوا" (they used to) to emphasize that this behavior is habitual and continuous, not occasional. The word "يستهزئون" (ridicule/mock) indicates that these people do not engage with the message intellectually or spiritually; instead, they belittle the messenger personally to undermine the credibility of the message itself. By mocking the bearer, they attempt to invalidate the truth he carries.

The deeper meaning highlights a psychological and spiritual truth: ridicule often serves as a defense mechanism for those who are too proud or too attached to their existing beliefs and lifestyles to accept correction. Rather than confronting the message's content—which might require changing their hearts and actions—they attack the messenger, thereby avoiding the uncomfortable demands of truth. This verse warns that this pattern is not unique to one community or era; it is a universal human tendency. Every nation that rejected its prophets exhibited this same attitude, and the consequence of such stubborn mockery is spiritual destruction. Thus, the verse serves both as a description of historical reality and as a warning to the listener: beware lest one fall into the same trap of dismissing divine guidance through arrogance disguised as humor or dismissal.

translation: Thus do We insert it (the denial/disbelief) into the hearts of the criminals/sinners.
interpretation: This verse describes a divine decree whereby rejection of truth is sealed within the hearts of those who persist in wrongdoing; their wrongdoing becomes a self-perpetuating condition in which guidance can no longer penetrate, so their hardened hearts become a fit vessel for further denial. The "slipping into" is not coercion into evil but rather Allah allowing the consequence of their own chosen disbelief to settle deeply within them, closing them off from faith as a natural outcome of their持续的罪恶。

translation: They do not believe in it, although the precedent of the former peoples has already passed.
interpretation: This verse points to a stubborn refusal to accept truth despite the clear historical pattern of consequences that befell earlier nations who rejected their prophets. The 'precedent of the former peoples' refers to the established divine law (sunnat Allāh) that those who deny the message of truth inevitably face destruction or severe punishment. The Arabic term 'sunnah' here carries a sense of an unalterable, recurring historical norm, implying that the disbelievers' attitude is not new; rather, it mirrors the obstinacy of past communities who similarly turned away from divine guidance. The verse thus serves as both a warning and a condemnation: by persisting in disbelief, the listeners are aligning themselves with a doomed historical lineage, demonstrating that their refusal is not due to lack of evidence but rather a deeper spiritual and moral corruption that makes them incapable of recognizing truth even when it is reinforced by the lessons of history.

translation: And [even] if We opened to them a gate from the heaven and they continued therein to ascend,
interpretation: This verse highlights the stubbornness and closed-mindedness of those who insist on denying the truth despite overwhelming evidence. Even if God were to grant them a miraculous experience—such as ascending through a gate in the sky—they would still find a way to reject the signs before them, accusing them of illusion or sorcery. It underscores that the issue is not a lack of evidence but a hardened heart and an unwillingness to submit to faith. The verse serves as a profound reminder that guidance ultimately depends on a sincere willingness to believe, not merely on the magnitude of proofs presented.

translation: They would say, 'Our eyes have been dazzled. Nay, but we are a people bewitched.'
interpretation: The verse describes the state of those who reject the truth and witness the clear signs of Allah. When confronted with undeniable proofs, they will claim that their perception is impaired or that they have been enchanted, as an excuse to deny reality and avoid submission. This reflects the depth of human denial and the refusal to acknowledge truth, even when it stands plainly before them. It highlights how arrogance and stubbornness can cloud one's ability to recognize the obvious, leading people to attribute their own blindness to external causes rather than to their own refusal to see.

translation: And We have certainly placed in the heaven constellations [of stars] and have beautified it for the observers.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the purposeful creation of the cosmos as a sign of divine wisdom and craftsmanship. The "constellations" mentioned refer to the zodiac and the ordered patterns of stars that serve as celestial markers, while the beautification of the sky with these luminous bodies invites human reflection and contemplation. The phrase "for the observers" indicates that the heavens are not merely functional but are aesthetically and spiritually designed to draw attention to the Creator's power and artistry. This calls upon believers to look beyond the material beauty of the night sky to recognize the underlying divine order, precision, and intentionality in creation, making the universe itself a source of guidance and a reminder of God's majesty.

translation: And We have protected it [the heavens] from every accursed devil.
interpretation: This verse affirms that Allah has guarded the heavens from the intrusion of evil, accursed devils who attempt to approach or eavesdrop on celestial matters. The protection mentioned here reflects divine sovereignty over creation, ensuring that corrupted forces cannot access or disrupt the higher realms or the sacred knowledge that descends from the heavens. This barrier is a sign of Allah's power and a safeguard for the purity of revelation and cosmic order, preventing the devils from interfering with divine communications or the spiritual integrity of the heavens.

translation: Except one who snatches (some words) by stealth, but is then pursued by a clear, flaming meteor.
interpretation: This verse describes the protective barrier Allah has placed between the heavens and the lower realms to guard against rebellious beings who might try to eavesdrop on divine knowledge. While the previous part of the verse acknowledges that some jinn or devils manage to ascend toward the lower heavens, they do not return with knowledge unchecked; rather, any fragment of information they steal is immediately followed and obliterated by a blazing celestial fire, rendering what they took useless or incomplete, which explains why false soothsayers and astrologers often mix fragments of truth with widespread error.

translation: And the earth We have spread out (like a carpet), and set thereon mountains standing firm, and produced therein all kinds of things in due balance.
interpretation: This verse portrays Allah as the wise and purposeful Designer of the universe. The imagery of the earth being spread out emphasizes the stability and suitability of the planet for life—it is not chaotic but purposefully arranged. The mountains 'standing firm' (rawasi) signify more than geological features; they are anchors that stabilize the earth's crust, preventing it from shaking, and they also serve as a metaphor for steadfastness in faith and life. The phrase 'from every thing in due balance' (min kulli shay'in mawzun) highlights the principle of cosmic equilibrium and moderation (mizan), meaning that everything in creation—whether elements, ecosystems, or resources—is created with precise proportion and measure. Nothing is in excess or deficient without purpose. For human beings, this verse calls to reflect on the signs of Allah in the natural world, to recognize the balance in creation as a sign of divine wisdom, and to embody balance and justice in their own lives, avoiding extremism and excess.

translation: And We have made for you therein [things of] livelihood, and [also for] those whom you do not provide for.
interpretation: This verse affirms that all the means of sustenance and provisions in the earth are ultimately established and arranged by God, not by human effort alone. While people work to earn their living, the true origin and guarantee of provision belongs to Allah. The phrase 'those whom you do not provide for' extends this divine sustenance to include all beings — children, dependents, animals, and creatures that humans cannot directly support — showing that Allah's mercy and provision encompass far more than what human hands can manage. It teaches reliance on God, gratitude for His unseen care, and recognition that no creature is beyond the reach of His mercy.

translation: And there is not a thing except that its sources are with Us, and We do not send it down except in a known measure.
interpretation: This verse conveys that all potentialities and causes of everything in existence originate from God's infinite treasury of power and wisdom. Nothing occurs by chance or from any independent source; rather, every created thing, every event, and every provision is brought into being only by God's will, according to a precise measure and determined wisdom known to Him. This affirms divine sovereignty over all affairs while also emphasizing that creation follows a purposeful order rather than randomness, reminding humanity that everything they encounter has been measured and ordained by God's knowledge.

translation: And We send the winds as pollinators, and We send down water from the sky, providing it to you to drink, and you are not its guardians.
interpretation: This verse illustrates a profound aspect of divine wisdom in the natural order: God employs the winds as agents of fertilization, carrying pollen to enable plant reproduction, and then descends rain from the sky as a source of sustenance for all creation. While humans may build reservoirs and channels to manage water, they possess no ultimate control over its origins or its preservation, emphasizing human dependence on divine providence and the limits of human authority over natural cycles.

translation: And indeed, it is We who give life and cause death, and We are the inheritors [of all].
interpretation: This verse affirms God's absolute sovereignty over the domain of existence, declaring that life and death originate solely from His will. The word 'الوارثون' (the inheritors) is profound, signifying that after everything else passes away, only God remains as the eternal possessor of all creation.

translation: And We have certainly known those who preceded you [in time] and We have certainly known those who are delayed.
interpretation: This verse affirms Allah's complete and perfect knowledge of all of humanity in relation to time—whether those who came before in the long span of history or those who will come later until the Day of Judgment. Nothing escapes His awareness, regardless of when or where a person exists. The word 'المستقدمين' (those who preceded) and 'المستأخرين' (those who came later) can be understood in several interconnected ways: it may refer to generations of people across history, to individuals who hurry ahead in worldly matters versus those who lag behind, or to those who strive in righteousness versus those who hold back. In every case, the verse is establishing that human beings cannot deceive or outmaneuver Allah by their choices or by the passage of time. A person cannot claim ignorance of divine guidance by saying they lived in a different era, nor can they claim they had no opportunity—Allah's knowledge and wisdom encompass every soul's circumstances. This serves as a foundation for divine justice: since Allah knows the full reality of every person's situation, the ultimate judgment in the Hereafter will be perfectly fair. It also calls humans to humility and accountability, recognizing that every thought, word, and deed is already known to the One before whom all creation will ultimately stand.

translation: And indeed your Lord, He will surely gather them. Indeed, He is Wise, All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse affirms that Allah will gather all people on the Day of Resurrection for accountability. The gathering is presented as a certainty tied to divine wisdom and knowledge, meaning that nothing escapes His awareness and every aspect of the reckoning—its timing, manner, and outcome—is grounded in perfect wisdom. The paired attributes of al-Hakim (the Wise) and al-Alim (the All-Knowing) emphasize that the resurrection is not arbitrary but a purposeful and precise act of a deity who understands the full reality of creation. This serves both as a warning to those who deny the afterlife and as reassurance to believers that justice will be executed with complete comprehension of all deeds and intentions.

translation: And We have certainly created man out of clay, from molded mud.
interpretation: This verse describes the origin of humanity as a deliberate act of divine creation, emphasizing that human beings are formed from humble, earthly materials—clay and molded mud. It highlights the transformation of inert matter into a living, conscious being through God's will and power, underscoring both the physical nature of human origin and the unique creative act that distinguishes humanity within the created order. The description serves to remind human beings of their humble beginnings, contrasting the frailty of their material composition with the noble status and responsibility bestowed upon them by their Creator.

translation: ,and the jinn We created before from smokeless fire.
interpretation: This verse refers to the origin of the jinn, who, unlike humans created from earth/clay, were brought into existence from a more subtle, intense element described as the fire of scorching winds. The mention that they were created 'before' highlights their precedence over humankind and underscores a hierarchy in God's creation. The reference to 'samum' (smokeless or piercing wind/fire) distinguishes the jinn's nature from ordinary material fire, suggesting a being composed of energy and spirit rather than physical substance. This origin shapes how the jinn are understood throughout the Qur'an: as powerful, invisible beings capable of great influence but still bound by divine authority and accountability.

translation: And [mention, O Muhammad], when your Lord said to the angels, 'Indeed, I am going to create a human being from clay from altered black mud.
interpretation: This verse marks the divine announcement before the creation of Adam, the father of humanity, signifying the intentionality and sovereign will of God in bringing forth human life from humble earthly elements. The mention of 'ṣalṣāl' (dried clay) and 'ḥamaʾ masnūn' (stagnant, fetid, or altered mud) emphasizes the lowly, transitional state of the raw material before it is given form, contrasting with the noble purpose it is destined for—bearing the divine trust and becoming God's vicegerent on earth. The pre-announcement to the angels serves to establish a cosmic context for humanity's arrival, inviting reflection on the mystery of creation from base substances to a being honored with the spirit of God, while also subtly preparing the angels—and through them, all conscious beings—to recognize the unique status humanity will hold within the created order.

translation: And when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, then fall down to him in prostration.
interpretation: This verse describes the culminating moment of the creation of Adam, where God instructs the angels to prostrate before him—not because of his inherent divinity, but as a recognition of the unique honor bestowed upon him through God's spirit and the divine breath that animated him. It signifies the singular status of humanity as a bearer of God's spirit, placed in a position of reverence among creation, and it also serves as a test of obedience for the angels, whose act of prostration demonstrates submission to God's command even when it involves acknowledging a being made from clay.

translation: So the angels prostrated, all of them entirely.
interpretation: This verse, situated within the account of God's creation of Adam and the command given to the angels, signifies the complete, unquestioning, and unanimous submission of the angelic realm to the divine will. The emphatic phrasing, 'all of them entirely,' highlights the absolute purity and perfection of the angels' obedience, which stands in deliberate contrast to the subsequent refusal of Iblis. The prostration here is understood not merely as a physical act of worship, but as an acknowledgment of a profound truth: Adam, the first human, was created to bear a nature and a knowledge—specifically, the names taught to him—whose very manifestation, or 'breath of the Merciful,' commanded a recognition from the highest order of creation. The verse thereby establishes a fundamental theological principle: true submission to God entails humility before His creative wisdom, even when that wisdom invests a being formed from clay with a status the angels themselves are called to venerate. The unanimity of the angels underscores the harmony of the celestial order with God's purpose for the human family.

translation: ,except Iblis, who refused to be with those who prostrated.
interpretation: This segment of the verse highlights Iblis's (Satan's) defiance against the command of Allah. While all of the angels prostrated before Adam out of obedience, Iblis arrogantly refused, driven by his pride and sense of superiority. His refusal marks the beginning of his rebellion against Allah and his enmity toward the progeny of Adam. The phrase carries a lesson that sincere obedience to Allah is incompatible with arrogance, and that refusing to submit to Allah's will leads to spiritual ruin.

translation: [Allah] said, 'O Iblees, what is [the matter] with you that you are not with those who prostrate?'
interpretation: The verse addresses Iblees (Satan) directly, questioning his deliberate refusal to join the angels in prostrating before Adam. The phrase 'ما لك ألا تكون' (what is the matter with you that you are not) conveys astonishment and rebuke, highlighting that his exclusion was a conscious, arrogant choice rather than an inability. This rhetorical question establishes the moment of divine confrontation following Satan's disobedience, marking the transition from a test of obedience to the declaration of his rebellion. It underscores the distinction between those who submit to God's will and those who, out of pride, refuse to do so, setting the theological stage for Satan's expulsion and his subsequent role as a tempter of humanity.

translation: He said, 'I would never prostrate to a human being whom You created from clay, from molded, odoriferous mud.'
interpretation: This statement is Iblis's (Satan's) defiant refusal to prostrate before Adam as commanded by Allah. It reveals the root of his arrogance: he deemed himself superior to Adam because he was created from fire while Adam was created from clay. The word 'masnun' indicates shaped or molded mud that has begun to change in consistency, emphasizing the humble origin of humanity. By framing his refusal in terms of what Adam was created 'from,' Iblis attempted to justify his disobedience through a false hierarchy of materials, exposing that his sin was not ignorance but pride and contempt for that which Allah chose to honor.

translation: He said, 'Then depart from it [i.e., Paradise], for indeed you are outcast.
interpretation: The verse addresses Iblis (Satan), where Allah commands him to leave His mercy and grace, declaring him an outcast and accursed. This signifies divine rejection and expulsion as a consequence of arrogance and disobedience. The phrase 'رَجِيم' (rajīm) implies being driven away and pelted, symbolizing rejection and isolation from divine favor. It serves as a warning against pride and defiance of divine authority, illustrating that transgression leads to alienation from grace. This command also initiates Satan's role as an open adversary to humanity, setting the stage for the ongoing spiritual struggle between good and evil. The verse underscores the principle that arrogance before God results in separation from His mercy, a theme that recurs throughout the Qur'an as a caution against self-exaltation.

translation: And upon you is the curse until the Day of Judgment (or Recompense).
interpretation: This verse is part of the Qur'anic dialogue between Allah and Iblis (Satan), who arrogantly refused to prostrate before Adam. When Iblis was given respite until the Day of Resurrection, he responded with defiance, declaring that he would misguide humanity. The curse mentioned here signifies Allah's expulsion of Iblis from His mercy and the lasting state of being far removed from divine favor. It serves as a profound warning against pride, disobedience, and arrogance, illustrating that those who reject humility before Allah's commands are subject to eternal alienation from His grace. The verse underscores the seriousness of defying divine will and the consequences of choosing rebellion over submission.

translation: He said, 'My Lord, then grant me reprieve until the Day they are resurrected.'
interpretation: Iblis's request for reprieve until the Day of Resurrection reflects his arrogance and his deliberate intention to persist in misguidance rather than seeking forgiveness. By asking for an extended period until the ultimate Day, he demonstrates not a desire for reform but a calculated resolve to continue leading humanity astray until the final accountability. This verse exposes the deceptive nature of those who, when confronted with truth, do not seek redemption but rather seek permission to continue in transgression. It also establishes the divine wisdom in allowing such trials to persist until a predetermined time, serving as a test for humanity's free will and ultimately revealing who sincerely seeks truth and who succumbs to persistent delusion.

translation: He said, 'Then indeed, you are among those reprieved'
interpretation: In this address, Allah conveys to Iblis that the plea he made for delay until the Day of Resurrection has been granted, meaning he has been granted a reprieve until a specified time. This delay, however, is not a sign of honor or forgiveness; rather, it is a strategic response from Allah, allowing Iblis a period in which he will exercise his rebellion fully so that his ultimate removal and punishment will manifest his arrogance and rebellion openly before all creation. The granting of this respite ultimately serves Allah's purpose of making clear the distinction between obedience and disobedience, truth and falsehood, and serves as a test for humanity regarding whether they will follow divine guidance or fall into the deceptions of the expelled one.

translation: . این میوه‌های آن بهشت است که به شما داده می‌شود،** تا روز معین و موعد مقرر ** (روز قیامت).
interpretation: این عبارت که در قرآن بارها تکرار شده است، بیانگر محدودیت نعمت‌های دنیوی و تأکید بر قطعی بودن روز قیامت است. «یوم الوقت المعلوم» به روزی اشاره دارد که زمان آن نزد خداوند معین و مشخص است، اما برای انسان‌ها ناشناخته و پنهان است. این مفهوم دو پیامد مهم دارد: نخست، انسان را از دلبستگی بیش از حد به دنیا و نعمت‌های موقت آن بازمی‌دارد و به او یادآوری می‌کند که این لذات فانی هستند و پایانی حتمی دارند. دوم، این عبارت به عدالت الهی اشاره دارد که در آن روز، پاداش و کیفر عادلانه به هرکس داده خواهد شد. «الوقت المعلوم» همچنین نشان‌دهنده علم مطلق خداوند به زمان دقیق قیامت است که از محدوده درک بشر خارج است، اما قطعی و حتمی خواهد بود.

translation: He (Iblis) said, 'My Lord, because You have put me in error, I will surely make [evil] attractive to them on earth, and I will surely mislead them all.'
interpretation: This verse captures the defiant declaration of Iblis (Satan) after his refusal to prostrate before Adam, as recorded in Surah Al-Hijr (15:39). When Allah questioned him about his disobedience, Iblis did not repent but instead blamed Allah for his misguidance—'because You have put me in error'—reflecting his arrogance and refusal to acknowledge his own choice. This statement is a manifestation of ingratitude and a justification of his rebellion. In response, Iblis vows to lead humanity astray by making sin appealing and beautifying vice in their eyes, leveraging human desires and weaknesses. His use of 'all' (أجمعين) reveals his boundless arrogance, assuming no one will escape his trap. Yet, his plan is limited by Allah's will; he can only misguide those who choose to follow him, while the sincere and faithful remain protected by divine guidance. The verse serves as a profound warning to humanity about the deceptive nature of evil, which often presents itself in attractive forms, and underscores the importance of seeking Allah's refuge from the whispers of Satan.

translation: Except Your sincere servants among them.
interpretation: This phrase concludes Iblis's declaration in Surah Al-Hijr (15:40) where he vows to lead humanity astray as a test, while acknowledging that those whom God has purified through sincere devotion and faith cannot be touched by his influence. The term 'المخلصين' (al-mukhlasin) refers to those whom God has chosen, purified, and granted steadfastness—people whose sincerity in worship protects them from deviation. The verse affirms that divine sincerity is a shield against misguidance and that God's protection is reserved for those who are wholly devoted to Him, suggesting that the quality of one's faith, not mere verbal claim, determines their spiritual immunity.

translation: He said, 'This is a path [leading] to Me, [a path that is] straight.'
interpretation: This statement emphasizes that there is a singular, direct way that leads back to the Divine, and that way is described as 'straight' because it requires no detours, distortions, or compromises. It affirms that ultimate closeness to God is not achieved through scattered or man-made routes, but through the clear path established by God Himself. In the broader Qur'anic context, this 'straight path' refers to total submission to God alone, undivided in devotion. It is 'straight' because it eliminates all crookedness of doubt, association, or desire that pulls the soul in multiple directions. Thus, the verse calls for sincere recognition that only the path defined and guided by God leads to Him, while all other directions—however appealing—deviate from that true destination.

translation: Indeed, [O Iblīs], you have no authority over My servants, except those who follow you from among the deviators.
interpretation: This verse establishes a fundamental principle of divine justice and human moral agency: Satan (Iblīs) has no dominion or compulsion over the believers, for genuine faith is a fortress against his whisperings. God limits Satan's influence strictly to those who choose to follow him, meaning that sin is never the result of forced necessity but of voluntary submission to misguidance. The phrase 'except the deviators' (الغاوين) refers to those who willingly stray from truth; their following of Satan is itself a consequence of their own deviation, not its cause. Thus, every human being bears full responsibility for their choices, and no one can blame Satan for their misdeeds, since he was given no authority except over those who surrender their will to him. The verse also reassures the righteous that their steadfastness places them outside the realm of Satan's coercive power, even as it warns that yielding to doubt and rebellion is what grants him a foothold.

translation: And indeed, Hell is the promised meeting place for them all.
interpretation: This verse affirms that Hellfire is the inevitable destination appointed for all those who reject faith and persist in wrongdoing, serving as a divine promise of ultimate accountability beyond worldly life.

. The traditional scholar is engaging with the image of Jahannam having seven gates in order to extract a theological point about gradations of punishment. He understands the gates not as a single entrance, but as distinct levels through which different categories of sinners are assigned their place. The phrase 'جزء مقسوم' is read as a precisely allotted portion, meaning that the share each group receives is not arbitrary but measured out according to their deeds. This reflects a broader Qur'anic theme that divine justice operates with exactitude, not excess. The scholar would likely situate this within discussions of divine sovereignty over punishment and the relationship between human accountability and the structure of the afterlife. In his broader work, this verse may function as evidence for the doctrine that hell itself has varying degrees of severity, supporting the view that eschatological realities are not uniform but differentiated in ways that mirror moral distinctions in earthly life. The interpretation remains grounded in the assumption that the 'gates' and their 'portions' describe real divisions within a literal hell, with the exegetical task being to identify which groups correspond to which levels.

translation: Indeed, the righteous will be among gardens and springs.
interpretation: This verse from Surah Al-Dhariyat (51:15) conveys a profound promise of divine reward for those who embody taqwa (God-consciousness or righteousness). The imagery of *jannat* (gardens) symbolizes a state of flourishing, peace, and spiritual fulfillment, while *'uyun* (springs or flowing waters) represents eternal life, purity, and the continuous outpouring of divine mercy and blessings. Together, these metaphors describe a paradisiacal reality that transcends the limitations of the material world, where the righteous experience a direct and unmediated connection with their Creator. The verse emphasizes that the rewards of piety are not merely abstract or deferred but are rooted in a tangible, sustaining, and life-giving reality—a return to a state of harmony with God's creation, echoing the original purpose of human existence as vicegerents on earth who live in alignment with divine will.

translation: Enter it in peace, safe [and secure].
interpretation: The verse indicates that the devoted servants of God will be invited to enter Paradise in a state of complete safety and tranquility, free from any fear of expulsion or harm, and they will be greeted with the salutation of peace, reflecting the eternal bliss and harmony of the Hereafter.

translation: And We will have removed whatever of resentment is in their breasts [of the people of Paradise]; [so they will be] brothers, [seated] on thrones facing each other.
interpretation: The verse portrays the purified state of the believers in Paradise, where all traces of worldly grudges, envy, and ill-feelings have been lifted from their hearts. The transformation is so complete that the inhabitants of Paradise regard one another with the purest affection, becoming like close brothers and sisters. They are then seated on adorned thrones facing one another, signifying mutual respect, equality, joy in each other's company, and the absence of any hierarchy or hidden animosity. The imagery of facing each other conveys open, honest fellowship, free from the secrecy and tension that often characterize human interactions in the worldly life. This state is presented as a divine gift, achieved not by human effort alone, but by God's mercy in cleansing the soul of its lower impulses.

translation: No fatigue will touch them therein [in Paradise], nor will they ever be made to leave it.
interpretation: The verse highlights a fundamental characteristic of the eternal state of the righteous in Paradise: their complete and perpetual rest. The mention of "no fatigue" (نصب) signifies the absence of any physical exhaustion, psychological strain, or emotional distress that characterizes worldly existence. By affirming that they will not be "made to leave" (بمخرجين) Paradise, the verse emphasizes the permanent, unending nature of this state of bliss, contrasting with the impermanence of worldly life where comfort is always temporary. This serves as a profound assurance of the unending nature of the reward for the righteous, presenting Paradise as a state of pure, uninterrupted peace that the inhabitants will never have to relinquish.

translation: Inform My servants that it is I who am the Forgiving, the Merciful,
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine reassurance that Allah's attributes of forgiveness and mercy take precedence over punishment, inviting all of humanity—especially those who have erred—to return to Him with sincere repentance. It emphasizes that no matter how far one has strayed, Allah's capacity to forgive is inexhaustible, and His mercy encompasses all things. The command to "inform My servants" underscores the importance of conveying this message of hope, reminding believers that the door to redemption remains perpetually open, and that turning back to Allah with humility and remorse is always met with compassion rather than rejection.

translation: And that My punishment is the painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the certainty and severity of the divine penalty reserved for those who reject truth and persist in wrongdoing, asserting that no other retribution can compare to the chastisement decreed by God.

translation: And inform them about the guests of Abraham.
interpretation: This phrase refers to the divine command to convey to the Prophet Muhammad (or his community) the account of Abraham's honored guests, who were actually angels sent by Allah. They came to him with glad tidings of a wise son and the forthcoming punishment of the wicked people of Lot. The verse emphasizes the continuity of prophetic revelation and the importance of reflecting on the stories of past prophets as sources of guidance, comfort, and warning. It also highlights the unique nature of true hospitality and the prophetic role of receiving divine messengers with reverence.

translation: When they entered upon him and said, 'Peace,' he said, 'Indeed, we are of you anxious/wearied in fear.'
interpretation: The verse captures the moment when the guests—angels sent to Abraham—offered him the customary greeting of 'salam' (peace), but Abraham sensed something unusual or foreboding about their presence, prompting him to express a feeling of unease or apprehension toward them. His response, 'we are of you wary,' reflects his cautious spiritual discernment rather than ordinary fear; as a prophet deeply attuned to the unseen, he perceived that these visitors were not ordinary travelers and felt a weighty concern about their true purpose. This anxiety proved justified, as their arrival carried the dual news of a promised son and the impending destruction of Lot's people. Thus, the verse illustrates that true prophetic consciousness involves an intuitive alertness to what lies beneath the surface of events, a vigilance that even God's messengers of glad tidings can stir in the heart of a believer who is watchful over the moral and spiritual dimensions of reality.

translation: They said, 'Do not be alarmed. Indeed, we bring you good tidings of a boy of [great] knowledge.'
interpretation: This phrase, spoken to the elderly Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham), captures a moment of profound reassurance following his natural astonishment or fear at the appearance of unexpected messengers (angels). The command 'Do not be alarmed' (la taajal) is a direct address to his human emotional reaction, acknowledging that such an encounter is indeed startling. The core of the message, however, is the promise of a 'boy of [great] knowledge' (ghulam 'alim). This is specifically understood to refer to Ismail (Ishmael), his firstborn son through Hajar (Hagar). The title 'alim (knowing, possessing knowledge) is significant and prophetic; it elevates the child not merely as offspring but as one destined for wisdom, understanding, and religious insight. This foretelling serves multiple purposes: it confirms divine power over natural law (granting a son to aged parents), it establishes a divine plan for the lineage that would continue through this child, and it immediately connects the physical gift of a son with the spiritual gift of knowledge, indicating that the son's significance lies as much in his future role as a bearer of divine guidance as in his biological relation to Ibrahim. The phrase thus transforms a moment of potential fear into an announcement of a sacred legacy centered on wisdom and knowledge.

translation: He said, 'Have you given me good tidings [of a son] although old age has touched me? Then of what [wondrous thing] are you giving me good tidings?'
interpretation: The verse captures the reaction of the elderly patriarch upon receiving the astonishing news that he will father a son in his old age. His question is not a denial but an expression of wonder and astonishment, highlighting the miraculous nature of the promise. It underscores a recurring theme in the Qur'an: that God's power is not bound by natural limitations such as age, and that His will prevails over human expectations. The verse invites reflection on humility before divine wisdom and encourages believers to recognize that miraculous events are meant to strengthen faith, not to be questioned with skepticism. It also serves to console those who feel that time has passed them by, reminding them that God's mercy and plans transcend human timelines.

translation: They said, 'We bring you good news of the truth, so do not be of those who despair.'
interpretation: This statement reflects the principle that divine mercy and hope are always accessible to the believer, regardless of the severity of one's circumstances. The addressees are urged against falling into despair (qunūṭ), a state condemned in the Qur'an as it contradicts tawḥīd and trust in God's infinite power and wisdom. The use of "good news" (bashar) signifies that what is being conveyed is not merely information but a transformative reality that should dispel despondency. In broader Qur'anic context, this phrase often appears following prayers or supplications, reminding the believer that God's response may come in forms unexpected or delayed, but it is always rooted in wisdom. Despair is thus a failure to recognize the scope of divine compassion ("Do not despair of God's mercy, for none despair of God's mercy except the disbelieving people" — 12:87). This verse calls for sabr (steadfastness) and yaqīn (certainty), teaching that hope in God is not wishful thinking but an active spiritual stance grounded in knowledge of His attributes as al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm.

translation: And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except for those who are astray?
interpretation: The verse addresses a fundamental aspect of the human spiritual condition: the danger of despairing of Allah's mercy. The rhetorical question form ('And who... except...') serves to emphasize that despair itself is a form of misguidance, because it fundamentally contradicts the nature of Allah, who is described throughout the Quran as infinite in mercy and forgiveness. The verse implies that the door of divine mercy remains open as long as a person is alive and capable of turning back to Allah; therefore, despairing of this mercy is not a realistic assessment of one's situation but rather a sign of being 'astray' (الضالون) from the correct understanding of Allah's attributes and from the path of hope and repentance. The term ' astray' (ضالون) here carries a strong meaning, referring to those who have deviated from the straight path of faith, suggesting that despair is not a minor sin or a momentary weakness but a major spiritual deviation that reflects a misunderstanding of who Allah is. In context, this verse comes after describing the rewards of the righteous and the punishments of the wicked, reminding the reader that no matter how severe one's sins or how dire one's circumstances, Allah's mercy is vast enough to encompass them if sought sincerely. The verse thus serves as both a warning against the spiritual disease of hopelessness and an invitation to maintain hope in Allah's infinite compassion.

translation: He said, 'Then what is your business, O messengers?'
interpretation: This verse is a profound dialogue within the narrative of Prophet Abraham (Ibrahim) and his guests. When he saw angels visiting him in human form, he approached them with hospitality and concern. His question, 'What is your business?' reflects a desire to understand their mission. In the broader context, it highlights a recurring Qur'anic theme: prophets and righteous servants of God are not passive recipients of revelation; they engage critically, seek clarity, and ensure they understand the divine purpose before committing to action. It demonstrates Abraham's courage to question even powerful supernatural visitors, showing that true faith is combined with reason and discernment.

translation: They said, 'Indeed, we have been sent toward a people of criminals,'
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the angels sent to Prophet Lot, illustrates that divine messengers are dispatched as agents of accountability and justice, targeting communities whose persistent transgression has reached a point of no return, signifying a universal principle in the Qur'anic narrative that divine mercy grants nations opportunities but ultimately delivers consequences when moral corruption becomes entrenched.

translation: Except the family of Lot; indeed, We will save them all.
interpretation: This phrase is a continuation of the narrative of Prophet Shu'ayb (or possibly Lot, depending on the surrounding context, as the verses differ between Surah Al-Hijr and Surah Ash-Shu'ara). In either case, it signifies Allah's specific intervention to exempt the believers among the family of the messenger from the general destruction decreed upon their people. The exception highlights the principle of divine mercy: faith serves as a shield against collective punishment. It indicates that even when a society reaches a point of total corruption warranting annihilation, Allah preserves those who have submitted to Him, demonstrating that salvation is tied to belief and not merely to biological or social kinship.

translation: Except his wife, [whom] We decreed will surely be among those who remain behind.
interpretation: This verse is part of the broader Qur'anic narrative concerning the punishment that was inflicted upon the people of Lot (Lut), who were destroyed for their persistent transgression of moral bounds, specifically the unnatural acts they engaged in as a community. The exception of Lot's wife is a profound theological and moral lesson: although she was married to a righteous prophet and shared his household and lineage, her inner reality was aligned with the corrupt beliefs and desires of her people. Divine decree operates upon the state of the soul and one's true allegiance, not merely upon outward associations. Her being 'decreed' to remain behind signifies that her ultimate end was already determined by God based on her hidden choices and affiliations, and no amount of physical proximity to righteousness could alter that destiny.

translation: When the messengers came to the family of Lot,
interpretation: This verse marks the arrival of the divine messengers (angels) at the household of the Prophet Lut (Lot), preceding the destruction of his people. The mention of 'the family of Lut' rather than the city itself indicates that the divine intervention began specifically with the household to deliver Lut and his believing family, separating them from the corrupt community that had rejected his message and engaged in immoral behavior. This event foreshadows the imminent punishment that would befall the people of Lut, emphasizing the mercy of God in first warning and granting the opportunity for the faithful to separate themselves before the coming wrath.

translation: He said, 'Indeed, you are a people of unknown [strangers, i.e., disbelievers].'
interpretation: This is the response of Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) to the people of Madyan, expressing his bewilderment or astonishment at their denial of the truth. The word 'munkar' (unknown, unfamiliar, or denied) here can be understood in two interconnected ways: it signifies that their behavior of rejecting the message of monotheism and engaging in immoral acts is 'munkar'—something disapproved and rejected by sound intellect and divine guidance. Simultaneously, it reflects Shu'ayb's feeling that they have become strangers to him, as their obstinacy and refusal to accept the divine warning have created an unbridgeable distance between them. This phrase encapsulates the Prophet's rejection of their persistent disbelief and his declaration that their nature and actions are entirely alien to the path of righteousness and submission to God.

translation: They will say, 'Rather, you have come to us with what they [i.e., the people before] used to doubt.'
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, the deniers will be told that the truth they now see before them is the very reality their predecessors had disputed and rejected out of stubbornness, so they have no excuse before God.

translation: And We came to you with the truth, and indeed we are of the truthful ones.
interpretation: This verse affirms that divine revelation and the messages brought by the prophets are grounded in absolute truth, as God and His messengers do not speak falsehood. It serves as a divine attestation of the integrity and sincerity of the prophetic mission, assuring believers that the guidance they receive is authentic and trustworthy, while also reinforcing the accountability of those who reject this truth despite clear evidence.

translation: Then set forth with your household in a portion of the night and follow behind them, and let no one of you look back, and go on to the place which you are commanded.
interpretation: This verse addresses Prophet Lut (Lot), commanding him to evacuate his family from the doomed city at night before its impending destruction, requiring that they march behind him and refrain from looking back in sorrow or attachment, proceeding directly to the designated place of safety. The directive emphasizes complete obedience, unwavering trust in divine instruction, and a decisive severance from the corrupt society about to face divine retribution.

translation: And We conveyed to him [Abraham] the decree that the root of these [people] would be cut off by morning.
interpretation: The verse describes a divine revelation to Abraham assuring him that the unjust people who opposed him would face a decisive end. The 'root being cut off' signifies the complete eradication of their influence and legacy, suggesting that their wrongdoing and opposition would not merely be punished temporarily but would come to a definitive conclusion with the dawn of a new day. This reflects the Quranic theme that injustice, no matter how entrenched, is ultimately overcome by divine will, and that those who persistently reject truth will be removed as a fundamental threat to the righteous community Abraham was establishing.

translation: And the people of the city came [to him], rejoicing.
interpretation: This verse describes the inhabitants of a city hastening toward a messenger with joyful anticipation, expecting glad tidings or celebration. It reflects a scene where news of the prophet's arrival or a promised blessing spread quickly, drawing crowds eager to witness the event. Theologically, it illustrates how communities often respond to divine messengers with enthusiasm when they perceive personal benefit, contrasting with later rejection when the message challenges their interests. It also highlights the communal nature of prophetic missions, where entire populations are drawn into the unfolding divine narrative.

translation: He said, 'Indeed, these are my guests, so do not shame me.'
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the prophet Lut (Lot) to his community, demonstrates a fundamental principle of honor and hospitality: the duty to protect one's guests from harm and humiliation takes precedence over social pressure or the behavior of the host's own people. Lut appeals to a shared cultural value of his time—the sacred duty to safeguard guests—using this moral obligation to confront the wrongdoing of those around him, showing that the ethics of protecting the vulnerable serve as a powerful standard by which to challenge injustice.

This is a fragment of a longer verse, most commonly associated with Qur'an 49:12 ("يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا اجْتَنِبُوا كَثِيرًا مِّنَ الظَّنِّ... وَلَا تَجَسَّسُوا وَلَا يَغْتَب بَّعْضُكُم بَعْضًا ۚ أَيُحِبُّ أَحَدُكُمْ أَن يَأْكُلَ لَحْمَ أَخِيهِ مَيْتًا فَكَرِهْتُمُوهُ ۚ وَاتَّقُوا اللَّـهَ ۚ إِنَّ اللَّـهَ تَوَّابٌ رَّحِيمٌ") and 49:2 (...فَإِذَا دُخِلْتُم بُيُوتًا فَسَلِّمُوا عَلَىٰ أَنفُسِكُمْ تَحِيَّةً مِّنْ عِندِ اللَّـهِ مُبَارَكَةً طَيِّبَةً ۚ كَذَٰلِكَ يُبَيِّنُ اللَّـهُ لَكُمُ الْآيَاتِ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَعْقِلُونَ), where the fragment "وَاتَّقُوا اللَّـهَ وَلَا تَخْزُونِ" appears to be a truncated version of an address to the believers. The phrase enjoins fear of God (taqwa) and prohibits "takhzūn," which most likely refers to disgracing, humiliating, or failing to uphold the trust/community bond (the root kh-z-y often means disgrace, shame, or disappointment). In context, particularly in Surah al-Hujurat, this is often interpreted as a command not to betray, embarrass, or bring shame upon fellow believers, especially in matters of trust, community standing, or when receiving delegations/guests, while simultaneously maintaining consciousness of God. The interpretation is that true taqwa entails protecting others from dishonor and preserving the dignity and trust within the believing community, for God is ever-watching and will hold each person accountable for how they treat others.
