The verse implicitly calls the reader to recognize divine sovereignty and to find signs ('ayat') in the natural world as evidence of purposeful creation.

translation: We did not grant any human being before you immortality; if you die, will they live forever?
interpretation: This verse reminds believers that every Prophet and messenger who came before Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) eventually passed away, and so he too must die. It challenges the false hope that some companions or later generations might cherish—that the Prophet would remain among them forever or that his message could be preserved through his physical presence alone. The verse underscores the transience of human life and warns against the delusion that death can be escaped. Instead, it points to the necessity of building a faith that does not depend on any individual's lifespan, but on the Qur'an and the guidance of God, which remain as the lasting legacy for all generations.

translation: Every soul will taste death, and We test you with evil and good as a trial, and to Us you will be returned.
interpretation: This verse presents three intertwined truths about the human condition. First, mortality is universal and inevitable—no being is exempt from death, which levels all distinctions of wealth, power, and status among people. Second, life's experiences, both the painful and the pleasant, serve as divine tests rather than rewards or punishments in themselves; adversity does not necessarily indicate God's displeasure, nor does prosperity necessarily indicate His favor. Third, ultimate accountability lies not in this temporary world but in the return to God, where the true significance of how one navigated these tests will be revealed. The verse calls believers to maintain perspective and moral equilibrium through all circumstances, recognizing that life's dualities are part of a purposeful divine trial with an eternal conclusion.

translation: And when the disbelievers see you, they take you not except in ridicule, [saying], "Is this the one who speaks [disparagingly] about your gods?" And they are, at the mention of the Most Merciful, disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse portrays the defiant hostility of the disbelievers toward the Prophet Muhammad, showing that their mockery of him stems from a deeper rejection of the very concept of divine mercy. Their ridicule is not merely a personal attack but a reaction to his call against idolatry, while their rejection of the mention of Allah, the Most Merciful, reveals that the root of their arrogance lies in their refusal to acknowledge divine compassion and grace. The verse thus exposes how mockery of truth often serves as a cover for an underlying unwillingness to submit to a higher power that demands humility.

translation: He created man from [a state of] haste. I will soon show you My signs, so do not hasten Me.
interpretation: This verse draws attention to a fundamental aspect of human nature: an inherent impatience and urgency in the way people are constituted. The phrase 'created man from haste' (خَلَقَ الْإِنسَانَ مِنْ عَجَلٍ) suggests that the very fabric of human existence is woven with a propensity for rushing—whether in desire, action, or judgment. Humans frequently want immediate results, demand swift answers to their questions, or grow restless in the face of divine wisdom that unfolds according to a higher timetable. This impatience reflects a limited perspective, one that cannot fully comprehend the purposes behind events or the wisdom in delays. God, in His omniscience, reassures that His signs will manifest in due course, and that this unfolding is part of a larger, purposeful design. The admonition 'do not hasten Me' (فَلَا تَسْتَعْجِلُونِ) is not merely a warning but an invitation to trust in divine timing, to cultivate patience (صبر), and to recognize that what may seem like delay is often part of a deeper mercy or a test of faith. The verse also subtly critiques the human tendency to challenge or question divine decree, urging instead a posture of humility and acceptance. In essence, it teaches that human impatience is a defining trait, but spiritual maturity lies in surrendering to the pace of divine wisdom rather than demanding immediate gratification or explanation. This balance between human nature and divine omniscience is central to the verse's message, calling believers to reflect on their own tendencies and to trust that God's plan unfolds precisely as it should.

translation: And they say, 'When will this promise come true, if you are truthful?'
interpretation: This verse refers to the demand made by disbelievers, who, in mockery and denial, challenge the truth of the promised Day of Judgment and divine accountability. By asking "when" it will occur, they intend to express their rejection of the reality of that day and to provoke doubt in the believers. The phrase "if you are truthful" reflects their false certainty that it will never happen, while the verse implicitly affirms that the promise is indeed true and will come to pass at the appointed time known only to God. It thus serves as a reminder that human impatience or disbelief does not alter the certainty of divine decree, and that the timing of divine matters is beyond human knowledge.

translation: If those who disbelieved only knew, when they will not be able to ward off the Fire from their faces or from their backs, and they will not be helped.
interpretation: This verse highlights the severe consequences faced by disbelievers in the afterlife, emphasizing their inability to protect themselves from the torment of Hellfire, which will engulf them from all directions—front and back—without any hope of rescue or divine aid.

translation: But it will come upon them suddenly and bewilder them, and they will not be able to repel it, nor will they be granted any respite.
interpretation: This verse conveys the sudden and inescapable nature of divine punishment or the Hour of Judgment. The word 'بغتة' (suddenly) emphasizes that the event will arrive without warning, catching people off guard. 'فتبهتهم' (and bewilder them) suggests that it will leave them utterly confused and stunned, unable to respond or formulate any defense. The phrase 'فلا يستطيعون ردها' (they will not be able to repel it) underscores their helplessness and lack of power to avert or resist the divine decree. Finally, 'ولا هم ينظرون' (nor will they be granted any respite) indicates that no delay or reprieve will be given; they must face the consequence immediately. The overall meaning is a stark warning about the inevitability and overwhelming nature of divine justice, which cannot be negotiated, delayed, or escaped.

translation: And certainly [O Muhammad] messengers were mocked before you, but those who mocked them were encompassed by what they used to ridicule.
interpretation: This verse offers profound comfort and warning simultaneously. For the Prophet ﷺ and the believers facing mockery and ridicule in Makkah, it affirms a divine principle: those who deride Allah's messengers eventually face the very consequences they dismissed as impossible. The word 'حَاقَ' (encircled/completely surrounded) indicates total envelopment, suggesting that the punishment came from where they least expected, consuming them entirely. More deeply, this reveals a spiritual law: mockery of truth is not merely an intellectual disagreement but an active opposition that builds a prison around the mocker's own heart. They become 'encompassed' by their ridicule because their arrogance blinds them to the signs until reality itself overtakes them. The verse thus serves as both consolation for the persecuted—history validates their patience—and a grave caution: rejecting prophetic guidance through mockery is self-defeating, for one inevitably becomes trapped by the very delusions one cultivates.

translation: Say, 'Who will protect you by night and by day from the Most Merciful?' But they are, from the remembrance of their Lord, turning away.
interpretation: The verse serves as a profound rhetorical challenge, compelling the listener to recognize human vulnerability and dependence on divine protection during both the unconscious hours of night and the active hours of day. By specifically referencing 'the Most Merciful' (الرحمن), it emphasizes that the source of safety is the very God whom these people reject, highlighting a profound irony: those who disregard God's remembrance still rely on His continuous mercy for their survival. The phrase 'turning away' (معرضون) indicates a deliberate, active avoidance of spiritual truth rather than mere ignorance, suggesting that disbelief is often a chosen defiance against the signs of a protecting and merciful Creator.

translation: Or do they have gods who defend them, other than Us? They are unable to help themselves, nor can they be escorted safely by Us.
interpretation: This verse challenges the belief in false deities by pointing out the absurdity of relying on powerless gods that cannot even protect themselves, much less their worshippers. It underscores the principle of monotheism, affirming that only Allah has the power to safeguard and provide refuge. The verse also serves as a warning that those who turn away from Allah will find no true protector or companion, leaving them vulnerable and alone. By highlighting the helplessness of these supposed protectors, it calls believers to reflect on the futility of false worship and to place their trust solely in Allah, who is self-sufficient and ever-watchful over His creation.

translation: Nay, but We gave these [people] and their fathers enjoyment until life was prolonged to them. Do they not see that We are approaching the land, reducing it from its borders? So is it they who will overcome?
interpretation: This verse addresses those who deny the reality of divine power and accountability by arguing that if God existed and were just, He would not grant the disbelievers prolonged worldly enjoyment and respite. God responds by stating that this extended worldly life is itself a test, a temporary allowance that should not be mistaken for divine approval or weakness. The 'reduction of the land from its borders' refers to the gradual advancement of the Islamic state and the decline of opposing civilizations, illustrating that the tide of truth is steadily progressing. Ultimately, the verse asserts that the ultimate victory belongs to God and His truthful servants; the disbelievers are deceived by immediate worldly gains and fail to perceive the larger, unfolding reality of divine sovereignty and the inevitable triumph of faith over falsehood.

translation: ,Say, 'I only warn you through revelation.' But the deaf do not hear the call when they are warned.
interpretation: The verse clarifies that the Prophet's role is strictly that of a warner who conveys divine revelation, not someone who compels belief; the inability of those who reject faith to respond is likened to the deaf being unable to hear a call, highlighting that spiritual deafness, not the Prophet's message, is the barrier to guidance.

translation: And if a breath of punishment from your Lord touches them, they will surely say, 'O woe to us! Indeed, we have been wrongdoers.'
interpretation: This verse reveals a profound truth about the nature of ingratitude and delayed remorse. Even when faced with the slightest taste of divine consequence, those who were previously heedless suddenly acknowledge their wrongdoing—but only when accountability becomes imminent. Their confession is not born of genuine repentance or a transformed heart, but of self-pity and regret over consequences. This pattern exposes how many people remain unmoved by blessings and signs throughout their lives, only awakening to moral reality when discomfort forces their hand. The phrase 'نفحة' (a breath, a mere whiff) emphasizes that even the smallest touch of accountability is enough to shatter their complacency. It serves as a mirror for every soul: transformation that comes only at the threshold of judgment is too late and insincere, whereas true righteousness lies in heeding guidance before consequences arrive.

translation: We will set up the scales of justice on the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged in the least. And if there be the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it forth. Sufficient are We as accountants.
interpretation: This verse affirms the absolute precision and perfect justice of God on the Day of Judgment. The imagery of the scale represents a divine standard of measurement that leaves no room for injustice, no matter how small the deed—whether a good or evil action as insignificant in human eyes as a mustard seed, the smallest of seeds. The verse reassures the believer that nothing escapes God's notice: every action, thought, and intention is recorded and will be weighed with exact fairness. The phrase 'Sufficient are We as accountants' underscores that God's accounting is flawless, complete, and beyond challenge, requiring no human auditor or standard. It serves as both a warning against trivializing sin and an encouragement for believers who may feel their small righteous deeds are overlooked, assuring them that divine justice operates on a scale infinitely more sensitive and accurate than any human measure. Ultimately, the verse calls humans to live with awareness that every atom of their deeds carries eternal weight in the sight of the All-Knowing, the All-Just.

translation: And We had certainly given Moses and Aaron the criterion and a light and a reminder for the righteous.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Anbiya (21:48), refers to the Torah (al-Furqan) granted to Moses and Aaron as a divine gift, which served as a means of distinguishing truth from falsehood. It is also described as 'light' (diya')—a guidance that illuminates the path of the believers—and as 'reminder' (dhikr) specifically for the God-conscious (al-muttaqin). The verse implicitly highlights that while divine guidance is universally offered, only those with taqwa (consciousness of God) truly benefit from it, deriving wisdom, moral direction, and spiritual enlightenment. The pairing of Moses and Aaron reflects their joint prophetic mission, with Aaron serving as a supportive figure in conveying God's message to the Israelites.

translation: Those who fear their Lord unseen, and they are apprehensive of the Hour.
interpretation: This verse describes a specific category of sincere believers whose piety is rooted in genuine inner awareness rather than outward display. The phrase "fear their Lord unseen" indicates that their reverence and consciousness of God (taqwa) is not contingent upon visibly witnessing divine signs or being observed by others in acts of worship; rather, their devotion persists in the hidden, private dimensions of life where human observation cannot reach. This points to an internalized faith that governs one's private thoughts, intentions, and secret deeds. The second clause, "and they are apprehensive of the Hour," complements this by showing that such believers maintain a constant awareness of eschatological accountability. Their consciousness of the final judgment shapes their present conduct, producing a state of reverent concern (taqwa). Together, these qualities describe believers whose righteousness is consistent and integrated—not performative for an audience but anchored in the reality of divine omniscience and the certainty of ultimate reckoning. This represents the highest form of moral and spiritual integrity in Islamic thought.

translation: And this is a blessed Reminder (the Qur'an) which We have sent down. Will you then (people) deny it?
interpretation: This verse emphasizes both the divine origin and the inherent value of the Qur'an, describing it as a 'blessed reminder' (dhikr mubarak), indicating that it is a source of guidance, wisdom, and spiritual benefit for humanity. The word 'mubarak' (blessed) suggests that engaging with it brings about positive outcomes in both this world and the hereafter. By declaring that We (Allah) have sent it down, it affirms that the Qur'an is not a human composition but a revelation from the Divine, possessing authority and authenticity. The rhetorical question 'Will you then deny it?' serves as a challenge to those who refuse to accept its truth, highlighting the irrationality and ingratitude of rejecting such a profound and beneficial guidance. It also carries a tone of warning, implying that denial or turning away from this message is a serious matter with consequences.

translation: }And We had certainly given Abraham his sound judgement before, and We were of him well-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse refers to a period before the events mentioned in the surrounding context, indicating that Abraham's prophetic mission and his role as a guiding figure were not sudden developments but had been prepared by God from his youth. The phrase 'sound judgement' refers to inner moral and intellectual insight, which enabled Abraham to distinguish truth from falsehood even before he publicly proclaimed his message. The divine affirmation that God 'was of him well-Knowing' underscores that Abraham's calling was part of a pre-eternal divine plan, and that his spiritual maturity was recognized and affirmed by God Himself, even before Abraham confronted his people or faced the trials recorded in his story.

translation: [Remember] when he said to his father and his people, 'What are these statues to which you are devoted?'
interpretation: This verse records Abraham's direct confrontation with the idolatry of his community. By questioning rather than immediately condemning, Abraham invites reflection on the practice of devotion to inanimate objects, challenging the assumption that such devotion holds meaning or worth. It marks the beginning of his prophetic call to question inherited traditions and to direct worship toward the One who truly deserves it. The use of 'these statues' emphasizes the tangible, manufactured nature of the idols, subtly exposing the absurdity of assigning divine status to human creations. This rhetorical approach models a method of dawah rooted in thoughtful inquiry rather than mere denunciation.

translation: They said, 'We found our fathers worshipping them.'
interpretation: This verse reflects a common human tendency to justify one's beliefs and practices by appealing to tradition and the example of ancestors, even when those practices lack genuine rational or spiritual basis. The speakers are using the argument of inherited custom as a defense for their idolatry or devotion to false deities, suggesting that they perpetuate these practices not necessarily out of personal conviction or understanding, but because it is what they were taught and what they observed in their forebears. This highlights the Qur'anic critique of taqlid (blind following) and emphasizes the importance of sincere reflection, critical thinking, and direct engagement with the truth, rather than simply conforming to inherited beliefs without examination. It serves as a caution against allowing ancestral customs to override reasoned faith and authentic spiritual commitment.

translation: He (Ibrahim) said, 'You have certainly been, you and your fathers, in manifest error.'
interpretation: This statement, attributed to Ibrahim (Abraham), is a declaration of the error and misguidance of idol worship and the worship of false deities, a practice common among his people and predecessors. It is a call to recognize the deviation from the truth and to turn away from baseless beliefs and traditions that have no foundation in divine guidance. The phrase highlights the clarity of the error ('ضلال مبين' - manifest misguidance), meaning the deviation is not subtle or hidden but evident, suggesting that those who cling to such practices do so out of stubbornness or blind adherence rather than ignorance alone. It is an invitation to reflect on the nature of worship and the source of true guidance.

translation: , they said, "Have you come to us with truth, or are you among those who jest?"

interpretation: The verse reflects a moment of defiant faith and confession. The speaker (Prophet Ibrahim, Abraham, in dialogue with his people regarding the idols) refuses to accept their claim or curse, instead affirming that their Lord—whom they may be calling upon—is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Creator who brought them into being. By placing himself among the witnesses (

translation: And by Allah, I will surely plan against your idols after you have turned away, departing.
interpretation: This statement, spoken by Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) in Surah Al-Anbiya (21:57), represents a firm resolve to challenge the falsehood of idol worship, not out of spite, but as a demonstration of the logical and spiritual bankruptcy of polytheism. The phrase emphasizes his determination to reveal the powerlessness of the idols, employing a strategic plan contingent upon the people's departure. It highlights the prophetic methodology of exposing falsehood through decisive action when its proponents are absent, relying on divine will rather than brute force. Importantly, this declaration is bound by an oath to Allah, indicating that the intended action is sanctioned by the Divine, serving a higher purpose of clarifying the truth and dismantling the influence of false deities. This is interpreted within the broader narrative as a catalyst for the confrontation that follows, which ultimately proves the idols' inability to cause harm or grant benefit, thereby affirming the Oneness of God. It also subtly critiques the superstitious attachment to inanimate objects and underscores the importance of rational inquiry and unwavering commitment to monotheistic truth, even when it invites opposition from the community. The statement thus functions as a pivotal moment in the prophetic narrative, shifting from verbal admonition to tangible demonstration of the futility of shirk (associating partners with God). It reflects the courage and strategic foresight required to confront deeply entrenched societal norms, all while maintaining absolute reliance on divine support and guidance. The verse also foreshadows the events leading to Ibrahim being thrown into the fire, which becomes another{

translation: And he reduced them to fragments, except a large one among them, that they might return to it [to seek guidance].
interpretation: This verse describes Prophet Abraham's decisive action against the idols his people worshipped: he smashed them all into pieces, sparing only the largest idol. By leaving the biggest idol intact, Abraham (peace be upon him) set up a rhetorical trap—when his people returned and saw the devastation, they would naturally turn to the largest remaining idol for answers about what happened, exposing the helplessness and absurdity of worshipping powerless objects they themselves had carved.

translation: They said, 'Who has done this to our gods? Indeed, he is of the wrongdoers.'
interpretation: This statement reflects the reaction of the disbelievers to the desecration of their idols (referring to Abraham smashing the idols, as mentioned in earlier verses, particularly in Surah Al-Anbiya 21:51-67). Their reaction reveals a deep irony: they quickly condemn Abraham as an oppressor for breaking their inanimate, powerless idols, yet they themselves oppress their own souls and intellects by worshipping false deities. The verse highlights the misplaced priorities and moral blindness of those who defend fabricated objects of worship rather than acknowledging the oneness of God. It also subtly mocks the idolaters' irrational attachment to objects they themselves fashioned, exposing the absurdity of polytheism.

translation: They said, 'We have heard a young man mentioning them, who is called Abraham.'
interpretation: The people of the fire, who had worshipped idols, claimed that they had been led astray by Abraham's denunciations of idolatry. This verse highlights Abraham's role as a monotheistic reformer and the reaction of his community to his message.

translation: They said, 'Then bring him forth before the eyes of the people that they may testify.'
interpretation: This verse describes a demand made by a group who were challenged to produce the object of their dispute or claim as a public spectacle, so that the people could witness and attest to its authenticity or nature. The instruction to bring forth something 'upon the eyes of the people' (على أعين الناس) signifies an appeal to public visibility and communal witness, suggesting that the matter cannot remain hidden or ambiguous, but must be confronted openly. The phrase 'لعلهم يشهدون' (that they may testify) implies an intention to establish undeniable proof or to mobilize collective testimony against the accused or claimant. This reflects a psychological mechanism where a dominant group uses public exposure as a tool to consolidate its narrative, pressuring the individual or minority party through collective observation rather than through reasoned dialogue. The verse thus critiques the use of public spectacle as a form of intimidation, turning the community into an instrument of judgment rather than allowing for fair inquiry.

translation: They said, 'Have you done this to our gods, O Abraham?'
interpretation: The phrase بآلهتنا ('to our gods') reflects the accusative case (منصوب) because it is the object of فعلت ('you did'), confirming that the addressees are attributing the act of breaking the idols to Abraham, interrogatively. The demonstrative pronoun هذا ('this') functions as the predicate of the subject بآلهتنا in the accusative position. The vocative يا إبراهيم ('O Abraham') serves to address Abraham directly, highlighting that the question is directed to him personally, which the verse answers in the following passage.

translation: Rather, it was their eldest [brother] who did it. So ask them if they can speak [for themselves].
interpretation: The meaning is that the younger brothers of Joseph—accused of having stained or torn his shirt—were not the true culprits; rather, the eldest among them was responsible for the act of misappropriation or concealment. By shifting blame to the elder brother, they are exposing internal discord and perhaps seeking to deflect guilt through the natural deference or scapegoating of an older sibling. The phrase “if they can speak” implies a challenge to their credibility and honesty, suggesting that their collective silence or stammering response reveals their complicity or fabrication. In context, this verse reflects the Qur'anic narrative of Joseph (Surah Yusuf), where the brothers return to their father Jacob, bringing a fabricated story. The verse thus serves both as a narrative device—revealing the brothers' moral failure—and as a moral lesson: that falsehood and manipulation of truth ultimately lead to self-contradiction and disgrace.

translation: Then they returned to themselves and said, 'Indeed, it is you who are the wrongdoers.'
interpretation: This verse describes a moment of moral awakening, where individuals who were engaged in wrongdoing or denial pause and reflect honestly upon their own conduct, acknowledging their own injustice rather than blaming external circumstances. It emphasizes the capacity for self-reflection and personal accountability within the human conscience, suggesting that ultimate truth is recognized not through external validation but through sincere inward recognition of one’s own misdeeds.

translation: Then they turned back on their heels, [saying], "You know indeed that these [idols] do not speak."
interpretation: In Surah Ya-Sin (36:65), this verse describes the moment when the disbelievers, after being confronted with the truth, retreat and arrogantly challenge the Prophet ﷺ, as if to say: "We know full well that these statues cannot speak—so why do you insist that they will speak on the Day of Judgment?" It reflects their obstinate denial and mockery, even as the Quran warns that on that Day, they will indeed bear witness against their worshippers.

translation: He said, 'Then do you worship besides Allah that which does not benefit you at all nor harms you?'
interpretation: This verse is part of Prophet Ibrahim's (Abraham's) confrontation with his people, who had turned to idol worship. Through this rhetorical question, Ibrahim emphasizes the absurdity of directing worship toward powerless objects—idols that possess no ability to bring benefit or cause harm. The verse highlights that genuine worship should be reserved for the One who truly has power over benefit and harm, namely Allah. It challenges blind attachment to false deities and calls for reflection on whether one's devotion is directed toward something capable of responding in any meaningful way, exposing the irrationality of worshiping that which is entirely inert. This rhetorical device serves to awaken critical thinking and reaffirm the logical foundations of pure monotheism (tawhid).

translation: Uff (enough) to you and to what you worship besides Allah! Do you not reason?
interpretation: The verse is a sharp rhetorical rebuke directed at those who take false deities as objects of worship. The repeated "uфф" expresses weariness, disgust, and distancing from both the people and the idols they worship, indicating that both the worshippers and their objects of devotion are blameworthy. The closing question, "Do you not reason?," is an invitation to reflection, challenging the addressees to use their intellect and recognize the absurdity of directing devotion to beings that possess no power to benefit or harm them. The verse implicitly affirms that sound reason, if employed honestly, leads to the rejection of false worship and the recognition of the oneness of God.

translation: They said, 'Burn him and support your gods - if you are going to act.'
interpretation: This verse captures the violent reaction of the polytheists to Abraham's (Ibrahim's) monotheistic message, revealing how entrenched idolatry resorts to coercion and persecution when challenged by truth. The conditional phrase 'if you are going to act' exposes the conditional nature of their devotion to their false gods - their worship is not rooted in sincere conviction but in selective self-interest that demands decisive retaliation against those who threaten it. By threatening to burn Abraham, they attempt to weaponize the very elements of creation against a prophet who taught that the same sun, moon, and fire are mere creations under the dominion of the One God. This verse thus illustrates a recurring pattern throughout the Qur'an: when rational discourse and the rejection of false authority threaten entrenched power structures, the response is often persecution rather than reflection. The command to 'support your gods' also exposes the transactional nature of their faith - these idols are not truly believed in but are upheld as social and political symbols whose defense requires coordinated action rather than genuine spiritual conviction.

translation: We said, 'O fire, be cool and safe upon Ibrahim (Abraham).'
interpretation: This verse describes a miraculous divine intervention in which God commanded the fire that Abraham was thrown into by his people to become cool and peaceful for him, rather than burning him. This event illustrates God's power over the natural order and serves as a profound demonstration of faith rewarded, showing that sincere trust in God can lead to extraordinary protection from harm. It is understood as a lesson that devotion and surrender to the divine will can bring safety in situations that appear to lead to certain destruction, and that God's command extends over all elements of creation.

translation: And they intended a plot against him, but We made them the greatest losers.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine principle that those who conspire against God's chosen servants ultimately bring destruction upon themselves, as divine will turns their schemes into the very means of their own downfall and loss.

translation: And We saved him and Lot to the land which We had blessed for the worlds.
interpretation: This verse refers to God’s rescue of Abraham and Lot from the oppressive environment of their people, guiding them to a land designated with divine blessing and sustenance for all creation. It underscores the concept that true salvation is not merely physical deliverance but also relocation to a place where spiritual growth, moral integrity, and divine favor can flourish. The 'blessed land' symbolizes an environment where God's signs are evident and where humanity can find guidance, prosperity, and a means to fulfill its higher purpose. This movement from a place of corruption to one of divine blessing illustrates that God provides His chosen servants with opportunities to thrive in surroundings conducive to righteousness, serving as a refuge and a source of goodness for all of mankind.

translation: And We granted him [Abraham] Isaac and Jacob as an additional gift, and We made each of them righteous.
interpretation: This verse highlights that the bestowal of Isaac and Jacob upon Abraham was not merely a fulfillment of his prayer for an heir, but a divine grace and an added bounty beyond what he asked for. The mention of 'nafilah' (additional gift) signifies that while Ishmael was the immediate answer to his supplication, Isaac and Jacob were a further, unasked-for blessing, demonstrating God's generosity and the unfolding of His covenant across generations. By describing both Isaac and Jacob as righteous, the verse underscores that righteousness is a divinely granted status and a legacy that can be passed down through a prophetic lineage, affirming God's active role in cultivating a community of faithful individuals to carry forward His message.

translation: And We made them leaders guiding by Our command, and We inspired to them the doing of good deeds, the establishment of prayer, and the giving of zakah; and they were worshippers of Us.
interpretation: This verse portrays a divinely appointed group of individuals elevated to the status of guiding exemplars (a'immah) whose leadership is not self-asserted but rooted in God's command ('amrina). The semantic pairing of 'leadership' (imamah) with 'guiding' (yahdun) implies a directional, normative function—these figures orient others toward a theocentric purpose. The mention of 'inspiration' (wahy) directed toward moral and ritual practices (ihya' al-khayrat, iqamat al-salat, ita' al-zakah) signifies that righteous conduct is not merely legislated externally but internalized through revelation, blending ethical volition with prescribed worship. The concluding phrase 'they were worshippers of Us' ('abiduna lana) employs the emphatic suffix -na to underscore exclusive devotion, suggesting that authentic guidance culminates in submission ('ibadah) as a comprehensive state of being rather than isolated acts. The verse thus constructs a paradigm of authority that is revelatory, ethical, and devotional in character.

translation: And Lot - We gave him judgment and knowledge, and We saved him from the city that was committing depravities. Indeed, they were a people of evil, defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: This verse highlights Prophet Lot's role as a recipient of divine wisdom and prophethood, distinct from familial lineage. It emphasizes that prophethood is a gift from Allah, not an inherited trait. The verse also illustrates that following divine guidance leads to salvation from environments characterized by moral corruption, even when surrounded by overwhelming evil. Lot's rescue serves as evidence that Allah protects those who remain steadfast in faith, while those who persist in wrongdoing will ultimately face consequences. The phrase "قَوْمَ سَوْءٍ فَاسِقِينَ" (a people of evil, defiantly disobedient) describes a society that had not only strayed from morality but had actively rebelled against divine guidance, becoming a cautionary example of the consequences of persistent wrongdoing.

translation: And We admitted him into Our mercy; indeed, he was among the righteous.
interpretation: This verse refers to God's compassionate acceptance of a righteous servant into His grace and care, affirming that the individual's moral integrity and devotion served as the qualification for divine mercy, thereby illustrating the inseparable connection between human righteousness and the bestowal of God's special favor in both this life and the Hereafter.

translation: And [remember] Noah, when he called [to Us] before [this]. So We responded to him and saved him and his family from the great distress.
interpretation: This verse presents Noah (Nuh) as a paradigm of prophetic steadfastness and divine responsiveness. It highlights a fundamental principle of the Quranic worldview: the relationship between sincere supplication (du'a) and divine mercy. Noah's call ('nada') is not merely an act of desperation but a sustained, earnest appeal to God amidst prolonged opposition from his people. The verse affirms that God's response (istijaba) is not delayed or absent but is assured for those who persevere in turning to Him. The salvation of Noah and his family from the 'great distress' (al-karb al-'azim) symbolizes deliverance from both external persecution and the existential burden of bearing a message rejected by one's community. Implicitly, the verse serves as an address to the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community, who faced similar rejection and hardship in Makkah. It functions as both a historical reminder and a source of consolation: just as Noah was ultimately vindicated through divine intervention, so too will the believers who remain patient and reliant on God. The verse thus intertwines themes of prophetic perseverance, the certainty of divine justice, and the redemptive promise that sincere faith, even when met with fierce opposition, will ultimately be preserved.

translation: And We supported him against the people who had denied Our signs. Indeed, they were a wicked people, so We drowned them all.
interpretation: This verse describes divine intervention to save a righteous figure (commonly understood to be Moses) from a corrupt and oppressive society that rejected divine guidance. The key idea is that when a community persistently denies truth and perpetuates wrongdoing, divine support is granted to the righteous, and collective accountability leads to the destruction of the evildoers as a whole.

translation: And [remember] David and Solomon, when they judged concerning the field when the sheep of a people wandered [at night] into it, and We were witness to their judgment.
interpretation: This verse highlights the Prophet David and his son Solomon as examples of righteous judgment, noting that even in matters involving property damage by animals, their rulings were just and divinely guided, serving as a lesson for all who arbitrate disputes.

translation: And We gave [understanding of the case to] Solomon, and to each [of the two] We gave judgment and knowledge. And We subjected the mountains along with David to glorify [Us], and the birds as well. And We were doers.
interpretation: This verse highlights God's favor upon David and Solomon, illustrating the divine wisdom and prophetic knowledge granted to them as well as the miraculous ability to command the natural world. By stating that Solomon was given the correct understanding in the matter of the dispute mentioned previously (regarding the sheep that damaged the field), the verse shows that prophetic insight surpasses ordinary human judgment, even when that judgment may seem logically sound. The mention of David's ability to lead the mountains and birds in glorifying God is a sign of his exalted spiritual station, indicating that true prophethood involves harmony between the human soul and all creation. Ultimately, the verse teaches that wisdom, knowledge, and miraculous power are gifts from God, and that prophets serve as exemplars of how these gifts are to be used in devotion to Him.

translation: And We taught him [David] the art of making garments (coats of mail) for you, that they may protect you from each other's violence. Will you then be grateful?
interpretation: This verse highlights a divine gift bestowed upon Prophet David: the knowledge and skill to craft armor (specifically coats of mail) for the Children of Israel. This innovation served a practical purpose—protection during warfare and defense against harm. The verse also calls believers to reflect on divine favors and respond with gratitude, acknowledging that true security and strength ultimately come from God, even when manifested through human ingenuity and craftsmanship.

translation: And to Solomon (We subjected) the wind, a stormy blast blowing at his command toward the land which We had blessed. And We are, of all things, Knower.
interpretation: This verse signifies that Allah granted Solomon a unique miracle—control over the wind, which carried him and his forces swiftly to distant lands. The mention of "the land which We had blessed" likely refers to the land of Palestine/Sham, highlighting its spiritual and historical significance as a site of many prophets and divine revelations. The wind was not merely a natural phenomenon but a divinely controlled force that responded to Solomon's command, demonstrating his divinely-ordained authority over parts of creation. The closing statement "And We are, of all things, Knower" affirms that Allah's knowledge encompasses all creation, including how these extraordinary powers were granted, their purpose, and their limits. This serves to remind believers that such miracles are not accidental or inherent to Solomon, but are deliberate grants from an Omniscient God who chooses to bestow such gifts upon His prophets for specific purposes, often to establish justice, propagate faith, or demonstrate divine power to humanity.

translation: And among the devils were those who dived for him [into the sea] and did [other] work besides that. And We were [constant] guardians over them.
interpretation: This verse, situated within the broader narrative of Solomon's (Sulaiman) remarkable dominion and authority, illuminates the multifaceted nature of the power granted to him by God. The mention of devils diving into the sea suggests they were tasked with retrieving precious materials, pearls, or other submerged treasures, thereby serving Solomon's grand projects and kingdom. The phrase 'and did other work besides that' indicates that their service was not limited to this single task; they were engaged in various labors, likely including construction, craftsmanship, and other demanding endeavors associated with Solomon's extensive building programs, such as the Temple in Jerusalem. Crucially, the concluding statement, 'And We were constant guardians over them,' signifies divine oversight and control. This implies that despite the seemingly autonomous actions of these beings, they operated strictly within the boundaries set by God. They did not act out of their own volition to harm or transgress, but were bound to fulfill the purpose for which they were subjected to Solomon. This serves as a reminder that all authority and power, even that exercised by extraordinary figures like Solomon, is ultimately subordinate to and regulated by the divine will, ensuring that such power serves a purposeful and constrained role within the cosmic order.

translation: And [mention] Job, when he called to his Lord, 'Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of those who show mercy.'
interpretation: This verse from Surah Al-Anbiya (21:83) presents the Prophet Job (Ayyub) as a model of patient reliance on God amidst profound suffering. His supplication is striking for its brevity and sincerity, containing two essential elements: an honest acknowledgment of his pain ('adversity has touched me') and an unwavering affirmation of divine mercy ('You are the Most Merciful of those who show mercy'). Rather than complaining against God or demanding immediate relief, Job's words demonstrate that true faith does not deny hardship but confronts it with transparency while maintaining trust in God's compassionate nature. The phrase 'the Most Merciful of those who show mercy' (arham al-rahimin) reflects a deeply personal recognition of God's mercy as incomparable, even in the midst of trials. This teaches that the proper human response to affliction is not despair or rebellion, but humble appeal coupled with confidence in divine benevolence. Job's subsequent restoration in the following verses serves as divine validation of this balanced spiritual posture, suggesting that patience combined with hopeful supplication is both the path through suffering and the foundation for its ultimate alleviation.

translation: So We responded to him, removed his affliction, and restored his family to him—and more besides—as a mercy from Us and a reminder for those who worship [Us].
interpretation: The verse illustrates a profound spiritual principle: that sincere supplication, accompanied by patient perseverance through trials, becomes the very means through which divine mercy arrives. The fact that affliction was "removed" (kushifnā) rather than the believer being removed from it suggests that trials serve a pedagogical purpose, and their alleviation is granted once their lesson is absorbed. The restoration of the Prophet Ayyub's (Job's) family "and more besides" (wa mithlahum ma'ahum) indicates that what is returned after patience surpasses what was originally lost—loss becomes a platform for greater bounty. The phrase "remembrance for those who worship" (dhikrā lil-ʿābidīn) frames the entire episode not merely as historical narrative but as an ongoing instruction: those who worship Allah earnestly find in this story a timeless pattern—that relief follows persistence, that hardship is temporary, and that divine response is assured for those who turn wholly to their Lord.

translation: And Ishmael, and Idris, and Dhul-Kifl — all of them were among the patient.
interpretation: The verse places Ishmael (Isma'il), Idris, and Dhul-Kifl within a sequence of prophets whom God highlights for their steadfastness and perseverance. By grouping them together under the descriptor 'the patient' (as-sabirin), the Qur'an signals that their defining characteristic was sabr — patience in the face of trials, constancy in obedience to God, and endurance in fulfilling prophetic duties. The mention of Ishmael, son of Abraham, affirms his prophetic status in Islamic theology and links him to the legacy of his father's household. Idris, often associated with Enoch in the Judeo-Christian tradition, is presented here as a model of enduring devotion. Dhul-Kifl, whose precise identity remains debated among scholars (with various identifications proposed), is nonetheless elevated to the rank of patient worshipper. Collectively, the verse serves a didactic function: by naming these particular figures, it encourages the Muslim community to emulate their example of patient perseverance in faith, especially when called upon to endure hardship, suffering, or opposition for the sake of God. The construction 'kullun min as-sabirin' — 'all of them were among the patient' — is an emphatic affirmation, indicating that patient endurance was not incidental but essential to their prophetic vocation. Thus the verse both honors these prophets and establishes patience as a fundamental virtue for the believing community to cultivate.

translation: And We admitted them into Our mercy. Indeed, they were of the righteous.
interpretation: This verse concludes a narrative account, likely referring to the prophets and righteous servants (such as Noah, Abraham, Moses, and others mentioned in the preceding context of Surah Al-Anbiya or a similar passage) whom Allah saved and encompassed in His grace. The phrase 'And We admitted them into Our mercy' signifies that their ultimate reward was not merely worldly salvation from trials or enemies, but a lasting inclusion in Allah's boundless mercy, which encompasses forgiveness, Paradise, and divine pleasure in the Hereafter. The statement 'Indeed, they were of the righteous' serves as a divine affirmation of their status; their righteousness was not merely a self-proclaimed virtue but a truth acknowledged by Allah Himself. This highlights a profound theological principle: true righteousness is measured not by human standards but by divine recognition, and it is this righteousness that becomes the cause—through Allah's mercy—of ultimate salvation and eternal honor.

translation: And [mention] the Man of the Fish [Jonah], when he went away in anger and thought that We would not decree [anything] upon him. And he called out within the darknesses, 'There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers.'
interpretation: This verse refers to the Prophet Jonah (Yunus), known here as 'Dhū al-Nūn' (the Man of the Fish). The phrase 'idh dhahaba mughāḍiban' indicates that Jonah left his people in a state of anger, likely because they refused to heed his message and he had grown weary of their rejection. The expression 'faẓanna an lan naqdira 'alayhi' carries the meaning that Jonah perceived, in his human limitation, that his situation could not be constrained or managed by divine decree. 'Nādā fī al-ẓulumāt' describes his call from within multiple layers of darkness: the darkness of the night, the depths of the sea, and the belly of the whale. His supplication 'lā ilāha illā ant, subḥānaka, innī kuntu min al-ẓālimīn' is considered a comprehensive invocation of repentance and monotheistic affirmation. The verse teaches that sincere repentance, even at the most extreme moment of distress, can lead to divine mercy, as God responded by delivering Jonah from his affliction. It also illustrates the prophetic virtue of returning to God with humility after a moment of impatience or error.

translation: So We responded to him and saved him from the distress.
interpretation: This part of the verse affirms that Allah’s response to the sincere supplication of His servant is assured, and that salvation from hardship comes solely through divine mercy and power. The subsequent phrase, 'and thus do We save the believers,' generalizes this specific historical event into a universal divine principle: Allah consistently delivers those who have faith from their trials and calamities. It indicates that while the immediate context may refer to the rescue of a prophet (such as Yunus from the belly of the whale), the mercy and salvation of Allah extend to all believers who call upon Him in sincerity and faith.

translation: And [mention] Zechariah, when he called to his Lord, 'My Lord, do not leave me alone [with no heir], while You are the best of inheritors.'
interpretation: This verse highlights the prophetic supplication of Zechariah, who, despite his advanced age and his wife’s barrenness, turned to Allah with a heartfelt plea for a successor. His request was not driven by a desire for personal legacy or worldly continuation, but rather by an earnest concern that the mission of conveying divine truth and guiding people would persist. By acknowledging Allah as 'the best of inheritors,' Zechariah expressed profound trust in God’s sovereignty over all affairs—recognizing that any heir would ultimately be a means through which Allah’s purpose would be fulfilled. The verse carries a powerful lesson for believers: sincere supplication combined with reliance on Allah can overcome seemingly impossible circumstances, and one’s concern should be for the preservation of faith and righteousness rather than merely personal lineage. It also underscores the value of du'a (supplication) as a means of drawing closer to Allah and seeking His help in matters of greatest importance.

translation: ,And We answered his prayer and gave him Yahya (John), and We made his wife fertile/reformed her for him. Indeed, they used to hasten to good deeds and call upon Us with hope and fear, and they were humble before Us.
interpretation: This verse from Surah Al-Anbiya (21:90) highlights several interconnected concepts regarding the nature of true servanthood and the Divine response to sincere devotion. The mention of Zakariya's prayer being answered, the miraculous gift of a son despite his advanced age, and the rectification of his wife's condition demonstrates that God responds to those who combine genuine supplication with righteous action. The verse characterizes the righteous as possessing four qualities: (1) hastening toward good deeds with enthusiasm and priority, (2) praying to God with both hope (raghaban) and fear (rahaban), (3) maintaining humility (khushu') before God, and (4) being proactive in worship. The pairing of hope and fear represents a balanced spiritual psychology: hope motivates one toward God's mercy and rewards, while fear restrains one from disobedience and arrogance. The concept of 'khushu'' refers to a deep inner humility and reverent awe that permeates one's entire being, not merely outward display. The verse also subtly indicates that God's response to prayer is not arbitrary but connected to the quality of the servant's relationship with Him—their consistent striving in good, their balanced emotional orientation toward God, and their genuine humility.

translation: And [mention] the one who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into her of Our spirit, and We made her and her son a sign for the worlds.
interpretation: This verse refers to Maryam (Mary) and her son Isa (Jesus). The phrase 'guarded her chastity' highlights her exceptional devotion to God and her moral purity. The 'breathing of His spirit' signifies the unique miraculous manner in which Isa was conceived without a father, through the command and power of God. The designation of Maryam and Isa as 'a sign for the worlds' indicates their extraordinary status and the miraculous nature of Isa's birth as a divine sign pointing to God's omnipotence and mercy for all of humanity across time. The verse also subtly affirms the Islamic belief in the virgin birth of Isa while maintaining the Islamic understanding of Jesus's nature.

translation: Indeed this, your religion, is one religion, and I am your Lord, so worship Me.
interpretation: The verse asserts the fundamental unity of the divine message and the singularity of God as the object of worship. It addresses the idea that all prophets and the religions they brought share a common origin and purpose: the call to monotheism and submission to the one God. By stating that their community (ummah) is one, it emphasizes that despite differences in laws, rituals, or languages across time and peoples, the core essence of faith remains consistent. The command 'so worship Me' reinforces that the ultimate aim of human existence and the unifying thread of all revelation is the worship and recognition of God alone, without intermediaries or partners.

translation: And [some of] you have taken to dividing your affairs among yourselves, [but] all [of you] will return to Us.
interpretation: This verse addresses the fragmentation and division that can occur among people, often in the context of worldly affairs or beliefs, where individuals break into groups and adopt conflicting paths. Rather than emphasizing mutual unity or shared purpose, the verse warns that every person will ultimately return to Allah for accountability, regardless of how divided they may become in worldly life. It underscores that the fragmentation of communities or beliefs into competing factions is a transient and illusory condition, as the ultimate reality is the meeting with Allah, where the truth of one's choices and affiliations will be laid bare. This serves as a reminder to remain mindful of one's ultimate return to Allah and to avoid becoming engrossed in divisions that may seem significant in the temporal world but hold no weight in the eternal reckoning.

translation: , and whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer – there will be no denial of his effort, and indeed We will be recording (it) for him.
interpretation: This verse affirms a fundamental theological principle within the Qur'an: the inseparability of faith and the acceptance of righteous deeds. The conditional structure 'whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer' establishes that true acceptance of good works is contingent upon faith, suggesting that deeds performed outside of belief lack the same spiritual weight. The phrase 'there will be no denial of his effort' serves as a divine guarantee that God does not waste, overlook, or minimize the sincere efforts of the believer; their striving will be acknowledged and rewarded rather than rejected or forgotten. The final clause, 'We will be recording it for him,' emphasizes divine omniscience and meticulous accountability, indicating that every righteous action is documented by God for ultimate reckoning. This reflects the Qur'anic worldview where human agency operates within a framework of divine knowledge and justice, encouraging believers that their sincere endeavors hold eternal value beyond any worldly dismissal or ingratitude.

translation: And [it is] forbidden for a city which We have destroyed that they (its people) will ever return [to life/worldly life].
interpretation: This verse states that once a community is destroyed by God's decree, they cannot return to the worldly life they once had; rather, their final return is to the Hereafter for accountability. The phrase 'حرام على قرية' (forbidden/impossible upon a town) indicates that the return of the people of that destroyed city to this world is something that will never happen by God's will, highlighting that divine punishment, once executed, is final and irreversible in terms of giving another chance in this worldly life. This emphasizes God's absolute sovereignty over life and death, and the certainty of the Hereafter.

translation: Until [the time] when Gog and Magog are released, and they rush down from every height.
interpretation: This verse describes a cataclysmic event that marks the approaching end of the world, when the barriers holding back the chaotic forces of Gog and Magog (Yajuj and Majuj) are broken, unleashing them to swarm forth in overwhelming numbers across the earth, signaling the fulfillment of divine decree and the onset of ultimate turmoil.

translation: And the true promise [the Day of Judgment] has drawn near, and suddenly the eyes of the disbelievers will stare in terror, and they will say: 'Woe to us! We were indeed heedless of this; rather, we were wrongdoers.'
interpretation: This verse describes the sudden and overwhelming onset of the Day of Judgment, a moment when the reality that was long promised becomes undeniably present. For the disbelievers, this arrival is not a relief but a source of profound shock and regret, as their eyes are transfixed by the terrifying sight. Their cry of 'Woe to us' is an acknowledgment of their former negligence—they were not simply unaware of the truth, but they chose to ignore it out of arrogance and indulgence in worldly life. By calling themselves 'wrongdoers,' they admit that their state was not mere ignorance, but a deliberate violation of the moral and spiritual order. The verse therefore carries a powerful warning: heedlessness toward truth is not a passive failing but an active injustice against one's own soul, and the consequences of that choice become painfully clear when the veil of worldly delusion is finally lifted.

translation: Indeed, you [disbelievers] and what you worship besides Allah will be the fuel of Hell. You will surely come to it.
interpretation: This verse addresses the inevitable consequences of misdirected worship and false devotion. It establishes that those who reject the truth and ascribe divinity to beings or objects devoid of divine power will be brought into judgment alongside the very entities or concepts they elevated. The imagery of being 'fuel' underscores a spiritual reality: misguidance possesses a self-consuming nature, meaning that whatever a person allows to dominate their heart—replacing the awareness of the Divine—becomes a source of inner ruin and ultimately leads to states of severe alienation from the Source of all being. However, the classical tradition holds that this ruling applies specifically to those who consciously chose ultimate misguidance and persisted in it, and that divine mercy and intercession may extend to others in ways beyond human comprehension. The verse thus serves as a stark warning about the gravity of misappropriating the highest human capacity—the orientation of the soul—while leaving the door open to the limitless possibilities of divine grace.} | (This interpretation is derived from classical Sunni exegesis, drawing on the works of scholars such as al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi, and Ibn Kathir, and reflects the broader interpretive tradition of Islam.)

translation: If these [the gods they worship besides Allah] were [true] gods, they would not have come to it [Hellfire], but all of them will be in it [eternally].
interpretation: This verse conveys a profound theological argument regarding the nature of divinity and the futility of polytheism. It states that if the deities the disbelievers worship alongside Allah were genuinely divine, they would never have entered the Hellfire. However, because these alleged gods are nothing more than powerless creations—be they idols, false deities, or even satans—they too will share the same fate as their misguided worshippers. The verse underscores the absolute sovereignty and uniqueness of Allah, demonstrating that anything besides Him is inherently weak and incapable of saving, even itself. The eternal nature of this punishment, indicated by the word 'خالدون' (eternal dwellers), emphasizes the severe consequence of associating partners with Allah (shirk) and rejecting His oneness.

translation: For them therein is furious breathing, and they therein do not hear.
interpretation: The verse describes the state of those in Hellfire: they will produce a horrific, agonizing sound (zafīr) as they gasp in their torment, yet despite this, they will not be able to hear anything—not even the cries of others in Hell—because their suffering is so intense and overwhelming that their senses are numbed and shut off from anything except their own anguish. The verse highlights both the physical torment (the rasping, desperate breathing) and the sensory deprivation (the inability to hear) that compound the punishment of the damned, emphasizing the completeness of their isolation and the extremity of their suffering in the Hereafter.

translation: Indeed, those for whom the best [reward] has preceded from Us—they will be far removed from it [the punishment of Hell]
interpretation: This verse conveys a powerful assurance from Allah regarding the ultimate destiny of those who have already been granted the foremost reward of divine acceptance. It affirms that a category of people—those whose sincere faith and righteous deeds have earned them Allah's prior favor and pledge of Paradise—will be completely distanced and insulated from the horrors of Hellfire, its torment, and even its hearing and awareness. The verse establishes a clear principle of divine mercy: those whom Allah has chosen to honor with His acceptance are eternally protected from the punishment, suggesting that genuine faith and good works, when preceded by divine grace, become an unbreakable safeguard against eternal ruin. It also implicitly serves as a call to believers, urging them to strive for such a state through devotion, righteousness, and reliance on Allah's mercy, knowing that the ultimate protection from damnation lies not in one's own efforts alone but in the prior favor and decree of the Most Merciful.

translation: They will not hear its slightest sound, and they will abide in whatever their souls desire.
interpretation: This verse refers to the reward for the people of Paradise, who will be granted an eternal state of bliss where they are completely insulated from any form of discomfort, including even the faintest sounds of Hell (such as its boiling, sighing, or torment). The phrase 'they will not hear its slightest sound' signifies a complete separation from the fears and horrors of punishment. The second part, 'and they will abide in whatever their souls desire,' emphasizes that they will remain forever in a state of perfect contentment, where every lawful and pure desire is fulfilled without limitation, pain, or end. It highlights the completeness of their joy and the perfection of their reward in the Hereafter.

translation: The greatest terror [i.e., the horrors of the Day of Judgment] will not grieve them, and the angels will meet them, [saying], 'This is your Day which you have been promised.'
interpretation: This verse describes a state of profound divine comfort bestowed upon the righteous believers on the Day of Judgment. The 'greatest terror' (al-faza'u al-akbar) refers to the overwhelming awe and dread associated with the ultimate reckoning and the cataclysmic events preceding it, such as the sounding of the Trumpet and the Day of Resurrection. Unlike the general state of horror that envelops all of creation, the God-fearing will be shielded from this consuming grief and anxiety. Instead, they will be greeted warmly by the angels, who announce that the Day they were promised—their entry into Paradise and ultimate recompense—has finally arrived. This signifies a transition from the trials of the worldly life to a state of secure, honored reception in the eternal realm, reflecting God's mercy and the reward for their steadfast faith.

translation: The Day when We will fold the heaven like the folding of a written scroll. As We began the first creation, We will repeat it. [That is] a promise binding upon Us. Indeed, We will do it.
interpretation: This verse describes the Day of Judgment with powerful imagery, emphasizing Allah's absolute sovereignty over creation. The folding of the sky like a scroll signifies the end of the current cosmic order, while the promise to recreate creation as it was first initiated demonstrates that resurrection is no more difficult for Allah than the initial act of bringing existence into being. The phrase 'a promise binding upon Us' functions as a divine guarantee, underscoring that human return to Allah is not merely possible but absolutely guaranteed by Allah's nature, which requires no effort to accomplish what it decrees ('indeed, We will do it'). This serves as both a warning of the certainty of accountability and a testament to divine power that operates beyond human limitations.

translation: And We have already written in the Psalms after the Reminder that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants.
interpretation: This verse refers to God's covenant and promise that the earth will eventually come under the dominion of the righteous, who are characterized by their faith and obedience to God. The phrase "after the Reminder" suggests a continuity of divine guidance revealed through previous scriptures, including the Zabur (Psalms) given to David, and it affirms that despite the temporary dominance of corrupt or oppressive forces, ultimate authority over the earth belongs to those who sincerely uphold God's commandments. It also serves as a consolation to the faithful that their struggles are not in vain, as divine justice will prevail in the fullness of time.

translation: Indeed, in this [Qur'an] there is a clear message for a people who worship [and serve Allah].
interpretation: This verse serves as a powerful declaration of the Qur'an's purpose and efficacy, functioning not merely as a book of information but as a transformative guide that yields tangible spiritual results. The word "balaghan" (بلاغًا) signifies the attainment of one's destination or objective, implying that the Qur'an successfully delivers the servant to their intended goal, which is salvation and closeness to the Divine. However, this profound success is conditional upon the recipient possessing the quality of 'ibadah' (عابدين), referring to those who engage in acts of devotion and servitude with sincerity and mindfulness of Allah. This indicates that mere knowledge or passive reading is insufficient; rather, the individual must actively turn to Allah in worship, allowing the divine guidance to permeate their inner consciousness and shape their actions. Consequently, the verse establishes a direct correlation between spiritual receptivity and the realization of truth: the more one immerses themselves in sincere worship, the more the Qur'an's message becomes a living reality that guides them through the trials of worldly existence toward eternal success.

translation: And We did not send you [O Muhammad] except as a mercy to the worlds.
interpretation: This verse declares Prophet Muhammad's mission as a universal mercy, encompassing both humanity and jinn across all times and places. It emphasizes that his prophethood was not a warning or punishment, but fundamentally an act of divine compassion aimed at guiding creation toward truth, righteousness, and ultimate salvation. The word "mercy" here carries comprehensive meaning: it includes the guidance of the Qur'an, the moral example of the Prophet, the easing of previous burdens, and the opening of a path to God's forgiveness. By describing his mission in this way, the verse establishes that Islam's purpose is not coercion but the manifestation of divine grace to all of existence.

translation:
, the translation of this verse is: "Say, 'It has been revealed to me that your God is one God. So will you submit?'"

This is a profound and direct call to monotheism (Tawhid). The verse emphasizes the exclusive oneness of God and presents Islam as a surrender and submission to this singular divine reality.
interpretation: The verse directly addresses Prophet Muhammad, commanding him to convey the core message of Islam: the absolute oneness of God (Tawhid). The phrase "your God is one God" establishes monotheism as the foundational truth and the central theme of the divine message. The concluding question, "So will you submit?" is both an invitation and a challenge, presenting Islam not merely as a belief system but as an active submission to God's will, urging humanity to recognize and accept His sovereignty.

translation: So if they turn away, then say, 'I have warned you all equally; and I do not know whether what you are promised is near or far.'
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet Muhammad to maintain a stance of detachment and clarity in the face of rejection: after fulfilling his duty of delivering the message, he is to declare a universal warning that applies equally to all, without showing preference or discrimination among people. The phrase 'آذنتكم على سواء' (I have warned you equally) signifies that the warning is impartial and applies to everyone alike, emphasizing that no one can claim ignorance or favoritism. The second part, 'I do not know whether what you are promised is near or far,' reflects the human limitation of the Prophet and, by extension, all human beings, regarding the timing of divine promises such as the Day of Judgment or punishment. This acknowledges that while the outcome is certain, its specific timing remains in the realm of divine knowledge alone, encouraging constant vigilance and preparedness rather than complacency based on assumed delays. The verse thus conveys the themes of universal accountability, the completion of prophetic duty regardless of the audience's response, and the exclusive divine sovereignty over matters of timing in the unseen.

translation: Indeed, He knows what is spoken aloud and He knows what you conceal.
interpretation: This verse affirms God's absolute omniscience, encompassing both the external and internal dimensions of human communication. It serves as a profound reminder that no utterance, whether openly proclaimed or secretly whispered, escapes divine awareness. This divine knowledge is not limited to surface-level words but extends to the intentions, thoughts, and concealed motives behind them. The verse functions as both a warning and a comfort: a warning to those who might outwardly profess righteousness while harboring hypocrisy, deceit, or evil intentions, assuring them that their hidden realities are fully exposed to God; and a comfort to the sincere, whose unspoken struggles, silent prayers, and private acts of devotion are equally witnessed and known. It establishes that authentic accountability before the Divine is measured not by external appearance but by the totality of what is expressed and what remains hidden in the heart.

translation: And I know not; perhaps it is a trial for you and an enjoyment for a time.
interpretation: This portion of the verse (from Sūrah al-Anbiyāʾ 21:111) refers to the Prophet's admission of his limited knowledge regarding the timing of the Day of Judgment or divine decree, suggesting that the deferral or withholding of certain knowledge serves as a test for humanity and a temporary provision, reminding believers that ultimate wisdom belongs solely to God.
