The verse therefore teaches that intellectual and spiritual attainment is not merely a product of human effort or natural maturation, but a divine reward bestowed upon those who strive to perfect their character. It establishes a link between moral excellence and epistemological insight, suggesting that those who cultivate virtue become fitting receptacles for sacred wisdom. The concluding phrase, "Thus do We reward the doers of good," generalizes the principle beyond a single individual, indicating that the divine pattern (*sunnat Allāh*) operates consistently: goodness is never wasted, and God honors those who honor Him through righteous living.

translation: And he entered the city at a time of unawareness of its people and found therein two men fighting – one from his faction and one from his enemy – and the one from his faction called him for help against the one from his enemy. So Moses struck him [with his fist] and ended him. He said, 'This is from the work of Satan. Indeed, he is a clear, misleading enemy.'
interpretation: The verse describes a critical turning point in Moses's early life, when he impulsively intervened in a conflict between two men in Egypt, striking down the oppressor. The phrase “at a time of unawareness of its people” (على حين غفلة من أهلها) indicates he chose a moment when he could act without being observed, suggesting an awareness that his intervention was risky and that Pharaoh's regime was hostile to his people. This reflects the condition of oppressed communities who must act covertly against tyrannical powers, unable to confront them openly without inviting further persecution. The striking of the Egyptian – “وكزه موسى” (Moses struck him) – is interpreted in classical exegesis as an unintended outcome of an impulsive act rather than a deliberate killing. Moses himself immediately recognized the moral gravity of his action, attributing the inner impulse that led to violence to the work of Satan (“هذا من عمل الشيطان”). This self-awareness and moral accountability represent a profound spiritual principle: that human beings must recognize when destructive impulses arise within them, identify their true source, and resist them before they manifest in harmful actions. By naming Satan as “a clear, misleading enemy,” Moses affirms that the path of violence, even when seemingly justified by the cause of justice, can be a deviation from righteousness when it bypasses lawful means or arises from uncontrolled anger. The verse also establishes the theme that legitimate defense of the oppressed must be exercised within moral and legal boundaries, and that hasty, unconsidered actions – even those motivated by sympathy for the suffering – can produce consequences that require repentance and accountability. This moment serves as a moral lesson for all who seek justice: that the means must be as righteous as the end, and that self-examination is essential before taking any action that affects another's life.

translation: He said, 'My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, so forgive me,' and He forgave him. Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.
interpretation: This verse depicts a profound moment of sincere repentance and divine mercy, often understood in the context of Prophet Moses (or another prophet, according to various scholarly opinions) after an unintentional wrongdoing. The plea 'My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself' reflects a profound consciousness of human fallibility before the Divine, acknowledging that all sin, regardless of intention or magnitude, constitutes an injustice against one's own soul by exposing it to spiritual detriment and separation from God's grace. The subsequent acceptance of this repentance, 'and He forgave him,' illustrates a fundamental attribute of the Divine: that sincere acknowledgment and turning back to God in humility always meets with pardon. This establishes a theological principle that divine mercy is not contingent upon perfection, but rather upon the genuineness of the heart's return to its Lord. The closing affirmation, 'Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful,' universalizes this particular instance into an eternal promise for all of humanity, offering hope that no matter how great one's transgression, the gates of repentance and forgiveness remain perpetually open for those who approach God with humility and sincerity.

translation: He [Moses] said, 'My Lord, because You have favored me, I will never be a helper to the criminals.'
interpretation: After Allah endowed Moses (peace be upon him) with knowledge, prophethood, and salvation from Pharaoh's oppression, Moses pledges to never side with or assist the wrongdoers. This reflects a profound principle of moral integrity: recognizing Allah's blessings strengthens one's resolve to dissociate from sin and injustice. It also implies that those who recognize Allah's grace upon them must actively oppose evil rather than remain neutral or complicit. Moses' statement serves as a model for believers: gratitude to Allah manifests not only in worship but also in taking a clear moral stance against wrongdoing, refusing to lend support—whether through action, silence, or approval—to those who transgress Allah's limits. It underscores the believer's responsibility to be an ally of righteousness, not of corruption.

translation: So he [Moses] awoke in the city, fearful and vigilant. Then behold, the one who had sought his help the day before was calling out to him for help [again]. Moses said to him, 'You are indeed a clear troublemaker.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates a critical moment in the story of Moses (Musa) after he accidentally struck and killed an Egyptian. The verse highlights that even a person who once had cause to seek assistance may, through their own contentious and aggressive nature, become a source of repeated distress rather than lasting alliance. Moses' statement that the man is 'a clear troublemaker' (la-ghawiyyun mubin) reflects the recognition that true danger often arises not from outright enemies, but from those who are perpetually embroiled in conflict, unable to live peaceably among their people. Spiritually, this can be seen as a warning against impulsivity, reckless speech, and choosing companions poorly. The verse also serves as a prelude to the unfolding of Moses' prophetic mission: his confrontation with injustice in the city eventually leads to his flight from Egypt, marking the beginning of a journey toward his ultimate destiny. The repeated cry for help from the same man foreshadows the chaos that will drive Moses out of the city and set the stage for his encounter with God at the burning bush. As such, the verse functions both as a character study of human folly and as a narrative pivot in the larger story of salvation and divine guidance.

translation: So when he intended to lay hold of the one who was an enemy to both of them, the man said, 'O Moses, do you intend to kill me as you killed someone yesterday? You only intend to be a tyrant in the land, and you do not intend to be of those who promote peace.'
interpretation: This verse continues the narrative from Surah Al-Qasas (28:19), recounting a pivotal moment in the story of Prophet Moses (Musa) before his prophetic mission. After Moses had intervened in a quarrel and accidentally killed an Egyptian the previous day, he now sees the same Israelite man he had previously helped being involved in another altercation, this time with an Egyptian (or possibly another adversary). When Moses moved to defend the Israelite and intended to strike his opponent, the man, fearing for his life, mistakenly assumed Moses was again acting with murderous intent. The man's accusation that Moses only wants to be a 'tyrant' (jabbar) reveals a profound irony and tension: Moses' intervention, though motivated by justice and a desire to protect his people, is perceived by others as violent aggression. This reaction highlights the danger of using physical force, even with good intentions, in a society where Moses is an outsider and his previous killing is remembered. The verse underscores the theme that hasty and forceful actions, even those aimed at justice, can be misinterpreted as tyranny. It also serves as a critique of those who resort to violence as the primary means of resolving conflict, contrasting this with the role of a 'muslih' (one who promotes reconciliation and reform). Theologically, this episode foreshadows Moses' later role as a prophet and lawgiver who would guide his people toward structured legal and moral systems rather than mere vigilantism. It also illustrates the psychological and social consequences of a single act of violence—it stains the perpetrator's reputation and makes genuine peacemaking difficult. Ultimately, this narrative invites reflection on the distinction between defense, aggression, and true reform, suggesting that lasting peace ('islah') requires wisdom, patience, and legitimate authority rather than individual acts of force.

translation: And a man came from the farthest end of the city, running. He said, 'O Moses, indeed the assembly is conspiring to kill you, so leave. Truly, I am among your sincere advisors.'
interpretation: This verse describes a pivotal moment of deliverance for Moses, where divine providence operates through an unnamed believer who, recognizing the imminent danger from Pharaoh's court, risks his own safety to warn Moses. The man's origin 'from the farthest end of the city' and his 'running' indicate urgency and the gravity of the threat—Pharaoh's elite ('الملأ') have convened specifically to plot Moses's assassination. This unnamed figure represents those who possess faith ('إني لك من الناصحين') yet operate within a hostile system, demonstrating that sincere advice often requires courage and sacrifice. The verse illustrates a recurring Qur'anic theme: when persecution becomes insurmountable, departure (hijrah) is divinely sanctioned as a means of preservation, not retreat. Moses's subsequent departure from Egypt fulfills this counsel and sets the stage for his prophetic mission to mature outside Pharaoh's reach, showing that divine plans often unfold through both warning and willing obedience to that warning. The unnamed man's sincerity stands in contrast to the collective treachery of the elite, highlighting how truth and genuine concern for the prophet exist even in the heart of oppressive societies, often in places least expected.

translation: So he left it (the land), fearful and anticipating (danger). He said, 'My Lord, save me from the wrongdoing people.'
interpretation: This verse refers to a prophet (commonly identified as Moses) who fled his homeland out of fear after committing an act that endangered his life, pleading to God for protection from those who had resolved to harm him. The verse illustrates the human condition of vulnerability and the appropriate response of turning to the Divine for refuge when facing the oppression of unjust people. It emphasizes that even those chosen for great missions can experience moments of fear and must rely on God's deliverance from tyrannical forces, reinforcing the theme that safety and justice ultimately come from God rather than from human efforts alone.

translation: And when he [Moses] directed his course toward Midian, he said, 'Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the right way.'
interpretation: This verse captures a moment of profound vulnerability and trust in God's guidance as Moses flees Egypt after inadvertently killing an Egyptian. His deliberate turn toward Midian—where he would encounter the well, the daughters of Jethro, and eventually receive his prophetic calling—symbolizes an outward journey that mirrors his inner spiritual turning toward God. The phrase 'perhaps my Lord will guide me' does not express doubt but rather humility and dependence; Moses acknowledges that human plans are fragile and that ultimate direction comes from the divine. The 'right way' (sawasāʾ al-sabīl) refers not only to a physical path but to the straight path of truth, justice, and ultimately, prophetic purpose. This moment exemplifies the Qur'anic theme that sincere seekers, even when displaced and uncertain, are led by God toward the fulfillment of a greater purpose they cannot yet see. Moses becomes a model of tawakkul (reliance on God), surrendering control while remaining active in seeking refuge, demonstrating that divine guidance often accompanies sincere human effort.

translation: And when he arrived at the waters of Madyan, he found a community of people watering [their livestock], and he found, besides them, two women holding back [their animals]. He said, 'What is your business?' They said, 'We do not water until the shepherds have finished, and our father is an old man.'
interpretation: This verse depicts a poignant moment of modesty, patience, and reliance on God in the face of vulnerability and difficulty. The two women are waiting at the well, not out of idleness, but because of social constraints and their father's old age, which prevents them from mingling among men or competing for water. Their statement reflects both dignity and a quiet surrender to circumstance: they do not complain about their hardship, nor do they abandon their duty; rather, they endure with patience. Their trust in God's timing—waiting for the crowd to disperse—is a subtle expression of tawakkul (reliance on God). The verse also sets the stage for divine providence: the one who will come to their aid (Moses, though unnamed here) is being prepared to meet them precisely because of their patience and honesty. In this way, the verse teaches that God often responds to those who remain steadfast and sincere, even when their situation seems impossible.

translation: So he watered [their flocks] for them; then he turned away to the shade and said, 'My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You would send down to me, in need.'
interpretation: This verse depicts a moment of sincere humility and reliance on God after an act of service. Having just assisted others without seeking recognition or reward, the person withdraws and turns to God in private supplication, acknowledging that any goodness in life comes solely from the Divine. The phrase 'whatever good You would send down to me' reflects an understanding that all blessings—material provision, strength, opportunity, and even the capacity to do good—are gifts from God, not personal entitlements or achievements. The admission 'I am in need' is not a confession of poverty in worldly terms, but a recognition of spiritual and existential dependence: that human beings, despite their abilities and actions, remain utterly reliant on God's mercy and grace. This teaching emphasizes that true gratitude is expressed not in public display, but in quiet, honest acknowledgment of one's need for God's continued generosity, and that sincere service to others flows naturally from a heart that remembers its own dependence on the Divine.

translation: Then one of the two women came to him, walking with shyness. She said, 'Indeed, my father invites you so he may reward you for having watered [our flock] for us.' When he came to him and told him the story, he said, 'Do not fear. You have escaped from the wrongdoing people.'
interpretation: This verse describes a young man, traditionally understood in Islamic tradition as the Prophet Shu'ayb or more commonly as the Prophet Moses, being approached by one of the two women who were previously prevented from drawing water for their flock due to the shepherds' haste and impropriety. Her approach 'walking with shyness' (al-istihya') demonstrates her modesty and moral character, as she does not directly engage him but conveys the purpose of her father's invitation through formal speech. The invitation to 'reward you' reflects a culture where compensation for services rendered was an established norm, but her father's intention here appears to be more than mere payment—it is a recognition of his chivalry and an opportunity to integrate him into their household. The father, upon hearing his story, offers reassurance: 'Do not fear. You have escaped from the wrongdoing people,' indicating that the young man had been fleeing from those who intended him harm—identified in Islamic exegesis as Pharaoh's people or an oppressive community. The verse emphasizes divine providence working through ordinary human interactions: a seemingly simple act of kindness toward strangers opens a path of safety and sustenance. It also illustrates the moral qualities honored in prophetic figures—compassion toward the vulnerable, respect for women even in distant interactions, and reliance on God's protection. The father's statement carries a tone of certainty and authority, suggesting either prophetic insight or trustworthy knowledge of the surrounding political situation, offering the young man both physical security and emotional relief.

translation: ,,قولُ إحدى ابنتي شعيب -عليه السلام-: يا أبتِ استأجِرْ هذا الرجلَ القويَّ الأمينَ ليرعى غنَمَنا.
interpretation: وهذا المشهد يُبرز صفتي القوة والأمانة بوصفهما المعيارَين الأساسيين لاختيار العاملين وأصحاب المسؤوليات؛ فالأمانةُ تُوجِبُ الثقةَ فيمن يُولّى أمرًا، والقوةُ تُكفلُ أداءَه على الوجه الأكمل؛ ولهذا امتدح القرآنُ هذين الخُلُقَيْن معًا، وفيه إشارةٌ إلى أنّ الكفاءةَ لا تنفكُّ عن الخُلُقِ، وأنّ استيفاءَهما جميعًا هو الأصلحُ للأمّةِ وأحوالِها.

translation: He said, 'Indeed, I wish to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine, on the condition that you work for me for eight years. But if you complete ten, that will be from you; and I do not wish to make things difficult for you. You will find me, if God wills, among the righteous.'
interpretation:
This verse from Surah Al-Qasas (28:27) presents the proposal of Shu'ayb (or, according to many scholars, an unnamed righteous man from the lineage of Shu'ayb) to Musa (Moses). The proposal contains several layers of meaning and wisdom:

1. **Divine Providence and Human Effort**: The verse illustrates how Allah orchestrates events to fulfill His plan. Musa had fled Egypt after accidentally killing an Egyptian and found himself in Midian, where he helped the daughters of this man water their flock. Now, the father offers him marriage in exchange for labor—a means of providing sustenance for Musa during his exile, while also giving him a family and a reason to stay.

2. **Fairness and Consent**: The father's approach demonstrates ethical conduct. He does not impose the marriage but presents it as a proposal ('I wish to marry you'), giving Musa the freedom to choose or decline. He also offers two daughters ('one of these two'), showing consideration for Musa's comfort rather than forcing a specific choice.

3. **Flexibility and Mercy in Contracts**: The father sets a baseline term of eight years but allows Musa to extend it voluntarily to ten for additional benefit. This reflects a balanced contractual arrangement where the worker is not exploited, and the additional two years are framed as a gift ('from you'), not a burden. This teaches the Islamic principle that agreements should be just, with room for generosity rather than coercion.

4. **Ease Over Hardship**: The statement 'I do not wish to make things difficult for you' reflects the Islamic value of removing hardship (mashaqqah) from human interactions. It echoes the Qur'anic principle that religion is meant to be easy, not burdensome.

5. **Trust in Divine Will**: The phrase 'if God wills' (in sha' Allah) acknowledges that outcomes depend on Allah, even in worldly affairs. This teaches the believer to attribute plans and hopes to Allah's will rather than relying solely on human arrangements.

6. **Character of Righteousness**: The father describes himself as being among the righteous (as-salihin), and Musa's later response in the following verses confirms his own good character. This highlights that righteous people recognize and associate with one another.

In essence, the verse portrays a model of just, kind, and God-conscious human interaction, while also showing how Allah uses ordinary circumstances—like labor, marriage, and contracts—to shape the lives of His prophets and fulfill greater divine purposes.

translation: That [agreement] is between me and you; whichever of the two terms I fulfill, there shall be no aggression against me, and Allah is Witness over what we say.
interpretation: This verse reflects the importance of fulfilling covenants and treating agreements with seriousness and integrity, even in matters of worldly benefit. The speaker (the wise man who freed Bilqis from her unjust trial system) sets clear conditions: the pact must be honored, the duration—whether shorter or longer—must be respected without violation, and the entire matter is placed under divine observation. On a deeper level, it underscores that all human commitments ultimately stand before God, who holds each party accountable for their promises, reminding believers that transparency, fairness, and trustworthiness in dealings are not merely ethical choices but spiritual responsibilities before the Almighty.

translation: And when Moses had completed the term and was traveling with his family, he perceived from the direction of the Mount a fire. He said to his family, 'Remain here; indeed, I have perceived a fire. Perhaps I will bring you from it some information or a burning branch from the fire that you may warm yourselves.'
interpretation: This verse marks a pivotal transition in the story of Moses, depicting the end of his years of service in Midian and the beginning of his prophetic mission. The completion of the appointed term signifies the fulfillment of his covenant with his father-in-law and a readiness for a new phase of life. The perception of fire on the mountain serves as both a literal and symbolic catalyst: literally, it draws Moses toward a source of warmth and information for his family in the darkness; symbolically, it represents the divine spark of prophecy and guidance that will illuminate not only his path but the path of an entire nation. The verse highlights the human vulnerability of Moses—his concern for his family's comfort in the cold night—while simultaneously illustrating how divine providence often intersects with ordinary human needs, turning a simple search for warmth into the inauguration of a prophetic encounter that will reshape religious history. The journey toward the fire thus becomes a journey toward destiny, where the mundane act of seeking warmth converges with the momentous event of receiving revelation.

translation: And when he came to it [the fire], he was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot from the tree: 'O Moses, indeed I am Allah, the Lord of the worlds.'
interpretation: This verse marks the pivotal moment of divine revelation to Moses at Mount Sinai, where the sacred and the ordinary intersect. The specific physical details—the right bank of the valley, the blessed ground, and the burning tree—are not merely geographical markers but symbolic of the precise location where the boundaries between the human and divine are transcended. The direct address, 'O Moses, I am Allah,' establishes the foundational concept of monotheism (Tawhid) in its purest form, emphasizing that the Lord of all existence is one, encompassing every dimension of creation. This moment initiates Moses's prophetic mission, transforming a solitary shepherd into the spokesperson for divine will, demonstrating that truth is often revealed not in grand palaces or centers of power, but in humble, overlooked places when the heart is ready to receive it.

translation: ...and 'Cast down your staff.' But when he saw it moving like a serpent, he turned back fleeing and did not look back. [Allah said], 'O Moses, come forward and do not fear; indeed, you are among the secure.'
interpretation: This verse portrays a pivotal moment in the encounter between Moses and the divine at the burning bush, where the miraculous transformation of his staff into a living serpent becomes a test of faith and fear. The vivid imagery of the staff writhing like a 'jann' (a swift, snake-like creature) triggers a deeply human, instinctive flight response in Moses—he runs away without looking back, symbolizing the raw vulnerability of even a chosen prophet in the face of the uncanny and overwhelming. Yet the divine reassurance, 'O Moses, come forward and do not fear; indeed, you are among the secure,' serves as a profound metaphysical declaration: true safety is not the absence of frightening phenomena, but the presence of divine protection that transcends natural terror. This moment foreshadows Moses's lifelong role as a leader confronting the might of Pharaoh, teaching that prophetic courage is not the absence of fear but the conscious return to it with trust in God's safeguarding. The verse thus establishes a foundational theme in the Qur'anic narrative: that proximity to the divine often first manifests through trembling awe, which must then be overcome by conscious submission, transforming fear into the basis for sacred mission.

translation: Put your hand into your bosom; it will come out white, without evil. And draw your arm close to you, to be free of fear. These are two proofs from your Lord to Pharaoh and his nobles. Indeed, they are a wicked people.
interpretation: The verse addresses the Prophet Moses (Musa) and reassures him during his daunting mission to confront the oppressive ruler of Egypt. The command to insert his hand into his bosom and withdraw it shining white, free from any disease, signifies a miraculous sign intended to authenticate his prophethood and captivate Pharaoh's court. The instruction to draw his arm close to him—often understood as pressing it against his chest to dispel dread—reflects divine comfort for the natural fear Moses felt before confronting tyranny. The two signs together—the radiant hand and the removal of terror—are framed as undeniable evidences from God to Pharaoh and his elite, emphasizing that rejection of the truth stems not from a lack of clarity but from moral corruption and defiance. The verse underscores the divine principle that prophets are supported by tangible proofs, yet guidance remains constrained by the readiness of the human heart to accept truth.

translation: He said, 'My Lord, indeed I have killed one of them, and I fear they will kill me.'
interpretation: This verse reflects a moment of human vulnerability and the tension between a sense of mission and the awareness of personal danger. The speaker, having taken a life out of conviction that it was necessary, acknowledges the potential consequences—namely, retaliation from those who would defend the slain individual. Despite being driven by a higher purpose, he does not deny the gravity of his act or dismiss the real threat it poses. Instead, he turns to God with honest, unvarnished concern, showing that genuine faith does not require the suppression of fear but allows for full transparency before the Divine. This admission also carries an implicit plea for protection and guidance, revealing that the path of righteousness often demands confronting not only external opposition but also the internal struggle of doubt and apprehension. It underscores the idea that moral courage is not the absence of fear, but the willingness to proceed faithfully while entrusting one's safety and outcome to God.

translation: And my brother Aaron is more eloquent than me in speech, so send him with me as a helper to confirm me. Indeed, I fear that they will deny me.
interpretation: Moses acknowledges his human limitation in speech and humbly requests divine support through his brother, recognizing that prophecy requires both divine authorization and human collaboration; this reflects the Qur'anic theme that prophets are chosen vessels who rely on God, and it legitimizes Aaron's role in confronting Pharaoh, emphasizing that faith, eloquence, and sincerity are necessary companions in conveying truth.

translation: He [Allah] will strengthen your arm through your brother, and give you both authority, so that they shall not be able to touch you. By Our signs, you two, and those who follow you, will be the victors.
interpretation: This verse refers to the support Allah gave to Moses by granting him his brother Aaron as a companion and helper in his mission against Pharaoh and his people. The divine promise contained here is twofold: first, a practical strengthening through human solidarity (Aaron's assistance to Moses), and second, an overarching spiritual guarantee that those who cling to faith and rely on God's signs will ultimately prevail against tyranny and oppression, regardless of how overwhelming worldly power may seem against them. The verse underscores the Islamic principle that victory is not determined by numerical or material strength alone but by divine support accompanying sincere faith and righteous struggle.

translation: When Moses came to them with Our clear signs, they said, 'This is nothing but invented magic, and we have not heard of this among our forefathers.'
interpretation: The verse describes the defiant rejection of truth by those who are deeply entrenched in inherited traditions. Despite being presented with evident signs from God, Pharaoh's people chose to dismiss Moses's message as fabricated magic, expressing that such teachings were alien to the legacy of their ancestors. This reflects a psychological and spiritual condition in which attachment to inherited customs and ancestral practices takes precedence over objective truth, causing people to deny even the clearest evidence when it challenges familiar norms. The verse thus critiques the human tendency toward dogmatic adherence to tradition and warns that reverence for the past can become a barrier to recognizing divine guidance, leading one to label truth as falsehood simply because it disrupts established beliefs.

translation: And Moses said, 'My Lord knows best who has come with guidance from Him and who will have the best outcome in the eternal home. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed.'
interpretation: Moses is expressing complete trust in God's exclusive knowledge of who sincerely follows His guidance versus who persists in arrogance and injustice. He acknowledges that ultimate success belongs only to those who submit to truth, while those who reject divine guidance and oppress others are destined to fail in both this world and the Hereafter. This reflects the fundamental Islamic principle that salvation is achieved through humility before God and adherence to His revealed way, not through worldly power or coercion.

translation: And Pharaoh said, 'O eminent ones, I have not known of any god for you other than me. So kindle for me, O Haman, a fire over clay and make for me a tower that I might look at the God of Moses. And indeed, I think he [Moses] is among the liars.'
interpretation: This verse unveils the inner reality of tyrannical authority, which inevitably produces a paradox of self-deification and existential insecurity. Pharaoh's claim to be the sole deity is not a genuine assertion of divinity; it is a desperate confession of cognitive and spiritual bankruptcy. By stating, "I have not known of any god for you other than me," Pharaoh admits the limits of his own knowledge—he knows no other god, because his arrogant attachment to worldly power has blinded him to any reality beyond his own dominion. The very fact that he commands Haman to construct a tower to "look at the God of Moses" demonstrates that his heart is haunted by a reality he cannot control. True sovereignty would not need to seek out a rival; it would be self-sufficient. Pharaoh's restless search for Moses's God reveals a gnawing doubt beneath his absolute claims. Furthermore, his statement, "I think he is among the liars," shows that Pharaoh's denial is not based on conviction but on defensive rejection. To call Moses a liar is easier for Pharaoh than to confront the terrifying possibility that there exists a Lord of the heavens and the earth whose authority supersedes his own. Thus, this verse portrays the tyrant as a tragic figure, one who builds towering monuments not out of strength, but out of a profound fear of being small in a universe governed by a higher Will.

translation: And he [Pharaoh] exalted himself, along with his soldiers, in the land without right, and they thought they would never be returned to Us.
interpretation: The verse condemns Pharaoh and his followers for their arrogant tyranny and false sense of invincibility. Their boastful claim that they would never be held accountable reflects a deeper spiritual delusion: the denial of divine justice and the inevitability of the return to God. This serves as a timeless warning against the corrupting nature of power when it is divorced from humility and accountability. The phrase "without right" emphasizes that their dominance was illegitimate, built on oppression rather than any moral or divine mandate. Ultimately, the verse underscores that all worldly dominion is temporary and that every soul will stand before God, regardless of how powerful or unassailable it appears in the present world.

translation: So We took him and his troops and cast them into the sea. So observe how the end of the wrongdoers was.
interpretation: This verse refers to the destruction of Pharaoh and his army when they pursued Moses and the Children of Israel; they were all drowned as a consequence of their persistent oppression and rejection of divine guidance. The verse then calls upon the listener to reflect upon this historical event as a moral lesson, demonstrating that tyranny and wrongdoing inevitably lead to ruin, and that worldly power cannot protect those who defy God's will from ultimate accountability.

translation: And We made them leaders inviting to the Fire, and on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped.
interpretation: This verse describes those whom God has appointed as examples of misguidance, whose legacy is an ongoing call toward falsehood and destruction, such that their influence persists in tempting others toward what leads to ruin in the hereafter. On the Day of Judgment, when they stand in need of rescue from the consequences of their actions, no helper or intercessor will come to their aid, emphasizing that ultimate success and salvation come only through sincere devotion to God and righteous conduct, and that those who lead others astray bear a heavy burden for which they alone must answer.

translation: And We followed them (the rejected) in this world with a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the despised.
interpretation: This verse establishes a comprehensive and terrifying consequence for those who reject the truth of Allah's message. The phrase "followed them in this world with a curse" indicates that their rejection is not a static event but one that generates continuous negative consequences throughout their worldly lives. This curse manifests as spiritual alienation, where they are deprived of true peace and guidance; social alienation, where their defiance isolates them from true human community; and material alienation, where their worldly success lacks true meaning or ultimate value. The progression from worldly curse to the Day of Resurrection demonstrates an unbroken continuum of alienation that begins in worldly life and culminates in the eschatological realm. The specific use of "among the despised" rather than "among the punished" suggests that their state will not merely involve suffering but a profound rejection and disgrace. This terminology implies that their eternal condition will be marked not only by pain but by a deeper sense of being condemned to a despised status before Allah and before all of creation.

translation: And We had certainly given Moses the Scripture after We had destroyed the former generations, [making it] insights for the people and guidance and mercy, that they might be reminded.
interpretation: This verse draws a connection between divine revelation and historical continuity: after the destruction of earlier civilizations that rejected their prophets, God granted Moses the Torah as a source of insight, guidance, and mercy for his people. The historical pattern suggests that divine guidance is not a single event but an ongoing mercy renewed for each generation, while the destruction of past nations serves as a warning of consequences for those who reject it. The triple description of the scripture as 'insights,' 'guidance,' and 'mercy' emphasizes that revelation addresses human needs on multiple levels—it clarifies truth, directs behavior, and ultimately represents God's compassionate provision for humanity. The phrase 'that they might be reminded' acknowledges that remembrance is an active process requiring willingness to reflect on both the scripture and the historical lessons embedded in it.

translation: And you were not on the western side [of the mountain] when We revealed to Moses the command, nor were you among the witnesses.
interpretation: This verse affirms the Prophet Muhammad's lack of direct, physical presence at the historical event of God communicating His command to Moses at Mount Sinai, thereby emphasizing that the knowledge he conveys about past prophets and divine events comes through authentic revelation from God, not from personal eyewitness experience or human transmission, which serves as a subtle validation of the divine origin of his prophethood.

translation: But We did raise up generations, and long ages passed over them. And you were not a dweller among the people of Midian, reciting to them Our verses, but We were the senders [of messengers].
interpretation: This verse responds to those who questioned the Prophet Muhammad's authority to warn his people, given that he had not been present among earlier communities like the people of Midian (the community of Shuʿayb). The verse affirms that although the Prophet did not personally witness those earlier times, the message he delivers is not his own invention; it is divinely revealed and continuously sent by Allah through successive messengers to every generation. This emphasizes the unbroken chain of divine guidance and the truth that the Qur'an's warning is part of Allah's eternal plan for humanity.

translation: And you were not on the side of the Mount [Sinai] when We called [Moses], but [you were sent] as a mercy from your Lord to warn a people to whom no warner had come before you that they might be reminded.
interpretation: This verse affirms the Prophet Muhammad's lack of physical presence at the historical event of God calling Moses on Mount Sinai, yet it situates his prophetic mission within the same divine purpose: to deliver a message of mercy and warning. The emphasis on "mercy from your Lord" frames prophethood not merely as a punitive or juridical function, but as an act of divine compassion extended to a community that had lived in spiritual ignorance—having received no direct prophetic guidance since earlier dispensations. The phrase "that they might be reminded" (لعلهم يتذكرون) suggests that while the warning is necessary, the ultimate aim is recollection: the awakening of a fitrah (innate moral awareness) that already bears witness to truth. The verse thus validates the continuity of prophetic revelation while distinguishing Muhammad's role as both culmination of prior messages and a specific mercy tailored to his audience's condition.

translation: And were it not that a disaster would strike them for what their hands have sent before them (i.e., their sins and misdeeds), they would say, 'Our Lord, why did You not send us a messenger so we could follow Your verses and be among the believers?'
interpretation: This verse, like others around it, serves to preemptively silence the excuses of disbelievers. It teaches that when punishment befalls people for their past sins, they would have complained that they were never given a messenger. In doing so, it warns that rejecting the Prophet ﷺ after clear evidence has reached them will leave no excuse, since earlier peoples were similarly held accountable and were not given a chance to fabricate justifications. The verse thereby affirms the seriousness of responding to divine guidance once it has been delivered. }

translation: And when the truth came to them from Us, they said, 'Why was he not given the same as what was given to Moses?' Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Moses before? They said, 'Both are magic, supporting each other,' and they said, 'Indeed we, to all [of it], are disbelievers.'
interpretation: This verse exposes the deep-seated dishonesty of those who reject divine guidance. When the Qur'an was presented to them, they demanded that Muhammad receive something akin to the miracles given to Moses—yet they had already rejected those very miracles. Their objection is not rooted in a genuine search for evidence but in stubborn defiance. By acknowledging that they disbelieved in what Moses received while simultaneously demanding the same for Muhammad, they reveal that no amount of miraculous evidence would satisfy them. Their claim that the Torah and the Qur'an are two cooperating magics is a rhetorical ploy to dismiss both revelations without engaging with their content. This verse critiques the pattern of selective skepticism, where disbelievers demand proof while ignoring existing proof, using superficial objections to mask their unwillingness to submit to truth. It underscores that faith is not contingent on the type or magnitude of miracles but on the orientation of the heart.

translation: Say, 'Then bring a book from Allah that is more guiding than these two, and I will follow it, if you should be truthful.'
interpretation: The verse presents a decisive challenge directed at those who reject the guidance brought by Prophet Muhammad. It calls upon them—if they are sincere in their claim that the Torah and the Qur'an are not true guidance—to produce a scripture from Allah that offers better direction than these two revealed sources. The phrase 'أهدى منهما' (more guiding than both of them) acknowledges the inherent guidance found within the Torah and the Qur'an, while simultaneously inviting a comparison that no human-made or alternative scripture could meet. This serves as both a theological argument and a test of sincerity: those who genuinely seek truth would recognize divine guidance when presented with it, while those who reject it out of stubbornness or pride are left without excuse.

translation: And if they do not respond to you, then know that they only follow their desires. And who is more astray than he who follows his desire without guidance from Allah? Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: This verse establishes a fundamental criterion for distinguishing truth from error: when people reject prophetic guidance, the cause is not intellectual confusion but the surrender to personal desires. The 'following of desires' (hawā) is identified as the root of misguidance, surpassing in its deviation any other form of error because it replaces divine guidance with subjective preference. This positions the unmoved self as the ultimate false deity. However, the verse also places this human failing within a divine framework. Allah does not guide the wrongdoers—this is not a punitive withdrawal but a natural consequence: those who orient their will toward self-interest rather than truth become structurally incapable of recognizing guidance. Divine guidance requires a receptive orientation, and those who have corrupted their moral compass through persistent wrongdoing find that the clarity of truth no longer reaches them. The verse thus describes both a human responsibility and a divine law: the heart that chooses preference over principle eventually loses the capacity to perceive what it refuses to accept.

translation: And We have certainly conveyed to them the Word [i.e., the Qur'an] in succession that they might remember.
interpretation: This verse affirms that Allah has progressively revealed His message to humanity, presenting it in a connected and coherent manner over time. The purpose of this revelation is to serve as a reminder, prompting people to reflect, take heed, and align their lives with divine guidance. The word 'وصلنا' (We have conveyed/connected) emphasizes the continuity and deliberate unfolding of the truth, while 'لعلهم يتذكرون' (that they might remember) highlights the ultimate goal: awakening human consciousness to recognize the signs of Allah, the reality of accountability, and the path to righteousness. It underscores that the Qur'an is not a random collection of statements but a purposeful, interconnected discourse meant to inspire reflection and remembrance of one's relationship with the Creator.

translation: Those to whom We gave the Book before it — they, [some of them] believe in it.
interpretation: This verse affirms that genuine faith in the Qur'an is not exclusive to those who heard it for the first time; rather, among the earlier communities who received prior scriptures (such as the Torah and the Gospel), there are sincere, devoted believers who recognize the Qur'an as the fulfillment and continuation of the same divine truth they were entrusted with. Their faith is a testament to the consistency of God's guidance across revelation, and their affirmation of the Qur'an demonstrates that sincere adherence to earlier scriptures naturally leads one to accept its message, rather than rejecting it out of tribal or sectarian attachment. The verse thus highlights the continuity of divine revelation and the universal potential for sincere faith, while implicitly contrasting these true believers with those among the People of the Book who reject the Qur'an out of prejudice rather than conviction.

translation: And when it [the Qur'an] is recited to them, they say, 'We have believed in it; indeed, it is the truth from our Lord. Indeed, we were, before it, among those who submitted [to Allah].'
interpretation: This verse describes the response of sincere believers when they hear the Qur'an recited. They affirmatively declare their faith in it, recognizing it as the undeniable truth originating from their Lord. Their declaration goes beyond mere acceptance; it reflects a deep spiritual awareness that their current belief in the Qur'an is a continuation of a faith that has existed within them even before the revelation reached them, signifying that their hearts had already been inclined toward submission to God, and the Qur'an merely confirmed and formalized a pre-existing state of belief (Islam).

translation: :Those will be given their reward twice for what they patiently endured, and they repel evil with good, and from what We have provided them they spend.
interpretation: :This verse describes the qualities and rewards of sincere believers, likely referring to those who accepted Islam after previously following another revealed scripture. The phrase 'given their reward twice' signifies an extraordinary divine bounty, possibly because their faith involves both affirming their original scripture and recognizing the final revelation. The believer is characterized by three traits: patience (steadfastness in trials and obedience), the proactive repelling of evil with good (responding to hostility with kindness, transforming enmity into harmony), and generous spending from Allah's provisions (detachment from material wealth, using it in service of others). These qualities reflect a soul purified from miserliness, rancor, and anxiety, embodying a holistic spiritual excellence that harmonizes inner perseverance with outward moral conduct.

translation: And when they hear ill speech, they turn away from it and say, 'Our deeds belong to us, and your deeds belong to you. Peace be upon you; we do not desire the ignorant.'
interpretation: The verse is from Surah Al-Qasas (28:55). It describes a defining ethical stance of the righteous: when confronted with frivolous talk, falsehood, or offensive speech, they do not engage in retaliation or argumentation, but instead withdraw with dignity. Their statement, 'Our deeds belong to us, and your deeds belong to you,' establishes a clear separation of moral responsibility—each person is accountable only for their own actions. This reflects a principle of non-codependence: one does not carry the burden of another's wrongdoing or foolishness. The phrase 'Peace be upon you' (Salamun 'alaykum) is not merely a greeting but a profound act of disengagement from conflict, expressing that they harbor no ill will but also no desire to participate in the ignorance of the other party. The concluding words, 'We do not desire the ignorant' (la nabtaghi al-jahilin), should not be understood as contempt for people, but rather as a refusal to immerse oneself in the characteristics of ignorance (jahiliyyah). It signals a conscious choice to pursue knowledge, wisdom, and righteous conduct over the entanglements of worldly discord. This verse is often cited as an Islamic model for conflict resolution: respond to hostility with peace, uphold personal accountability, and maintain spiritual integrity by refusing to lower oneself to the level of foolishness.

translation: Indeed, you [O Muhammad] do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills. And He is most knowing of the [rightly] guided.
interpretation: This verse addresses the limits of human agency in matters of faith and guidance, making a profound theological point about divine sovereignty. It arose in the context of the Prophet Muhammad's deep personal concern for the guidance of certain individuals close to him, such as Abu Talib (his uncle who died without embracing Islam) or others among his relatives and companions whom he earnestly wished to see accept faith. The verse gently but firmly corrects any notion that the Prophet's persuasive abilities, sincere supplications, or emotional bonds could compel divine guidance. It establishes that faith is not a product of human effort or relational influence, but flows from God's will and wisdom. The concluding phrase, "He is most knowing of the rightly guided," carries a subtle but powerful implication: what appears to humans as misguidance may, in God's ultimate knowledge, be part of a different path or test, and what seems like guidance may require further purification. This teaches believers that true love for another is expressed not in coercing their beliefs but in sincere concern and trust in God's greater knowledge, while also relieving the Prophet and future messengers of the emotional burden of feeling personally responsible for the faith choices of those they cherish. It is a verse that simultaneously offers consolation—human failure in guiding others is not a failure of one's effort—and warning—spiritual guidance remains exclusively within God's domain, to be sought earnestly but accepted with humility.

translation: }They say, "If we follow the guidance with you, we will be snatched away from our land." Have We not established for them a safe sanctuary, to which the fruits of all things are brought, as provision from Us? But most of them do not know.
interpretation: This verse critiques those who reject the Prophet's guidance by claiming that following his message would expose them to danger, likely losing their lands or security. In reality, God has already granted them a secure sanctuary (Mecca, where the verse was revealed), where provisions flow freely from all directions. The verse refutes their excuse by highlighting their ungratefulness and ignorance: the very security they fear losing was bestowed by God. Their refusal to follow the truth stems not from rational concern but from a failure to recognize divine favors, showing that material attachment and ignorance blind them to the blessings already in their midst. The verse invites reflection on how people often resist spiritual guidance under the pretext of worldly risks, while overlooking the divine protections they already enjoy.

translation: And how many a town have We destroyed that was insolent in its [own] ease of life, and those are their dwellings which have not been inhabited after them except briefly. And it is We who were the inheritors.
interpretation: The verse serves as a stern warning against complacency born of prosperity. It reminds humanity that many communities, granted ease and abundance, grew arrogant and ungrateful, leading to their destruction. Their homes now stand empty, briefly visited or known only through traces, as a testament to divine sovereignty—God ultimately inherits all, and worldly power inevitably fades before His eternal reign.

translation: ,,and your Lord would not have destroyed the cities until He had sent a messenger to their mother city reciting to them Our signs. And We would not have destroyed the cities except when their people were wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse articulates a core principle of divine justice: accountability requires knowledge and warning. God does not destroy a community without first sending a messenger to its central or principal settlement, ensuring the message reaches the wider population. Even then, destruction only comes when the people choose persistent wrongdoing after clear guidance has been delivered. The phrase 'mother city' (ummiha) can mean the main city of a region, which would serve as the conduit for the message to spread, or it can mean the origin point of a people, emphasizing that guidance is sent first to where it will be most effective. The verse asserts that punishment is never arbitrary or premature; it follows a prophetic warning and is then triggered by the community's own injustice. This establishes that human beings are granted the opportunity to know the truth before facing consequences for rejecting it.

translation: And whatever you have been given is [nothing but] an enjoyment of the worldly life and its adornment. And what is with Allah is better and more lasting. Then will you not reason?
interpretation: The verse reveals a profound spiritual reality about the relative value of worldly possessions versus eternal spiritual rewards. The Arabic term 'متاع' (mataa') conveys the concept of temporary enjoyment or provisional benefit, emphasizing the transient nature of worldly gains. 'الحياة الدنيا' (the lower life) deliberately juxtaposes the fleeting material world against the enduring realm of divine presence. 'زينة' (adhinat) refers to the decorative allure that distracts humans from recognizing deeper spiritual realities. The rhetorical question at the end challenges listeners to engage their rational faculties, suggesting that true intelligence involves perceiving beyond surface appearances. The verse implicitly criticizes attachment to material wealth by highlighting its temporal quality compared to the 'أبقى' (more lasting) divine rewards, encouraging a shift in perspective from immediate gratification to eternal significance.

translation: Then is one to whom We have promised a good promise, and he attains it, like one whom We have given enjoyment of worldly life, and then on the Day of Resurrection he will be among those brought [to punishment]?
interpretation: This verse draws a sharp contrast between two categories of people in terms of their ultimate destiny. The first is the believer who sincerely believes in God’s promise of Paradise; God has guaranteed them a beautiful reward, and they will surely receive it. The second is the disbeliever who indulges in worldly pleasures and lives as if this fleeting life is everything; they will face a reckoning, and they will be brought to face punishment on the Day of Judgment. The verse emphasizes that apparent enjoyment in this world is no measure of true success, and that the real outcome is determined by one's relationship with God and one's response to His promises, whether one embraces faith or rejects it.

translation: And [warn of] the Day when He will call them and say, 'Where are 'My partners' which you used to claim?'
interpretation: This verse describes a scene of the Day of Judgment when Allah will address the disbelievers, confronting them with their past claims. During worldly life, they associated partners with Allah—whether idols, false deities, or ideologies they venerated alongside Him. On that Day, these false objects of worship will offer no help or intercession. The rhetorical question 'Where are My partners?' exposes the futility of their previous beliefs. The interrogative form is not for seeking information but for rebuke and humiliation, forcing the disbelievers to acknowledge their own delusion. The verse highlights the contrast between human forgetfulness in this life and the absolute clarity of the Hereafter, where every allegiance and claim will be scrutinized. It also serves as a warning: what people assume to be divine or sacred in worldly life has no reality before Allah, and reliance on such 'partners' leads only to spiritual loss.

translation: Those against whom the word [of punishment] has been justified will say, 'Our Lord, these [the misleaders] are the ones whom we led astray; we led them astray just as we ourselves were astray. We declare our disassociation [from them] before You; we had not been worshipping them.'
interpretation: This verse describes a profound moment of accountability on the Day of Judgment, where those who followed misleaders and deviant paths will attempt to deflect blame onto those who led them astray. The repetition of 'أغوينا' (we led astray) paired with 'كما غوينا' (just as we were astray) reveals a critical spiritual truth: moral responsibility cannot be transferred, for every soul willingly chose to follow falsehood. The misleaders, in turn, reject this accusation by declaring complete disassociation ('تبرأنا إليك') from those who worshipped them, exposing the reality that no false object of worship ever actually commanded devotion to itself—the followers had constructed their own delusions of worship around these entities. The verse dismantles the illusion that anyone can bear the burden of another's sin, affirming that each person possessed the innate capacity to recognize truth and chose otherwise, making their misguidance a self-inflicted consequence of willful turning away from divine guidance.

translation: And it will be said, 'Call upon your partners [i.e., the false deities you worshiped].' So they will call upon them, but they will not respond to them, and they will see the punishment. If only they had been guided!
interpretation: This verse describes the state of the deniers of truth on the Day of Judgment, when they are commanded to seek help from the deities they associated with God during their worldly lives. These false gods will utterly fail to answer their desperate pleas, leaving the disbelievers to face the consequences of their misguidance alone. The verse highlights a profound regret: the realization that had they accepted true guidance during their earthly lives, they would have been spared this terrible abandonment and ultimate doom.

translation: And [mention] the Day when He will call them and say, 'What did you answer the messengers?'
interpretation: This verse describes a profound moment of reckoning on the Day of Judgment, when Allah will directly address those who were sent prophets and messengers throughout their lives. The question is not merely a request for historical information but a confrontation meant to expose the reality of one's response to divine guidance. Those who rejected the messengers will be left speechless, as their worldly excuses will dissolve, while the believers will be granted the strength and clarity to affirm their faith. The verse underscores that every person was given the opportunity to recognize truth through chosen messengers, and accountability rests entirely on how one responded to that divine invitation.

translation: Then they were blinded from the news (or evidences) that day, and they will not ask one another.
interpretation: This verse describes the state of those who denied the truth in this life when they face the consequences of their denial on the Day of Judgment. The term 'anba'' (أبناء), often translated as 'news' or 'tidings,' can also refer to the evidences, signs, or pieces of knowledge that were available to them in the worldly life. The word 'fَ‘umiyat' (فعميت) conveys a sense of being blinded or becoming unable to perceive. On that Day, these former signs and evidences will become obscured or irrelevant to them, leaving them in a state of confusion and helplessness. Consequently, they will not be able to inquire from one another about their situation or seek guidance, indicating their utter isolation and the severity of their condition.

translation: As for the one who repents, believes, and does righteous deeds, then perhaps he will be among the successful.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that sincere repentance, genuine faith, and righteous action form the essential triad for spiritual success. The use of 'asā' (perhaps) reflects divine wisdom, not uncertainty, since ultimate success rests in Allah's hands while remaining a hopeful promise contingent upon sincerity and perseverance. This conditional framing teaches humility, as salvation cannot be assumed through mere claims but is contingent upon a transformed heart and consistent deeds. For modern readers, it offers reassurance that no past is beyond redemption if accompanied by authentic change and ethical living. The verse also positions worldly success as secondary to moral-spiritual flourishing ('falāḥ'), redefining achievement in terms of ethical integrity rather than material gain.

translation: Your Lord creates whatever He wills and chooses. They have no choice whatsoever. Glory be to God, exalted above what they associate with Him.
interpretation: The verse affirms the absolute sovereignty of God in creation and choice, emphasizing that human beings do not possess the authority to dictate what should exist or not exist; rather, everything is subject to the divine will. The phrase 'They have no choice whatsoever' rejects any notion that creatures share in God's prerogative of determining outcomes, directly countering the polytheistic belief that other beings or false deities have the power to choose alongside God. The concluding declaration of God's transcendence ('Glory be to God, exalted above what they associate with Him') serves as a theological corrective, distancing the divine nature from any partnership, similarity, or association with created beings, thereby establishing a strict monotheistic framework where God's will is unchallenged and His essence is incomparable.

translation: And your Lord knows what their breasts conceal and what they declare.
interpretation: This verse affirms Allah's absolute and all-encompassing knowledge of the inner states of human beings—the secrets hidden within the heart (such as doubts, intentions, grudges, or hypocrisy) as well as the words and actions made publicly known. It serves as a profound reminder that nothing in the realm of human thought or expression is concealed from the Divine, which carries with it a sense of divine oversight, accountability, and the ultimate justice that will be meted out based on the full truth of one's inner and outer states.

translation: And He is Allah; there is no deity except Him. To Him belongs all praise in the first [life] and the Hereafter. And to Him belongs all authority, and to Him you will be returned.
interpretation: The verse states that there is absolutely no one worthy of worship besides God alone.  He alone deserves all praise and gratitude for His countless blessings, both in this worldly life and in the eternal life of the Hereafter.  Furthermore, all matters of judgment, authority, and sovereignty belong to Him entirely.  Ultimately, all beings will be returned to Him for their final reckoning.  This emphasizes God's absolute singularity, the importance of praising Him in all circumstances, His complete control over existence, and the certainty of an ultimate meeting with Him for accountability.

translation: Say, 'Have you considered: if Allah should make the night perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what deity other than Allah could bring you light? Will you not hear?'
interpretation: This verse presents a rhetorical challenge to those who deny or neglect Allah, urging them to contemplate a scenario where divine mercy is withheld. By posing the hypothetical of endless darkness, it starkly highlights human dependence on Allah's continuous grace, as the alternation of night and day is not a mechanical inevitability but a deliberate, benevolent provision. The questioning 'Will you not hear?' appeals to human capacity for reason and reflection, suggesting that recognizing such profound reliance logically compels acknowledgment of a single, sovereign deity worthy of worship and gratitude, rather than relying on the false security of perceived natural autonomy.

translation: Say, 'Have you considered: if Allah should make the day continuous over you until the Day of Resurrection, what deity other than Allah could bring you a night in which you may rest? Will you not then see?'
interpretation: This verse presents a profound argument for monotheism by pointing to the divine mercy manifest in the alternation of day and night. The rhetorical challenge is designed to lead listeners to recognize that the very rhythm they take for granted—day for activity and night for rest—is a deliberate, ongoing gift from Allah alone. No other deity possesses the power to alter this cosmic order. The sequence of light and darkness is not a natural accident but an expression of divine wisdom, sustaining human life and providing relief from toil. By asking whether they do not

translation: And of His mercy He made for you the night and the day that you may rest therein and seek from His bounty and that you may be grateful.
interpretation: The verse is addressed to all people, inviting them to reflect on the alternation of night and day as a manifestation of divine mercy. The darkness of night provides a natural opportunity for rest and the renewal of the body, while the light of day enables activity, work, and the pursuit of livelihood. The verse encourages believers to recognize that both rest and the means of sustenance are gifts from God, not mere natural occurrences, and that proper gratitude involves acknowledging this divine favor. The reminder that the ability to work, earn, and rest in turn comes only through God's mercy reinforces the connection between human well-being and divine will, urging a mindset of humility, reliance on God, and thankfulness for His continuous provisions.

translation: And the Day He will call them and say, 'Where are My 'partners' that you used to claim?'
interpretation: This verse depicts a pivotal moment of divine confrontation on the Day of Judgment, where God directly addresses those who associated others with Him during their earthly lives, exposing the hollowness of their beliefs. The rhetorical question is not asked for informational purposes, as God is fully aware of the falsehood of their claims, but rather to compel the disbelievers to face the consequences of their own fabrications and to silence any excuse they might attempt to make. The term 'partners' (shurakā') is used ironically, as nothing in creation truly shares in divine authority or divinity. The phrase 'that you used to claim' (kuntum taz'umūn) carries a tone of rebuke, emphasizing that their attribution of partners to God was based on mere assumption, delusion, or stubborn assertion rather than genuine knowledge or evidence. This moment serves as a ultimate vindication of divine unity (tawḥīd) and a demonstration that false deities possess no power to intercede or respond, leaving the misguided believers with no refuge or justification for their misdirected devotion.

translation: , and We will bring forth from every community a witness, and We will say, "Produce your proof," and they will know that the truth belongs to Allah, and lost from them is that which they used to invent.
interpretation: This verse describes the Day of Judgment when every nation will be confronted with the testimony of their own prophets who witnessed against them regarding their faith and deeds. The phrase 'Produce your proof' is an ironic challenge to those who fabricated lies about Allah, as they will have no evidence to support their false beliefs and practices. The ultimate truth of Allah's sovereignty and the falsity of all human-made doctrines will be made manifest, demonstrating that whatever fabrications they created in worldly life will be completely exposed and invalidated in the Hereafter.

translation: Indeed, Qarun was from the people of Moses, but he oppressed them. We gave him such treasures that their keys would burden a company of strong men. When his people said to him, 'Do not exult; indeed, God does not love the exultant,
interpretation: This verse narrates the story of Qarun (often identified with the biblical Korah), a man from the generation of the Prophet Moses who, despite belonging to the community of a messenger, succumbed to arrogance and transgression (bagha) against his own people through his vast wealth and influence. The sheer magnitude of his riches is illustrated by the vivid image of a group of strong men struggling under the weight of the keys to his storehouses. The verse warns against the corrupting nature of wealth, which often leads to moral decay and a sense of self-sufficiency. The counsel given to Qarun—'do not exult'—is a profound moral directive: joy derived from material accumulation is incompatible with reverence for the Divine, as true joy should be anchored in spiritual contentment rather than worldly possessions. The verse establishes a foundational ethical principle in the Qur'anic worldview: the believer's ultimate allegiance and source of joy must be rooted in the Divine, not in transient material wealth, lest such attachment lead to oppression and hubris.

translation: ...And seek, through that which Allah has given you, the home of the Hereafter; and [yet], do not forget your share of the world. And do good as Allah has done good to you. And desire not corruption in the land. Indeed, Allah does not like corrupters.
interpretation: This verse establishes a principle of balanced religious conduct: prioritizing eternal reward while remaining engaged with worldly responsibilities, all within the framework of moral excellence and the prohibition of causing harm or disorder.

translation: He said, 'I was only given it because of knowledge I have.' Did he not know that Allah had destroyed before him generations who were greater than him in strength and greater in accumulation [of wealth]? And the criminals will not be asked about their sins [because they will be recognized by their marks].
interpretation: This verse condemns the arrogance of a person who attributes his worldly success solely to his own merit and intellect, failing to recognize that all outcomes are governed by divine will. It serves as a sobering reminder that material strength and wealth are not shields against Allah's decree, as entire civilizations with far greater power and resources were previously obliterated. The final clause, stating that criminals will not need to be questioned about their sins, implies that their offenses are so evident—either through their deeds or their recognizable state in the Hereafter—that no interrogation is required to expose their guilt.

translation: And he (Qarun) went forth before his people in all his finery. Those who desired the life of the world said, 'Ah, if only we had like what Qarun has been given! Indeed, he is a man of great fortune.'
interpretation: This verse describes Qarun (Korah) emerging in splendid attire, showcasing the material wealth and worldly status he had accumulated. The reaction of those whose aspirations are confined to the immediate, transient life is captured vividly: they express a wistful longing to possess a similar portion of worldly abundance, and openly acknowledge Qarun as a man of immense good fortune. The verse critiques a worldview that equates human success, favor, and blessing solely with outward material possessions and visible luxury. It illustrates how a society captivated by the fleeting glamour of worldly gain tends to celebrate the wealthy, overlook the means by which their riches were obtained, and fail to recognize the deeper dimensions of true prosperity—such as righteousness, integrity, and ultimate accountability before Allah. The verse implicitly sets the stage for the moral lesson that follows: such material splendor, however dazzling, is temporary and does not reflect true worth or divine approval, since Qarun's wealth was destined to become a source of his downfall.

translation: And those who were given knowledge said, 'Woe to you! The reward of Allah is better for whoever believes and does righteousness. But none will attain it except the patient.'
interpretation: This verse, following the preceding discourse on worldly pursuits and negligence of the Hereafter, depicts the response of the people of knowledge to those who dismiss faith and righteous deeds. The phrase 'وَيْلَكُمْ' (woe to you) is not merely an expression of condemnation but also of sorrow and warning, as those possessing knowledge recognize the gravity of the error in prioritizing temporary worldly gains over eternal recompense. The statement 'ثَوَابُ اللَّهِ خَيْرٌ' (the reward of Allah is better) establishes a fundamental principle of Quranic ethics: that whatever blessings, honors, or profits the world offers are negligible compared to the boundless, eternal reward that Allah has prepared for the believers who act righteously. This challenges the human tendency to measure value by immediate, tangible returns and calls for a radical reorientation of priorities. The concluding clause 'وَلَا يُلَقَّاهَا إِلَّا الصَّابِرُونَ' (and none will attain it except the patient) adds a crucial spiritual dimension: this eternal reward is not achieved merely through belief or aspiration, but requires steadfastness (sabr)—patience in trials, perseverance in obedience, resistance against temptation, and consistency in righteousness. It implies that the path to divine reward is demanding and that only those who endure with unwavering commitment will ultimately reach it. The verse thus serves as both a consolation to the faithful who may feel their worldly share is diminished and a caution to those who abandon eternal values for transient ones.

translation: We caused him [Qarun] to sink into the earth along with his dwelling, and he had no party to assist him against the will of Allah, nor was he among those who could save themselves.
interpretation: This verse refers to the fate of Qarun (Korah), a figure from the story of Prophet Moses (Musa) who was known for his immense wealth and arrogance. The verse illustrates the ultimate powerlessness of those who rely on material wealth and worldly status to protect themselves from divine punishment. When Allah's will decides to punish, no earthly force—no group of supporters, allies, or resources—can avert the consequence. The imagery of being swallowed by the earth signifies a complete, inescapable destruction that targets not just the person but their entire foundation, including their home and the social standing it represented. The verse serves as a profound warning against pride, greed, and the false sense of security that comes from worldly possessions, emphasizing that true power belongs only to Allah and that those who turn away from Him, no matter how powerful they appear, cannot escape His decree.

translation: And those who had wished for his position the day before were saying, "Ah, how Allah extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts [it]! If not that Allah had conferred favor on us, He would have caused the earth to swallow us. Ah, how the disbelievers do not succeed."
interpretation:
This verse refers to the aftermath of the Prophet Qarun's destruction and the reaction of those who had previously envied his wealth and status. The day before, these people wished they could be in Qarun's place, admiring his riches. However, after witnessing the sudden punishment that engulfed him, their tone changes drastically. They now acknowledge that wealth and provision are entirely under Allah's control; He grants abundance to whomever He chooses and withholds it from whomever He chooses, based on His perfect wisdom, not necessarily as a reward for righteousness or a punishment for sin in worldly terms.

The phrase "Wai'kana" (ويكأن) is an Arabic expression indicating astonishment or realization, often translated as "Ah, how..." or "Indeed, it is as if..." The people express their shock, recognizing that if Allah had not shown them mercy, they too could have been destroyed. They realize their vulnerability and that any worldly status they covet is meaningless if it leads to divine displeasure. This realization leads them to the concluding statement: the disbelievers—those who reject Allah's signs, act arrogantly, and covet worldly wealth without regard for the Hereafter—will never attain true success or salvation. This highlights that genuine success (falah) is measured by one's relationship with Allah and adherence to His will, not by the accumulation of material possessions. The verse serves as a powerful reminder that envy of the worldly possessions of those who defy Allah is misguided, and that divine mercy alone protects the believers.

translation: That final home — We assign it to those who do not desire exaltedness upon the earth nor corruption, and the outcome is for the righteous.
interpretation: This verse defines the spiritual qualifications for attaining ultimate success in the afterlife. The 'final home' refers to Paradise, which is reserved not for the powerful or wealthy, but for those who embody humility and integrity. The rejection of two specific traits is highlighted: 'exaltedness upon the earth' (al-'uluww) refers to arrogance, the desire for superiority, and the oppression that comes from seeking to dominate others; 'corruption' (fasad) refers to the active spreading of disorder, whether through injustice, deceit, or harming societal harmony. Thus, the verse establishes that true nobility lies in self-restraint and ethical conduct rather than in worldly status or the exercise of power over others. The concluding statement that 'the outcome is for the righteous' (al-muttaqin) reinforces that ultimate victory and a blessed end belong to those who maintain conscious awareness of the divine and restrain themselves from base desires and harmful actions. It presents a worldview where moral character, rather than material achievement, determines one's eternal destiny.

translation: Whoever comes with a good deed will have better than it, and whoever comes with an evil deed—then those who did evil deeds will not be recompensed except for what they used to do.
interpretation: This verse establishes the principle of divine justice and mercy in the Hereafter: those who present sincere good deeds before God will be rewarded with even greater blessings, reflecting His generosity, while those who come with evil deeds will face a punishment exactly proportionate to their wrongs—neither more nor less.
