The ultimate purpose (illa, 'except') of allowing Iblis to continue his activity is a divine means (li-nalama, 'that We may make known' or 'know') to reveal, through human choice and action, those who sincerely believe in the unseen reality of the Akhirah (Hereafter) from those who are doubtful or uncertain about its occurrence. The 'knowing' here is not an acquisition of new divine knowledge, but rather a manifestation and demonstration of that knowledge in the external reality of human conduct. The verse concludes by affirming Allah's absolute attribute of being al-Ḥafīẓ, the Guardian or Preserver of all things, ensuring that this test unfolds according to His divine wisdom and justice, and that He is fully aware of every action, thought, and intention, holding His creation accountable.

translation: Say [O Muhammad]: 'Call upon those you claim besides Allah; they do not possess an atom's weight [of ability] in the heavens or on the earth, and they have no share in [either of] them, nor has He among them any assistant.'
interpretation: This verse asserts the absolute sovereignty and unshareable power of God, directly refuting polytheism by stating that any being worshipped besides God possesses no independent authority or capability whatsoever in creation. By emphasizing that these supposed deities have no partnership with God in the heavens or earth, and that God does not rely on them as supporters, the verse dismantles the logical and theological foundation of associating partners with the Divine. It challenges the believer to examine the nature of what they invoke in prayer, demanding that true power and ownership reside exclusively with the One who created and sustains all that exists.

translation: And intercession does not benefit with Him except for one whom He permits. [And when] terror is removed from their hearts, they will say, 'What has your Lord said?' They will say, 'The truth.' And He is the Most High, the Grand.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute sovereignty of God over the matter of intercession, indicating that no being can intercede on behalf of another unless God explicitly grants permission. It conveys that on the Day of Judgment, even those in the highest celestial ranks will await God's command with hearts free of anxiety and dread, ready to affirm whatever He decrees as the unalterable truth. This highlights the boundless majesty and supreme authority of God, who alone determines what is just and true.

translation: Say, 'Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?' Say, 'God.' And indeed, we or you are either upon guidance or in clear error.
interpretation: This verse presents a rational argument for monotheism by pointing to divine providence as the basis for accountability, while acknowledging the human condition of either being rightly guided or manifestly astray. By framing the choice between guidance and misguidance in terms of 'we' and 'you', it implies that the distinction between belief and disbelief is not merely theoretical but has tangible consequences in this life and the Hereafter, since it is God who sustains all of creation and will hold all accountable.

translation: Say: 'You will not be questioned about what sins we have committed, nor will we be questioned about what you do.'
interpretation: The verse emphasizes a principle of moral accountability and spiritual detachment. It teaches that each soul is responsible for its own deeds and cannot bear the burden of another's transgressions. The Qur'an, through the Prophet Muhammad, is essentially telling the disbelievers that their attempts to involve the believers in their misdeeds or vice versa are futile. On the Day of Judgment, every person will stand alone before God, answerable solely for their own actions. This underscores the Islamic teaching of individual responsibility, rejecting any notion of inherited guilt or collective sin. Moreover, it serves as a powerful reminder to maintain moral integrity without being swayed by the actions of others, focusing instead on one's own spiritual journey and accountability to God. It also reflects a stance of peaceful disengagement from those who reject the message, refusing to be drawn into cycles of blame or argument, thereby promoting dignity and steadfastness in faith.

translation: Say, 'Our Lord will gather us together, then He will judge between us with truth, and He is the Judge, the All-Knowing.'
interpretation: This verse affirms that ultimate justice rests solely with God, who will assemble all of humanity and render a perfectly truthful and knowledgeable verdict on the Day of Judgment. It encourages patience and trust in divine wisdom, reminding believers that any present injustices or unresolved disputes will be settled by the One who fully comprehends all intentions, actions, and circumstances. The response 'Say' indicates that believers should make this declaration of faith in God's ultimate adjudication, turning away from seeking vindication through worldly means and placing their trust in His absolute knowledge and fair judgment. The divine names al-Fattah (the Opener/Judge) and al-'Alim (the All-Knowing) emphasize that God's decisions are based on complete wisdom and that He alone has the authority to reveal truth and resolve all matters definitively.

translation: Say: 'Show me those whom you have attached to Him as associates. No! Rather, He is Allah, the Almighty, the Wise.'
interpretation: This verse is a direct challenge to those who associate partners with Allah (shirk). It demands them to present evidence for the deities they claim share divinity with Him, exposing the baselessness of polytheism. The emphatic 'No' (كَلَّا) decisively rejects any notion of partners, affirming that Allah alone is worthy of worship. The attributes 'Al-'Aziz' (the Almighty, the Invincible) and 'Al-Hakim' (the Wise) underscore His supreme power and perfect wisdom, rendering any rivals to Him both impossible and absurd. The verse thus dismantles the logical and theological foundation of shirk, calling humanity to pure monotheism (tawhid) and reminding them that all authority and wisdom rest solely with Allah.

translation: And We have not sent you except as a mercy to all the worlds, as a bearer of good tidings and a warner—but most of mankind do not know.
interpretation: This verse establishes the universal and compassionate nature of the Prophet Muhammad's mission, presenting him as a blessing for all of creation rather than limited to a specific community or era. The phrase "كافة للناس" (unto all people) affirms the expansive scope of his prophethood across time and geography, while the pairing of "بشيراً ونذيراً" (bearer of good tidings and warner) illustrates the balanced nature of his message—offering hope and reward to those who believe, while also serving as a sincere warning of consequences for those who turn away. The concluding observation that "most of mankind do not know" serves as both a poignant reality and a subtle invitation: it acknowledges human forgetfulness and heedlessness as the primary obstacle to recognizing truth, suggesting that ignorance rather than malice often prevents people from benefiting from prophetic guidance. This creates an implicit call to reflection, urging individuals to move from a state of unawareness to conscious engagement with the message presented to them.

translation: And they say, 'When will this promise be fulfilled, if you are truthful?'
interpretation: This verse highlights the demand of disbelievers for immediate proof of the promised divine reckoning, exposing both their denial of the unseen and their arrogant mockery of the prophets' warnings. Their request for a specific timeline reflects not genuine seeking of truth, but rather a defiant challenge rooted in pride and refusal to submit to faith. Qur'anic context indicates that such demands arise from hearts already veiled from recognizing the signs already present in creation and divine revelation, serving as a test of whether one will respond with humility or obstinacy.

translation: Say [O Muhammad]: 'Your appointment [for the Day of Judgment] is on a Day which you cannot postpone for an hour nor hasten.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute certainty and fixed timing of the Day of Judgment as determined by God alone. It conveys that no creature has any power to alter, delay, or bring forward this appointed time, even by the briefest measure. The warning embedded in this statement is meant to instill a sense of urgency and seriousness, reminding humanity that their worldly pursuits and excuses will be rendered meaningless when this inevitable moment arrives. It underscores divine sovereignty over time and events, while calling people to live in constant awareness of their accountability before God.

translation: And those who disbelieve say, 'We will never believe in this Qur'an, nor in that which was before it.' But if you could see when the wrongdoers are brought to a stop before their Lord, returning [blame] to one another, those who were oppressed saying to those who were arrogant, 'If not for you, we would have been believers.'
interpretation: This verse portrays the ultimate futility of the disbelievers' defiance against the Qur'an and previous scriptures, revealing that their stubbornness is not rooted in rational inquiry but in arrogant self-assertion. On the Day of Judgment, when they stand before their Lord, the facade of worldly power and influence collapses. The scene of mutual recrimination illustrates how systems of oppression function in this world: the powerful (the arrogant) impose their will upon the vulnerable (the oppressed), and the vulnerable internalize the false belief that their subjugation is somehow incompatible with faith or righteousness. Yet, in that moment of absolute clarity, the oppressed will recognize that the arrogant were the true barrier to their acceptance of truth. This exposes a profound spiritual truth: disbelief is often not merely an intellectual position but a social construct enforced by power. The verse condemns those who use their authority to obstruct others from faith, warning that no worldly dominion can shield one from ultimate accountability, nor can the oppressed escape responsibility by blaming the powerful for their own hearts' surrender.

translation: Those who were arrogant said to those who were weak, 'Did we turn you away from guidance after it had come to you? Rather, you were criminals [yourselves].'
interpretation: The verse depicts a confrontation in the Hereafter between two groups: the powerful elite who persecuted the weak followers of truth, and the oppressed believers who were prevented from embracing faith. The tyrants, refusing to accept responsibility for leading others astray, deflect the blame onto the weak themselves, accusing them of being sinners and thus deserving of their fate. This rhetorical reversal exposes the arrogance of the powerful, who even in the afterlife refuse to acknowledge their role in hindering others from truth. The verse condemns this self-serving denial, affirming that every soul bears responsibility for its own choices, while also highlighting the moral corruption of those who used their power to obstruct others from faith. It serves as a warning against both spiritual complacency and the manipulation of the vulnerable by those in positions of authority.

translation: And those who were oppressed will say to those who were arrogant, 'Rather, [it was your] scheming day and night, when you were commanding us to disbelieve in Allah and set up rivals to Him.' And they will [all] hide [their] regret when they see the punishment. And We will put shackles on the necks of those who disbelieved. Will they be recompensed except for what they used to do?
interpretation: This verse portrays a pivotal moment of confrontation on the Day of Judgment, where the fundamental ambiguity of worldly power dynamics is completely dissolved. Those who were labeled 'weak' or 'insignificant' during their earthly lives will directly address their former oppressors, exposing the manipulative tactics—described as 'scheming day and night'—that were used to enforce ideological conformity and social pressure toward disbelief and polytheism (shirk). The verse highlights how systemic evil often operates not just through overt force, but through persistent propaganda and psychological manipulation. When the consequences of these actions are finally made manifest in the form of divine punishment, all parties will experience profound regret, but this remorse will be internal and concealed ('they will hide their regret'), as it serves no purpose for redemption at that stage. The imagery of shackles on the necks of the disbelievers symbolizes the inescapable binding nature of their consequences; their own deeds have literally forged their restraints. Ultimately, the verse establishes the principle of absolute divine justice: there is no arbitrary punishment, only a precise, exact requital for the choices and actions humans consciously undertook.

translation: And We did not send any warner to a town except that its affluent said, 'Indeed, we disbelieve in what you have been sent with.'
interpretation: This verse describes a recurring pattern in human history: when divine guidance arrives through prophets, it is consistently rejected not by the weak or marginalized, but by the wealthy, privileged, and powerful elite within society. The term "مترفوها" (mutrafuha, "its affluent") specifically refers to those accustomed to luxury and ease, whose material comfort has made them resistant to messages that challenge their status quo or call them to accountability. Their comfortable existence becomes a barrier to recognizing truth, as accepting prophetic guidance often demands relinquishing unjust privileges, altering exploitative systems, or submitting to moral accountability. The verse reveals that opposition to divine messengers is rarely rooted in intellectual objections alone but is frequently driven by class interests—the elite perceive prophets as threats to their wealth, power, and social hierarchies. This pattern of affluent rejection serves as both a historical observation and a warning, suggesting that material prosperity without spiritual awareness can become an obstacle to faith, and that those most blessed with worldly comforts are sometimes least receptive to transcendent truth.

translation: And they say, 'We have more wealth and children, and we are not going to be punished.'
interpretation: This verse exposes the false sense of security that material wealth and numerous offspring can create in a person's mind, leading them to believe that such blessings are signs of divine favor and immunity from accountability. In reality, worldly possessions and lineage have no bearing on one's ultimate standing before God, and such arrogant assumptions only deepen a person's distance from truth and from the moral responsibility required of every soul. The verse thus critiques the delusion that abundance equates to righteousness or safety, reminding the reader that true measure lies in one's relationship with God and adherence to divine guidance, not in external accumulations.

translation: Say, 'Indeed, my Lord extends provision for whom He wills and restricts [it], but most of the people do not know.'
interpretation: This verse from Surah Saba (34:36) teaches a profound lesson about divine wisdom and human limitations in understanding the distribution of wealth and sustenance. While people often observe the rich becoming richer and the poor remaining in hardship, leading them to assume that worldly success is a sign of divine favor or that poverty is a punishment, the Qur'an corrects this misconception by revealing that the true wisdom behind sustenance is known only to Allah. Provision (rizq) is not merely material wealth; it encompasses spiritual, intellectual, emotional, and eternal blessings that may not be visible in this worldly life. A person who appears to have abundant material wealth may be spiritually deprived, while someone with limited material means may possess rich faith, wisdom, and inner peace. Therefore, believers are reminded not to envy the apparent prosperity of others or to despair over their own circumstances, but to trust in Allah's perfect knowledge and wisdom, knowing that what is hidden in this life will become clear in the hereafter. The verse also serves as a call to gratitude and contentment, urging humans to recognize that their understanding of 'plenty' and 'scarcity' is limited, and that true provision extends far beyond what the material eye can perceive.

translation: And it is not your wealth or your children that bring you nearer to Us in [terms of] rank, but whoever believes and does righteousness — it is they for whom there is a multiplied reward for what they did, and they will be in the upper chambers [of Paradise], safe [and secure].
interpretation: This verse reorients the believer's understanding of value and success in God's sight. In societies where material wealth and lineage often determine honor and closeness to power, the Qur'an dismantles this hierarchy. True proximity to the Divine is not inherited through bloodlines or accumulated through possessions; it is cultivated through the inner state of faith (iman) translated into outward ethical action (amal salih). The mention of 'doubled reward' (ziyadah or double recompense) reflects a divine economy of generosity where sincere, small acts of righteousness are magnified beyond their human measure. The image of the 'upper rooms' (ghurafat) being a place of safety conveys an intimacy with God that is both protected from fear and elevated above ordinary worldly attainment. Ultimately, this verse teaches that the only lasting inheritance one gathers in this life is the currency of sincere belief and righteous deeds, which become the sole means of drawing near to God.

translation: And those who strive against Our signs, seeking to weaken [Our message] — they will be brought into the punishment.
interpretation: This verse serves as a stern warning against those who actively oppose, distort, or attempt to undermine the signs and revelations of Allah. The term "يسعون في آياتنا" (striving against Our signs) implies a deliberate and persistent effort to obstruct the truth, while "معاجزين" suggests a futile attempt to overpower or frustrate Allah's will. Such individuals, despite their efforts, are assured of being brought into punishment, indicating that their defiance will not avert divine justice but instead guarantee their exposure to consequence. The verse underscores the futility of resisting Allah's plan and affirms that opposition to His guidance leads only to accountability and suffering.

translation: Say, 'Indeed, my Lord extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts [it] for him. And whatever thing you spend [in His cause], He will compensate it; and He is the best of providers.'
interpretation: This verse establishes the principle that all sustenance originates with God, who determines its flow based on His infinite wisdom rather than human effort or merit alone. The fluctuation of wealth and poverty among people is part of a divine design that extends beyond surface-level causes. The second part of the verse addresses the human response to this divine sovereignty: whatever one gives in charity or spends for good causes, God will not only repay it but provide better compensation. This creates a paradox where apparent loss becomes gain, and generosity becomes the most reliable investment. The verse subtly counters materialist thinking by encouraging detachment from wealth while assuring believers that their generosity will never result in genuine loss. The characterization of God as 'the best of providers' (khayr al-raziqin) implies that no worldly source of sustenance can rival His generosity, and that trust should ultimately rest in Him rather than in material means or human guarantees.

translation: And [mention] the Day when He will gather them all together and then say to the angels: 'Did these [people] used to worship you?'
interpretation: This verse addresses the ultimate futility and misguidance of associating partners with God (shirk), particularly by directing worship toward beings other than Him—such as angels, saints, or other created entities. On the Day of Judgment, God will gather all of humanity together and will directly question the angels regarding the worship that the disbelievers had directed toward them. This confrontation serves to fully expose the error of the polytheists: the angels themselves will neither acknowledge nor accept this worship, and it will be revealed that such devotion was entirely misplaced and unauthorized. The verse underscores God's exclusive right to be worshipped, while also absolving the angels of any complicity in the false veneration offered to them, demonstrating that idolatry is a deviation invented by human beings themselves rather than any genuine invitation from the divine or angelic realm.

translation: , they said, 'Exalted are You! You are our protector instead of them. Rather, they used to worship the jinn; most of them were believers in them.'
interpretation: This verse highlights the absurdity of taking false deities as protectors, emphasizing that the jinn themselves did not accept responsibility for being worshipped, as they acknowledge God's supreme authority and their own servitude to Him. The verse critiques the practice of associating partners with God, noting that the jinn were the true objects of devotion, yet even they disavow this misplaced worship. This reflects the broader theme of misdirected faith, where humans attribute divine status to created beings, leading to spiritual misguidance and a false sense of security in their supposed protectors.

translation: So today no one will have any power to benefit or harm another, and We will say to those who wronged, 'Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny.'
interpretation: This verse describes the absolute helplessness and irrevocable separation of the Day of Judgment. The mutual bonds that existed in worldly life—whether of kinship, alliance, or shared wrongdoing—are entirely dissolved, as no soul can intercede for or deliver another from divine decree. The emphasis on neither benefit nor harm being possible underscores that all authority belongs solely to God, stripping human beings of any illusion of autonomous power. For those who persisted in wrongdoing and rejected the truth of the warning, the verse concludes with a direct address confronting them with the very punishment they dismissed as fabrication, thereby vindicating the truth of God’s promise and sealing the contrast between their former denial and their present, inescapable reality.

translation: And when Our clear verses are recited to them, they say, 'This is not but a man who wishes to turn you away from what your fathers used to worship.' And they say, 'This is not but a fabricated falsehood.' And those who disbelieve say of the truth when it comes to them, 'This is not but clear magic.'
interpretation: This verse describes the three-pronged rejection employed by the disbelievers (kuffar) when confronted with the unequivocal signs of Allah and the message of Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Their objections, despite their variety, all stem from a stubborn refusal to submit to the truth out of blind adherence to ancestral traditions, intellectual arrogance, and a desire to discredit the Prophet ﷺ by labeling his message as magic or lies. First, they accuse the Prophet ﷺ of having a personal, ulterior motive: he wants to divert them from the deities of their forefathers. This reveals their inability to conceive of pure sincerity and their suspicion that anyone challenging their inherited customs must be driven by selfish ambition. Second, they brand the Qur'an itself as a 'fabricated falsehood' (إفك مفترى), implying that it is a human invention rather than divine revelation. Third, they dismiss the Prophet's message and the miracles accompanying it as 'clear magic' (سحر مبين), an attempt to reduce a spiritual and rational challenge to mere illusion and trickery designed to manipulate the masses. Together, these three responses—ad hominem accusation, denial of the scripture's divinity, and reduction of the miraculous to sorcery—form a comprehensive defense mechanism against faith. Allah presents this not as a genuine debate, but as a diagnostic of the sealed heart: when truth arrives, it is met only with deflection, lies, and condemnation, because acknowledging it would demand a surrender of the ego and ancestral authority that the disbelievers worship instead of Allah.

translation: , and We did not give them any scriptures that they could study, and We did not send to them before you any warner.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that the disbelievers of Makkah had no prior revealed scripture or prophet sent specifically to them before Muhammad (peace be upon him), meaning they cannot claim ignorance of prior divine guidance. It highlights that the Qur'an and the Prophet are the first direct admonition they received, making their rejection entirely without excuse and rooted in willful denial rather than lack of knowledge.

translation: And those before them denied, and they had not attained the tenth of what We had given them; they denied My messengers, so how was My disapproval?
interpretation: The verse contrasts the relative power and resources of earlier nations with their ultimate downfall after rejecting divine guidance, serving as a warning that worldly strength cannot protect against the consequences of rejecting faith and prophets, and that divine retribution (nakir) is inescapable when communities persist in denial despite clear evidence.

translation: Say, 'I only advise you of one thing: that you stand for Allah, in pairs and individually, and then reflect. There is no madness in your companion; he is only a warner to you before a severe punishment.'
interpretation: This verse establishes that authentic spiritual counsel is singular in essence though plural in application: the one thing that matters is standing before God with full awareness, both in communal reflection and solitary contemplation. The negation of madness (جنّة) in Muhammad is not merely a psychological defense but a metaphysical assertion—true revelation cannot coexist with mental disorder, because the order, beauty, and consistency of the Qur'anic message testify against any derangement. The phrase "between the hands of a severe punishment" (بين يدي عذاب شديد) frames the prophetic function eschatologically: the warner comes before consequence, not after, meaning that the present moment of hearing is itself a threshold that will not recur. Reflection (تفكّر) is prescribed as the proper response to standing, indicating that mere emotion or ritual is insufficient; intellect must engage reality until the heart is transformed. The progression from pairs to individuals suggests that genuine understanding often requires withdrawal from group conformity, since collective settings can dilute or distort perception.

translation: Say, 'Whatever reward I have asked of you, it is for yourselves. My reward is only from Allah, and He is a Witness over all things.'
interpretation: This verse establishes a clear separation between the Prophet's spiritual authority and any worldly transaction. By stating that any benefit or payment demanded is for the people themselves, it negates the accusation that he is a mercenary for personal gain. Instead, ultimate accountability rests solely with God, who observes all actions, thereby legitimizing his mission as divinely mandated rather than self-serving.

translation: Say, 'Indeed, my Lord projects the truth. [He is] the Knower of the unseen.'
interpretation: This verse establishes the divine nature of truth's projection and the absolute knowledge of God. 'Yaqdhifu bil-haqq' (projects the truth) means that God casts or sends forth the truth decisively to dispel falsehood, often understood in context as revealing the truth to Prophet Muhammad against the disbelievers' opposition, particularly regarding the events at Badr. 'Allam al-ghuyub' (the Knower of the unseen) affirms that God's projection of truth is based on His omniscience, encompassing all that is hidden from creation. The verse serves as a divine authorization and encouragement to the Prophet to confront falsehood with truth, trusting that God's knowledge and power guarantee the triumph of what is real over what is fabricated. It underscores a fundamental Islamic principle: truth is not a human construct but a divine reality that God Himself asserts and protects.

translation: Say, 'Truth has come, and falsehood can neither initiate nor repeat.'
interpretation: This verse from Surah Saba (34:49) establishes a profound metaphysical principle about the nature of truth and falsehood. The command 'Say' (قل) indicates that this is a declaration to be proclaimed universally. Truth (الحق) has arrived definitively, which many scholars interpret as referring to the revelation of the Qur'an or the establishment of Islam as the final message. The phrase 'وما يبدئ الباطل وما يعيد' (falsehood can neither initiate nor repeat) uses the Arabic words يبدئ (initiate/begin) and يعيد (repeat/return), meaning falsehood has lost all power—it cannot begin anything new nor restore what has been undone. This implies a permanent, decisive victory of truth over falsehood. Truth possesses inherent creative power and durability, while falsehood is essentially parasitic and dependent, requiring truth to exist. The verse encourages the believer to understand that aligning with truth is aligning with the ultimate victorious reality, while falsehood, despite its apparent manifestations, is ultimately self-defeating and transient.

translation: Say, 'If I have gone astray, I have only gone astray to my own detriment. But if I am guided, it is only by what my Lord reveals to me. Indeed, He is All-Hearing, All-Near.'
interpretation: This verse establishes a fundamental principle of divine accountability and human responsibility before God. The Prophet is commanded to declare that any error he may fall into does not harm God in any way, but only harms himself, because deviation from truth brings spiritual loss upon the one who deviates. Conversely, when he remains upon guidance, it is solely because of divine revelation from his Lord, meaning he attributes all righteousness and correct guidance to God alone, not to his own effort or intellect. The verse concludes by affirming two divine attributes: God is All-Hearing, meaning He hears the prayers, supplications, and circumstances of His servants, and He is Near, meaning He is close to those who call upon Him, responding to them and aware of their state. This statement also serves as a teaching for all believers, reminding them that misguidance brings harm only to the one who chooses it, while true guidance comes solely from God, and that turning to Him in repentance and reliance is always met with His hearing and nearness.

translation: And if you could but see when they are terrified... and there will be no escape, and they will be seized from a place nearby.
interpretation: This vivid scene depicts the moment of death or the Day of Judgment when those who denied the truth are overwhelmed with terror and realize that no avenue of escape remains. The phrase 'from a place nearby' signifies that the punishment or reckoning seizes them swiftly and inescapably, suggesting that their reckoning has always been close at hand, perhaps delayed in worldly time but immediate in its certainty. The terror described here is not merely physical fear but the existential dread of beings confronted with the absolute reality of their accountability, where all delusions of refuge vanish. The verse thus serves as a stark warning about the suddenness and proximity of divine justice, which, though it may appear distant in worldly perception, is ever-approaching and cannot be evaded.

translation: And they say, 'We have believed in it,' but how can they reach [faith] from a place far away?
interpretation: This verse describes a profound spiritual irony: those who reject the Qur'an and its message, and then later—when facing the consequences of their rejection—claim belief, are in a state of spiritual impossibility. The word 'التناوش' (al-tanāwush) means 'to reach' or 'to grasp something from a distance,' implying that true faith requires a genuine openness of heart that they have already forfeited through their stubborn rejection. Their belated claim of belief is hollow because the disposition to receive faith has been closed off by their earlier defiance; they are trying to grasp something that is now beyond their spiritual reach. The verse condemns not merely disbelief itself but the self-inflicted inability to return to faith once the heart has been hardened against truth.

translation: And they had already disbelieved in it before, and they were casting accusations from a place far off.
interpretation: The verse refers to the disbelievers' prior rejection of the truth and their habit of making baseless accusations against the Prophet and the revelation. Their disbelief is established long before any argument is presented, and their accusations stem not from knowledge or evidence but from a distant, detached position—symbolizing their willful ignorance and opposition to divine guidance.

translation: And a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire, as was done with their counterparts before. Indeed, they were in disquieting doubt.
interpretation: This verse describes a moment of profound regret and divine justice in the afterlife. The 'barrier' (حِيلَ) refers to an insurmountable obstacle placed between the disbelievers and the things they used to desire or seek in the world—such as faith, repentance, or the mercy of God. Having rejected truth in life, they find themselves eternally cut off from what could have saved them. The phrase 'as was done with their counterparts before' links their fate to previous generations of deniers, affirming a consistent moral order in God's dealings with humanity. The final clause, 'they were in disquieting doubt,' exposes the root cause of their downfall: not ignorance, but a persistent, unsettling hesitation that prevented them from committing to faith. Their doubt was not neutral; it was an active state of spiritual paralysis that distanced them from certainty. Thus, the verse illustrates how unresolved doubt, when clung to, becomes a self-imposed barrier to truth, and divine justice responds by sealing off the very opportunities that were once available.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. [All] praise is [due] to Allah, Creator of the heavens and the earth, [who] made the angels messengers having wings, two, three, or four. He increases in creation what He wills. Indeed, Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: This verse presents a theological argument for Allah's absolute sovereignty and creative power by establishing Him as the unique originator of both the cosmos and the spiritual hierarchy. The pairing of 'heavens and earth' as Allah's creation underscores His dominion over both the seen and unseen realms, while the specific description of angels as messengers 'with wings—two, three, or four' emphasizes that even beings who operate in the invisible realm are bound by a created order subject to divine will. The phrase 'He increases in creation what He wills' is particularly significant: it asserts that Allah's creative act is not static or exhausted by initial creation but remains an ongoing, dynamic process through which He introduces novelty, abundance, and gradation into existence as He chooses. This implies that the diversity, complexity, and continuous development observed in creation are not accidents but expressions of deliberate divine will. The concluding affirmation that 'Allah is over all things competent' (Qadir) serves as the foundational premise for the entire passage: it is precisely because Allah possesses unqualified power over all things that His creative acts—whether establishing the heavens, fashioning winged messengers, or adding to creation—are perfectly executed and purposeful. The verse thereby invites contemplation of the visible signs of divine power as evidence of the same unlimited competence that governs the unseen order, urging the reader to recognize that no aspect of existence lies beyond Allah's sovereign capability.

translation: Whatever mercy God opens to people, no one can withhold it; and whatever He withholds, no one can release it after Him. He is the Almighty, the Wise.
interpretation: This verse affirms that all benefit and harm in creation flow from God's sovereign will alone. No human power or worldly authority can block the blessings, opportunities, or relief that God decrees, nor can anyone force open what He chooses to withhold. The closing names remind the reader of the proper posture this truth should produce: recognizing God's irresistible might (Al-Aziz) should free the believer from attachment to worldly means and fearful grasping, while trusting in His wisdom (Al-Hakim) should bring peace that apparent closures or openings are part of a perfect divine plan that operates beyond human comprehension.

translation: O people, remember the favor of Allah upon you. Is there any creator other than Allah who provides for you from the heaven and earth? There is no deity except Him, so how are you deluded?
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound call to reflection and recognition of divine grace, urging humanity to contemplate the origins of their sustenance and existence. By posing a rhetorical question about creation and provision, it dismantles the illusion of multiple sources of power, directing attention to a singular, transcendent source of life. The phrase "how are you deluded" challenges complacency and ingratitude, suggesting that turning away from this reality is a form of self-inflicted misguidance. It emphasizes the importance of acknowledging divine unity not merely as a theological concept but as a lived awareness that shapes one's relationship with the world and gratitude for its blessings.

translation: And if they deny you, then already messengers before you were denied. And to Allah return all matters.
interpretation: The verse responds to the Prophet's grief over his people's rejection by reminding him that this is not unique—earlier prophets faced denial too. It shifts the axis of concern from the immediate failure to persuade to the eternal return of all affairs to God, meaning that ultimate accountability, judgment, and resolution belong solely to Him. The believer is thus freed from the burden of forcing acceptance; his duty is to convey, while outcomes rest with the Divine. This brings both solace and moral clarity: perseverance in the mission, without attachment to immediate results, because history and final judgment belong to God alone.

translation: O mankind, indeed the promise of Allah is true. So let not the worldly life delude you, nor let the Deceiver (Satan) delude you concerning Allah.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine awakening to humanity, emphasizing the certainty of Allah's promise regarding the Day of Judgment and the Hereafter. It warns against two major sources of delusion: the temporary allurements of worldly life—such as wealth, status, pleasure, and power—which can make people forget their ultimate purpose and accountability, and the deceptive whispers of Satan, who beautifies sin and misguides people by making them feel secure from Allah's oversight or punishment. The verse calls for spiritual vigilance, urging believers to anchor their consciousness in the certainty of divine accountability rather than the fleeting illusions of material existence or the false assurances of evil, thereby cultivating a life of purpose, responsibility, and sincere devotion to truth.

translation: Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy. He only invites his party to be among the companions of the Blaze.
interpretation:
This verse presents a direct warning and command regarding the nature of Satan's relationship with humanity. Satan is described as an outright enemy, and believers are urged to respond to this enmity with conscious opposition rather than passive neglect. By labeling Satan as an 'enemy,' the Qur'an frames the spiritual struggle not as a distant myth but as a real and ongoing battle that requires vigilance, awareness, and active resistance.

The second part of the verse reveals Satan's true agenda: he does not merely tempt individuals out of personal malice, but systematically recruits a following—'his party'—whose ultimate destination is the Blaze (Hellfire). This implies that temptations are not random; they are part of a structured opposition to truth. Sin, corruption, and disbelief are portrayed as consequences of heeding a call that leads to collective ruin.

For believers, the verse calls for spiritual discernment: recognizing that every path which normalizes sin, desensitizes the heart, or distances one from divine consciousness is, in essence, an invitation from this enemy. True faith, therefore, is not merely about avoiding major sins but about adopting a stance of conscious opposition to anything that pulls one away from God—whether through desire, ideology, or worldly attachment.

The verse also carries a subtle warning about complacency. Many fall into error not because they deliberately choose evil, but because they underestimate the subtlety of this enemy's call. By urging believers to 'take him as an enemy,' the Qur'an emphasizes that awareness itself is a form of protection—knowing the nature of the threat is the first step in defending against it.

In essence, this verse transforms the believer's worldview: life becomes a field of conscious choice where one must recognize the adversary, reject his invitations, and align with divine guidance as an act of both loyalty to God and self-preservation from ultimate ruin.

translation: Those who disbelieve will have a severe punishment, and those who believe and do righteous deeds will have forgiveness and a great reward.
interpretation: This verse establishes a fundamental principle of divine justice: human actions in this life have corresponding consequences in the next. The contrast between the two groups serves not merely as information but as a profound motivation for the listener. The mention of 'severe punishment' for disbelievers and 'forgiveness and great reward' for the righteous creates a clear dichotomy that calls for self-reflection. The pairing of belief (iman) with righteous deeds (amal salih) is particularly significant—mere faith without action is insufficient, and righteous actions without faith lack foundation. The 'great reward' (ajr kabir) suggests that the blessings awaiting the righteous are beyond human comprehension, encouraging perseverance in faith and good works despite worldly challenges.

translation: Then is one who has been adorned [by Satan] with the evil of his deeds so that he sees it as good [like one who is rightly guided]? Indeed, Allah sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. So do not let yourself perish over them in regret. Indeed, Allah is Aware of what they do.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad regarding those who reject faith despite clear guidance. It draws a sharp contrast between two types of people: those whose evil deeds have been made alluring to them by Satan so that they perceive their wrongdoing as righteous conduct, and those whom Allah has guided. The verse clarifies that divine misguidance and guidance are rooted in Allah's ultimate wisdom and sovereign will—He misguides the willful rejecter who clings to falsehood, and guides the sincere seeker who turns toward truth. Crucially, the verse is a profound pastoral instruction to the Prophet: do not consume yourself with grief, sorrow, or self-blame over the stubbornness of those who refuse to believe, for their fate rests in Allah's omniscient knowledge. It teaches that the messenger's duty is to deliver the message with clarity and compassion, not to bear the crushing emotional weight of human rejection. This verse also serves as a timeless lesson for all believers called to spread truth: one must plant the seed of truth without taking ownership of the response, trusting that Allah sees every hidden motive, every closed heart, and every sincere effort, and that ultimate judgment belongs to Him alone.

translation: And Allah is the one who sends the winds, so they stir up clouds, and We drive them to a dead land, and thereby revive the earth after its death. Thus will be the resurrection.
interpretation: The verse employs the natural phenomenon of wind bringing rain to barren lands as a profound metaphor for the resurrection (al-nashur) that will occur on the Day of Judgment. By presenting this as a visible, recurring example of Allah's power to bring life from death in the physical world, the verse establishes the logical and theological foundation for the certainty of the afterlife. Just as the earth's revival through rain is a tangible reality, the resurrection of human beings from the state of death is an inevitable reality under Allah's command. The divine 'We' (sightings) emphasizes the majesty and authority of Allah's action in driving the clouds, which humans cannot control, paralleling the impossibility of preventing the divine act of resurrection. Thus, the verse invites reflection on the visible signs of Allah's creative power as a precursor to understanding the unseen reality of the afterlife, transforming a natural observation into a certainty of faith.

translation: Whoever desires honor [should know that] all honor belongs to God. To Him ascend good words, and righteous deeds uplift them. But those who plot evil deeds will suffer a severe punishment, and the plotting of those [people] will perish.
interpretation: This verse reorients the human pursuit of power and prestige by declaring that true honor ('izza) is an attribute of God alone. Any glory a person achieves in worldly terms is only a temporary, derivative reflection of the divine nature, not an independent possession. Therefore, those who seek real, lasting honor must seek it through God—by aligning their lives with His will rather than through political maneuvering, tribal allegiance, or self-assertion. The verse then establishes a spiritual mechanism: righteous deeds are the means by which a person's good intentions and words ('the good word that ascends') are elevated and accepted by God. In other words, sincerity must be actualized through action to have any lasting weight. In contrast, those who scheme and plot ('makar') to achieve their aims through deception and wrongdoing—seeking honor through domination rather than through righteousness—are warned that their plots will ultimately collapse and backfire upon them ('their plotting is what causes them to perish'). The Quranic concept of 'makar' here carries a strongly negative connotation: any cunning strategy that operates outside the bounds of justice and truth is inherently self-destructive, because it misreads the nature of reality, where only God possesses ultimate sovereignty. Thus the verse offers both a diagnosis of corrupt ambition and a remedy: humility, sincerity, and righteous conduct are the only paths to genuine, enduring honor.

translation: And Allah created you from dust, then from a sperm-drop, then He made you mates. And no female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge. And no one is granted long life or has his life shortened without being in a Book. Indeed, that is easy for Allah.
interpretation: This verse presents a profound theological reflection on divine sovereignty, human origins, and the meticulous governance of creation. By tracing human existence from dust to sperm-drop to paired beings, it emphasizes that human life in its entirety—from biological genesis to relational formation—is an intentional act of divine craftsmanship, leaving no room for accidental or autonomous origins outside Allah's will. The mention of conception, birth, longevity, and lifespan reduction being recorded in a 'Book' (likely the Preserved Tablet, *al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*) asserts that every detail of existence is known and decreed from eternity, not a product of blind fate or human agency alone. The closing declaration that this is 'easy for Allah' serves to comfort believers: what appears overwhelmingly complex to humans—the orchestration of life, death, and destiny—is effortlessly managed by the Divine. The verse thus functions as both a reminder of human humility before the Creator and an invitation to trust in His encompassing knowledge and decree, free from the illusion that any part of life occurs beyond His awareness or control.

translation: And not equal are the two seas: one fresh and sweet, pleasant to drink, and the other salty and bitter. Yet from both you eat fresh meat, and you extract ornaments that you wear. And you see the ships sailing through them, that you may seek of His bounty, and that you may give thanks.
interpretation: This verse draws attention to the divine wisdom behind the creation of two different kinds of water sources: sweet, fresh water and salt, bitter water. Although they appear contradictory in nature, both serve human needs in multiple ways. The sweet water is pleasant for drinking, while the salty seas provide food (such as fish and seafood), raw materials for ornaments (such as pearls and coral), and a medium for transportation through ships. This serves as a sign of God's mercy, provision, and thoughtful design for humanity. The verse calls on human beings to recognize these blessings and respond with gratitude, acknowledging that everything they enjoy comes from God's bounty. It also subtly encourages reflection on the balance and purpose in creation, urging believers to move beyond mere consumption to conscious appreciation of the divine gifts around them.

translation: He inserts the night into the day and inserts the day into the night, and He has subjected the sun and the moon, each running [its course] for a specified term. That is Allah, your Lord; to Him belongs sovereignty. And those you call upon besides Him do not possess even the membrane of a date seed.
interpretation: This verse presents a profound argument for divine sovereignty through observable natural phenomena, inviting reflection on the nature of ultimate authority and the futility of false dependencies.

translation: If you call upon them, they do not hear your call; and if they heard, they would not respond to you. And on the Day of Resurrection they will deny your associating them with Allah, and none can inform you like [an] All-Knower.
interpretation: The verse makes a profound declaration about the absolute inability of false deities—whether idols, abstract concepts, or even worldly powers that people turn to instead of God—to fulfill the role of the divine. It states that these objects of worship are completely deaf to the supplications directed at them; moreover, even if they somehow possessed the capacity to hear, they would lack the power and will to respond. The verse further emphasizes that on the Day of Judgment, these false deities will themselves disown the act of worship directed toward them, denying any partnership or association with the divine and thereby exposing the folly of those who ascribed divinity to them. The concluding phrase, "and none can inform you like an All-Knower," underscores that only Allah, who possesses perfect and intimate knowledge of the inner realities of actions, intentions, and consequences, can truly clarify the nature of this error and its ultimate outcome. Thus, the verse dismantles the illusion that anything other than Allah possesses independent power to hear, respond, or benefit the one who calls upon it.

translation: O mankind, you are those in need of Allah, and Allah is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: The verse establishes a fundamental relationship between creation and the Creator: all human beings exist in a state of perpetual dependence upon Allah. This need is not merely material—such as requiring sustenance, guidance, or mercy—but encompasses every dimension of human existence, including spiritual, intellectual, and moral aspects. No matter what a person achieves, possesses, or understands, they remain fundamentally reliant on Allah's continuous support and will. In stark contrast, Allah possesses absolute self-sufficiency (الغني), meaning He has no need of any being or thing. His attribute as the Praiseworthy (الحميد) indicates that He is inherently worthy of all praise, regardless of whether creation acknowledges it. This serves as a profound reminder that humility before Allah is the natural posture of the human soul, while arrogance or self-sufficiency represents a fundamental misrecognition of one's true condition. The verse also implicitly calls for trust in Allah alone, since He who is self-sufficient is the only one truly capable of providing for all needs without Himself being in need of anything in return.

translation: If He wills, He can take you away and bring a new creation.
interpretation: This verse conveys the absolute power and sovereignty of God over human existence, emphasizing that humanity is not permanent or indispensable in the divine plan. It serves as a reminder that God's will operates independently of human desire or attachment, and that the continuation of any group of beings depends solely on His choice. The phrase 'new creation' (khalq jadid) suggests not merely replacement but the possibility of an entirely different order of beings, underscoring the contingency of creation itself. This carries an implicit call for humility and reflection: human beings should not become complacent or arrogant about their existence, but recognize their dependence on God's will and live in accordance with that awareness.

translation: And that is not difficult for Allah.
interpretation: The phrase conveys that the matter being discussed—whether it is resurrection, the transformation of state, or the execution of divine will—is not challenging or burdensome for God. It highlights the absolute ease with which Allah accomplishes His purposes, underscoring that His power is limitless and unconstrained by the complexities or obstacles that might hinder human effort. This statement is often used to emphasize that whatever Allah intends to do, He does effortlessly, reflecting His sovereignty and omnipotence over all creation.

translation: ...and no bearer shall bear the burden of another; and if a heavily burdened soul calls [for help with] its burden, none of it shall be carried [by another], even if he should be a kinsman. You only warn those who fear their Lord unseen and have established prayer. And whoever purifies himself - then only for himself does he purify. And to Allah is the final return.
interpretation: This verse establishes several profound principles of individual accountability and spiritual responsibility in Islam. First, it affirms the absolute nature of personal responsibility before Allah—each soul will be judged solely on its own deeds, with no transfer of moral or spiritual burden between individuals, even if they are close relatives. This rejects any notion of inherited sin or vicarious salvation. Second, it indicates that prophetic warning and guidance are effective only for those who possess a genuine consciousness of Allah ('fear their Lord unseen') and who translate that inner awareness into concrete action through establishing prayer. The 'unseen' element emphasizes that authentic piety is not performative but rooted in sincere private belief and conduct. Third, spiritual purification ('tazkiyah') is framed as a wholly self-serving act—meaning that ethical self-development and inner refinement are pursued for one's own benefit, not for any external reward or to impress others. Finally, the verse closes by redirecting all human striving toward its ultimate endpoint: the return to Allah, where every soul will encounter the consequences of its choices. The verse thus weaves together divine justice, personal agency, sincere faith, and eschatological accountability into a unified moral vision, encouraging believers to take ownership of their spiritual development while trusting that Allah alone is the ultimate arbiter of their fate.

translation: And not equal are the blind and the seeing,
interpretation: id

translation: Nor the darkness, nor the light.
interpretation: This phrase, from Surah Al-Falaq (113:3), is part of the prayer for refuge with Allah from the evil of what He has created. The mention of darkness and light together signifies that evil can manifest in any form, hidden or apparent. By seeking refuge from 'whatever Allah has created,' the believer acknowledges that all creation contains potential trials and that ultimate protection lies solely in divine will, transcending human comprehension of good and bad.

translation: Neither the shade nor the scorching heat (will avail them).
interpretation: This phrase completes the imagery of complete futility regarding what false gods can offer or what people rely upon besides God. The shade (الظل) represents comfort, refuge, and protection, while the scorching heat (الحرور) represents harshness, torment, and affliction. Together, they encompass the full spectrum of human experience—both relief and hardship. The verse suggests that neither the comforts people seek nor the afflictions they endure through false means or intermediaries will benefit them in the sight of God. Everything is under divine control, and salvation comes only through God alone. This challenges the pre-Islamic Arabian practice of seeking refuge or making oaths at various objects and shrines, emphasizing that ultimate protection and judgment belong exclusively to God.

translation: And not equal are the living and the dead. Indeed, Allah causes to hear whom He wills, but you cannot make those in graves hear.
interpretation: This verse draws a clear distinction between those who are spiritually alive—responsive to the truth of God—and those who are spiritually dead, closed off to divine guidance. The living, in a metaphorical sense, are those whose hearts are open, while the dead are those who have hardened themselves against faith. The statement that Allah causes whom He wills to hear signifies that genuine spiritual awakening is ultimately a gift from God, granted according to His wisdom and will. The latter part, addressing the Prophet Muhammad, emphasizes that no matter how earnestly he delivers the message, he cannot reach those who have chosen to remain heedless—those who are, as it were, in their graves, both literally and spiritually. It underscores the limits of human effort in the face of divine decree and the reality that guidance is ultimately in God's hands.

translation: You are not but a warner.
interpretation: This verse establishes the Prophet Muhammad's role strictly as a bearer of warning, emphasizing that he holds no divine authority to compel belief or punish disbelievers; salvation and guidance remain in God's hands alone. By defining his mission through this singular function, the verse also reassures him against the heavy burden of people's rejection, reminding both him and his audience that conveying the message is his duty, while ultimate judgment, reward, and accountability belong solely to Allah.

translation: And if they deny you, then already those before them denied; their messengers came to them with clear proofs, with written scriptures, and with the illuminating Book.
interpretation: This verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ by drawing a parallel between the rejection he faces and the rejection endured by earlier prophets and their communities. Those nations also refused the truth even when divine evidence was presented in three successive and complementary forms: 'الْبَيِّنَات' (clear proofs and miracles manifesting divine power directly), 'الزُّبُر' (sacred scrolls and revealed admonitions addressing the heart and moral conscience), and 'الْكِتَابِ الْمُنِيرِ' (the illuminating scripture that dispels darkness through knowledge, law, and guidance). The verse teaches that rejection of truth is a recurring pattern of human history, not a unique failure of this ummah. At the same time, it affirms the consistency of the divine message across all prophets: every nation received the same essential components of guidance, so no community can claim it was left without clear evidence. The believer is thus called to patience and steadfastness, trusting that falsehood cannot ultimately prevail over the light of revelation, just as it never did against the prophets of the past.

translation: Then I seized the disbelievers, and how severe was My reproach.
interpretation: This divine statement follows a passage recounting the fates of past nations who rejected their prophets, emphasizing that after patiently warning them, God ultimately seized them with a dreadful punishment, demonstrating the severe and devastating nature of His response to persistent disbelief and defiance.

translation: Do you not see that Allah has sent down rain from the sky, and through it We bring forth fruits of varying colors? And from the mountains are pathways, white and red, of varying shades, and [others] intensely black.
interpretation: This verse draws the human attention to Allah's creative power manifested in the natural world, using rain as the central mechanism through which diverse life emerges. The phenomenon of rain falling uniformly from the sky yet producing fruits of strikingly different colors, tastes, and forms illustrates that the apparent sameness of cause does not dictate sameness of effect when the Creator's will is operative. The verse then shifts imagery to mountains, where 'judad' refers to the visible tracks, veins, or strata running through mountain formations. These pathways appear in contrasting colors—some white, some red, and others ('ghurabib') so intensely black they seem to absorb light. The word 'ghurabib' is particularly evocative, suggesting a deep, lightless blackness. The progression from white to red to black demonstrates an entire spectrum within a single geological structure. The verse's rhetorical question 'alam tara' (do you not see) challenges the observer to move beyond superficial perception toward recognition of deliberate design. The underlying theological point is that variation and diversity within creation are not accidents but signs requiring reflection. From a single source of water, infinite variety emerges; within a single mountain, complete color spectrums exist. This challenges any reductive worldview that would attribute such systematic diversity to chance, pointing instead to a Creator who, through uniform means, produces inexhaustible variety as a demonstration of attributes such as power, knowledge, and purposeful design. The verse invites the reader to recognize that the natural world functions as evidence (ayah) requiring not merely visual observation but contemplative understanding.

translation: And among people and animals and livestock are various colors (and types). Similarly, only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Almighty, Forgiving.
interpretation: This verse draws attention to the diversity found throughout creation—among humans, animals, and livestock—each with distinct colors, forms, and characteristics, reflecting the boundless creative power and wisdom of God. Yet, true reverence and awe of Allah are not simply a matter of acknowledging His existence outwardly; rather, such genuine fear and consciousness of God arise from deep knowledge and understanding. Those who possess true knowledge—scholars who reflect upon the signs of creation, the divine attributes, and the purpose behind existence—are the ones who truly grasp the magnitude of God's majesty and mercy. Their knowledge leads them to humility, reverence, and a conscious awareness of God's presence in every aspect of life. The verse concludes by affirming two divine attributes: 'Al-'Aziz' (the Almighty), emphasizing God's supreme power that no one can resist, and 'Ghaffur' (the Forgiving), highlighting His mercy toward those who turn back to Him in repentance and knowledge. Thus, the verse links understanding creation with understanding God Himself, and shows that genuine faith is rooted in knowledge that inspires both awe and devotion.

translation:
:
Indeed, those who recite the Book of Allah, establish prayer, and spend from what We have provided them—secretly and openly—hope for a trade that will never perish.
That He may pay them their rewards in full and give them more out of His bounty. Indeed, He is All-Forgiving, Most Appreciative.
interpretation: This verse refers to Allah's promise to those who are patient, steadfast, and conscious of Him, especially in the context of the previous verse about worship, remembrance, and the establishment of prayer. The phrase 'to pay them their rewards in full' indicates that Allah will not allow any good deed of the believers to be lost or diminished, no matter how small. The addition 'and give them more out of His bounty' points to the concept of divine grace (fadl), which is over and above what is strictly due to them according to the measure of their deeds. This reveals that human effort alone cannot encompass the fullness of divine reward; it is Allah's generosity that completes and multiplies the recompense. The concluding attributes, 'All-Forgiving' (Ghaffur) and 'Most Appreciative' (Shakur), highlight two dimensions of divine response to human conduct: forgiveness covers the shortcomings and sins that inevitably accompany human striving, while gratitude (in the sense of divine response) acknowledges and rewards even the smallest acts of obedience. Thus, the verse assures believers that their efforts are never in vain, that divine justice is balanced with divine mercy, and that the relationship between the servant and Allah is characterized by both accountability and boundless generosity.

translation: And that which We have revealed to you, [O Muhammad], from the Book is the truth, confirming what was before it. Indeed Allah, with His servants, is Acquainted and Seeing.
interpretation: This verse affirms the divine origin of the Qur'an revealed to Prophet Muhammad, establishing it as the ultimate truth that validates the previous scriptures revealed before it. It emphasizes that God is fully aware of and attentive to the condition of His servants, indicating that the revelation is not arbitrary but tailored with perfect knowledge of human needs and circumstances.

translation: Then We caused to inherit the Book those We have chosen from Our servants. And among them is he who wrongs himself, and among them is he who is moderate, and among them is he who is foremost in good deeds by permission of Allah. That is the great bounty.
interpretation: This verse refers to the ummah of Prophet Muhammad ﷺ as the inheritors of the revealed scripture, the Qur'an, distinguishing within the community three categories of believers based on their spiritual stations and levels of commitment: (1) the *ẓālim li-nafsihī* (one who wrongs himself), who commits sins but still holds onto faith, falling short in deeds though not abandoning the covenant entirely; (2) the *muqtasid* (one who is moderate), who balances between obedience and occasional neglect, fulfilling obligations without excess or falling into grave error; and (3) the *sābiq bi'l-khayrāt* (foremost in good deeds), who races toward righteous actions through sincere devotion and spiritual striving, attaining this rank only by Allah's permission and grace rather than solely through personal effort. The closing statement, *dhālika huwa'l-faḍl al-kabīr*, affirms that being granted inheritance of the divine book and being distinguished among communities is itself an immense favor, irrespective of one's individual station, because the ultimate outcome for each category—despite differing levels in this world—is paradise and divine pleasure in the hereafter.

translation: [They will be in] Gardens of Eden, which they will enter. They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their garments therein will be silk.
interpretation: This verse depicts a tangible aspect of the reward for the righteous in the Hereafter, using imagery of beauty and luxury familiar to its original audience to convey the overwhelming nature of divine favor. The mention of 'Gardens of Eden' symbolizes a state of eternal, unending bliss, free from the trials and transience of worldly existence. The specific adornments—gold bracelets, pearls, and silk garments—while materially luxurious, also carry symbolic meaning: gold signifies purity and incorruptibility, pearls represent perfection attained through enduring pressure (a metaphor for trials leading to spiritual refinement), and silk, known for its smoothness, suggests comfort and the absence of friction or hardship. Collectively, these elements illustrate a reality where the soul's deepest desires for honor, beauty, and comfort are fulfilled perfectly and eternally, transcending mere physical pleasure to represent a holistic state of grace and divine closeness.

translation: And they will say, 'Praise be to Allah, who has removed all sorrow from us; indeed, our Lord is Forgiving, Appreciative.'
interpretation: This verse reflects a state of ultimate relief and gratitude experienced by the righteous in the afterlife. Having endured the trials, anxieties, and grief of worldly existence, they now stand before their Lord in a state of complete peace, free from any lingering distress. Their praise acknowledges Allah as the sole source of this removal of sorrow, recognizing His forgiveness that pardoned their shortcomings and His appreciation that rewarded their sincere efforts and faith. The pairing of these divine attributes—Forgiving and Appreciative—highlights a profound spiritual truth: Allah's mercy encompasses both the overlooking of human failings and the generous recognition of good deeds, even those imperfectly performed. For believers, this verse offers comfort that the hardships of this life are temporary, while divine compassion and recognition are eternal.

translation: [He is the One] who has settled us in the Home of Eternal Stay (Dār al-Maqāma) by His grace, wherein no fatigue (naṣab) touches us, nor does exhaustion (lugūb) touch us.
interpretation: This verse portrays the ultimate reward of the people of faith as a state of perfect, uninterrupted tranquility granted solely by divine grace. The phrase 'Dār al-Maqāma' signifies a permanent, stable abode, contrasting sharply with the transient, effortful nature of worldly life. The negation of both 'naṣab' (toil and hardship) and 'lugūb' (weariness and its resulting debility) emphasizes that the divine reward is not merely the absence of suffering, but the complete transcendence of the conditions that make existence laborious. It teaches that true and lasting peace is not something human beings can achieve through their own striving; it is a gift ('faḍl') from God that transforms existence into a state of pure ease, where the very possibility of exhaustion has been removed. This reflects the Qur'anic vision that the highest human fulfillment lies in being settled by mercy into a realm beyond effort and fatigue.

translation: ,And those who disbelieve will have the Fire of Hell; they will neither be finished off by it so that they die, nor will its punishment be lightened for them. Thus do We reward every ungrateful one.
interpretation: This verse describes the eternal, unending torment awaiting those who reject faith. The fact that death does not come to relieve them and the punishment is never lessened signifies a state of perpetual suffering with no escape or mercy. The phrase "Thus do We reward every ungrateful one" (كلكفور) links the consequence to the attitude of ingratitude and denial of truth. It serves as a stark warning that disbelief is not merely an intellectual position but carries severe, everlasting consequences. The verse emphasizes divine justice, where the rejection of guidance leads to a punishment that matches the gravity of the offense—ingratitude toward the Creator who provided everything.

translation: And they will cry out in it, 'Our Lord, remove us, and we will do righteousness instead of what we used to do.' But did We not grant you a lifetime during which anyone who reflected could have reflected? And the warner came to you, so taste [the punishment]. For the wrongdoers, there is no helper.
interpretation: This verse confronts the belated remorse of those in Hell, who beg for a second chance to amend their deeds after having spent a lifetime in heedlessness. The rhetorical question—'did We not grant you a lifetime…?'—stresses that human beings were given ample years of opportunity, intellect, and the arrival of warners (prophets or reminders) to awaken conscience and turn toward righteousness. The failure was not due to ignorance or lack of time but to a deliberate neglect of moral reflection. Thus, their plea for return is rejected not out of cruelty but because the natural order of accountability has been exhausted: when guidance is offered and refused, consequences follow. The closing declaration—that the wrongdoers have no helper—underscores that no intercession or worldly power can rescue those who consciously chose wrongdoing despite every chance for repentance. The verse is ultimately a warning in this life: reflection and reform must happen now, while the opportunity still exists, because the moment of death seals the door to change.

translation: Indeed, Allah is the Knower of the unseen of the heavens and the earth. He is the All-Aware of what is in the hearts (of His creation).
interpretation: This verse affirms Allah's absolute and encompassing knowledge, extending to all hidden matters, both in the vast cosmos of the heavens and the earth, and in the most intimate aspect of His creation: the inner workings of the human heart. It serves as a profound reminder of divine omniscience, emphasizing that no secret, intention, or concealed reality is hidden from Allah. This awareness of the unseen and the thoughts within the chest is not merely passive observation but reflects a perfect, encompassing, and continuous understanding. The verse calls individuals to recognize that their inner states are fully exposed to Allah, which instills a profound sense of accountability and encourages sincerity in belief and action, knowing that all intentions and thoughts are subject to divine knowledge.

translation: He is the one who placed you as successors on the earth. So whoever disbelieves – upon him is his disbelief, and the disbelief of the disbelievers does not increase their Lord with them except in disgust, and the disbelief of the disbelievers does not increase them except in loss.
interpretation: This verse conveys that the privilege of human stewardship on Earth is not an absolute or unconditional gift; rather, it functions within a moral and covenantal framework tied to accountability. By establishing humanity as khalifs (successors or vicegerents), the verse implies a transfer of responsibility where each generation, and each individual, inherits the duty to uphold divine guidance. The phrase 'faman kafara fa'alayhi kufruhu' ('so whoever disbelieves, upon him is his disbelief') emphasizes personal moral responsibility and the absence of coercion in matters of faith – a foundational principle in Qur'anic theology. The repetition of the phrase regarding the disbelievers ('la yazidu al-kafirin kufruhum') serves a rhetorical purpose: to underscore a profound psychological and spiritual reality. Disbelief does not harm God, nor does it diminish His sovereignty; instead, it invites divine 'maqt' (deep displeasure, wrath, or detestation) and results in 'khasara' (loss, ruin, deficit). The dual repetition is significant – it stresses both the relational rupture between the Creator and the creation, and the existential, spiritual, and eschatological loss incurred by the one who rejects faith. Importantly, the verse does not deny God's mercy to disbelievers, nor does it assert that their fate is eternally sealed by their initial choice; rather, it describes the immediate consequence and trajectory of persistent, willful rejection. The term 'maqt' is distinct from 'ghayd' (anger) or 'la'n' (curse); it suggests a profound turning away in divine regard – a state of being held in contempt due to persistent ingratitude and denial, despite clear signs and rational proofs. This concept is reinforced elsewhere in the Qur'an (e.g., 9:96, 40:10), where God's 'maqt' falls upon those who knowingly reject truth after it has been made clear. The term 'khasara' encompasses loss not only in the afterlife but also in this world – loss of moral direction, spiritual insight, and ultimate purpose. This aligns with a broader Qur'anic theme where faith is described as a source of 'falah' (success, welfare, flourishing), and its absence as 'khusran' (loss, ruin). Thus, the verse functions simultaneously as a warning and a theological statement: human stewardship on Earth carries moral weight, disbelief does not diminish God's majesty but corrupts the human soul, and such corruption inevitably manifests as both estrangement from the divine and as self-inflicted loss.

translation: Say, 'Have you considered your 'partners' whom you call upon besides Allah? Show me what they have created of the earth, or do they have a share in the heavens? Or have We given them a book so that they are on a clear proof from it?' Rather, the wrongdoers only promise one another delusion.
interpretation: This verse is a direct rhetorical challenge from Allah to the polytheists, demanding them to produce tangible evidence of their idols' divine power or legitimacy. By questioning whether these false deities created anything on earth, participated in the heavens, or received divine scripture, the verse exposes the unfounded nature of shirk (associating partners with Allah). The concluding statement warns that any promises or reassurances made among those who persist in injustice are nothing more than empty delusion, highlighting that the entire basis of polytheism rests on illusion rather than truth.

translation: Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth, lest they cease [to function]. And if they were to cease, no one could hold them [in place] after Him. Indeed, He is Forbearing and Forgiving.
interpretation: This verse highlights Allah's absolute sovereignty and power in sustaining the universe. The heavens and the earth remain in their stable orbits and continue to function only because Allah sustains them; were He to withdraw His support, nothing in existence could maintain them. The mention of Allah's attributes as "Forbearing" (Halim) and "Forgiving" (Ghafoor) at the conclusion connects His infinite might with His mercy, suggesting that He grants time and pardons humanity despite our failings, rather than holding the universe accountable for the corruption caused by human deeds.
