Thus, believers are called to trust in God's quiet, often unseen workings in their lives, recognizing that His provisions come from a source of complete authority and unmatched strength, even when the means appear humble or the timing unclear. The verse reassures the faithful that nothing escapes God's grasp, and His kindness is neither accidental nor limited.

translation: Whoever desires the harvest of the Hereafter – We will increase for him his harvest. And whoever desires the harvest of this world – We will give him thereof, but in the Hereafter he will have no share.
interpretation: This verse establishes a fundamental principle of divine justice: human intentions and goals determine one's eternal recompense. Those who sincerely strive for everlasting reward through righteous deeds will find their efforts multiplied and blessed by God, while those whose ambitions are confined solely to material, worldly gains will receive their portion in this life but will be excluded from the blessings of the next. The verse underscores that the pursuit of the Hereafter is not a negation of worldly engagement but a reorientation of purpose—prioritizing eternal outcomes over temporal ones, and recognizing that worldly success without spiritual orientation leaves one spiritually bankrupt in the ultimate reality.

translation: Or do they have partners [in divinity] who have ordained for them a religion that God has not authorized? And if not for the decisive word, it would have been judged between them. And indeed, the wrongdoers will have a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse condemns those who fabricate religious laws and rituals based on human desires or cultural traditions rather than divine revelation, asserting that any religious legislation must originate from God's permission alone. It warns that while divine justice may be delayed by God's predetermined decree, those who unjustly ascribe partners to Him or distort His religion will ultimately face severe retribution in the hereafter, emphasizing that accountability for such transgressions is certain.

translation: You will see the wrongdoers fearful of what they have earned, when it has befallen them. And those who believe and do righteous deeds will be in the flowery meadows of the Gardens; they will have whatever they wish from their Lord. That is the great bounty.
interpretation: This verse establishes a stark contrast between two groups on the Day of Judgment. The wrongdoers, burdened by the weight of their sins, are seized by overwhelming terror as they face the inescapable consequences of their deeds. Their fear reflects the reality that worldly gain purchased through injustice yields only punishment. In contrast, the believers who performed righteous actions are granted a place of beauty and delight—'the flowery meadows'—a metaphor for the expansive, flourishing bliss of Paradise. Crucially, the verse emphasizes that the believers receive 'whatever they wish' from their Lord, suggesting that their reward is not limited or measured but flows from divine generosity. The concluding phrase, 'that is the great bounty,' highlights that entrance into Paradise and the unlimited favor of God constitute the supreme honor one can attain, far surpassing any worldly status or achievement.

translation: That is the good tidings which Allah gives to His servants who believe and do righteous deeds. Say, 'I do not ask you for it any payment except love of [my] relatives. And whoever commits a good deed — We will increase for him good therein. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Appreciative.
interpretation:
This verse presents a profound synthesis of divine mercy, prophetic sincerity, and the reciprocal nature of righteousness. The 'good tidings' are not abstract promises but the very announcement of divine favor bestowed upon those whose faith manifests in righteous action — a reminder that belief without ethical embodiment remains incomplete.

The Prophet's declaration that he seeks no material compensation from his community, only love for his near relatives (ahl al-bayt, or his kinsfolk according to various interpretations), reveals a spiritual economy that inverts worldly expectations. He asks not for wealth, status, or obedience to himself, but for love to be cultivated among those bound by sacred kinship — suggesting that the health of the ummah depends on the bonds of affection between those who share proximity to the Messenger.

The verse then affirms a divine principle: every good deed, however small, is multiplied in goodness by God. This is not transactional arithmetic but an expression of divine generosity. The closing divine attributes — Forgiving and Appreciative — frame the entire passage: God pardons human shortcomings while recognizing and rewarding sincere effort, however modest. Together, these attributes assure the believer that the path of righteousness is walked not in fear of divine severity but in trust of a Lord who overlooks faults and values intention.

translation: Or do they say, 'He has fabricated [something] about God'? Then [if] God willed, He could seal over your heart. And God eliminates falsehood and establishes truth by His words. Indeed, He is Knowing of that within the breasts.
interpretation:
This verse addresses the accusations of disbelievers who claimed that the Prophet Muhammad fabricated lies about God, meaning he invented the Quran or the message of Islam himself. God consoles and strengthens His Prophet, assuring him not to be distressed by their false claims. 

The verse is a powerful statement about divine will and the preservation of truth. It begins with a rhetorical question challenging the disbelievers' accusation of fabrication. It then affirms that if God had willed, He could have sealed the Prophet's heart, preventing him from receiving or conveying the message, meaning the Prophet's ability to receive revelation is entirely under God's control, not his own invention. The emphasis here is that the Prophet's role is passive in receiving revelation; he is a vessel for God's words. 

The core of the verse is a promise: God will eliminate falsehood (الباطل) and establish truth (الحق) through His words (بكلماته). This signifies that despite the temporary triumphs of falsehood and the doubts cast by disbelievers, ultimate victory belongs to truth. God's knowledge encompasses the innermost thoughts, intentions, and certainties within human hearts (ذات الصدور). This reinforces the idea that human judgment is fallible, and God alone knows the true nature of the Prophet's sincerity and the reality of the message.

translation: And He is the One Who accepts repentance from His servants and pardons the evil deeds, and He knows what you do.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes three interconnected divine attributes that form the foundation of the believer's relationship with Allah. First, Allah actively accepts repentance (tawbah), meaning that turning back to Him is not merely a private matter but one that He receives and responds to, provided it meets the conditions of sincerity, cessation of the sin, and determination not to return. The use of the active verb 'yaqbalu' (accepts) implies continuous readiness—Allah's mercy is perpetually available, not closed at any moment. Second, He 'yafū' (pardon/wipes away) the evil deeds, which goes beyond mere acceptance of repentance; it involves the actual erasing of sins as if they never occurred, reflecting a boundless generosity that exceeds the gravity of human error. Third, the mention that He 'knows what you do' serves as both a warning and a comfort—it warns against heedlessness since actions are never hidden, yet it also reassures that sincere repentance is recognized by One who is fully aware of the circumstances and intentions behind every deed. The verse, coming in the context of God's response to those who despair of His mercy or assume He is unaware, encourages believers to never abandon hope, for the divine door of return remains open as long as the soul has not reached its final moment.

translation: And those who believe and do righteous deeds are responded to (by Allah), and He increases them from His bounty. But the disbelievers will have a severe punishment.
interpretation: This verse establishes a fundamental reciprocity in the relationship between the believer and the Divine: faith (iman) when paired with righteous action (amal salih) is not a passive state but an active appeal that elicits a response from Allah. The word 'yastajib' (responds to) implies that Allah turns toward the servant who turns toward Him, meeting sincere belief and ethical effort with an answering grace. Moreover, the addition 'wa yaziduhum min fadhlihi' (and He increases them from His bounty) reveals that divine response is not merely reciprocal in kind but is always superabundant—Allah gives more than what was asked or earned, which is the very meaning of grace (fadl). This contrasts sharply with the second clause, where the disbelievers, who withhold both belief and righteous deeds, receive what corresponds to their state: not bounty but 'adhab shadid' (a severe punishment). The juxtaposition illustrates an ongoing cosmic moral order in which human choices—faith with action, or rejection with indifference—determine the quality of what returns to them, either multiplied grace or severe reckoning.

translation: And if Allah were to extend provision to His servants, they would surely commit transgression on the earth, but He sends down what He wills in a measured way. Indeed, He is, of His servants, Aware and Seeing.
interpretation: The verse establishes the divine wisdom behind the measured distribution of sustenance in the world: boundless wealth, absent of struggle or accountability, would corrupt human nature and lead to widespread transgression, as people forget their dependence on the Divine when basic needs are effortlessly met; therefore, Allah deliberately apportions provision according to a precise wisdom that balances human testing with mercy, for He alone fully perceives the inner states, capacities, and inclinations of every servant, knowing precisely what each individual or community requires to be tried, refined, and brought back to Him.

translation: And it is He who sends down rain after they have despaired and spreads His mercy. And He is the Protector, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: This verse affirms that Allah's mercy and power manifest through His response to human desperation, as He sends rain after people have lost all hope, demonstrating that His assistance often comes precisely when circumstances seem most bleak. The divine attributes mentioned here—Al-Wali (the Protector/Guardian) and Al-Hamid (the Praiseworthy)—indicate that Allah's intervention is not arbitrary but stems from His caring guardianship over creation and His inherent worthiness of praise regardless of whether His mercy is visibly evident. The verse carries a profound message about patience and trust in divine timing, teaching that periods of hopelessness are not permanent states but often precede the greatest demonstrations of divine grace.

translation: And of His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth and whatever living creatures He has dispersed throughout them. And He is able to gather them whenever He wills.
interpretation: This verse points to the diversity and distribution of life across the cosmos as a sign of God's creative power, while affirming that the same power that scattered living beings throughout creation will, by His will, bring them all together on the Day of Judgment—demonstrating that resurrection and ultimate accountability are as certain and within His capability as His original act of creation.

translation: Whatever misfortune befalls you is because of what your hands have earned, and He pardons much.
interpretation: This verse affirms the principle of moral cause and effect: human suffering and adversity generally arise from the consequences of one's own choices and actions, reflecting accountability in the moral order. Simultaneously, it acknowledges divine mercy by stating that God pardons far more than He punishes, indicating that what people endure is only a fraction of what their actions might warrant, while much is overlooked through divine grace.

translation: And you cannot escape [Him] in the earth, nor do you have besides Allah any protector or helper.
interpretation: This verse, revealed in the context of the Meccan period, addresses the disbelievers who denied the Prophet Muhammad and the resurrection, reminding them that Allah's power and knowledge encompass the entire earth. No one can flee from His grasp or escape His decree. The verse underscores that human beings are utterly dependent on Allah and possess no inherent ability to save themselves from His authority. Any protector or helper they seek must ultimately come from Him alone. It serves as a warning that attempts to evade accountability for one's actions, particularly denial of truth and rejection of divine guidance, are futile. The verse emphasizes tawhid (the absolute oneness of Allah) and human vulnerability, calling for reliance on Allah rather than false attachments to worldly powers or idols.

translation: And among His signs are the ships sailing through the sea like mountains.
interpretation: The Arabic phrase "كَالْأَعْلَامِ" (ka-al-aʿlām) literally means 'like banners' or 'like flags/poles,' though classical commentators have commonly rendered it as 'like mountains.' This comparison reflects the awe-inspiring scale of ships traversing the ocean, drawing attention to humanity's reliance on divine design in both natural and constructed realms. The verse emphasizes that sailing vessels are a manifestation of divine power (āyah), suggesting that human ingenuity and engineering exist only through Allah's will. The reference to the sea connects to several Qur'anic themes of divine power over nature, while the comparison to mountains (aʿlām, which can also mean 'tall structures' or 'poles') highlights the imposing presence of these ships on the water. The verse invites contemplation of the balance between human capability and divine sustenance: while ships are human-made, their ability to navigate the sea depends entirely on natural laws established by Allah.

translation: If He wills, He can still the wind, and they would remain motionless on its surface. Indeed in that are signs for everyone patient and grateful.
interpretation: This verse highlights the power and will of Allah over the natural world, specifically the sea and the winds. It illustrates that the ability to still the wind and halt ships on the water's surface is a divine prerogative, not a human one. By mentioning that

translation: Or He may destroy them for what they have earned, and He pardons much.
interpretation: This verse refers to God's power and choice regarding the consequences of human wrongdoing: He could destroy people for their sins, but instead He often chooses to forgive and show mercy, overlooking many offenses rather than punishing every transgression.

translation: And He will teach those who argue about Our verses that they have no refuge [i.e., no escape from punishment].
interpretation: This verse addresses those who engage in disputes and arguments regarding Allah's signs and revelations, denying or distorting them. It warns them that their argumentation will not avail them before Allah, and they will find no escape or place of refuge from His punishment. It serves as a divine reminder that defiance of the truth through debate and sophistry will only lead to accountability, as Allah knows the intentions behind such disputes and will expose the falsehood of those who persist in opposing His guidance.

translation: And whatever you have been given is [only] a temporary enjoyment of the life of this world, but what is with Allah is better and more lasting for those who believe and put their trust in their Lord.
interpretation: This verse presents a profound contrast between the fleeting nature of worldly possessions and the enduring rewards of the Hereafter. It acknowledges that any material wealth, status, or comfort attained in this life is merely a temporary provision, subject to inevitable decay and loss. The phrase 'what is with Allah' signifies divine favor, spiritual fulfillment, and eternal reward, which transcends the transient nature of worldly gains. The verse specifically addresses 'those who believe and rely upon their Lord,' highlighting that true security and lasting benefit are found not in amassing worldly treasures but in faith and dependence on God. This calls believers to shift their aspirations from ephemeral worldly pursuits to the enduring blessings of the divine realm, fostering a perspective that values spiritual richness over material accumulation.

translation: And those who avoid the major sins and immoralities, and when they are angry, they forgive.
interpretation: This verse describes a noble moral quality of the believers, who are conscious of God and strive to live a righteous life. They are mindful to avoid committing major sins and shameful acts, yet they are not immune to human emotions such as anger. When anger arises, they choose the path of forgiveness rather than retaliation. This reveals that true righteousness is not merely the avoidance of sin but the mastery of one's impulses, responding to provocation with clemency and grace, reflecting a heart anchored in mercy and self-restraint.

translation: And those who respond to their Lord, establish prayer, conduct their affairs by mutual consultation, and spend from what We have provided them,
interpretation: This verse outlines the defining qualities of the successful servants of Allah (الْفَالِحُونَ) within the broader context of Surah Ash-Shura. It describes a comprehensive model of faith that integrates four essential principles: spiritual commitment, social responsibility, collective governance, and economic solidarity. First, responding to the Lord signifies obedience that arises from a conscious recognition of Allah's authority, going beyond mere ritual to encompass a sincere engagement with divine guidance. Second, establishing prayer represents the foundational pillar of worship that anchors the believer's daily life and maintains spiritual consciousness. Third, the principle of mutual consultation (شُورَى) is particularly significant as it establishes that legitimate decision-making within the believing community must be based on collective dialogue and deliberation rather than autocratic imposition, establishing a foundational Islamic principle of participatory governance. Fourth, spending from what Allah has provided reflects the economic dimension of faith, where wealth is viewed as a trust from Allah to be shared with those in need, thereby preventing hoarding and fostering social cohesion. These four traits together illustrate that true success in Islam requires harmony between the individual's relationship with Allah, their conduct within the community, their method of making collective decisions, and their approach to material resources—portraying the ideal Muslim as someone who is spiritually grounded, socially responsible, politically consultative, and economically generous.

translation: And those who, when wronged, defend themselves.
interpretation: This verse affirms the moral legitimacy of self-defense and standing up against injustice. It establishes that retaliation in the face of oppression is not merely permissible but a characteristic of the righteous, distinguishing between patience as forbearance and patience as surrender to wrongdoing. The verse implicitly condemns passivity in the face of tyranny, suggesting that allowing oneself to be wronged without response can embolden the oppressor and betray the trust Allah places in believers as stewards of justice. However, this self-defense must remain within the bounds of proportionality and justice, as the broader Qur'anic ethic insists that even resistance to oppression cannot become an excuse for excess or further transgression.

translation: The recompense for an evil is an evil like it, but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is due from Allah. Indeed, He does not like the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse establishes a foundational principle of justice tempered with mercy in Islamic ethics. While it affirms the moral law of equivalence—that wrongdoing deserves proportionate consequences—it immediately elevates forgiveness as the superior moral response. The phrase "his reward is due from Allah" transforms pardon from passive non-retaliation into an active, rewarded act of righteousness, suggesting that restraint in the face of provocation carries spiritual weight beyond human calculation. The concluding warning, "He does not love the wrongdoers," carries a layered meaning: while forgiveness is commended, this divine disapproval targets those who persist in injustice, implying that the ethical duty remains on both sides—the wrongdoer must cease, and the wronged must choose mercy when possible. The verse thus balances accountability with grace, teaching that true moral strength lies not in retaliation but in the courage to forgive while trusting divine justice to complete what human mercy leaves undone.

translation: But whoever defends himself after he has been wronged – there is no blame upon them.
interpretation: This verse establishes a foundational principle of justice in Islamic law: the right of self-defense against oppression. When a person has been subjected to wrongdoing, their subsequent act of retaliation or defense to restore their rights is not only permissible but carries no sin or legal penalty. This is part of a broader ethical framework that distinguishes between aggression—which is condemned—and the legitimate response of a victim seeking justice or repelling harm. The verse implicitly acknowledges human vulnerability to injustice and provides moral and legal cover for those who stand up against it, reinforcing the Qur'anic value that oppression cannot go unanswered, while still maintaining that the response must be proportionate and aimed at justice rather than excess.

translation: ...Indeed, the way [to blame] is only against those who wrong the people and transgress upon the earth without right. These will have a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse clarifies that legitimate retaliation or blame is directed solely against those who commit injustice and spread corruption in the land unjustly, and that such transgressors will face a severe reckoning in the hereafter.

translation: But indeed, if one endures patiently and forgives, that is among the matters of determination (and courage).
interpretation: This verse praises the qualities of patience in the face of wrongdoing and forgiveness toward those who have caused harm. Rather than retaliating, a person restrains their anger, bears the offense with composure, and pardons the offender. The Qur'an elevates this conduct as a hallmark of strength of character and firm resolve, suggesting that true moral courage lies not in aggression or vengeance but in self-control and magnanimity. Forgiveness here is framed not as weakness but as an active, disciplined choice that reflects inner fortitude and a higher ethical standard.

translation: And whoever Allah leads astray, there is no protector for him after Him. And you will see the wrongdoers, when they see the punishment, saying, 'Is there any way to return?'
interpretation: This verse underscores a profound theological reality in Islam regarding the nature of divine guidance and misguidance. It establishes that ultimate misguidance comes from Allah, and once He withdraws His guidance from a person due to their persistent rejection of truth, no other protector or intercessor can save them from the consequences of their own choices. The second part of the verse vividly portrays the regret of the wrongdoers on the Day of Judgment when they witness the punishment—they desperately seek any avenue of return to the worldly life to rectify their deeds. This reflects the Islamic teaching about the irreversibility of the Hereafter and the agonizing realization that opportunities for repentance and amendment have passed. It serves as a powerful warning about the importance of heeding divine guidance in this life, as the chance to return and change one's course will not be available after death.

translation: And you will see them being exposed to it, humbled in abasement, looking with a furtive glance; and those who believed will say, 'Indeed, the losers are those who lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection.' Unquestionably, the wrongdoers will be in a lasting punishment.
interpretation: This verse depicts the contrasting states of two groups on the Day of Judgment: the wrongdoers and the believers. The wrongdoers are shown in a state of utter humiliation and disgrace, being exposed to the punishment of Hellfire. Their posture is one of complete submission and dejection, "humbled in abasement," and they can only look at the horror before them with a "furtive glance," too terrified to stare directly. This description emphasizes the magnitude of their loss. In contrast, the believers, observing this scene, articulate the ultimate nature of that loss: the wrongdoers are not merely deprived of paradise, but have fundamentally lost their very selves and, by extension, their families, who would have been their companions in salvation. The verse concludes with a definitive statement that this punishment is not temporary but "lasting," underscoring the eternal consequence of their injustice in the world.

translation: And they will have no protectors to help them besides Allah. And whoever Allah leads astray – for him there is no way [to guidance].
interpretation: This verse establishes a fundamental principle of divine sovereignty in matters of guidance and misguidance. It teaches that no created being—whether human, jinn, or idol—possesses any power to save or guide those whom God has determined to be astray. The verse underscores that ultimate authority rests solely with the Divine, and that misguidance is not an accidental occurrence but part of a purposeful divine pattern tied to a person's inner disposition and choices. This serves as both a warning against false attachments to powerless intermediaries and a call to recognize that sincere, correct guidance comes only from turning to God. It also implicitly encourages self-reflection: if a person finds themselves in confusion or misguidance, they should examine their own relationship with God rather than seeking salvation elsewhere.

translation: Respond to your Lord before there comes a Day from Allah that cannot be averted. On that Day, you will have no refuge, nor will you be able to deny [anything].
interpretation: This verse is a powerful summons to obedience and repentance before the inevitable arrival of the Day of Judgment. The phrase 'respond to your Lord' (استجيبوا لربكم) is an active call demanding immediate action—turning toward Allah in obedience, worship, and submission before a time arrives when such response will be impossible. The 'Day that cannot be averted from Allah' (يوم لا مرد له من الله) emphasizes that this Day will come by Allah's decree alone, unstoppable by any human effort, influence, or intercession. The verse highlights the helplessness of humanity on that Day: 'you will have no refuge' (ما لكم من ملجإ) means there will be no place to hide or seek protection, and 'nor will you be able to deny [anything]' (وما لكم من نكير) means one cannot refute, argue against, or conceal one's deeds. Together, this serves as a profound warning that the opportunities for repentance, correction, and choice exist only in this worldly life; once the Hereafter begins, the soul stands exposed before Allah with no escape and no defense, making the present moment a critical opportunity for sincere return to the Lord.

translation: If they turn away, We have not sent you as a guardian over them; your duty is only to convey [the message]. And when We give man a taste of mercy from Us, he rejoices in it; but if evil befalls him for what his hands have earned, then indeed, mankind is ungrateful.
interpretation: This verse outlines the limits of the Prophet's mission and the nature of human disposition. He is not charged with compelling belief or protecting people from the consequences of rejecting faith; his role is exclusively one of clear delivery of divine guidance. The second part highlights a fundamental contradiction in human behavior: when blessings are received, there is celebration, but when hardship comes—as a consequence of one's own actions—ingratitude and denial of divine wisdom prevail, revealing the tendency to acknowledge favors only in comfort and to blame fate or God in times of trial.

translation: Or He may marry them together [providing them] with males and females, and He makes whom He wills barren. Indeed, He is Knowing and Competent.
interpretation: This verse highlights the absolute sovereignty of God over the most intimate aspects of human life—procreation and family formation. It states that God can grant a person male children, female children, or a combination of both, just as He can withhold the ability to bear children entirely by making someone barren. The concluding attributes of God being 'Knowing' (Alim) and 'Competent' (Qadir) emphasize that these divine decisions are not random but are based on perfect wisdom and boundless power, reminding believers to trust in God's plan regarding their progeny and to recognize that such matters lie entirely within His will.

translation: And it is not for any human being that Allah should speak to him except by revelation or from behind a veil or by sending a messenger (angel) who reveals, by His permission, whatever He wills. Indeed, He is Most High, All-Wise.
interpretation: This verse establishes that direct, unmediated communication between Allah and a human being is not the norm in Islamic theology; rather, divine guidance comes through specific channels: (1) *wahy* (revelation), an internal inspiration bestowed upon prophets such as Muhammad, Moses, or Muhammad; (2) speech from behind a veil, as occurred when Allah spoke to Moses at Sinai without Moses seeing Him; or (3) the sending of an angel, such as Gabriel, who delivers the message to the prophet. The phrase 'by His permission, whatever He wills' emphasizes Allah's absolute sovereignty in choosing what to reveal and to whom, while 'He is Most High, All-Wise' underscores that this method of communication is rooted in divine wisdom and purposes beyond human comprehension.

translation: And thus We have revealed to you, [O Muhammad], an inspiration of Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor what was faith, but We have made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants. And indeed, [O Muhammad], you guide to a straight path.
interpretation: This verse describes the revelation of the Qur'an to the Prophet Muhammad as a divine gift of 'spirit' (rooh) from God's command, emphasizing that the Prophet did not acquire knowledge of previous scriptures or the essence of faith through human learning, but received it through this inspired revelation. The revelation functions as a 'light' (noor), an illuminating guidance whose recipients are chosen by God's will, highlighting divine sovereignty in guiding humanity. While the message and Prophet serve as guidance toward a straight path (siraat al-mustaqeem), this guidance is ultimately facilitated by God, who activates its impact in the hearts of those He selects among His servants, underscoring that true guidance is a divine act rather than a purely human achievement.

translation: The path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Unquestionably, to Allah all matters return.
interpretation: This verse affirms that the Straight Path is ultimately Allah's path, because sovereignty over all creation belongs to Him alone. By stating that everything in the heavens and earth is His, the verse establishes that no other being shares in His authority or deserving of ultimate allegiance. The closing statement, that all matters ultimately return to Allah, functions as both a warning and a comfort: human affairs, judgments, injustices, and choices will all be brought before Him for ultimate resolution. Thus, following this path is not merely a matter of personal preference but aligns one's life with the very order of reality, since every outcome is already returning to its true Owner.

Its description as 'exalted' (alin) indicates its lofty station and incomparability, while 'full of wisdom' (hakim) signifies that it contains profound, purposeful, and immutable divine wisdom. The verse reassures believers of the Qur'an's divine preservation, authority, and the deliberate wisdom underlying its revelation, distinguishing it from any human composition or alteration.

translation: And how many a prophet We sent among the former peoples.
interpretation: This verse serves as a rhetorical device to emphasize the continuity and abundance of divine guidance throughout human history, reminding the Quraysh and the broader audience of Mecca that Allah’s message of monotheism and moral accountability is not novel but part of an ongoing tradition of revelation sent to every nation. The word *nabī* (prophet) here denotes messengers chosen by God to deliver His commands and warn their communities, while the phrase *fī al-awwalīn* (among the former peoples) underscores that previous generations also received prophets, suggesting that Muhammad ﷺ is not an isolated phenomenon but the culmination of a divine pattern. The verse implicitly calls the listeners to reflect on the fate of those who rejected earlier prophets, inviting recognition of the seriousness of their own response to the message of Islam.
