Such individuals perceive in the ruins of these nations a tangible warning: that worldly might, technological advancement, and material progress cannot save a people from divine retribution when they transgress the bounds set by their Creator. Therefore, the verse calls upon the believer to extract from history a lesson of accountability, to recognize that civilizations rise and fall by the will of Allah, and that ultimate safety lies only in piety and submission to Him, lest the same fate befall those who heed not the signs.

translation: And [mention] Moses, when We sent him to Pharaoh with a clear authority.
interpretation: This verse calls attention to the mission of Prophet Moses as a divinely appointed messenger who confronted a tyrannical ruler with undeniable proof of his prophetic commission, highlighting that even the most powerful earthly authorities are subject to God's will and cannot withstand the truth when it is delivered with divine authority.

translation: Then Pharaoh withdrew with his clique and said, 'I am your supreme chief; I know not any god for you besides me.'
interpretation: The leaders of oppression often retreat to their inner circle of advisors and supporters, seeking validation for their tyranny and false claims of divinity, which highlights how arrogance blinds them to the reality of the Creator.

translation: So We seized him and his soldiers and threw them into the sea, and he was blameworthy.
interpretation: This verse refers to the downfall of Pharaoh and his army, who were drowned as a consequence of their persistent arrogance, oppression, and rejection of divine guidance. The word 'mليم' (blameworthy) highlights that Pharaoh's destruction was not an unjust act but a deserved punishment for his defiance and tyranny. It serves as a powerful reminder that those who transgress against truth and oppress others, despite clear signs, ultimately face consequences, and that divine justice prevails over worldly power.

translation: And in 'Aad, when We sent against them the barren wind.
interpretation: This phrase is part of a longer passage (Qur'an 51:41–42) reminding the Quraysh of past destroyed nations as warnings. The verse specifically references the ancient tribe of 'Aad, who were destroyed by a divinely sent, sterile ('aqim) wind — one that brought no benefit, only destruction. The word 'aqim (عقيم) literally means barren or sterile; it is used metaphorically here to describe a wind that does not produce rain or life but instead destroys crops, people, and livestock. Some classical scholars, like Al-Tabari, note that the wind was called 'aqim because it did not carry rain or because it left nothing behind that could reproduce or regrow. The verse is generally understood to refer to the wind mentioned in Surah Al-Ahqaf (46:25) and Surah Al-Haqqah (69:6–8), which tormented the people of 'Aad for several nights and days. The mention of 'Aad serves as a warning to the Quraysh (the immediate audience of Surah Adh-Dhariyat) that those who reject divine messengers face severe consequences. Theologically, this affirms God's power over natural elements, which He uses as instruments of punishment when communities persistently transgress. The barren wind also symbolizes futility: it represents a message of warning that, when ignored, results in complete spiritual and physical barrenness.

translation: There is not a thing but that it destroys it, leaving it like [fine] dust.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the Angel of the Wind regarding the wind sent against the people of 'Ad, emphasizes the totality and irresistibility of divine power. Nothing—whether solid structures, human life, or natural elements—can withstand or evade the destructive command of Allah, once He sends it forth. What was once substantial, thriving, or alive is reduced to 'ar-ramīm,' meaning fine, crumbling dust scattered in the air or on the ground. The verse invites reflection on the illusion of permanence in worldly life: strength, civilization, and even identity can be erased in a single moment. It also underscores a deeper theological message about Allah's control over both creation and destruction—He is not only the giver of life and stability but also the One who returns all things to nothingness when He so wills. This is not merely a story of ancient ruin; it is a warning that any nation, however powerful, exists only by Allah's permission and can be made to vanish like dust in the wind. The linguistic force of the verse—through the use of 'mā tatharu' (it leaves nothing)—amplifies the idea that no remnant of the arrogant or the rebellious remains to boast or endure. It calls for humility, remembrance of consequences, and recognition of the transient nature of all that opposes the divine will. In essence, the verse reveals that true power belongs to Allah alone, and all worldly might is but a passing shadow.

translation: And among the people of Thamud, when they were told, 'Enjoy yourselves for a while.'
interpretation: This verse alludes to the Thamud people, who were given a period of respite to enjoy the pleasures of this world, but it was only a temporary reprieve before the consequence of their denial and transgression caught up with them. It serves as a warning that any period of ease or comfort granted to those who reject truth is not a sign of divine approval, but merely a delay before accountability.

translation: But they defied the command of their Lord, so the thunderbolt seized them while they were looking on.
interpretation: This verse describes a people who consciously witnessed divine warnings and signs yet deliberately chose disobedience and arrogance, refusing to heed the guidance sent to them. Their downfall came not out of ignorance, but as a direct consequence of their willful rebellion. It serves as a sobering reminder that spiritual heedlessness, when combined with stubbornness against truth, invites divine chastisement even upon those who have seen the proofs before their very eyes. The verse underscores that no amount of knowledge or observation protects a person who rejects accountability, and that divine justice responds to conscious defiance with decisive punishment.

translation: And they were unable to resist [or withstand] it, nor could they protect themselves [or avert it].
interpretation: The verse expresses that those who are confronted with Allah's power are utterly helpless: they can neither mount a defense against His command nor avail themselves of any support or means of escape, making their incapacity a vivid reflection of the futility of opposing the divine will.

translation: And the people of Noah before them; indeed, they were a transgressing people.
interpretation: This verse refers to the people of the Prophet Noah, who lived before the people addressed in the preceding verses (the people of 'Aad and Thamud). It emphasizes that the people of Noah were transgressors (fasiq), meaning they openly disobeyed God, transgressed His limits, and rejected His guidance. The verse serves as a warning to all subsequent generations that those communities who knowingly reject divine guidance and persist in transgression will face consequences, highlighting the moral decline and persistent wickedness that characterized Noah's people, making them deserving of the divine punishment they eventually received through the flood.

translation: And the heaven We constructed with strength, and indeed, We are [its] expander.
interpretation: This verse refers to the vastness of the heavens and their ongoing expansion, reflecting the Qur'an's engagement with cosmology. The word 'aīdin' (strength/power) emphasizes Allah's absolute capability in creating such a magnificent structure, while 'mūsiʿūn' (expander) is frequently understood by scholars as referring to the continuous expansion of the universe—a phenomenon confirmed by modern astronomy, though such scientific correlations are matters of reflection rather than the verse's primary purpose. The deeper meaning points to divine omnipotence and the boundless nature of creation, inviting believers to recognize that the same power that built the heavens governs all existence, including human affairs. It serves as a sign (āya) that connects the observable cosmos to the reality of the Creator, urging humility and awe before a power that transcends human comprehension.

translation: And the earth We have spread out (like a carpet), so how excellent (are) the Makers (of it)!
interpretation: This verse highlights a profound truth about the concept of design and purpose in the universe. By describing the earth as something spread out like a carpet or a resting place, it draws attention to the deliberate planning involved in creating a habitable surface for living beings. The rhetorical question that follows, acknowledging the excellence of the Makers, serves to direct the observer's mind away from seeing the earth's flatness and stability as mere coincidence, and instead toward recognizing an intentional act of creation. It suggests that human comfort and stability on earth are not accidental but are the result of careful arrangement, inviting reflection on the wisdom behind natural phenomena that might otherwise be taken for granted.

translation: And of all things We have created pairs, that you may remember (or reflect).
interpretation: This verse draws attention to the fundamental principle of duality and complementary opposition woven through all of creation, pointing the contemplative mind toward the reality that existence itself is structured upon paired contrasts—night and day, earth and heaven, sweet and bitter, male and female—so that human beings, through observing the created order, are reminded that God is One, unpaired and incomparable, and that the multiplicity of the cosmos ultimately testifies to the singularity of its Creator.

translation: So flee to Allah. Indeed, I am to you a clear warner from Him.
interpretation: This verse is a direct and urgent summons to turn away from all that is false and transient and to seek refuge exclusively in Allah. The word 'flee' (فروا) is not a call to physical escape but to an inward detachment — a decisive break from idols, desires, and delusions of self-sufficiency, and a return to the only Source of safety and truth. The one making this call is not speaking from personal ambition or speculation; he is a 'clear warner,' one whose warning is unmistakable in its sincerity and evident in its source, which is divine revelation itself. The verse places the believer at a crossroads: either continue clinging to what inevitably leads to ruin, or take swift, wholehearted refuge in Allah before the moment of reckoning arrives. It underscores both Allah's mercy — in providing a way of escape — and His justice — in making clear what is at stake before holding creation accountable. The command is timeless, addressed to every soul standing between attachment to the fleeting and surrender to the Eternal.

translation: And do not make [or set up] with Allah another deity; indeed, I am to you a clear warner from Him.
interpretation: This verse is a direct and unequivocal command from Allah prohibiting polytheism (shirk), which is the act of associating partners with Allah in worship. It commands believers to maintain pure monotheism (Tawhid). The verse emphasizes the exclusivity of worship due to Allah alone, as He is the sole creator, sustainer, and worthy of devotion. The phrase "another deity" refers to anything or anyone worshipped besides Allah, whether idols, human figures, natural phenomena, or abstract concepts. By stating "indeed, I am to you a clear warner from Him," the speaker (Prophet Muhammad ﷺ) affirms that his warning against polytheism comes directly from Allah's authority. This underscores the seriousness of the command and serves as a stern caution of the severe consequences—namely, divine punishment in the Hereafter—that await those who defy this fundamental tenet of faith. The clarity ("mubeen") of the warning suggests that the message is unambiguous, leaving no excuse for misunderstanding. Ultimately, this verse establishes the foundational principle of Islamic theology: absolute devotion to Allah alone, free from any form of idolatry or associating partners with Him.

translation: Likewise, there came not to those before them any messenger except that they said, 'A magician or a madman.'
interpretation: This verse highlights a recurring pattern in human history: whenever prophets and messengers were sent to guide people, they were met with rejection and ridicule from their communities. The accusers, unable or unwilling to recognize the divine truth of the message, resorted to defaming the messengers by calling them either sorcerers or lunatics. This reveals the psychological defense mechanism of denial used by those resistant to change or accountability, as well as the nature of worldly opposition to divine guidance. The verse underscores that the rejection faced by the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was not unique; rather, it mirrors the experiences of all previous prophets, indicating that opposition is a hallmark of the human response to revelation. This serves as both a source of comfort for the messenger, who need not feel isolated in facing hostility, and a warning to communities to reflect on their predecessors' mistakes and avoid repeating the same patterns of denial and mockery.

translation: Do they enjoin one another to this [message]? Rather, they are a transgressing people.
interpretation: This rhetorical question highlights the absurdity of the disbelievers' situation. God points out that they are not merely passively hearing the message, but actively encouraging each other to reject it, mock it, or persist in denial—suggesting a collective, stubborn defiance rather than ignorance. The verse condemns their transgression ("ṭughyān"), indicating that their rejection stems not from a lack of awareness but from an arrogant overstepping of moral and spiritual boundaries, a deliberate rebellion against divine guidance that has become a entrenched communal trait.

translation: So turn away from them; you are not to be blamed.
interpretation: This verse conveys divine reassurance to the Prophet Muhammad, instructing him to disengage from those who reject the message and finding no fault in him. It signifies that after fulfilling his duty of delivering the warning, the Prophet bears no responsibility for the choices or fates of those who turn away. The verse highlights a principle of accountability in Islam: the messenger's obligation is to convey the truth, not to compel belief or bear the guilt for human rejection. By being told he is not to blame, it affirms that the Prophet has fulfilled his prophetic mission and absolves him of any moral burden for the disbelief of others, while also serving as a subtle indication that a reckoning awaits those who persist in denial.

translation: And remind, for indeed, reminder benefits the believers.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the Prophet (peace be upon him), commands him to continue delivering reminders and admonitions to the people, assuring him that although the message may be rejected by many, it will certainly benefit the believers—those whose hearts are open to faith. The verse conveys that sincere remembrance and admonition from the Prophet will not be in vain; it will serve as a source of guidance, increase in faith, and spiritual nourishment for those who believe. It also implies that the Prophet's duty is merely to convey the message and remind, while the actual benefit is reserved for those with receptive, believing hearts. This verse highlights the value of constant reflection upon divine truths and the role of prophetic guidance in strengthening the faith of believers.

translation: And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me.
interpretation: This foundational verse from Surah Adh-Dhariyat (51:56) establishes the central purpose of human and jinn existence as the worship and conscious acknowledgment of Allah alone. The use of the emphatic 'lam' (لِ) clarifies that worship is the singular, deliberate purpose of creation, ruling out any alternative primary reason. Worship here encompasses not merely ritual acts like prayer, but the entire spectrum of submission, remembrance, gratitude, and adherence to divine guidance in every aspect of life. By including both the jinn—an unseen creation made of smokeless fire—and humans, the verse affirms that this purpose applies universally to both realms of conscious beings, regardless of their nature or worldly circumstances. The verse implicitly conveys that worship is not a burden but the fulfillment of the innate disposition (fitrah) with which both beings are created, linking their existence intrinsically to their Creator and His commandments. This singular focus on divine worship also distinguishes the purpose of life from worldly pursuits, material success, or mere biological existence, asserting that ultimate meaning is derived only through the conscious, voluntary service of Allah. The verse thus serves as a theological cornerstone for understanding why life, with its trials and responsibilities, is inherently purposeful, and how true success in both this world and the hereafter is measured by one's devotion to this divine mandate.

translation: I do not want from them any provision, nor do I want them to feed Me.
interpretation: The verse is part of Allah's address to humanity through the Prophet, emphasizing God's absolute self-sufficiency (al-Ghaniyy). He does not stand in need of His creatures' worship, charity, or sustenance. By stating that He wants neither provision from them nor that they feed Him, Allah negates any notion of divine need or dependency, thereby affirming that human obedience and devotion are acts of self-purification and moral benefit for the people themselves, not for fulfilling a requirement on God's part. This concept also dissolves anthropomorphic misconceptions of divinity, reinforcing pure monotheism (Tawhid) and divine transcendence, and it serves as a reminder that sincere faith and righteous deeds are pursued solely because they bring the soul closer to its Creator, not because the Creator is in need of them.

translation: Indeed, Allah is the Provider, the possessor of strength, the firm/mighty.
interpretation: The verse affirms that all sustenance in the universe originates from Allah alone, emphasizing that He is not merely a giver of provision but the ultimate source and sustainer of all that exists. The description 'Possessor of Strength' (Dhū al-Quwwah) highlights that His authority and capability to provide are rooted in an absolute, unmatched power, while 'the Firm/Mighty' (al-Matīn) intensifies this attribute by pointing to a strength that is unyielding, unwavering, and beyond any weakness or depletion. Theologically, the verse teaches that because Allah Himself is the foundation of sustenance, human beings are called to rely upon Him with complete trust (tawakkul), free from anxiety over provision, since no worldly power can withhold what He grants or give what He withholds. It also subtly warns against attaching the heart to apparent means of livelihood, reminding the believer that all strength behind those means belongs to Allah, who distributes His bounty according to wisdom, mercy, and an eternal will that no creature can resist or alter.

translation: But those who have wronged [themselves] deserve a punishment like the punishment of their peers, so let them not ask to hasten it.
interpretation: This verse addresses those who commit wrongdoing and acts as a divine warning that they will receive a portion of punishment commensurate with what previous generations of wrongdoers endured, and the divine decree cannot be rushed; the inevitability of accountability should inspire reflection and repentance rather than heedlessness.

translation: So woe to those who disbelieve from their Day which they are promised.
interpretation: The verse delivers a stern warning to those who reject faith, proclaiming a day of reckoning and punishment that awaits them. It underscores the inevitable consequence of disbelief and serves as a reminder of divine justice and the fulfillment of divine promises.

translation: By the mount (Ṭūr).
interpretation: The opening of Sūrah al-Ṭūr draws the reader's attention to the towering mountain as a sacred emblem of stability, revelation, and the meeting place between heaven and earth, reminding believers that just as the mountain stands firm upon divine command, the truth of the Qur'an and the message of Muhammad stand immovable and cannot be shaken by human opposition or falsehood.

translation: And a written book,
interpretation: This phrase alludes to a record of deeds inscribed clearly and unmistakably, symbolizing the transparency with which human actions will be brought to account, leaving no room for denial or distortion on the Day of Judgment.

The phrase "في رق منشور" (fī raqqin manshūr) appears in Surah At-Tur (52:3) as part of a series of divine oaths: "By the Mount [of Sinai], And by a Book inscribed, In parchment unfolded" (Wa aṭ-ṭūri wa kitābin masṭūrin fī raqqin manshūrin).

Translation: "In an unfolded parchment/scroll" or "In a spread-out sheet of paper/parchment."

Interpretation: This phrase describes the Quran as a recorded, inscribed book written on parchment that is spread out (unfolded), meaning it is open, clear, and accessible for reading and understanding. The image is of a scroll that has been unrolled so that its contents are exposed and visible. In classical tafsir, many commentators (such as Ibn Kathir, At-Tabari, Al-Qurtubi) explain that "al-raqq" (الرَّقّ) refers to parchment or vellum (prepared animal skin used for writing), and "manshūr" (منشور) means unfolded, spread out, or open. The implication is that the Quran is written in a clear, expanded form that is available for people to read, reflect upon, and derive guidance from—it is not hidden or concealed but rather openly presented. Some scholars also note that this implies the Quran's preservation and accessibility across time and space.

The image conveys that divine guidance is not concealed or hidden but plainly set forth for all to read, reflect upon, and take heed of. It also reflects the Quran's preservation in a form that is available to people across time and space—openly presented rather than restricted or secret. The unfolding implies that its meanings and rulings are to be progressively engaged with and applied, inviting continuous reflection and study.

translation: And the [heavenly] frequented house (al-bayt al-ma'mur).
interpretation: Al-Bayt al-Ma'mur is understood in classical tafsir as a celestial sanctuary above the seventh heaven—paralleling the Kaaba on earth—that is continuously encircled by angels in worship, analogous to how pilgrims circumambulate the Kaaba. Its mention here, immediately before the title 'Sidrat al-Muntaha' (the Lote-Tree beyond which no creation passes), is theologically significant: it places the Prophet ﷺ's vision of the heavens within a framework of cosmic order and sacred geography. The verse thereby links earthly pilgrimage (Hajj) to a heavenly prototype, affirming that the ritual centered on the Kaaba is not a merely human convention but participates in a celestial reality perpetually observed by angelic beings. The definite article 'al-' before both 'bayt' and 'ma'mur' signals that this is a uniquely known, singular entity—a counterpart to 'al-Kaaba al-Musharrafa,' both being 'axially' significant. In being mentioned in the context of the Night Journey (al-Isra' wa al-Mi'raj), the verse further underscores that the Prophet ﷺ was shown the ultimate reality of creation, in which every earthly locus of worship has its heavenly archetype.

translation: And the raised ceiling (sky),
interpretation: This phrase, from Surah At-Tariq (86:13), refers to the vast, lofty expanse of the sky. The term المرفوع (al-marfu') conveys not only physical elevation but also purposeful design and exaltation, suggesting that the heavens were raised by Allah's will, power, and wisdom. It invites reflection on the immensity, order, and stability of the cosmos, pointing to the greatness of the Creator who established it as a protective canopy and a sign for those who reflect. The verse uses this majestic imagery as part of an oath emphasizing the truthfulness of the Qur'an and the reality of divine guidance and accountability.

translation: And the sea that is filled [with flame].
interpretation: This phrase, following verses that mention signs and warnings to humanity, points to the sea as another awe-inspiring manifestation of God’s power. The term *masjur* carries layers of meaning: on one level, it describes the sea as filled with waves, tides, and currents, perpetually in motion and restless. On a deeper eschatological level, many scholars read it as a reference to the sea being filled with fire on the Day of Judgment, an apocalyptic transformation where its very nature changes. In this sense, the verse uses the familiar to point toward the terrifying: a creature of beauty and sustenance becoming a creature of destruction. The sea, which humans rely upon for travel, trade, and sustenance, is a reminder of God’s sovereignty over creation, the fragility of what seems permanent, and the certainty of accountability before the One who commands all waters. The verse invites reflection on the transient nature of worldly benefits and the ultimate return to God, when even the most stable elements of the natural order will be reshaped by divine decree.

translation: Indeed, the punishment of your Lord will surely occur.
interpretation: This verse affirms the certainty and inevitability of divine retribution in the Hereafter. The word 'لَوَاقِع' (surely to occur) emphasizes that Allah's punishment for those who reject faith and transgress His limits is not a mere possibility but an absolute reality that will befall them as a consequence of their actions. It serves as a solemn warning, reminding humanity that divine justice is an established part of the cosmic order, tied to the natural consequences of moral and spiritual choices.

translation: No one can avert it [or defend him]
interpretation: In this phrase, derived from the broader context of the Day of Judgment in Surah Al-Haqqah, the term "دافع" (dafi') refers to a defender, intercessor, or one who could repel the punishment. The negation "ما له" indicates total helplessness and absolute vulnerability. Here, the emphasis lies on the concept that on the Day of Resurrection, no human being will possess any power, authority, or capacity to protect themselves from Allah's decree. The phrase reveals the principle that all forms of worldly influence, wealth, power, social status, and even familial ties become completely meaningless before the sovereignty of Allah. A person cannot bribe, manipulate, or rely on any worldly connection to escape divine justice. This linguistic construction underscores the absolute monarchy of Allah over His creation on the Day of Judgment, where His will is final, His decree is irresistible, and His authority is uncontested. It serves as a profound warning that every soul must ultimately face its Creator alone, stripped of all earthly support systems and human alliances, emphasizing the importance of self-accountability and righteous conduct in one's earthly life. The negation here is absolute, not partial, reinforcing the comprehensive nature of divine power and the futility of any human attempt to evade ultimate accountability.

translation: The day when the sky will be convulsed in a tremendous manner (or will be turned upside down).
interpretation: This verse describes a cataclysmic event on the Day of Judgment, indicating a profound and overwhelming transformation of the sky as it currently exists. The word 'mawr' (مَوْرًا) implies an intense, rolling movement, suggesting that the heavens will undergo a radical restructuring, losing their stability and order. This serves as a vivid warning of the magnitude of the eschatological upheaval, where the familiar cosmos will be dismantled, emphasizing the absolute power of God to bring about the ultimate reckoning and the helplessness of creation before the divine decree.

translation: And the mountains will be made to pass away, becoming [like] scattered dust.
interpretation: The verse employs vivid eschatological imagery common in the Quran, depicting the Day of Judgment when the seemingly permanent and immovable structures of the world—including the mighty mountains—will be utterly demolished and reduced to scattered particles of dust blown by the wind. This serves as a powerful warning of the impermanence of worldly grandeur and stability, emphasizing that nothing in this created realm possesses inherent permanence before the power and decree of Allah. The juxtaposition of the mountain's traditional symbolism of strength, steadfastness, and permanence being made to 'pass away' underscores the transient nature of all material existence and the ultimate reality of the hereafter, where only the eternal nature of Allah and the consequences of human deeds endure.

translation: So woe on that Day to those who deny the truth.
interpretation: This verse functions as a stark warning of impending divine retribution, declaring a state of 'woe'—a profound ruin and sorrow—upon those who persistently reject the truth of God's revelation on the Day of Judgment. The repetition of such warnings throughout the Qur'an highlights a core spiritual principle: the denial of divine truth, often out of arrogance, willful ignorance, or attachment to worldly desires, carries inescapable consequences in the afterlife. The verse underscores the gravity of rejecting faith, not merely as an intellectual error but as a moral and spiritual choice that leads to ultimate loss and anguish in the presence of God. It serves as a divine call to self-reflection, urging humanity to recognize the signs of truth before the arrival of the inevitable Day when denial will be of no avail.

translation: Those who are in [empty] discourse, playing [with truth].
interpretation: This verse condemns those who, instead of engaging sincerely with divine revelation and matters of ultimate consequence, trivialize them through frivolous argument and diversion, treating sacred realities as objects of sport rather than earnest reflection, reflecting a deeper spiritual malaise in which willful playfulness masks an unwillingness to confront truth.

translation: The Day they will be called to the Fire of Hell with a [violent] pushing.
interpretation: This verse describes the terrifying and forceful manner in which the wrongdoers will be driven toward the punishment of Hellfire on the Day of Judgment. The word 'دعا' (pushing or driving) signifies not a gentle summoning, but a harsh, violent thrusting, reflecting the horror and disgrace awaiting those who rejected faith and righteousness. It serves as a stark warning of the severe consequences of turning away from God's guidance, emphasizing that the journey to punishment will be one of humiliation and compulsion, devoid of any dignity or comfort.

translation: This is the Fire which you used to deny.
interpretation: This verse is a divine address to those who rejected the truth of the Hereafter and mocked the warning of Hellfire during their worldly lives; it is spoken on the Day of Judgment when they are confronted with the very punishment they had deemed impossible, exposing the fatal consequences of arrogant disbelief and the delusion of those who considered themselves beyond divine accountability.

translation: , so is this magic? Or do you not perceive?
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical question posed by the Qur'an that confronts the listeners—particularly the disbelievers—with the miraculous nature of the Qur'an itself. The phrase 'so is this magic?' mocks their attempts to dismiss the Qur'an as sorcery or illusion, while 'or do you not perceive?' challenges their capacity to recognize clear truth when it is presented to them. It serves as an indictment of willful ignorance and intellectual stubbornness, suggesting that those who reject the message do so not because the evidence is unclear, but because they refuse to see. The verse emphasizes human accountability in distinguishing truth from falsehood, implying that perception is both a physical and moral faculty that can be deliberately closed.

translation: Enter it [the Fire]! Whether you are patient or impatient, it will be the same for you. You will only be requited for what you used to do.
interpretation: This verse presents a profound divine address to those who have earned Hell, stripping away any illusion of bargaining or negotiation in the afterlife. The command 'اصلبوها' (enter it) is not an invitation but a decisive, authoritative declaration that the destination is sealed. The phrase 'فاصبروا أو لا تصبروا' (whether you are patient or impatient) shatters the worldly logic that endurance leads to relief and impatience leads to worsening. In eternity, such categories collapse; time, as a mechanism of change, no longer functions as it did in the duniya (worldly life). Patience and impatience become psychologically indistinguishable because the outcome is fixed and unalterable. This divine rhetoric exposes a deeper truth: the suffering of the people of the Fire is not punitive in the temporal sense (a temporary consequence meant to correct), but retributive in the ultimate sense (a perfect, eternal recompense). The verse concludes with the foundational principle of divine justice: 'إنما تجزون ما كنتم تعملون' (you are only recompensed for what you used to do). This is not merely a statement of fairness, but a profound ontological assertion. It means that the punishment is not arbitrary or excessive; it is the exact, intrinsic consequence of the soul's own choices, crystallized into an eternal state. The suffering is, in a sense, the self-made reality of the soul finally made manifest without any worldly veils. Thus, the verse teaches that the afterlife is not a place for appeals or second chances, but the ultimate revelation of the soul's own truth, where divine justice is not imposed from outside but unfolds from within the consequences of one's own deeds.

translation: Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and [in] bliss.
interpretation: This verse states that those who are conscious of Allah through faith, obedience, and piety—by fulfilling His commands and avoiding what He has forbidden—will be rewarded in the Hereafter with a place of eternal delight, residing in elevated gardens of Paradise that contain bliss which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human mind has imagined. The term "muttaqīn" (the righteous or the God-conscious) encompasses believers who carry within them a sense of reverence and awe before Allah, which restrains them from sins and motivates them toward acts of righteousness, leading ultimately to this sublime, everlasting reward.

translation: }Delighting in what their Lord has given them, and their Lord has protected them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire.
interpretation: This verse describes a state of bliss and contentment for the faithful in the Hereafter. The phrase 'delighting in what their Lord has given them' suggests that the believers will experience profound joy and satisfaction from the rewards bestowed upon them by Allah. These rewards are not merely material but encompass spiritual fulfillment and nearness to the Divine. The mention of their Lord 'protecting them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire' underscores a dual aspect of divine mercy: not only are the believers rewarded with blessings, but they are also shielded from the ultimate punishment. This protection serves as a reassurance of Allah's grace and the efficacy of sincere faith and righteous deeds. Together, these elements paint a picture of paradise as a place of eternal joy, free from suffering, where the faithful enjoy the fruits of their devotion in the presence of their Lord's favor and protection.

translation: Eat and drink with satisfaction because of what you used to do.
interpretation: This verse describes the reward awaiting the righteous in Paradise. It indicates that the enjoyment of the bounties therein is not arbitrary but is a direct consequence of one's own deeds in the earthly life. The phrase "hinan" (هنيئا) implies complete ease, contentment, and absence of any ill consequence from what is consumed, contrasting with the temporary and often anxiety-laden consumption in worldly life. Thus, it establishes a principle of divine justice: the quality of one's eternal sustenance corresponds to the sincerity and righteousness of one's past actions, and the joy experienced in the Hereafter is a pure return free from sin or harm.

translation: Reclining on lined-up couches, and We will pair them with houris (companions) of beautiful, wide eyes.
interpretation: The verse describes the ultimate state of rest and companionship awaiting the righteous in Paradise. The image of reclining on couches arranged in perfect order conveys peace, ease, and a sense of harmony, free from hardship. The mention of being paired with 'houris of wide, beautiful eyes' symbolizes pure, refreshing, and delightful companionship—emphasizing that Paradise is not only a place of physical comfort but also of soulful joy, intimate connection, and beauty that fulfills the deepest human longing for serenity and belonging.

translation: And those who believed and whose descendants followed them in faith – We will join them with their descendants, and We will not deprive them of any of their deeds. Every person is pledged for what they have earned.
interpretation: This verse affirms that for those who sincerely embrace faith (iman), God will not only honor their own deeds but will also elevate their righteous descendants to be united with them in eternal reward, even if the descendants did not achieve the same spiritual rank. It underscores a divine mercy that honors familial continuity in faith, suggesting that the moral and spiritual efforts of believing parents can have a lasting impact on their lineage. Simultaneously, the verse firmly establishes the principle of individual accountability—each soul remains fully responsible for its own actions (kasb), indicating that no one can rely on another's piety or deeds for salvation. The balance between divine grace in uniting families in faith and personal responsibility for one's actions is central to the verse's meaning, portraying a God who is both compassionate toward human relationships and perfectly just in judgment.

translation: And We will provide them with fruit and meat from whatever they desire.
interpretation: This verse from Suraṭ al-Wāqiʿah (56:21) illustrates the boundless generosity and mercy of Allah toward the inhabitants of Paradise. The emphasis is placed not on the specific kinds of fruit or meat, but on the phrase 'مِمَّا يَشْتَهُونَ' (from whatever they desire), which signifies that in Paradise, every craving and longing of the soul and body will be fully and perfectly satisfied without restriction, fatigue, or want. Unlike the worldly pursuit of desires, which is often tainted by effort, excess, guilt, or unattainability, the fulfillment in the Hereafter is pure and free from any negative consequence. The pairing of fruit and meat represents a harmony of delight—fruit symbolizing delicate, natural sweetness, and meat representing rich, substantial nourishment—showing that Paradise contains a comprehensive and balanced abundance of all that brings joy. Ultimately, this verse reminds believers that the ultimate reward of righteousness is not merely the absence of pain, but the presence of perfect, eternal contentment granted by the unlimited grace of Allah.

translation: They will pass to one another a cup [of wine] wherein there is no idle talk and no sin.
interpretation: This verse describes the pure and exalted nature of the social gatherings in Paradise, where every interaction is free from the foolishness, slander, and sins that characterize worldly conversations, reflecting an environment of complete spiritual purity and purposeful communion.

translation: And there will circulate among them young boys (servants) of theirs, as if they were hidden pearls.
interpretation: This verse describes one of the delights of Paradise: youthful, eternally youthful servants will attend to the people of Paradise, moving gracefully to fulfill their wishes. Their beauty and purity are likened to pearls preserved in their shells—untouched, radiant, and flawless. The imagery emphasizes the idea of preservation and pristine beauty; just as a pearl hidden in its shell has not been exposed to the wear of the world, these servants are untouched by age, fatigue, or impurity. This serves not only as a depiction of luxurious service but also as a symbol of the flawless, untainted nature of the Paraíso itself, where everything exists in a state of eternal perfection. The verse reflects the Qur'anic theme that the rewards of the Hereafter are beyond human imagination, presenting them in imagery that conveys beauty, purity, and eternal freshness.

translation: And they will approach one another, asking each other (questions).
interpretation: The verse describes a scene on the Day of Judgment where people, in a state of shock and accountability, turn to one another with questions, reflecting their confusion and the overwhelming reality of the Day of Reckoning, where each person is eager to know the fate of others and seek clarity about what has befallen them.

translation: They will say, 'Indeed we were, before among our families, fearful [of displeasing Allah].'
interpretation: This verse depicts a moment of reflection in the Hereafter, where the inhabitants of Paradise—those who attained salvation—acknowledge that their success was rooted in a profound, conscious awareness of Allah's presence and authority while they were still living among their families and communities. The term "mushfiqeen" (fearful/conscious) carries a dual meaning encompassing both the awe-inspired dread of falling short before the Divine and the deep-seated anxiety about the moral and spiritual responsibilities they bore in worldly life. Their prior state of God-consciousness acted as a divine preservative, shielding them from heedlessness, sin, and the corrupting influences of society, and it is precisely this internal vigilance that Allah ultimately rewarded with peace and security in the eternal life. Thus, the verse highlights that true righteousness is cultivated through persistent mindfulness of one's ultimate accountability to Allah, even amidst the distractions and attachments of earthly existence. It serves as an encouragement for believers to maintain spiritual vigilance and a sense of敬畏 (reverent fear) toward Allah in all circumstances, knowing that such consciousness is the means to attaining eternal tranquility.

translation: But Allah has favored us and protected us from the punishment of the scorching wind.
interpretation: This verse expresses profound gratitude to Allah for His divine favor and protection from a severe, burning torment, both literal and metaphorical. It reflects the human condition of vulnerability and the recognition that ultimate safety lies only in Allah's mercy. The

translation: .Indeed we used to call upon Him before; indeed He is the Kind, the Merciful
interpretation: This verse appears at the conclusion of a passage in Surah Adh-Dhariyat (51:56–58) emphasizing that the fundamental purpose of human creation is to worship God alone. The statement “Indeed we used to call upon Him before” reflects the faithful’s acknowledgment that prior to receiving the full guidance and wisdom of this message, they were already engaged in supplicating God, turning to Him in need, devotion, and reliance. Their earlier worship, though perhaps less complete or informed, was directed to the same God who now reveals His command to worship none other than Him. The verse then affirms two of God’s most beautiful names: *Al-Barr* (البر), meaning the Kind, the Righteous, the Source of All Goodness who fulfills His promises and responds to those who turn to Him; and *Ar-Rahim* (الرحيم), the Merciful, whose compassion encompasses His servants in every state—whether in heedlessness or in guidance, in sin or in repentance. The conjunction of these two names signifies that God’s kindness is not withdrawn from those who previously erred but persists through His mercy, accepting their return to sincere devotion. Thus, the verse reassures the believers that their past calling upon God was not in vain, for the One they invoked is inherently good and ever merciful, ready to receive their renewed commitment to worship Him alone.

translation: So remind; you are, by the blessing of your Lord, neither a soothsayer nor a madman.
interpretation: This verse affirms that the Prophet Muhammad's role is to convey reminders and divine guidance, not to practice fortune-telling or speak from madness; rather, his message is a mercy and favor from Allah, given in a state of soundness, balance, and divine inspiration.

translation: Or do they say, 'He is a poet — we await for him some misfortune of time?'
interpretation: The verse exposes the dismissive and mocking attitude of the disbelievers toward the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, accusing him of being merely a poet whose words hold no divine weight, and maliciously expressing their wish that he would suffer some misfortune or death to prove their false claim false. This rejection reflects a deeper refusal to engage sincerely with the message, choosing instead to belittle revelation through comparison to poetry, while their

translation: Say, 'Wait! Indeed, I am with you among those who wait.'
interpretation: This verse is a statement of confidence and steadfastness in the face of opposition. When Prophet Muhammad was threatened by disbelievers who claimed they would soon overcome him or see his message fail, he responded with calm assurance, affirming that only God knows the outcome of events. The 'waiting' here carries the meaning of anticipating divine judgment and ultimate vindication, where truth and falsehood will be distinguished by God's will. It reflects the prophetic principle of patience (sabr) combined with reliance on God, where the Prophet acknowledges that while his opponents wait for his downfall, he waits alongside them for God's decree—trusting that victory ultimately belongs to those who are steadfast in faith. The verse also implicitly warns that the same time that awaits the oppressors also awaits the oppressed, making all accountable to divine justice.

translation: Or do their intellects command them to do this? Or are they a transgressing people?
interpretation: This verse, revealed in the context of the Quraysh's rejection of the Prophet Muhammad, presents a rhetorical challenge questioning the source of the disbelievers' obstinacy. It asks whether their rational faculties are truly directing them to oppose the truth, or whether their transgression and defiance have so clouded their judgment that they can no longer recognize the signs of God. The verse highlights a profound spiritual condition: when people persistently reject divine guidance, their capacity for sound reasoning becomes impaired by arrogance and rebelliousness. Thus, their denial is not necessarily a product of logical assessment but rather a consequence of a disposition that has willfully transgressed its moral and intellectual boundaries. It serves as a warning that persistent ingratitude and defiance can corrupt the very faculty meant to discern truth.

The disbelievers accuse Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) of fabricating the Quran, but the real issue is not that he composed it; rather, it is their refusal to believe in its divine origin due to their stubbornness and denial of truth.

translation: Then let them bring a discourse like it, if they are truthful.
interpretation: This verse is a direct challenge from God to those who reject the Qur'an, demanding that they produce even a single writing of similar literary perfection, prophetic depth, and spiritual guidance if they claim it is merely a human invention. It highlights the unique, inimitable nature of the Qur'an as a definitive proof of its divine origin, exposing the hollowness of those who dismiss it while being unable to match its magnitude.

translation: Or were they created from nothing, or are they the creators?
interpretation: This verse poses a rhetorical challenge to deny the possibility that human beings arose without a cause or that they brought themselves into existence, emphasizing that the only logical explanation for their existence is creation by Allah, the ultimate Originator.

translation: Or did they create the heavens and the earth? Rather, they have no certainty (of the truth).
interpretation: This verse challenges the ingratitude of those who deny or turn away from the truth, pointing out the impossibility of their pride: they did not create the heavens and the earth, so why do they act as if they are independent of their Creator? The phrase 'blā lā yūqinūn' indicates that their deeper problem is not just ignorance, but a lack of inner certainty and conviction. They refuse to grasp the clear signs of God's power and the reality of their own dependence, choosing instead to live in doubt and spiritual blindness. It is a call to recognize that everything—galaxies, mountains, and the human soul itself—bears witness to a Creator, and that denial stems not from an absence of evidence but from a failure to allow that evidence to reach the heart.

translation: Or do they have the treasuries of your Lord, or are they the controllers [of destiny]?
interpretation: This verse challenges those who deny or resist the message of truth, pointing out the absurdity of their position. It asks whether they possess the boundless treasures of God’s mercy, power, and sovereignty, or whether they hold the authority to determine outcomes and control affairs. The rhetorical question is designed to expose human limitations and the futility of opposing divine will. It emphasizes that all resources, authority, and dominion belong exclusively to God, and no creation—regardless of status or strength—can override His decisions or monopolize His blessings. The verse calls for humility, urging individuals to recognize their dependence on God and to abandon arrogance, since true control and provision rest only with Him.

translation: Or do they have a stairway [to heaven] by which they listen? Then let their listener produce a clear, supporting authority.
interpretation: This verse challenges those who reject the Prophet's message by mocking the idea that they could have access to divine knowledge. It sarcastically asks whether they have some elevated means—like a ladder or staircase—to the heavens that allows them to overhear angelic communications. If they truly claim access to such knowledge, they are demanded to produce undeniable proof supporting their denial. The verse thus exposes the absurdity of their position and demands evidence rather than baseless rejection.

translation: Or has He [only] daughters while you [have only] sons?
interpretation: This verse from Surah As-Saffat (37:159) is a rhetorical question posed by the Qur'an to mock the false claims of the polytheists. It highlights the absurdity of attributing daughters to Allah — whom the pre-Islamic Arabs considered a sign of weakness or shame — while reserving for themselves the honor of having sons. The verse condemns this distorted logic and exposes the irrationality of their beliefs, emphasizing that such an unequal and demeaning assignment does not befit the Majesty and Perfection of God. It serves as a powerful critique of the cultural biases that devalued daughters, urging a reassessment of human-made hierarchies in relation to divine attributes.

translation: Or do you ask them for a payment, so they are burdened with debt?
interpretation: This rhetorical question is posed to reassure the Prophet Muhammad that his message is delivered sincerely without any worldly motive. The verse implies that if he were demanding a material reward for his prophethood, the burden of this debt would weigh heavily on his listeners, and they would have a reason to reject his call. Since he asks for no such compensation, their rejection cannot be justified on grounds of greed or financial strain, highlighting the purity of his intentions and the divine origin of the Qur'anic revelation.

translation: Or have they [access to] the unseen, so they are writing [it] down?
interpretation: This verse challenges those who deny the truths revealed by Allah, questioning whether they possess knowledge of the unseen (الغيب) that is beyond human perception—such as future events, the nature of the afterlife, or divine decrees. By asking if they are

translation: Or do they intend a plot? But those who disbelieve are themselves the object of a plot.
interpretation: This verse responds to the disbelievers' attempts to undermine the message of Islam, affirming that any schemes they devise against the truth or its messengers will ultimately backfire, as divine wisdom ensures that their plots become the very means of their own downfall.

translation: ... أم لهم إله غير الله، سبحان الله عما يشركون.
interpretation: تستخدم هذه الآية الكريمة أسلوب الاستفهام الإنكاري لتوبيخ المشركين على شركهم، فكأنه يقول: كيف يعقل أن يكون لهم معبود بحق غير الله، أو أن يتخذوا آلهة من دونه، مع أنه هو وحده المستحق للعبادة، فلا شريك له ولا نظير؟ والاستفهام هنا يرمي إلى إظهار بطلان ما عليه المشركون من تعدد الآلهة، وإثبات أن الوحدانية لله وحده. وقوله: «سبحان الله عما يشركون» يعني: تنزيه الله وتقديسه عن كل ما يشركه المشركون معه من الأنداد والأصنام والآلهة الباطلة، فهو سبحانه منزه عن النقص والشبيه والمثيل، لا يشاركه أحد في ألوهيته وربوبيته، فكل ما يعبد من دونه فهو باطل وضلال، والله هو الإله الحق المعبود بحق. وفي هذا تنبيه على أن الشرك بالله منافٍ لكمال الإلهية، وأن العقل والفطرة السليمة يأبيان من قبوله، فلا إله إلا الله وحده لا شريك له.

translation: And if they saw a fragment of the sky falling down, they would say, 'A piled-up cloud.'
interpretation: This verse portrays the stubbornness and denial of the disbelievers. Even if confronted with a clear, miraculous sign from the heavens—a piece of the sky actually falling—they would refuse to acknowledge it as a divine warning. Instead, they would dismiss it as nothing more than an ordinary meteorological phenomenon, a mass of clouds. This illustrates how a heart closed to faith will rationalize or explain away even the most extraordinary evidence, choosing denial over recognition of divine truth.

translation: So leave them until they meet their Day in which they will be struck down.
interpretation: The verse is a statement of divine forbearance coupled with a stern warning. God instructs the Prophet (and by extension, the believers) to disengage from futile arguments with those who reject the truth. The phrase يَلاقُوا يَوْمَهُمُ الَّذِي فِيهِ يُصْعَقُونَ ('they meet their Day in which they will be struck down') refers to the Day of Judgment, characterized here by an overwhelming, paralyzing terror—the root ص ع ق conveys the idea of being seized by a thunderous, annihilating force. The command فَذَرْهُمْ ('leave them') implies that divine justice will inevitably arrive; human effort cannot hasten or prevent it, and the believers are not responsible for forcing acceptance. It serves as a reminder that ultimate accountability belongs solely to God, who alone knows the appointed time of reckoning.

translation: A Day when their scheming will not avail them aught, nor will they be helped.
interpretation: This verse declares that on the Day of Judgment, the cunning plots and strategic maneuvers that people relied upon in worldly life will lose all power and effect. No amount of deception, alliances, or worldly influence will provide protection or rescue from divine justice. The verse emphasizes human helplessness before God's ultimate sovereignty, stripping away the false sense of security derived from worldly tactics and reminding that true deliverance comes only from Allah, not from any human stratagem or external support.

translation: And for those who have wronged, there is a punishment before that [resurrection], but most of them do not know.
interpretation: This verse serves as a stern warning that the ultimate punishment of the Hereafter is not the only consequence for the wrongdoing of oppressors; rather, they will also face a form of retribution or hardship in this worldly life, a consequence rooted in the natural order of existence that often manifests as suffering, loss, or societal collapse. The concluding phrase highlights a profound spiritual tragedy: the heedlessness of the majority of wrongdoers is so deep that they fail to recognize the causes of their afflictions and the impending ultimate accountability. This spiritual blindness perpetuates their cycle of injustice, as they do not connect their actions to their worldly suffering, nor do they look ahead to the final judgment, rendering them incapable of repentance and correction.

translation: And be patient for the decision of your Lord, for indeed you are under Our Eyes. And glorify with praise of your Lord when you rise.
interpretation:
This verse is addressed to Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and, by extension, to all believers who follow his example. Its central message is a divine exhortation to steadfastness in the face of trials and the challenging responsibilities of the prophetic mission. To be patient for the 'decision' (حكم) of the Lord means to rely entirely on divine wisdom and timing, to cease striving through personal anxiety or impatience, and to await Allah's ruling with absolute trust, knowing that His judgment is always perfect and just. 

The phrase 'you are under Our Eyes' (بأعيننا) offers profound solace. It does not merely mean divine surveillance, but rather conveys a sense of close watchfulness, care, honor, and protection. The Prophet is being assured that he is never alone, nor is he abandoned in his struggles; every hardship he endures and every effort he makes is witnessed, valued, and guarded by Allah Himself. This care is not restricted to moments of trial, for the subsequent command to 'glorify with praise of your Lord when you rise' (سبّح بحمد ربّك حين تقوم) extends divine attention into the ordinary rhythms of life. Rising—whether from sleep, from a seated position, or to undertake one's daily duties—is presented as an opportunity to remember and praise Allah, transforming mundane acts into worship. 

The verse, therefore, balances the weight of duty with the comfort of divine nearness. Patience is not mere passive waiting, but an active state of trust combined with constant remembrance of God. The believer is called to endure, knowing that their life is held in divine sight, and to sanctify their movements through constant praise, weaving devotion into the fabric of daily existence.

translation: And during the night, glorify Him, and at the setting of the stars.
interpretation: This verse commands believers to remember and glorify Allah through prayer and remembrance during the specific times of night and at the dawn when the stars begin to fade, emphasizing the importance of consistent devotion across different periods of the day and night.

translation: By the star when it descends (or falls).
interpretation: This opening verse of Surah An-Najm (Chapter 53) draws attention to the celestial phenomenon of a falling star as a divine sign. Some scholars suggest that the reference to the descending star alludes to the shooting stars used by Allah to repel the eavesdropping devils, as mentioned in other Quranic passages. The verse serves as a solemn oath, emphasizing the magnitude of what is about to be revealed in the surah. It also functions as a reminder of Allah's power over the heavens and the natural order, preparing the listener or reader to receive the profound truths that follow, including the account of Prophet Muhammad's ascension (Mi'raj) and the unambiguous affirmation that Allah is the sole God worthy of worship.

translation: Your companion [Muhammad] has not strayed, nor has he erred,
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine reassurance regarding the spiritual integrity and sincerity of the Prophet Muhammad. The dual mention of misguidance (ضلال) and error (غواية) is significant, as it refutes any notion that his teachings are based on personal desire, ignorance, or madness. The word 'companion' (صاحب) is used to address the believers, implying that those who live with the Prophet and witness his character can attest to the truth of this divine statement. Consequently, the verse establishes the Prophet as a trustworthy guide and a clear example, demanding that his words and actions be received with trust and followed with devotion, rather than being doubted or rejected.

translation: And he does not speak from [his own] desire.
interpretation: This part of the verse from Surah An-Najm (53:3) emphasizes that the Prophet Muhammad is not conveying his own thoughts, opinions, or personal whims, but rather he is transmitting divine revelation from Allah. The word 'الهوى' refers to personal desire or caprice, which is often associated with subjectivity and human inclination. By stating that the Prophet does not speak from his own desire, the Qur'an asserts the authenticity and divine origin of the message he delivers, distinguishing it from personal interpretation or human fabrication. This highlights the concept of Prophethood in Islam, where the messenger serves as a conduit for divine guidance, remaining free from personal biases and ensuring that the message remains pure and untainted by human error.

translation: It is not but a revelation revealed.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that the Quran is not a product of human composition or personal desire, but rather a divine message communicated to the Prophet Muhammad by Allah through the angel Gabriel. By stating that the Quran is only

translation: Taught by one of fierce power,
interpretation: The verse refers to the angel Gabriel (Jibril), describing him as possessing immense and overwhelming strength, underscoring the awe-inspiring nature of the divine revelation conveyed to Prophet Muhammad.

translation: Possessor of power, then He established/exalted Himself [over the Throne].
interpretation: This phrase describes Allah as the One who possesses perfect, absolute power and might, free from any weakness or imperfection. Following this, His 'istiwa' (establishing Himself) over the Throne signifies His supreme authority, sovereign dominion, and uncontested rule over all creation. It emphasizes that His authority is not delegated but inherent to His nature as the Most Powerful. The verse serves to remind humanity that all true power belongs to Allah alone, and that human strength or worldly authority is transient and ultimately subordinate to His eternal majesty.

translation: .تفسير: والله سبحانه كان في أعلى موقع من الأفق، يعني في أرفع الأماكن وأسماها، حيث ظهر للرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم في ححَوته الأولى بشكل واضح ومشاهدة عيانية، دون أي شك أو تأويل، في أعلى رتبة من الأفاق، ليعلم أنه صادق فيما يبلغه عن ربه، وأن الحق بين يديه، فلما عاين الأعلى بعينه صار أكثر تسليما وثباتا على الدعوة والرسالة، وذلك في غار حراء حين فجأه الوحي وهو في أعلى الأفاق من سماء الدنيا، فرأى من آيات ربه الكبرى، فكانت هذه الرؤية تأسيسا لمبدأ الوحي والنبوة، وتشريفا للرسول بالمرتبة العليا في التكليل بحمل الأمانة، فمن عاين الأعلى علم أنه صادق بلا جدال، ومصطحب بلا غلط.
interpretation: God, glorified be He, was at the highest position of the horizon, meaning in the loftiest of places and the highest heavens, where He appeared to the Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, in his first encounter in a clear and observable manner, without any doubt or interpretation, at the highest rank of horizons, so that he would know that he is truthful in what he conveys from his Lord, and that the truth is in his hands. When he witnessed the highest with his own eyes, he became more surrendered and steadfast in his call and message, and that was in the cave of Hira when the revelation came to him while he was at the highest horizon of the worldly sky, and he saw the great signs of his Lord. This vision was the foundation for the beginning of revelation and prophethood, and an honor for the Messenger with the high rank of being entrusted with the trust. Whoever saw the highest with his own eyes knew that he is truthful without dispute, and accompanied without mistake.

translation: Then he approached and descended closer.
interpretation: This verse describes the closest encounter between the Prophet Muhammad and the divine presence, during which he drew near and descended in a state of intimate proximity, signifying the pinnacle of spiritual elevation and direct communion with the divine.

translation: And was at a distance of two bow lengths or nearer.
interpretation: This verse describes the intimate closeness the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ experienced during his encounter with the divine presence, symbolized by the image of being only two bow-lengths away—or even closer. It conveys the idea of extraordinary nearness to the source of revelation, while also implicitly affirming the Prophet's high spiritual rank and the reality of a direct, unmediated connection between him and God. The phrase serves both as a description of his unique experience and as a means to inspire believers to aspire toward closeness with the Divine.

translation: So He revealed to His servant what He revealed.
interpretation: This verse from Surah An-Najm (53:10) describes the moment when Allah communicated directly with the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) during the Night of Ascension (Laylat al-Miraj). The phrase emphasizes the profound nature of this divine communication, where Allah conveyed His guidance, knowledge, and spiritual realities to the Prophet. The deliberate repetition of the word 'orbi/a' (revealed) underscores the magnitude and significance of this revelation—something beyond ordinary human experience. The verse affirms that Muhammad was indeed chosen as Allah's servant and messenger, and that the knowledge he received came directly from the Divine, distinguishing this encounter from ordinary prophetic inspiration. It also highlights the intimate connection between Allah and His chosen servant, reinforcing the Prophet's elevated spiritual station while affirming his role as a vessel through whom divine guidance reached humanity. This event set the foundations for the obligations of the five daily prayers and marked a pivotal moment in Islamic spiritual history.

translation: The heart did not lie about what it saw.
interpretation: This affirms that the Prophet Muhammad’s inner certainty matched the outward vision he experienced—truth and inner perception were in perfect alignment.

translation: Do you dispute with him over what he sees?
interpretation: This rhetorical question challenges those who doubt the veracity of the Prophet's vision, affirming that his spiritual sight is a certainty bestowed by God, not something subject to human debate or skepticism. It underscores the divine origin of his experience, calling people to accept it rather than contest it.

translation: And he certainly saw him [Gabriel] in another descent.
interpretation: This verse affirms that the Prophet Muhammad experienced multiple encounters with the angel Gabriel, with this particular vision occurring during a second, distinct descent, likely referring to the Prophet's Night Journey and Ascension (Isra and Mi'raj), where he saw definitive signs from his Lord, reinforcing the reality of the divine message he received and his own status as a witness to the unseen realms.

translation: At the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary,
interpretation: This phrase marks the furthest limit of created existence, beyond which even the highest created beings cannot pass. It signifies that the Prophet Muhammad's Night Journey reached the ultimate frontier of the knowable and tangible cosmos, where ordinary perception gives way to direct encounter with the Divine, indicating that the reality of what lies beyond can only be experienced, not conceptualized or grasped through ordinary means of knowledge.

translation: With it is a garden of refuge (jannat al-ma'wa),
interpretation: This phrase refers to the ultimate destination promised to the righteous and the God-conscious: a secure, tranquil garden that serves as their final abode. The term 'al-ma'wa' (المأوى) implies a place of ultimate shelter and return, suggesting that the trials and hardships of worldly life are temporary, while this divine sanctuary represents the eternal, settled state of the soul. It speaks to the promise that those who are mindful of God will not be left to drift in a state of anxiety or homelessness, but will find a permanent resting place characterized by peace, security, and proximity to the Divine.

translation: When the Lote-tree was covered with what it was covered with.
interpretation: This verse refers to a profound mystical event in which the Prophet Muhammad, during his ascension (Mi'raj), encountered the Lote-tree (Sidrat al-Muntaha), a celestial boundary beyond which no creation can pass. The verse alludes to an overwhelming divine manifestation that engulfed the tree—be it light, angels, or a reality beyond human comprehension—signifying a moment where the boundaries of ordinary perception dissolved. It suggests that divine realities can transcend human intellect and language, emphasizing the limits of human understanding when confronted with the infinite nature of the divine. This encounter also symbolizes the Prophet's proximity to Allah, representing the ultimate spiritual ascent and the unveiling of truths that cannot be fully grasped by the human mind or expressed in words.

translation: The sight did not swerve, nor transgress.
interpretation: This phrase emphasizes steadfastness and precision in observation, particularly in the context of witnessing truth or revelation. It suggests that true perception remains anchored and does not deviate into distortion or excess. In spiritual terms, it implies that genuine insight or divine vision is unwavering, untainted by illusion, exaggeration, or misguidance. It speaks to the idea that authentic encounter with reality—whether through revelation, experience, or understanding—maintains balance and clarity, neither falling short nor overreaching. This balance is often seen as a hallmark of divine guidance, where the observer remains firmly grounded in truth without distortion or bias.

translation: He certainly saw of the greatest signs of his Lord.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Prophet Muhammad's experience of receiving divine revelation, understood within Islamic tradition as the Night Journey and Ascension (Isra and Mi'raj). The phrase 'the greatest signs' (al-ayat al-kubra) points to extraordinary manifestations of divine power that transcend ordinary human perception. The word 'ra'a' (saw) here is understood by scholars not as physical sight but as a spiritual and prophetic vision, since the realities of the unseen realm cannot be grasped through ordinary senses. The verse affirms that the Prophet was granted direct access to truths beyond the material world, establishing his unique station as a recipient of revelation. Rather than depicting him as a passive observer, the verse presents him as a witness to divine realities, which then authorized his mission to humanity. The use of 'kubra' (greatest) emphasizes the magnitude and unparalleled nature of what was revealed to him, setting his prophetic experience apart from all others.

translation: Have you then considered the Lat and the 'Uzza?
interpretation: This verse confronts the Meccan pagans with a direct, challenging question, forcing them to acknowledge the absurdity of their devotion to false deities like al-Lat and al-'Uzza, who were merely powerless idols incapable of providing any benefit or harm, thereby exposing the futility of their polytheistic beliefs.

translation: And al-Manāt, the third (goddess), the other one.
interpretation: This verse references al-Manāt as the third deity that the disbelievers worshipped alongside two others, alluding to the false idols (commonly identified as al-Lāt and al-‘Uzzā) whose worship was deeply entrenched in pre-Islamic Arabian custom. By naming this third entity, the Qurʾān exposes the arbitrary and fabricated nature of the pagan pantheon, emphasizing that these so-called deities are powerless and lack any divine reality, thereby contrasting them with the oneness of God.

translation: Is the male for you and for Him the female?
interpretation: This verse confronts the patriarchal and anthropomorphic biases of pre-Islamic Arabian society by challenging the listeners' sense of propriety. God rhetorically questions why they would ascribe to themselves the gender associated with strength and preference (the male), while attributing to God the gender they consider weaker or lesser (the female). The rhetorical force lies in exposing the absurdity of their logic: if they would be offended by being given daughters, why do they imagine God would accept what they themselves reject? It dismantles the tendency to project human social hierarchies onto the divine, asserting that God's nature transcends gendered categories and that such divisions are merely human constructs rooted in preference and bias, not in any reality of the divine.

translation: That is an unjust division!
interpretation: This verse condemns the practice, prevalent in pre-Islamic Arabian society, of allotting inheritance exclusively to male relatives while excluding women, children, and other dependents. The term 'ضيزى' signifies a distribution that is inherently inequitable and biased. By denouncing such practices as unjust, the Qur'an establishes the principle of equitable distribution and respect for the rights of all individuals, laying the groundwork for just and compassionate societal structures.

translation: They are nothing but names which you have named—you and your forefathers—for which God has sent down no authority. They follow nothing but conjecture and what their souls desire, although guidance has already come to them from their Lord.
interpretation: This verse is a powerful condemnation of those who fabricate false deities or ideologies based on nothing but tradition, hearsay, and personal desire, while clear guidance from God has already been provided to them. It serves as a warning against blindly following inherited beliefs and superstitions that lack any divine sanction, emphasizing that truth is found only in revelation from God, not in human invention or wishful thinking.

translation: Or does man have what he desires?
interpretation: This verse is a sharp rhetorical rebuke, challenging the false assumption that human beings can dictate the course of events or that all their ambitions and desires will be fulfilled. It serves as a reminder that ultimate control belongs solely to Allah, not to human aspiration. The interrogative tone dismantles human arrogance by exposing the gap between wishful thinking and divine will, teaching that success, provision, and destiny are not granted based on mere desire but according to Allah's wisdom and decree.

translation: So to Allah belongs the Hereafter and the first [life] (i.e., this world).
interpretation: The verse indicates that both the afterlife and the worldly life belong to Allah alone in terms of sovereignty, creation, and authority. It implies that the transient nature of this world is a preparation for the eternal abode, and that ultimate success and value lie in the Hereafter, while this world serves as a means and a test. A believer is therefore called to prioritize actions that have lasting significance for the Hereafter over fleeting worldly pursuits, recognizing that all phases of existence—temporal and eternal—fall under divine dominion. }

translation: And how many angels there are in the heavens whose intercession will not avail at all except [only] after Allah has permitted [it] to whom He wills and approves.
interpretation: This verse establishes that intercession (shafa'ah) is entirely subject to God's sovereign permission and pleasure, correcting any notion that angels, prophets, or other celestial beings possess independent power to influence divine judgment. The phrase 'how many angels' serves as a rhetorical device to emphasize abundance—despite the vast multitude of noble beings in the heavens, none can intercede autonomously. The condition of divine permission ('after Allah has permitted') affirms God's absolute authority, while 'approves' (yurda) introduces a moral dimension, suggesting that only those aligned with God's will and wisdom are granted this privilege. The verse thus dismantles hierarchical or patron-saint mentalities often associated with later theological traditions, reinforcing a strict monotheism where all created beings, regardless of status, remain subordinate to the divine will. It also implies that intercession is not a mechanical transaction but a grace contingent upon God's infinite knowledge and mercy, leaving ultimate judgment solely in His hands.

translation: Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter name the angels with female names.
interpretation: This verse condemns the practice of those who deny the resurrection and ultimate accountability, assigning female identities to the angels—a practice rooted in pre-Islamic Arabian polytheism and ignorance. By labeling the angels as female, these disbelievers attribute to them offspring and lineage (associating them with God as daughters, as in the claim that the angels are God's daughters), which contradicts the nature of the angels as honored, obedient servants of God. The verse thus exposes a fundamental error in their theology: rejecting the Hereafter leads to distorted conceptions of the unseen, including mischaracterizing the nature of the angels, who are neither male nor female in the human sense but are created beings wholly devoted to glorifying and serving God.

translation: They have no knowledge of it; they follow nothing but assumption, and assumption avails not against the truth at all.
interpretation: This verse condemns those who claim certainty about matters beyond their knowledge, relying instead on conjecture, speculation, or inherited assumption rather than verified truth. It establishes an epistemological principle that human cognition must be grounded in genuine knowledge (ʿilm) rather than mere probability (ẓann), because conjecture, however sincerely held, cannot substitute for or overcome objective reality. In the broader Qur'anic context, this verse critiques the attitude of disbelievers who fabricate beliefs about Allah or the unseen without evidentiary basis, and it serves as a caution against all forms of dogmatism unsupported by sound reasoning or revelation. The verse also implicitly elevates the value of intellectual humility, urging the believer to distinguish between what is known and what is merely guessed, since only truth itself can serve as a reliable foundation for belief and action.
