interpretation: This is part of the verse 70 of Surah Al-Qalam (68:70), where Allah addresses the Prophet Muhammad regarding the disbelievers of Quraysh who denied the Quran and the Day of Judgment. The full verse reads: 'It may be that he (the Prophet) will say, 'If only a treasure had been given to me, or if only I could have a shade (of shade)!' And We will say to them, 'Indeed, the criminals are in a far-off error.' The word 'زعيم' (za'eem) in Arabic means a guarantor, sponsor, or one who takes responsibility. Here, it carries a tone of sarcasm and mockery. The disbelievers had certain leaders and prominent figures who claimed responsibility for their religious beliefs and decisions. In the context of the verse, it is said that on the Day of Judgment, when the reality is exposed, every disbeliever will disavow his leader and every leader will disavow his followers. 'زعيم' also refers to a 'master' or 'lord' — someone who is obeyed. In this context, the verse warns that the disbelievers' leaders (those whom they followed in disbelief) will become their worst enemies, and they will wish they could return to the world to separate themselves from them. The verse uses a tone of warning and admonition, indicating that the relationship between the leader and the followers in disbelief is not based on truth but on mutual manipulation and interest, and on the Day of Judgment, this relationship will collapse, and each party will blame the other. This verse is a stern warning to those who follow others without thought or evidence, reminding them that every individual is responsible for their own choices and deeds.

translation: Or do they have partners [false deities]? Then let them bring their partners, if they are truthful.
interpretation: This verse is a direct challenge to polytheists, asserting that if they believe their claimed deities share divine authority with God, they should produce evidence of their existence and power. It underscores the Islamic principle of strict monotheism (Tawhid), emphasizing that God's oneness is absolute and unchallengeable, while exposing the baselessness of shirk (associating partners with God). The rhetorical force of the verse invites believers and skeptics alike to consider the emptiness of polytheistic claims, which lack any tangible proof or rational foundation. In essence, it calls upon those who dispute God's exclusive divinity to substantiate their beliefs, reinforcing that truth stands evident and self-evident against all falsehood.

translation: The Day the shin is uncovered and they are called to prostration, but they will not be able to do it.
interpretation: This verse describes a terrifying moment of the Day of Judgment, using the vivid image of an uncovered shin (a traditional Arabic idiom for a moment of intense, grave seriousness and hardship, like when one tucks up one's garment for serious action or battle). It depicts the sudden unveiling of the stark reality of the Hereafter, stripping away all worldly pretense. In that moment, those who in worldly life were arrogant and refused to bow to God, or whose prostration (symbolizing submission, humility, and acknowledgment of the Truth) was merely outward and hypocritical, will be commanded to prostrate but will find themselves utterly unable to do so. Their backs will become rigid like a locked joint (as described in the preceding verses), and they will be in a state of humiliation and helplessness, exposed before the Almighty. It emphasizes that true submission and the ability to humble oneself before God are gifts of this world; when the moment of ultimate truth arrives, insincerity and arrogance become a prison, and the soul is left unable to perform the very act of acknowledging its Creator.

translation: ,And their eyes humbled, humiliation shall cover them; and they were [already] called to prostration while they were sound.
interpretation: In this powerful verse, the imagery is one of profound spiritual reversal and the ultimate consequence of rejecting divine guidance. The "humbled eyes" and "humiliation covering them" depict a state of absolute powerlessness, shame, and the removal of all worldly pride or false confidence. This is contrasted with their previous state on Earth, when they were physically and mentally capable of performing prostration—the most humble and physically grounded act of worship in Islam—yet chose to reject it out of arrogance or heedlessness. The phrase "while they were sound" (وَهُمْ سَالِمُونَ) emphasizes that they had full physical and mental capacity, opportunity, and well-being to submit to God, but deliberately refused. The verse thus serves as a stark warning about squandering the gift of ability, health, and time to turn toward God. On the Day of Judgment, their state will be the opposite of their former potential: from being able to bow in voluntary humility before God, they will be forced into a state of utter lowliness. The deeper meaning highlights that true dignity lies in voluntary submission to the Divine, while rejection of this path, despite ability, leads to an enforced and far more painful humiliation in the end. It underscores the themes of moral accountability, the gravity of rejecting sincere worship, and the profound loss incurred by those who let arrogance or negligence override the opportunity for spiritual connection in this life.

translation: So leave Me alone with whoever denies this hadith. We will lead them on step by step from where they do not know.
interpretation: This verse from Surah Al-Qalam (68:44) is a divine admonition directed at Prophet Muhammad regarding those who reject the Qur'an. It conveys two key messages: first, that the Prophet should entrust the matter of disbelievers entirely to Allah, refraining from grieving over their rejection; second, that Allah will gradually lead them further into misguidance in ways they may not perceive. This

translation: And I will give them respite; indeed, My plan is firm.
interpretation: This verse expresses divine patience and strategic certainty. The phrase "وَأُمْلِي لَهُمْ" (And I will give them respite) reflects the deliberate and measured response of the divine will. It suggests that what appears to be inaction or delay is not weakness but a calculated allowance of time. The word "إِنَّ كَيْدِي مَتِينٌ" (indeed, My plan is firm) reinforces the idea that this apparent leniency is not indifference but rather a steadfast and unyielding design. It conveys that those who persist in wrongdoing or opposition may be given the illusion of freedom or success, yet they remain within a larger framework of inevitable consequence. The verse emphasizes that true power lies not in immediate intervention but in the certainty that justice will prevail in due course. It also carries an implicit warning: any sense of security based on delay is misplaced, as the underlying structure of events is already determined and resolute. This juxtaposition of respite and firmness invites reflection on the nature of divine wisdom—where patience is not passivity, and delay is not defeat. Ultimately, it assures the righteous and warns the wrongdoer that all actions are observed and accounted for within a plan that cannot be subverted or resisted.

translation: Or do you, [O Muhammad], ask them for a payment? But they are in a burden of debt?
interpretation: This verse challenges the disbelievers' resistance to faith by pointing out that the Messenger is not demanding worldly compensation for his prophetic mission. The 'burden of debt' (mighram) refers to the heavy toll they imagine would be imposed upon them if they accepted his message—suggesting their reluctance stems from a fear of spiritual or material cost rather than from any genuine intellectual objection. By framing their evasion in terms of imagined financial burden, the verse exposes the pettiness of their excuses: they cling to disbelief not because the truth is unclear, but because they perceive faith itself as an unwelcome expense.

translation: Or have they [knowledge of] the unseen, so they are writing it down?
interpretation: This rhetorical question challenges those who deny the truth of divine revelation and prophetic warning. It asks whether such people possess knowledge of the hidden, unseen realities—the ultimate outcomes of human conduct, the fate of souls, and the nature of the afterlife—which are known only to God. By asking whether they are 'writing it down,' the verse exposes the absurdity of their position: they speak as though they have authoritative access to unseen truths and are recording definitive judgments, when in reality they are merely speculating and fabricating claims without divine knowledge. The question underscores that ultimate truth belongs to God alone, and any attempt to set their own words or judgments alongside divine decree is unfounded arrogance.

translation: So be patient with the decree of your Lord, and do not be like the companion of the whale [i.e., Jonah] when he called out, while he was distressed.
interpretation: The verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad, urging him to remain steadfast in the face of opposition and persecution he faced from the Quraysh, as divine outcomes unfold in their own time. The reference to 'the companion of the whale' alludes to the Prophet Jonah (Yunus), who, overwhelmed by the burdens of his prophetic mission and the reluctance of his people to heed his message, became angry and despondent when they did not respond, eventually abandoning his community. After being swallowed by the whale (or great fish), Jonah cried out from within its belly in a state of profound distress ('makzum', meaning laden with grief, choked by anguish, or overcome with resentment). The verse serves as a cautionary reminder that the Prophet Muhammad must not resemble Jonah's impatience or the internal emotional turmoil that arises when one's efforts seem unrewarded. Instead, he is called to exercise unwavering patience and submission to the divine will, trusting that Allah's timing and judgment are supreme. By drawing this parallel, the verse teaches a profound lesson about maintaining composure, trust, and perseverance in fulfilling one's mission, even when facing hardship, and about the danger of allowing personal frustration to cloud one's commitment to the divine path.

translation: If it had not been for a favor from his Lord reaching him, he would have been cast forth upon the shore, blameworthy.
interpretation: The verse speaks of a person (commonly understood to refer to the Prophet Jonah/Yunus) who was in a state of distress and deserved blame or rejection, but was saved from being cast out naked and disgraced only because a mercy and favor from his Lord intervened to rescue him from his plight; thus, it teaches that human beings are dependent on divine grace to escape the consequences of their own faults and that even those who err may be spared disgrace and ruin through God's compassion.

translation: So his Lord chose him, and made him among the righteous.
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Ayyub (Job), whose patient endurance through immense suffering was rewarded by God. After his prolonged trials, God selected him and restored him to a state of righteousness and spiritual soundness. The word 'اجتباه' (istajāba/ijtabā) implies a special selection or election by God, indicating divine favor bestowed upon those who demonstrate unwavering faith and submission during times of hardship. It underscores the principle that steadfastness in faith, particularly under duress, leads to divine recognition and inclusion among the righteous. This concept serves as an encouragement for believers to remain patient and trustful in God's wisdom, knowing that perseverance can lead to elevated spiritual status in God's sight.

translation: And those who disbelieve almost make you slip with their eyes when they hear the Reminder and say, 'He is indeed a madman.'
interpretation: This verse describes the intense hostility and malicious envy of the disbelievers toward the Prophet Muhammad, suggesting that their hateful gazes alone almost cause him to stumble or be harmed, while they dismiss his message by labeling him as insane.

translation: And it is not but a reminder to the worlds.
interpretation: This statement from the Qur'an affirms that the message of Islam is fundamentally a universal reminder and guidance for all of humanity, regardless of race, time, or geographical location. The word 'dhikr' (reminder) suggests that the truths contained within the Qur'an are not entirely new concepts, but rather a renewal and clarification of the primordial truths that have been conveyed to humanity through previous prophets. The universality implied by 'al-'alamin' (the worlds) emphasizes the comprehensive scope of this message, intended to reach beyond the immediate audience to encompass all of creation, including jinn and humans, and extending through all generations until the Day of Judgment.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. The Reality (the Inevitable Event).
interpretation: This opening of Surah Al-Haqqah introduces one of the divine names for the Day of Judgment. The term 'Al-Haqqah' signifies the truth that must inevitably come to pass, the event whose occurrence is undeniable and absolute. It refers to the Day of Resurrection, which is described here as a certainty beyond any doubt. By naming this surah after this attribute, the Qur'an emphasizes the undeniable reality of ultimate accountability before God, calling all of humanity to recognize that this momentous event will surely arrive, disrupting worldly assumptions and establishing a true reckoning of deeds.

translation: , the Inevitable Reality
interpretation: This opening phrase, which begins Surat Al-Ḥāqqah (Chapter 69), employs the Arabic interrogative form "mā" (what?) not as a request for information but as a rhetorical device to express awe, astonishment, and overwhelming magnitude. By asking "What is the Inevitable Reality?" the verse immediately captivates the listener's attention and compels them to contemplate something beyond ordinary human experience. The term "Al-Ḥāqqah" (the Inevitable Reality or the Sure Reality) refers to the Day of Judgment—known in Islamic theology as one of several names for the Day of Resurrection, including Al-Qāriʿah (the Striking), Al-Ṣākhkhah (the Shatterer), and Al-Ṭāmmah (the Overshadowing). Each name emphasizes a different terrifying attribute of this day. The word "Ḥāqqah" is derived from the root letters ḥā-qāf-qāf, conveying meanings of truth, certainty, inevitability, and established occurrence. It indicates something that will undoubtedly come to pass with absolute certainty and necessity, leaving no room for doubt or escape. This is a day whose arrival is guaranteed by divine promise, beyond the reach of human denial or avoidance. The rhetorical question form is characteristic of the early Meccan surahs, designed to shake the indifferent and arouse those who had become heedless of life's ultimate purpose. By presenting the Day of Judgment as something so awe-inspiring that mere words cannot adequately describe it, the verse establishes from the very beginning the profound gravity and terror of what will follow in the rest of the surah—detailing scenes of divine punishment upon past nations who rejected their prophets, including the peoples of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, Lot, and Pharaoh, followed by descriptions of the events of the Day itself and the differing fates awaiting those who receive their records in their right hands versus those who receive them in their left. The verse thus serves as a powerful wake-up call, demanding reflection on mortality, accountability, and the temporary nature of worldly existence.

translation: ,And what can make you know what is the Inevitable Reality?
interpretation: This verse, at the end of Surah Al-Haqqah, serves as a powerful rhetorical device that emphasizes the awe-inspiring and overwhelming nature of the Day of Judgment. The phrase 'Al-Haqqah' (the Inevitable Reality) refers to the Day of Resurrection, which is absolute, undeniable, and will manifest with undeniable certainty. By asking 'what can make you know what it is?', the verse underscores the limitations of human understanding in comprehending the full magnitude, terror, and reality of that Day. It is a divine warning meant to instill a sense of urgency, humility, and fear in the hearts of those who hear it, urging them to prepare through faith and righteous deeds before the inevitable truth is revealed.

translation: The people of Thamud and 'Aad denied the Striking Blow [of Judgment].
interpretation: This verse signals a direct confrontation with disbelief. By naming Thamud and 'Aad, two ancient communities destroyed for their refusal to accept divine guidance, the verse establishes a sobering precedent: nations that turn away from truth invite their own downfall. The mention of 'the Striking Blow' (al-Qari'ah) references the unmistakable, overwhelming reality of accountability that will arrive without ambiguity. The purpose is not merely historical remembrance but a warning delivered to the listener that the same pattern of denial followed by decisive consequence remains in effect. Anyone who encounters clear evidence of truth and still chooses denial should understand that what came before them is not ancient folklore but an operative reality that awaits repetition.

translation: As for Thamud, they were destroyed by the overwhelming [blast]
interpretation: This phrase, appearing in Surah Al-Haqqah (69:5), refers to the destruction of the ancient Arab tribe of Thamud through a tremendous, overwhelming catastrophe. The Arabic word "الطاغية" (at-tāghiyah) comes from the root meaning to exceed bounds or transgress, and here it refers to a violent force or blast that transgressed all limits—commonly understood as the mighty cry or earthquake sent upon them for their refusal to accept the Prophet Salih. The verse serves as a warning to the Quraysh of the consequences of stubbornness in rejecting the Prophet Muhammad, drawing a parallel between the fate of Thamud and the potential downfall of any community that denies divine truth. It emphasizes that Allah's punishment, when it comes, is sudden and overwhelming, sparing no one.

translation: }And as for 'Ad, they were destroyed by a screaming, raging wind.
interpretation: This verse describes the specific nature of the punishment inflicted upon the ancient tribe of 'Ad. Unlike other nations destroyed by earthquakes, floods, or other calamities, the people of 'Ad were annihilated by a fierce, relentless wind. The use of the word 'sari' ( صرصر ) emphasizes the piercing coldness and harshness of the wind, while 'atiyah' ( عاتية ) describes it as exceeding all bounds of intensity and fury. This serves as a powerful reminder that divine punishment comes in various forms, often corresponding to the blessings or strengths in which a people place their arrogance. The people of 'Ad were known for their immense physical strength and impressive architectural achievements, yet they were reduced to nothing by a force they could not withstand, highlighting that no worldly power can protect against the will of the Divine.

translation: He subjected it [the wind] to them for seven nights and eight days in succession, so you would see the people therein [fallen] as if they were hollow trunks of palm trees.
interpretation: This verse refers to the punishment sent against the people of 'Aad, to whom the prophet Hud was sent. They were a powerful and arrogant people who rejected their prophet and his message. As a consequence, God subjected a violent, devastating wind to them that lasted for seven nights and eight days without interruption. The wind was so fierce and destructive that it uprooted them and threw them to the ground dead, their bodies looking like the hollow trunks of fallen palm trees—a vivid image of complete destruction and emptiness. The verse serves as a powerful reminder of the consequences of stubbornness, arrogance, and rejection of divine guidance. Despite the great physical strength and worldly power that 'Aad possessed, they were unable to withstand the wind sent by God, highlighting that no worldly power can protect one from divine punishment. The vivid imagery of the bodies as hollow palm trunks emphasizes the totality of the destruction—nothing remained of them but empty shells, devoid of life and meaning.

translation: So do you see any remnant of them?
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical question posed to the Prophet Muhammad, emphasizing that the disbelieving peoples who rejected the truth—such as the people of Noah, 'Aad, and others—have been utterly destroyed, leaving no trace of their existence as communities; it serves as a powerful warning that those who stubbornly oppose divine guidance will ultimately face complete annihilation, while also highlighting Allah's absolute sovereignty in deciding the fate of nations.

translation: And there came also Pharaoh and those before him, and the overturned cities [of Lot] with sin,
interpretation: This verse references three distinct historical communities that rejected divine guidance and were subsequently destroyed: Pharaoh (and his people in Egypt), earlier civilizations that had similarly defied God's prophets, and the cities of Lot (often identified with Sodom and Gomorrah), which were 'overturned' by a catastrophic divine punishment. The phrase 'بالخاطئة' (with sin) serves as the unifying cause of their downfall, indicating that their transgression—not mere disbelief but a persistent commitment to wrongdoing, corruption, and rejection of prophetic warnings—was the reason they were overtaken by ruin. The verse thus presents these accounts as cautionary examples, illustrating that every nation that persists in sin and refuses to heed divine admonition faces consequences, reinforcing the Qur'anic theme that God's justice operates across generations and civilizations.

translation: So they disobeyed the messenger of their Lord, so He seized them with a seizing that overwhelms.
interpretation: This verse from Sūrah al-Ḥāqqah (69:10) refers to the fate of past nations—such as the people of Pharaoh, Thamūd, ʿĀd, and others—who rejected the messengers sent to them. The phrase *faʿaṣaw rasūla rabbihim* (

translation: Indeed, when the water [of the flood] overflowed, We carried you [i.e., your ancestors] in the sailing vessel (the Ark).
interpretation: This verse refers to the great flood sent upon the people of Noah. It conveys the idea that when wrongdoing and corruption reach extreme levels, divine intervention comes to reset the balance. The saving of Noah's followers in the Ark symbolizes preservation of truth and righteousness amid overwhelming chaos, and serves as a reminder to future generations that human beings are ultimately accountable for their actions and can be rescued through faith and obedience.

translation: That We might make it a reminder for you, and that an ear attentive may retain it.
interpretation: The verse draws attention to the preservation of divine messages through attentive listening and reflects on the responsibility of the individual to absorb guidance with a discerning mind. It emphasizes that sacred truths are meant to be internalized by those who are consciously receptive, indicating that meaningful understanding comes not from passive hearing but from active reflection and remembrance, and that wisdom is retained only by those who cultivate an 'ear' that is both willing and aware.

translation: .When the Trumpet is blown with a single blast
interpretation: This verse describes the first of two trumpet blasts that herald the Day of Judgment in Islamic eschatology. The singular, powerful blast signifies the moment of cataclysmic transformation when the present world order is destroyed and all creation is summoned before God for final reckoning.

translation: And the earth and the mountains will be lifted up and crushed with a single blow.
interpretation: This vivid depiction signifies the immense power and irresistible nature of the Day of Judgment, where the established structures of the world, no matter how grand and unshakeable they may seem—like towering mountains—will be utterly obliterated by a singular, catastrophic event. It serves as a stark reminder of the transience of worldly existence and the ultimate authority of the divine command, rendering all human constructs insignificant in the face of the hereafter.

translation: So on that Day the [cataclysmic] event will have come to pass (or befall).
interpretation: This verse marks the certainty and inevitability of the Day of Judgment, emphasizing that its arrival is fixed and unavoidable. It serves as a sobering reminder of human mortality and the transient nature of worldly life, urging believers to prepare through faith and righteous deeds before that momentous day arrives when all will be held accountable.

translation: And the heaven will split asunder, for that day it will be frail (and easily broken).
interpretation: This verse depicts the profound and terrifying reality of the Day of Judgment. It employs the image of the sky splitting apart to convey a universe in complete disintegration, where the very fabric of the cosmos as we know it collapses. The word “واهية” (wāhiyah), often translated as frail, weak, or fragile, signifies a total loss of its usual strength and structure. On the one hand, it describes the physical shattering of the heavens; on the other hand, it serves as a powerful metaphor for the fragility of all worldly power and permanence. What appears steadfast and unchangeable becomes utterly vulnerable when God commands it to be so. This is meant to evoke awe and a sense of urgency, reminding human beings that the entire order of existence is contingent upon the will of God and that ultimate authority belongs to Him alone. The verse challenges any human attachment to the material world by showing that even the heavens themselves, often seen as the epitome of stability, will be undone. It is a call to recognize human vulnerability and to place trust not in worldly structures, but in the eternal nature of God. The awe-inspiring nature of this scene is intended to shake complacency and inspire reflection, repentance, and spiritual readiness for what lies beyond this life. In essence, the verse is not merely a prediction of cosmic destruction, but a profound theological statement about power, impermanence, and divine sovereignty. The splitting of the heavens becomes a visual symbol of the collapse of all false securities, leaving only the truth of God’s absolute dominion.

translation: And the angels will be at its edges. And the Throne of your Lord will be borne above them that Day by eight [angels].
interpretation: This verse portrays the profound reality of the Day of Judgment, emphasizing the vastness and majesty of the divine court. The mention of angels stationed at the 'edges' of the heavens or earth signifies the encompassing nature of the divine order, where creation is fully under the authority and watchfulness of Allah. The depiction of eight angels carrying the Throne of Allah above them symbolizes the immense power, nobility, and reverence of the angelic realm tasked with this supreme honor. It serves to illustrate the awe-inspiring scale of the afterlife, where earthly concepts of power and stability are transcended, and the sovereignty of Allah is manifested in its fullest, most absolute form, reminding humanity of the ultimate return to their Creator.

translation: That Day, you will be fully exposed, and no secret of yours will remain hidden.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment when every person will be presented before Allah in a state of total exposure—nothing hidden, no facade, no disguise. It speaks to the absolute accountability that awaits each soul, where inner intentions and concealed deeds become manifest. The verse serves as a profound warning that private actions, thoughts, and motives, even those never disclosed to others, will be scrutinized and revealed. It calls individuals to self-reflection and integrity in this worldly life, emphasizing that ethical conduct must be maintained not merely for public reputation but for one's ultimate accountability before God. The concept of 'خافية' (that which is hidden) encompasses all forms of concealment, reminding believers that sincerity and righteousness must permeate every aspect of life, as ultimate justice requires complete transparency before the Divine.

translation: As for him who is given his record in his right hand, he will say, "Here, read my record!
interpretation: This verse portrays the joyful and confident state of the righteous believer on the Day of Judgment. Receiving the book of deeds in the right hand is a traditional symbol of honor, salvation, and success in the Qur'anic worldview. The exclamation 'Here, read my record!' is not merely an instruction to others, but an eager invitation, reflecting a heart at peace, confident in the record of good deeds it has accumulated through a life of faith and righteousness. The believer's readiness to have their deeds read publicly demonstrates transparency and a deep inner assurance that nothing has been hidden or falsified. It also conveys a sense of pride—not arrogant, but gratefully acknowledging the mercy and guidance of Allah that enabled such a outcome. This scene stands in contrast to those who receive their record in their left hand or from behind their back, illustrating the ultimate fruit of sincere faith and righteous action.

translation: Indeed, I am certain that I will meet my account.
interpretation: This verse expresses the personal conviction of the speaker—likely from the story of the owner of the two gardens in Surah Al-Kahf—who acknowledges with certainty that he will eventually face divine reckoning for his deeds in the Hereafter, reflecting a moment of truthful self-reflection before acknowledging the transient nature of worldly life.

translation: He will be in a life of contentment/satisfaction.
interpretation: This verse depicts the ultimate state of the righteous believer in the afterlife as one of complete and lasting fulfillment, where every desire is satisfied and no suffering or discontent exists. It signifies that such a person has attained the highest possible existence, one free from hardship, grief, and unfulfilled longing, having earned divine approval and eternal bliss through faith and good deeds. The word "rādiyah" emphasizes a state of perfect self-contentment and divine pleasure combined, suggesting harmony between the soul's inner state and its external circumstances in Paradise.

translation: In a lofty Paradise.
interpretation: This phrase points to the ultimate reward for those who have attained spiritual success and inner peace. It describes a state of existence beyond the limitations of the material world, where one dwells in a reality that is pure, elevated, and free from corruption. The word "high" suggests that this station transcends the ordinary levels of being, offering a closeness to the divine and a vision that sees things as they truly are. It is a place where the heart finds its rest and the soul experiences fulfillment, untouched by the trials and tribulations of the lower world.

translation: [And] its fruit hanging low within reach,
interpretation: When the Quran describes the fruits of Paradise as "hanging low within reach," it paints a vivid picture of ease, accessibility, and effortless abundance in the afterlife. The word *qutūf* (قطوف) refers to gathered clusters or fruits that one plucks, and *dāniyah* (دانية) means near, close, and lowered. This imagery conveys that in Jannah (Paradise), the believer will not need to toil, struggle, or exert effort to obtain sustenance or pleasure. What was once difficult to attain in the worldly life—patience, perseverance, hardship, and striving—will yield a reward that comes to the believer with complete ease. The verse also carries a deeper spiritual meaning: the fruits of one's righteous deeds, sown through trials and discipline in this world, will be brought close and made easily accessible in the Hereafter. It reflects the Quranic theme that the struggles of the present life are temporary, while the fruits of faith and good character are everlasting and graciously within reach. The verse invites believers to endure life's challenges with patience, knowing that what is prepared for them by Allah is not only magnificent but also effortlessly attainable, free from any form of difficulty or deprivation.

translation: Eat and drink with satisfaction because of what you sent forth in the days gone by.
interpretation: This verse, spoken to the people of Paradise, encapsulates the principle of divine justice and the ultimate meaning of human action. The 'days gone by' refer to the earthly life, where every deed—every act of obedience, patience, charity, and remembrance—was essentially a deposit ('aslamtum') placed in trust for the Hereafter. The pleasure of Paradise is not arbitrary; it is the direct, unadulterated return on the investment of one's earthly deeds. The words 'eat and drink' signify complete, wholesome satisfaction ('hanna-an'), a state free from the anxieties of provision, physical ailment, or psychological distress that characterized worldly existence. The verse thus redefines the purpose of temporal life: it is a field of sowing whose harvest is eternal, and the bliss of the afterlife is the fruit of righteous conduct in the former.

translation: }But as for he who is given his record in his left hand, he will say, "Oh, I wish I had not been given my record,"
interpretation: This verse portrays the deep regret and despair of the one who receives the book of his deeds in his left hand—a symbol in Qur'anic imagery of misfortune, rejection, and failure on the Day of Judgment. The phrase "يا ليتني لم أوت كتابيه" ("Oh, I wish I had not been given my record") expresses an intense longing for non-existence of that moment, reflecting the crushing realization that one's deeds stand as undeniable testimony against oneself. This figure represents those who lived in denial of accountability, pursued worldly desires without heed to divine guidance, and now face the consequence of spiritual bankruptcy. The regret here is not merely about punishment but about the lost opportunity for repentance and righteous action. It conveys a profound moral lesson: the eternal consequences of one's choices are fixed, and no worldly success or evasion can alter the record written by one's own actions. The left hand in this context signifies disgrace and separation from divine mercy, contrasting with the right hand, which represents honor, success, and salvation. This verse invites the reader to reflect on the transient nature of worldly life and the importance of preparing for an irreversible reckoning through sincere faith and righteous conduct.

translation: And I do not know what my account will be.
interpretation: The speaker in this verse expresses profound uncertainty and humility regarding the ultimate reckoning of their deeds, acknowledging that despite their efforts and awareness, the final outcome of their life and deeds remains beyond their knowledge, thereby emphasizing human limitation and the exclusive domain of divine omniscience over the true state of one's record on the Day of Judgment.

translation: Oh, I wish it [the death] had been the final one [i.e., the first death that ends life]!
interpretation: This is an utterance attributed to some of the disbelievers or wrongdoers on the Day of Judgment, expressing a desperate wish that the death they had already experienced in the worldly life had been the ultimate end of their existence, so they would not have to face the horrors, accountability, and punishment of the Hereafter. It reflects the regret of those who rejected faith and lived in disobedience, realizing too late that resurrection and divine reckoning are real; they would rather have never been brought back to life than endure the terrifying consequences of their deeds. The verse highlights the profound remorse and hopelessness that grip those who denied the truth when they finally encounter the undeniable reality of the afterlife.

translation: What will my wealth avail me?
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the Pharaoh as he is drowning, reflects the ultimate futility of material power and arrogance before God. Having relied on his armies, riches, and political might throughout his life, Pharaoh finally confronts the truth that none of it can save him from divine punishment. It serves as a timeless warning that worldly possessions are temporary and meaningless when weighed against the eternal consequences of one's deeds, reminding believers that true security lies only in faith and accountability to God.

translation: Perished from me is my authority.
interpretation: This is the anguished cry of the Pharaoh as he realized his worldly power had failed to save him. At the moment of drowning, he confessed to belief in the God of the Children of Israel, but his claim to authority collapsed entirely. The verse illustrates the ultimate futility of worldly dominion and the absolute helplessness of human power before divine decree. Pharaoh's lament exposes a profound truth: the sovereignty he wielded over others was itself subordinate to a higher authority, and once life ends, all such illusions dissolve. It serves as a warning that no worldly status, however vast, can shield one from the consequences of one's actions or grant control over one's ultimate fate.

translation: Seize him and shackle him,
interpretation: This phrase refers to the stern command given to the angelic guardians of Hell regarding a specific individual who rejected faith and turned away from the Quran; it signifies the severe accountability and binding restraint that await the defiant disbeliever in the hereafter, emphasizing that ultimate authority belongs to God and that no one can escape His grasp when summoned for judgment.

translation: Then the Hellfire - they will be burned in it.
interpretation: This verse presents a stark warning about the ultimate destination of those who reject truth and persist in wrongdoing. The use of 'then' (ثُمَّ) indicates a progression or consequence, suggesting that after certain stages of accountability or judgment, the ultimate penalty is the Hellfire. The verb 'صَلَوْهَا' (they will enter/burn in it) implies an ongoing, active experience of punishment, not merely passive residence. This emphasizes the active, suffering nature of the consequences in the afterlife.

translation: Then [the angel will say], 'Tie him in a chain seventy cubits long.'
interpretation: This vivid imagery depicts a soul confronted with the consequences of rejecting divine guidance, being utterly restrained by an immensely long chain. The symbolic number seventy suggests a completeness or totality of constraint, implying that the soul is bound inescapably by its own accumulated misdeeds and the weight of its heedlessness. The chain is not merely an external punishment but a manifestation of the inner shackles forged by the soul's turning away from truth. This verse calls the reader to reflect on the profound nature of spiritual bondage—the idea that distance from the divine results in a self-imposed captivity, one far more confining than any physical restraint, and serves as a sobering reminder of the gravity of moral and spiritual negligence.

translation: Indeed, he used not to believe in Allah, the Supreme,
interpretation: This verse condemns a man's refusal to acknowledge the absolute authority and greatness of Allah, highlighting that his denial stemmed from arrogance and a refusal to submit to the ultimate truth, leading to his moral and spiritual ruin.

translation: And does not encourage feeding the poor.
interpretation: This phrase is part of a longer passage describing the negative qualities of the disbeliever or the one who denies the religion (ad-Din). Specifically, it highlights that such a person is not motivated by compassion or generosity toward the needy. By mentioning the lack of encouragement—even if it implies they do not personally feed the poor—the verse critiques a heart hardened against the suffering of others. It points to a deeper spiritual flaw: denying the Day of Judgment leads to a withdrawal from moral responsibility. When a person does not believe in accountability before God, they become indifferent to the welfare of the vulnerable. This serves as a powerful reminder that true faith manifests in action, particularly in caring for those in need. The verse calls believers to reflect on whether their lives reflect the opposite attitude—actively promoting generosity and ensuring that the poor are not forgotten or neglected.

translation: So [i.e., after the judgment] he will have no true friend here today, nor any intercessor who might be obeyed or heeded.
interpretation: This fragment from Surah Haqqah (69:35) is spoken by the inhabitants of Hellfire as they describe the condition of the wrongdoer cast into the Fire. The word "حميم" (ḥamīm) in classical Arabic carries a powerful range of meaning: it denotes a true, intimate companion, a close kinsman, or a heartfelt friend. It comes from the root meaning of intense, boiling heat, but in this context it refers to someone who shares the inner warmth of genuine, loyal friendship. The addition of "اليوم هاهنا" — "today, here" — emphasizes a shocking, absolute finality. On the Day of Judgment, at the very moment when a person most desperately needs someone to stand by them, to plead their case, to shield them, or simply to share the burden of their anguish, they discover that every such bond has been severed. No blood relation, no close companion, no one who once shared their secrets and their joys will step forward to advocate for them, because such bonds, if not rooted in taqwa (God-consciousness), dissolve before the terrifying reality of the Hereafter. The verse is a profound meditation on the nature of human relationships in light of eternity: those connections we cling to as ultimate sources of security — family, tribe, inner circle — prove utterly powerless when stripped of divine sanction. It calls the believer to reflect deeply: are the relationships we cultivate in this life oriented toward the Divine, or do we treat them as substitutes for our ultimate reliance upon Allah? The chilling truth conveyed is that on that Day, a person's only true intercessor and protector will be Allah Himself, and only those who lived in conscious alignment with His will will find refuge.

translation: And no food will there be except from the washing of wounds (or filth).
interpretation: This verse depicts a scene of severe punishment and deprivation in Hell, where the inhabitants are deprived of any wholesome nourishment and are instead given a foul, repulsive substance to eat. The phrase "from the washing of wounds" refers to the pus and excrement that wash down from the bodies of the tormented, serving as their only sustenance, emphasizing the degradation and suffering of those who rejected faith and righteousness.

translation: Let none eat it except the sinners.
interpretation: This phrase refers to a tree in the Hellfire called Zaqqum, which is described elsewhere in the Qur'an (such as in Surah Al-Waqi'ah and Surah Al-Isra) as a bitter and foul food that grows from the depths of Hell. The verse indicates that this tree will be a source of nourishment exclusively for the disobedient and unrepentant sinners who rejected Allah's guidance and earned His punishment. By restricting its consumption to the sinners, it serves as a powerful symbol of their alienation from all goodness, as even its consumption is portrayed as an act exclusive to those who transgressed against divine commands, emphasizing both the severity of their punishment and their complete separation from the mercy and blessings enjoyed by the righteous in Paradise.

translation: So I swear by what you see (i.e., all that you perceive with your senses)
interpretation: This verse marks the beginning of a powerful oath by Allah, emphasizing that He swears by the observable phenomena of creation and all that is within human perception, as well as what is hidden from them. The phrase 'فلا أقسم' (So I swear) serves as a solemn prelude to an impending declaration about the certainty of the Hereafter and the truth of the Qur'an, or the consequences of denying it. By swearing by 'what you see'—the visible world, the heavens, the earth, and all sensory experiences—Allah draws attention to the signs embedded in creation that point to His power and the reality of the afterlife. This rhetorical oath underscores the gravity of the truth about to be revealed, urging reflection on the tangible and intangible aspects of existence as evidence of divine authority and the inevitability of resurrection and judgment.

translation: And what you do not perceive (or see)
interpretation: This phrase highlights the limits of human perception and knowledge in contrast to the boundless knowledge and awareness of Allah. It serves as a reminder that there are countless realities, truths, and dimensions of existence—whether spiritual, cosmic, or metaphysical—that are beyond human sensory perception and intellectual grasp. Humans tend to evaluate reality based on what they can see, hear, or rationally deduce, but this verse reminds believers that divine wisdom encompasses far more than what is apparent. It encourages humility, faith in the unseen (al-ghayb), and reliance on divine revelation, since finite human senses cannot fully comprehend the infinite nature of Allah's creation, will, and plan. This concept is central to Islamic theology, which maintains that belief in the unseen is a fundamental aspect of faith, as mentioned in Surah Al-Baqarah (2:3).

translation: It is truly the saying of a noble messenger.
interpretation: The verse affirms that the Qur'an is not the speech of a human or a jinn, but a message delivered by a noble messenger (Jibreel) who brings it from Allah, emphasizing its divine origin and the high rank of the angel entrusted with its conveyance.

translation: And it is not the word of a poet. Little do you believe.
interpretation: The statement emphasizes a contrast between divine revelation and human poetic speech, asserting that the message being conveyed does not originate from poetic imagination or personal expression. It highlights a spiritual deficiency in human belief, suggesting that limited faith prevents full recognition of the divine nature of the message. This serves to distinguish the sacred text from literary art, pointing toward its transcendent origin beyond human creativity.

translation: Nor is it the speech of a soothsayer; little do you reflect.
interpretation: This verse firmly denies any attribution of the Qur'an to the utterances of fortune-tellers or diviners, suggesting that humanity fails to contemplate deeply enough to recognize its divine origin, as it is distinguished from humanly fabricated or supernatural claims.

translation: [This is] a revelation from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: This phrase affirms that the Qur'an is not a human fabrication, poetry, or magic, but a divine message sent down by Allah, who is the Cherisher and Sustainer of all creation. By describing Allah as the 'Lord of the worlds' (Rabb al-'Alamin), it emphasizes His absolute sovereignty, authority, and care over every realm of existence—whether they are the worlds of humans, jinn, angels, animals, or the cosmos. This establishes the Qur'an's authenticity and authority as a source of guidance, demanding that it be accepted with reverence and submission, as it originates from the ultimate source of truth and power. It also serves as a foundational principle of the Islamic faith: that true knowledge, guidance, and legislation come only from divine revelation, not from human conjecture or desire.

translation: If [Muhammad] had invented something about Us,
interpretation: This hypothetical scenario establishes the impossibility of fabrication in the Qur'an through a logical consequence: had Muhammad invented statements and falsely attributed them to Allah, he would have faced severe divine retribution. The verse thus affirms both the human role of the Prophet as a transmitter and the divine origin of the revelation, making any notion of human authorship inconceivable given the reality of his protected prophethood.

translation: We would have seized him by the right hand.
interpretation: The verse describes God's absolute power to instantly halt any falsehood or false claim-maker. The 'right hand' symbolizes might, strength, and decisive action. It means that if a liar forged something against God (contextually referring to fabrications about divine revelations), God would immediately destroy that fabricator with overwhelming force. The verse underscores that no false statement can stand against divine authority and that God's grasp is inescapable and absolute.

translation: Then We would have severed his aorta.
interpretation: This verse describes a hypothetical scenario in which a determined opponent of the Prophet Muhammad's message persists in denial and opposition despite clear evidence. The 'awtin' (وتين) refers to the aorta or the vital sinew that connects the body to life, and severing it would mean instant death. The verse employs a powerful conditional statement to demonstrate that had Allah willed to destroy the denier, He could have done so instantly and decisively; however, divine wisdom chooses patience and respite, granting the individual time to reflect and turn back from falsehood. It highlights both Allah's absolute power over life and death and His attribute of forbearance, showing that restraint does not arise from inability but from purposeful mercy.

translation: And there is not one of you who could prevent [Him] from it.
interpretation: This statement emphasizes God's absolute sovereignty and irresistible power, asserting that no human being can act as an intercessor or barrier against His decree. It serves as a powerful reminder of human helplessness before the divine will, contrasting the limited agency of humanity with the unchallengeable authority of God. Such a verse is intended to inspire humility and a recognition of submission to God, while also reinforcing the futility of relying on any power other than the divine for protection or salvation. In classical tafsir, this phrase is often paired with reflections on the Day of Judgment, where no created being can shield another from God's ultimate justice. It strips away any illusions of self-sufficiency, urging believers to place their trust solely in God, who alone has the capacity to withhold or grant mercy as He wills.

translation: And indeed it is a reminder for the muttaqeen (the God-conscious, those who fear Allah).
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that the Qur'an serves as a profound source of guidance and admonition specifically for those who possess taqwa—inner awareness of and reverence for Allah. While the Qur'an's message is universally accessible, its transformative power, depth of meaning, and spiritual benefit are fully realized only by individuals who approach it with sincere piety, humility, and a conscious effort to live in accordance with divine guidance. For such people, the Qur'an functions as an ongoing reminder that nurtures their faith, corrects their conduct, and strengthens their relationship with Allah.

translation: And indeed, We know that among you are those who deny,
interpretation: This verse acknowledges that while the Prophet is delivering the divine message with sincerity and truth, there will inevitably be some among his audience who reject it. It reflects the Quranic theme that disbelief is a known outcome of prophetic mission, yet it does not diminish the truth or weaken the responsibility of the messenger, nor does it give those who deny any justification before God.

translation: And it will surely be a regret for the disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse expresses that the Quran, or the truth presented within it, will become a source of deep regret and sorrow for those who reject faith. The 'regret' here refers not merely to a momentary feeling of remorse, but to an intense, enduring grief that the disbelievers will experience when they realize the magnitude of what they have forfeited by their rejection of divine guidance. This regret is distinct from the regret of the hypocrites and sinners mentioned elsewhere, as it is rooted in a fundamental denial of the truth itself. The verse underscores the irreversible loss incurred by those who turn away from faith, highlighting the gravity of disbelief and the eternal consequences that follow from rejecting the clear signs and guidance offered by God.

translation: And it is surely the certain truth.
interpretation: This phrase emphasizes the absolute, unquestionable certainty of the message being conveyed, which is understood in context to refer to the Qur'an or the realities of the Hereafter, judgment, and divine promise. The use of the emphatic form 'لحق اليقين' (the certain truth) underscores that this matter is beyond doubt, conjecture, or denial; it is an established reality that will inevitably come to pass, demanding sincere reflection and preparation from those who hear it.

translation: So glorify the name of your Lord, the Magnificent.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound directive to turn away from worldly preoccupations and engage in the remembrance and glorification of God. The word 'Subhan' (glorified/exalted) implies a recognition of God's absolute perfection, sovereignty, and transcendence above any imperfection, weakness, or human conception. By commanding the Prophet to glorify His name, it calls for an active, continuous state of spiritual awareness—a life oriented toward acknowledging God's majesty. The attribute 'Al-Azim' (the Magnificent/Great) points to God's overwhelming greatness that encompasses all of existence, reminding humanity that true power, authority, and significance belong solely to Him. This teaching offers comfort and guidance to believers: when facing trials, awe, or challenge, the response is not helplessness but a conscious elevation of God, which realigns the heart and mind with a higher, eternal perspective, fostering inner peace, humility, and resilience through a profound connection with the Divine.

translation: :The asker has asked for a punishment that is bound to come
interpretation: This verse refers to a person, identified by many scholars as al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who challenged the Prophet Muhammad by demanding that God's promised punishment of disbelievers be brought upon him immediately. The Quran responds by affirming that such punishment is inevitable and decreed, though its timing is known only to God. It serves as a warning that divine justice cannot be rushed or manipulated, and that those who doubt or mock the promise of accountability will face its reality. The verse also subtly shifts the perspective, reminding the questioner that certainty about the unseen, including the timing of divine retribution, rests with God alone, not with human demand.

translation: .لِلكَافِرِينَ لَيْسَ لَهُ دَافِعٌ
interpretation: The verse expresses that for the disbelievers, the punishment or consequence they face has no one to repel or avert it from them.

translation: From Allah, the Lord of the ascending stations.
interpretation: This phrase appears as part of a longer verse (Surah Nuh 71:3-4) where Allah commands Prophet Nuh to warn his people. The mention of 'the Lord of the ascending stations' (ذي المعارج) refers to Allah's sovereignty over the heavens and the means by which angels and souls ascend to His presence. The term 'ma'arij' (plural of mi'raj) signifies elevated ranks, degrees, or paths of ascent, which can be understood as the celestial spheres, the ranks of angels, or the stages of spiritual elevation that exist in Allah's creation. This description serves to remind Nuh's people—and by extension, all of humanity—that the one issuing the warning is not a mere mortal but Allah, who holds supreme authority over all realms of existence, including those beyond human perception. The phrase emphasizes divine transcendence and the obligation to recognize Allah's majesty and respond to His call.

translation: The angels and the Spirit will ascend to Him on a Day whose duration is fifty thousand years.
interpretation: This verse describes the profound and awe-inspiring nature of the Day of Judgment. The 'ascension of the angels and the Spirit'—where 'the Spirit' is often understood as the angel Jibreel (Gabriel), distinguished here by his supreme rank—refers to their return to Allah's presence following their cosmic duties throughout the created order. The staggering measurement of 'fifty thousand years' is not intended as a literal chronological span for human calculation, but rather as a metaphor to convey the immense, terrifying gravity of that Day. It emphasizes that what might seem an instantaneous event in divine reality corresponds to an eternity of intense experience within human perception. The verse underscores the absolute sovereignty and majesty of Allah, before whom even the highest of creation must stand in awe, and the incomparable weight of accountability that awaits humanity in the Hereafter.

translation: So be patient with gracious patience.
interpretation: This verse, revealed during a period of intense persecution and opposition in Mecca, calls upon the Prophet to endure hardship with a specific kind of patience: sabran jamila (gracious, beautiful, or noble patience). The word 'jamīl' (beautiful) carries the meaning of patience that is free from complaint, protest, or resentment toward God. It is not merely passive endurance, but an active, dignified resilience that maintains inner composure and trust in God's wisdom. It implies accepting trials without despair, maintaining moral integrity under pressure, and persisting in one's mission without becoming harsh, bitter, or vengeful. The verse establishes that steadfastness in faith requires not just physical endurance, but a beautiful and disciplined character—one that reflects trust in the divine plan even when circumstances appear adverse. This 'beautiful patience' becomes a model for how believers should navigate their own trials: not with anger or self-pity, but with quiet strength and grace.

translation: Indeed, they see it [as] far off,
interpretation: This verse highlights the contrast between human perception and divine truth. From the perspective of those being addressed—often understood as disbelievers or heedless people—the Day of Judgment, divine accountability, or the consequences of their actions seem impossibly distant, unlikely, or remote. Their sense of distance reflects spiritual heedlessness, as they are absorbed in worldly life and unmindful of the transient nature of this existence. The verse underscores that what appears far to finite human perception is near in God's encompassing knowledge and timing. It serves as a warning that such delusion of remoteness does not diminish the certainty of what is promised; rather, it only increases the heedless one's lack of preparation.

translation: But [if you do so], We will make you taste a [painful] punishment very soon.
interpretation: The verse serves as a divine warning: those who deviate from God's signs and persist in denial will inevitably face a swift and severe consequence, emphasizing that ultimate accountability rests with God, not human conjecture.

translation: }On the Day the sky will be like molten copper,
interpretation: This vivid image describes the terrifying transformation of the sky on the Day of Judgment, comparing it to 'muhl' (مُهْل), which scholars interpret as molten metal, bubbling pus, or the residue of boiling oil. The verse captures the complete dissolution of the heavens' familiar order, replacing cosmic stability with a horrifying, fluid chaos. This is not merely physical destruction but signifies the unraveling of the entire created order, leaving nothing but Divine sovereignty. The image evokes visceral fear, warning that the stability people take for granted is temporary and contingent upon Allah's will, and that on that Day, all of creation will be exposed to the raw, unrelenting reality of divine power and judgment.

translation: And the mountains will be like carded wool.
interpretation: This vivid image portrays the Day of Judgment, when the firm and majestic mountains that once seemed eternal and unshakeable will lose their solidity. 'الصهل' or 'العهن' refers to loose, fluffed, or carded wool—something light, scattered, and easily blown about by the wind. The verse depicts a complete transformation of the natural order: what appeared strong and stable becomes insubstantial and fragmented. Beyond its literal meaning, the image conveys profound truths: earthly powers, no matter how towering or imposing, are ultimately fragile and temporary when measured against divine eternity. The scattering of mountains like wool also suggests a release of burdens, as if the earth itself sheds its weight and form, preparing for a new state of existence in which worldly hierarchies and structures hold no sway. It calls the listener to recognize the temporary nature of all material certainty and to place trust in what endures beyond the physical world.

translation: And no close friend will ask about [the welfare of] another close friend.
interpretation: This phrase conveys the idea that on the Day of Judgment, the intense fear and awe of that moment will be so overwhelming that even the closest human relationships—such as between intimate friends or relatives—will dissolve. The bonds that tie people together in worldly life will become irrelevant, as each individual will be wholly consumed by their own accountability before God. It underscores the ultimate solitude of the soul in the afterlife, where no intercession or concern from loved ones can shield one from divine judgment.

translation: They will see them [i.e., the criminals will see those whom they used to lead astray]. The criminal would wish to ransom himself from the punishment of that Day by his children.
interpretation: This verse portrays a scene of the Day of Judgment where those who committed crimes and led others astray will be confronted by the consequences of their actions. The criminals, upon seeing those whom they misguided, will be filled with such intense regret and terror that they would wish to offer their own children as a ransom to escape the impending punishment. The mention of one's own children, who are typically the most cherished and beloved in worldly life, signifies the extreme desperation and helplessness the criminal will feel. It underscores the reality that no worldly possession, relationship, or bond can intercede or compensate on the Day of Judgment. The verse serves as a profound warning about the gravity of misleading others and the ultimate accountability each soul bears, emphasizing that the ties of kinship and material attachments will hold no value in the face of divine justice.

translation: And his companion, and his brother
interpretation: This phrase, spoken by the people of Pharaoh as they dispute with him in the Hellfire, refers to the worldly ties that once defined his life—his wife, his close associate, and his brother. These were the relationships he prioritized and relied upon, yet they offer him no protection or salvation from divine punishment. The verse underscores the futility of worldly attachments when they are severed from faith and righteousness, illustrating how material bonds cannot shield a person from the consequences of rejecting truth and perpetuating injustice.

translation: And his close family who sheltered him [i.e., who gave him refuge and protected him]
interpretation: This part of the verse refers to the close family members who provide shelter, protection, and refuge to a person. In the broader Qur'anic context, it points to the ties of kinship and the responsibility of family members to offer support and sanctuary. It can also imply that those who shield a person from harm—often at personal cost—share in the consequences of that person's fate, whether in this world or the Hereafter. The word 'فصيلته' (faseelah) specifically refers to one's immediate family or close relatives, emphasizing the bond of blood and the duty of care within the family unit. In the context of the verse in Ma'arij (70:13), it warns that even those who protected and sheltered a person cannot ultimately save him from the torment of the Hereafter, highlighting that ultimate salvation depends on one's relationship with Allah, not human ties alone.

translation: And whoever is on earth entirely - then it (the earth) could not save him.
interpretation: The phrase indicates that even if all of humanity were to unite, they would be unable to rescue a person from the consequences of their denial and disbelief when divine punishment comes, highlighting the helplessness of creation before the power and decree of the Creator.

This phrase describes the blazing fire of Hell, which Allah uses as a vivid metaphor for the intensity of the punishment awaiting those who reject faith and indulge in wrongdoing. The word 'لظى' (laza) is derived from the Arabic root meaning 'to flame' or 'to blaze,' and the addition of the emphatic prefix 'إِنَّهَا' (innaha - 'indeed it') underscores the certainty and severity of this punishment. In the broader context of Surah Al-Ma'arij, the verse serves as a stark warning about the consequences of human transgression and ingratitude toward Allah. The imagery evokes not just physical torment but also spiritual anguish—the burning realization of one's own accountability before the Divine. Classical commentators such as Ibn Kathir note that 'لظى' is one of the names of Hell, emphasizing its consuming nature. The verse challenges the reader to reflect on the transient nature of worldly desires versus the eternal consequences of one's choices, urging a return to consciousness of Allah and righteous conduct.

interpretation: }This is a reference to the severe heat and scorching fire of Hell. The 'Shawa' refers to the outer layers of the body, particularly the limbs and skin. The imagery suggests that the fire not only burns the surface but actively pulls and strips away these outer parts, emphasizing the intense and excruciating nature of the punishment in the Hereafter. It serves as a powerful warning about the consequences of one's actions in this life.

translation: calling out to one who turns his back and flees
interpretation: The verse depicts the Day of Judgment as a stark and terrifying reality where the soul, or the record of deeds, relentlessly pursues the person who turned away from the truth in the worldly life. The word تَدْعُو (calling out) conveys an image of urgency and insistence, as if the consequence itself is summoning the individual with no possibility of evasion. The phrase مَنْ أَدْبَرَ وَتَوَلَّى (one who turned his back and turned away) refers to those who, during their earthly existence, deliberately rejected faith and withdrew from the remembrance and obedience of Allah. The use of both أَدْبَرَ (turned his back) and تَوَلَّى (turned away) emphasizes a compounded rejection: not only did they retreat from the truth, but they actively chose a path of opposition and avoidance. This paints a vivid picture of accountability, where one's past choices cannot be undone or hidden; rather, they pursue the person relentlessly, demanding acknowledgment and facing the ultimate consequence of their denial of the divine message.}Interpretation: The verse portrays the Day of Judgment as a moment of inescapable confrontation, where the consequences of one's choices actively pursue and summon the individual. translation: And he gathered [wealth] and hoarded it.
interpretation: This verse criticizes those who become consumed with the accumulation of wealth, treating the gathering and stockpiling of material possessions as the ultimate purpose of life. It describes a mindset that is so fixated on collecting and storing riches—often beyond what is needed or rightfully earned—that the individual neglects the spiritual, moral, and social responsibilities that faith demands. The act of 'hoarding' implies not only the gathering of wealth but also an unwillingness to circulate it through charity, fair trade, or the support of others, which stands in opposition to the principles of generosity, balance, and accountability emphasized throughout the Qur'an. Thus, the verse serves as a warning against greed and the delusion that material abundance can secure one's status or safety in this world or the hereafter.

translation: Indeed, mankind is created anxious/eager.
interpretation: This verse describes a fundamental aspect of the human condition: an inherent anxiety and desperation. The term 'haloo' (هلوعا) encompasses intense worry, greed, and impatience, suggesting that human beings are naturally predisposed to negative emotional states, especially when faced with loss or potential gain.

translation: when evil touches him, he is despondent and complaining
interpretation: This phrase describes the extreme vulnerability and ingratitude of the human condition when afflicted by hardship or misfortune. At the very moment a person is struck by adversity—whether loss, pain, or difficulty—the instinctive reaction is despair, panic, and lamentation. This reveals a fundamental weakness of the soul: that man quickly forgets the blessings he enjoyed and instead collapses into complaint, as though the hardship is unbearable and will never end. The verse is a mirror held up to human nature, exposing how swiftly faith and patience dissolve in the face of trials. It contrasts sharply with the earlier description of man boasting and exulting when times are good, showing the inconsistency of a heart that swings between arrogance in prosperity and hopelessness in adversity. The deeper message is a call to reflection: true strength of character is measured not by how one behaves when life is pleasant, but by how one maintains trust in God, gratitude, and composure when tested. The human being who falls into despair under hardship has, in effect, failed to recognize that all affairs belong to God alone, and that trials are a natural part of life that can bring purification, growth, and deeper reliance on the Divine if faced with patience and faith rather than with bitterness and despondency.

translation: And when good touches him, he is grudging.
interpretation: This verse describes the behavior of the miserly person, the "منوع" (mun'ū'), who is the one who withholds, refuses to give, or is extremely niggardly. The verse highlights a specific trait of this miser: if any blessing, benefit, or good fortune touches him, instead of being grateful and sharing it with others, he becomes stingy and withholds what he has. He hoards it, refuses to give charity, and tightens his grip on his wealth, as if giving would diminish it. This paints a picture of the miser's character as both ungrateful to Allah for the blessing and selfish toward his fellow human beings, turning the very good that was meant to be shared into something he selfishly keeps to himself.

translation: Except those who pray...
interpretation: This phrase, from Surah Al-Ma'un (107:5), refers to those who are sincere and consistent in their prayers, who do not consider prayer a burden or a habit, but rather establish it with full presence of mind, humility, and devotion to Allah, fulfilling its rights and conditions both outwardly and inwardly.

translation: Those who are constant in their prayer.
interpretation: This phrase from Surah Al-Ma'un (107:23) describes a defining characteristic of the truly devout: they are not merely performers of prayer, but those who maintain a steadfast, unwavering commitment to it. The emphasis on being 'constant' (دائمون) suggests that the value of prayer lies not just in its occasional performance, but in its persistence and regularity, reflecting a continuous state of spiritual devotion and mindfulness of God. Such constancy in prayer indicates a person whose entire life is oriented around this fundamental act of worship, making it the steady axis around which their daily existence revolves.
