interpretation: This verse condemns the attitude of arrogant disbelievers who reject the Qur'an not based on rational inquiry or evidence, but out of pride and prejudice. By dismissing the divine revelations as 'legends of the ancients,' they refuse to engage with the transformative message in front of them, preferring instead to cling to inherited skepticism. This reflects a spiritual condition where willful ignorance hardens the heart against truth, making one incapable of recognizing the living, miraculous nature of divine guidance.

translation: Nay! Rather, what they used to earn has rusted over their hearts.
interpretation: This verse addresses the spiritual condition of those who persist in wrongdoing and reject divine truth. It explains that their hearts have not simply been neglected; rather, the accumulated weight of their own sinful actions and persistent disobedience has created a spiritual veil—a rust, as it were—that hardens the heart and renders it impervious to faith, reflection, and sincere remembrance of Allah. This is a profound statement of human moral responsibility: it is not external circumstances that seal a person's heart against guidance, but the internal consequences of choices they freely made. Each sin, when unrepented, leaves a residue that further darkens the soul until the heart becomes unable to recognize or respond to truth. The verse therefore serves as a warning about the incremental, self-inflicted nature of spiritual corruption. Since the rust is produced by one's own deeds, reversal is also possible through sincere repentance, remembrance of Allah, and righteous action. The passage underscores that the human being is not a passive recipient of guidance or misguidance but an active agent whose behavior shapes the very capacity of the heart to receive divine light.

translation: No! Indeed, on that Day they will be blocked from their Lord.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the ultimate separation that will occur on the Day of Judgment between the disbelievers and the mercy and presence of Allah. While the believers will be granted nearness to their Lord, the disbelievers and sinners who turned away from His signs and commandments will be veiled and barred from His grace. The word *mahjubun* (blocked or veiled) signifies a state of being cut off, not merely spatial distance, but a deprivation of the divine mercy, light, and approval that comes from being in the presence of Allah. It highlights the gravity of rejecting faith and the consequences of deliberate disobedience, as it results in the most profound loss a soul can experience.

translation: Then indeed they will be cast into Hellfire.
interpretation: This verse describes the ultimate fate of those who rejected the truth and persisted in wrongdoing. The word "لصالو" comes from the root ص-ل-و (to be cast, to be roasted, to enter), and it is intensified to indicate a severe, continuous entry into the Fire. The word "الْجَحِيم" refers specifically to the intensely hot and fierce layer of Hell, reserved for the worst of the wrongdoers. This conveys that their destination is not merely a passing through punishment, but a permanent, agonizing plunge into the deepest levels of divine retribution.

translation: Then it will be said, "This is what you used to deny."
interpretation: On the Day of Judgment, after the reality of the punishment or the falsehood of the promised resurrection becomes undeniably manifest, the truth of the warning will be pointed out to the deniers. The phrase serves as a divine rebuke, highlighting their former obstinacy and mockery. By saying 'This is what you used to deny,' the confrontation is direct, forcing the deniers to recognize that the very thing they dismissed as impossible or fabricated was, in fact, undeniably true. It underscores the ultimate triumph of truth over rejection and serves as a solemn reminder of the accountability that awaits those who chose to reject divine signs and warnings.

translation: No indeed! Truly the record of the righteous will be in 'Illiyyun (the highest ranks).
interpretation: This verse, following the previous warnings about human ingratitude and denial of the Hereafter, presents a powerful contrast by emphasizing that the book of deeds—the record of every action, word, and intention—of those who are genuinely righteous and devoted to obedience to Allah is preserved in a station of supreme honor and elevated rank ('Illiyyun), known only to Allah. While the wicked and disbelievers will have their records placed in Sijjin (the lowest depths), the righteous enjoy a status so lofty that it defies full human comprehension. The emphatic 'kalla' (No indeed!) signals a shift from a tone of rebuke to one of definitive reassurance and promise, assuring the believers that their sincere efforts and virtuous lives are not in vain but are valued and safely preserved. It serves as a profound source of hope, indicating that true success lies not in worldly status or wealth but in attaining this exalted spiritual position through faith, piety, and good deeds.

translation: And what can make you know what is 'Illiyyun (the lofty ranks/record of the righteous)?
interpretation: This rhetorical question emphasizes that the true nature and exalted reality of 'Illiyyun—a realm or record reserved for the most righteous—transcends human comprehension. By asking 'what could tell you what it is?' the verse directs attention away from speculation and toward reverent awe of what Allah has prepared for those who attain the highest stations of faith and virtue. It signals that the loftiness of this state is known only through divine revelation, urging believers to seek understanding not from conjecture but from God’s guidance, while inspiring aspiration toward righteousness whose reward surpasses ordinary worldly imagination.

translation: [This is] a written record,
interpretation: The phrase suggests that the deeds, destinies, or souls of individuals are inscribed in a preserved, unalterable divine register. It implies that nothing in creation is left to chance or forgotten; rather, every matter is documented with precision by God. This concept serves as a reminder of accountability, emphasizing that human actions are recorded and will be presented before the divine court on the Day of Judgment.

translation: Witnessed by those brought near [to Allah].
interpretation: This phrase indicates that the events spoken of—such as the rewards of the Hereafter or the realities of the divine decree—are observed and attested to by the highest ranking angels, those nearest to Allah’s presence. Their witnessing serves as a mark of the supreme significance and certainty of what is being affirmed, since they are the most noble of creation and the closest in proximity to divine truth. Their attestation removes all doubt about the matter, as they perceive the realities of the unseen with unwavering clarity and stand as truthful witnesses before all of creation on the Day of Judgment.

translation: Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss.
interpretation: This verse assures believers that those who lived a life of righteousness—characterized by faith, good deeds, and obedience to God—will be rewarded with a state of profound joy and comfort in the hereafter. It contrasts the ultimate fate of the pious with that of the sinful, highlighting the principle of divine justice that good is rewarded and evil is punished.

translation: On thrones (or cushions) they will be gazing (around).
interpretation: The verse is set in the context of the eternal bliss awaiting the righteous in Paradise, describing them as reclining on elegant furnishings and observing the wonders and delights prepared for them. It symbolizes their state of complete ease, honor, and contemplative joy—free from any hardship or grief. The act of looking around reflects their wonder at the beauty of Paradise, the rewards bestowed upon them, and possibly the contrast with the punishment of the inhabitants of Hellfire. This imagery emphasizes a transition from worldly trials to a state of serene dignity and fulfillment.

translation: You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss.
interpretation: This verse describes the visible marks of divine favor and joy upon the faces of the righteous in Paradise, a luminosity that reflects the inward delight of being in Allah's presence and having attained ultimate fulfillment, distinct from worldly contentment as it is a manifestation of eternal grace granted by the Most Merciful.

translation: They will be given to drink from a sealed wine.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Mutaffifin (83:25), describes a drink given to the righteous in Paradise that is "sealed" or "finished," meaning it is pure, untouched by human hands, and reserved exclusively for them. The sealing implies that its delightful fragrance and essence remain intact and untainted, and some scholars suggest the seal refers to the final taste of the drink being preserved from any sourness or alteration, symbolizing a perfect, everlasting bliss that is uniquely theirs and uncontaminated by the impurities or trials of the worldly life.

translation: , final is musk. And in that let the competitors compete.
interpretation: , this is a profound allegory describing the ultimate state of those who attain divine pleasure, suggesting that the journey itself is the destination - that genuine, elevated souls are not enticed by this world's fleeting guarantees, but rather compete only for what is intrinsically perfect and pure. The closing image of musk evokes an ineffable fragrance whose essence permeates without diminishing, an unalterable purity - the true reward of those who traverse the path of sincerity with excellence. The call to competition here redefines success itself: the only rivalry worth pursuing is that of spiritual refinement, where the victor is he who most fully aligns his inner reality with the divine. This is a complete vision - the reward is not separate from the journey, but is its natural culmination.

translation: And its mixture is from Tasnim.
interpretation: The phrase 'مزاجه من تسنيم' (its mixture/seasoning is from Tasnim) refers to the unique and exquisite quality of the drink enjoyed by the righteous in Paradise. Tasnim is described elsewhere in the Qur'an (Surah Al-Insan 76:18) as a fountain from which the chosen servants of Allah drink, and here it emphasizes that the wine or drinks of Paradise are blended or flavored with the water of this lofty spring. The point is not intoxication or indulgence, but the unparalleled purity, elevation, and delight of the blessings of the Hereafter. Tasnim is derived from the root meaning 'elevation,' indicating that the source itself is lofty and near to the Throne, reserved for those whom Allah has honored and purified. Therefore, the verse highlights the supreme honor and exquisite nature of the reward of the pious, whose drink is distinguished by being mixed with water from a source of the highest rank in Paradise.

translation: A spring from which the chosen ones drink
interpretation: This verse depicts a spring reserved exclusively for those nearest to God (al-muqarrabūn). After describing rivers of wine, milk, and honey as rewards for the righteous, the Qur'an singles out a special fountain for the elect among the saved. Unlike the other beverages, which the pious drink, this spring is reserved for those of the highest rank. In early tafsīr (such as al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr), some commentators identify this spring with the Fountain of Abundance (Kawthar) entrusted to the Prophet, or with the Ṭasnīm spring, and others name it al-Rawḥ and al-Rayyān. Some Sufi commentators read the verse as symbolizing direct, unmediated knowledge of God: the intimate servants drink directly from the source, while others receive it filtered through intermediaries such as intellect, law, or grace. The verse thus expresses a hierarchy of spiritual attainment within paradise, where proximity to the divine grants access to a knowledge or bliss unavailable to lesser ranks.

translation: Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed.
interpretation: This verse depicts a profound spiritual reversal: those who persisted in wrongdoing and arrogance in the worldly life mocked and derided the believers, considering them foolish for their faith, devotion, and moral restraint. The verse exposes a tragic miscalculation—the criminals viewed their worldly success and the believers' apparent vulnerability as evidence of their own superiority, oblivious to the fact that their contempt would one day be answered. On the Day of Judgment, the tables will be turned entirely: the believers will look upon the criminals from a position of fulfilled promise and realized truth, while the criminals will face the consequences of having rejected faith and mocked those who embraced it. The verse thus serves as both a warning against the spiritual blindness of arrogance and a consolation to believers who endure ridicule, affirming that worldly mockery is a fleeting illusion compared to the eternal weight of divine justice.

translation: And when they pass by them, they exchange glances, mocking.
interpretation: This verse describes the attitude of those who reject faith toward the believers who sincerely strive in righteousness. The verb يتغامزون (yaghamizūn) implies more than casual glancing; it conveys a furtive, contemptuous sneering—a covert ridicule meant to belittle the believers' devotion without confronting them openly. The act of passing by (مرور) suggests that these mockers are so confident in their own position that they treat the righteous as objects of derision rather than as equals worthy of dialogue. At its core, the verse exposes a spiritual truth: those who ridicule sincere faith reveal their own inner emptiness and insecurity. True conviction does not need to mock the devotion of others; it is the fragile ego that must belittle what it cannot emulate. The believers, meanwhile, are portrayed as steadfast—unmoved by the sneers of the arrogant. This serves as both a comfort to the faithful and a warning: contempt for righteousness is not a sign of strength, but a symptom of a heart darkened by arrogance, one that will ultimately be held accountable for its disdain.

translation: And when they return to their families, they return indulging in idle talk and falsehood.
interpretation: This verse condemns hypocrisy and deceit, describing those who, after performing acts of worship or interacting with the Prophet and believers, return to their families and boast or spread falsehoods about what they witnessed or heard, using it for amusement or to mislead others. It serves as a warning against using religion or knowledge as a means for personal gain, showing off, or spreading misinformation, and emphasizes the importance of sincerity and integrity in one's speech and actions.

translation: And when they saw them, they said, 'Indeed, these people are truly astray.'
interpretation: This verse describes the reaction of those who rejected faith when confronted by the believers. Instead of recognizing the truth or engaging in sincere reflection, they dismiss the believers as misguided. This statement reflects a psychological defense mechanism: those who are entrenched in falsehood often label those who follow the truth as being lost, because the believers' commitment to principles and accountability challenges their own lifestyle of heedlessness. The verse also highlights the irony of misguidance—the ones who claim to be guided are themselves blind to their own deviation, while accusing others of being lost. It serves as a caution that truth is not determined by popular opinion or by the consensus of those who reject it, but by sincere adherence to divine guidance.

translation: And they were not sent as guardians over them.
interpretation: This phrase emphasizes that previous messengers and warners were not appointed as permanent overseers or custodians of every individual's spiritual journey; rather, their role was to deliver the message and provide guidance, while ultimate accountability rests with each person themselves.

translation: So today [on the Day of Judgment] the believers, in regard to the disbelievers, are laughing
interpretation: This verse describes the Day of Judgment from the perspective of divine justice, where the roles between believers and disbelievers are reversed in the afterlife. The disbelievers, who mocked and ridiculed the believers in worldly life, now face the consequences of their rejection of truth, while the believers experience relief and vindication. The laughter mentioned here is not mockery but rather a natural expression of the believers' realization that the promises of Allah have been fulfilled and that they are now in a state of bliss and security. It signifies the ultimate triumph of faith over disbelief and serves as a reminder that worldly mockery is temporary, while the consequences of one's choices in the hereafter are eternal. This reversal also highlights the Quranic theme that true judgment belongs to Allah alone, and that human arrogance and rejection of faith will inevitably lead to a position of vulnerability before divine justice.

translation: On thrones, looking [around].
interpretation: This verse describes the blessed condition of the inhabitants of Paradise, who will be seated comfortably on elevated thrones (arāʾik), enjoying a position of honor and dignity. The word yunẓurūn ('looking') indicates their attentive observation of various scenes of bliss, whether witnessing the rewards of their own companions, gazing upon the fruits of Paradise, or witnessing the punishment of the disbelievers in Hell. This visual element emphasizes that their enjoyment is not static but involves active, joyful observation from a place of elevated status. The thrones also symbolize the completeness of their reward, as seating on thrones signifies authority, rest, and honor—contrasting with the exhaustion and humiliation experienced in the worldly life. Thus, the verse paints a picture of ultimate spiritual fulfillment, combining physical comfort, noble status, and the delight of witnessing the fruits of divine justice and mercy.

translation: We will let the disbelievers taste a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: This verse expresses a divine promise that those who persist in disbelief and reject faith will face a severe and degrading consequence. The phrase 'humiliating punishment' underscores not only the intensity of the suffering but also the shame and disgrace that accompany it, reflecting the ultimate loss of dignity for those who deliberately turn away from the truth. It serves as a warning about the spiritual and existential degradation that results from choosing disbelief, and it implies that such punishment is a natural consequence of their persistent rejection of divine guidance rather than an arbitrary decree.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. When the sky is split asunder.
interpretation: This opening of Surah Al-Inshiqaq presents a vivid depiction of the Day of Judgment, where the sky will be torn apart—a sign of the immense power of Allah and the radical transformation of the cosmos as we know it. The 'splitting of the sky' symbolizes the dissolution of the physical order, marking the transition from the temporal world to the eternal realm of accountability. This imagery serves as a stark reminder of human fragility and the certainty of resurrection, urging the listener to reflect on their deeds and prepare for the inevitable meeting with their Creator. The verse also evokes awe, illustrating that nothing in creation is permanent except Allah Himself, and that even the heavens, which appear solid and unchanging, will yield to His command.

translation: And [the earth] will permit its Lord to take it [i.e., to judge it], and it will be fit for that.
interpretation: This verse describes the Day of Judgment, when the earth will bear witness to and acknowledge the authority of Allah, allowing His decree to be executed upon it without resistance. The earth itself will be in a state of readiness and submission, reflecting the universal acknowledgment of Allah's sovereignty and justice at the end of time, when all creation testifies to His perfect wisdom and power.

translation: And when the earth is stretched out,
interpretation: This vivid image from the Qur'an depicts the profound transformation of the earth on the Day of Judgment. Stretching here signifies the earth's expansion and leveling, removing its mountains, valleys, and divisions, becoming a single, flat expanse. This change dismantles the familiar structures and hierarchies of the present world, presenting humanity before their Lord on entirely new terms. The verse emphasizes the radical alteration of physical reality as part of the ultimate transition to the afterlife.

translation: And it (the earth) shall cast forth what is within it, and shall be empty (of all that it contained).
interpretation: This vivid eschatological image portrays the earth as a vessel or a pregnant entity that finally yields its contents. It depicts the Day of Judgment when the earth will be compelled to reveal all the hidden deeds, secrets, and remains of the dead buried within it. 'Throwing out what is inside it' suggests a violent expulsion or disclosure, leaving no secret concealed. 'Becoming empty' (takhal-la) implies a state of absolute bareness after this revelation, where nothing remains hidden, and all that was concealed—whether good or evil—comes to light for divine reckoning.

translation: And she (the soul) has been permitted [to leave] by her Lord, and that is what was ordained for her.
interpretation: This verse refers to the moment of death, when the soul is given permission by God to depart from the body. It signifies that the departure of the soul is not a random or accidental occurrence, but rather a divinely ordained event that takes place exactly as God has decreed. The phrase 'وُضعت' (was ordained/placed) emphasizes that every soul has a predetermined time and manner of death, established by God's wisdom and will. This serves as a reminder of human mortality and the ultimate authority of God over life and death, encouraging believers to live in consciousness of their eventual return to Him and to prepare for the Hereafter through righteous deeds.

translation: O mankind, indeed you are laboring toward your Lord with [great] exertion and will surely meet Him.
interpretation: This verse addresses the universal human condition of striving, emphasizing that all efforts in life—whether in obedience, sin, success, or hardship—are a journey toward ultimate accountability before God. The word 'كادح' (laboring) carries the nuance of relentless, often difficult effort, suggesting that human existence is inherently a pursuit shaped by intention and consequence. The concluding 'فملاقيه' (and will meet Him) is a profound declaration of certainty, stripping away any illusion that one's actions are without ultimate reckoning. It serves both as a warning and a source of hope: for the righteous, it affirms that their striving will be met with divine reward; for the heedless, it is an undeniable reminder that no effort goes unnoticed or unjudged. The verse encapsulates the Islamic worldview that life is a purposeful test, and every moment draws one closer to an inescapable encounter with the Creator, where truth and justice will prevail.

translation: As for the one who is given his record in his right hand
interpretation: This opening phrase sets the stage for one of two contrasting fates on the Day of Judgment. The 'right hand' symbolizes honor, acceptance, and salvation in the Quranic worldview. Receiving one's book (of deeds) in the right hand signifies that the person has been deemed righteous by God and will be granted entry into Paradise. It evokes a state of ease, dignity, and divine approval, as opposed to receiving it in the left hand, which denotes disgrace and punishment.

translation: Then he will have an easy account (settled with)
interpretation: This divine statement carries a profound message of mercy that stands as one of the most comforting principles in Islam. When a person embraces faith, lives with sincerity, and prioritizes the eternal over the temporary, the reckoning on the Day of Judgment becomes light and gentle. The Arabic word 'hisab' (account) here refers not to a mere review of deeds, but to a comprehensive accountability where every action, intention, and moment is laid bare before the Divine. An 'easy account' does not necessarily mean fewer sins or less scrutiny; rather, it signifies an account settled with grace, where shortcomings are overlooked through divine mercy, and the scale of one's good deeds, though perhaps modest in worldly estimation, tips the balance favorably. This reflects a spiritual truth that the quality and sincerity of one's faith carries greater weight in Allah's judgment than the sheer volume of one's deeds. The person whose worldly attachment was weak, whose heart remained connected to the Creator, and whose life was oriented toward the Hereafter experiences a gentle transition into eternity. Contrastingly, those who immersed themselves in worldly accumulation, who treated this temporary existence as their ultimate purpose, and whose hearts grew distant from remembrance of Allah, will face what scholars describe as a 'difficult account,' where every minor detail is examined and nothing is overlooked. This verse therefore serves as both an invitation and a warning, urging the soul to reorient its priorities while there is still time, recognizing that true ease in the afterlife is cultivated through the choices made in this life.

translation: , and he will return to his family in joy (Surat Al-Qalam, 68:9).
interpretation: The happiness described is not merely the absence of sorrow or a passing feeling of delight, but rather the profound, lasting joy that comes from a life lived in accordance with divine guidance. The imagery of returning to one's family in joy suggests that the righteous person's inner state of contentment radiates outward, bringing light and warmth into the lives of those closest to them. The family, in turn, shares in this blessing, creating a home filled with tranquility and mutual love. This verse, coming as it does after the description of the obstacles placed before the Prophet ﷺ, serves as a powerful affirmation that genuine success is not measured by the world's standards of wealth or status, but by the strength of one's relationship with Allah and the quality of one's character. The joy is, in essence, the joy of inner peace—the certainty that one is on the right path and that Allah's favor rests upon them.

translation: But as for he who is given his record behind his back,
interpretation: This verse describes the state of the disbelievers and hypocrites on the Day of Judgment who will be handed their book of deeds from behind their backs, a sign of their being turned away from Allah's mercy and their rejection of the truth they once acknowledged in worldly life. This act of receiving the record behind the back symbolizes their detachment from their own deeds, as if they are in denial or unwilling to face the reality of their actions. It also reflects their being driven toward punishment, as the direction of receiving the record is opposite to how the righteous will receive theirs in their right hand. Behind the back can also symbolize being deceived by the worldly life, turning one's back on the remembrance of Allah, and ultimately facing the consequences of that turning away.

translation: Soon he will call for destruction.
interpretation: This verse expresses the inevitable consequence awaiting those who oppose divine guidance: a state of such profound ruin and regret that they will cry out for annihilation, wishing for a 'thubūr'—a complete and irreversible downfall—as an escape from the severe accountability that comes from turning away from the truth and choosing falsehood.

translation: , and he will be burned in a blazing fire.
interpretation: The verse is part of a larger passage addressing the consequences for those who reject faith and deny the signs of God. The "blazing fire" refers to the severe punishment in the Hereafter, emphasizing the painful fate awaiting those who persist in disbelief and wrongdoing. The verse serves as a warning about the ultimate outcome of rejecting divine guidance and moral responsibility.

translation: Indeed, he was among his people [living] in delight/amusement.
interpretation: This verse refers to a person (identified in Qur'anic commentary as the 'man of the book' or the owner of the two gardens mentioned in Surah Al-Kahf) who was engrossed in the pleasures and comforts of his worldly life. The term 'مسرورا' (musrifan, sometimes read as 'musirran') conveys a sense of someone so absorbed in delight, luxury, and self-satisfaction that he became heedless of the Hereafter and the ultimate accountability before God. His 'delight' was not merely enjoyment but a state of arrogance and ingratitude, as if the worldly blessings were permanent and there would be no return to his Lord. The verse critiques such complacency, contrasting it with the reality that all worldly possessions and joys are transient, and that true success lies in righteousness and acknowledgment of the Hereafter.

translation: Indeed, he thought that he would never return [to Allah].
interpretation: This verse describes a fundamental delusion of the disbeliever: the assumption that death is final, that there is no return to one's Lord for accountability. This false certainty of never returning to Allah leads him to arrogance, transgression, and heedlessness of moral consequences. The verse exposes the root of human wrongdoing as a mistaken belief in the absence of resurrection and divine reckoning, reminding that the conviction of returning to Allah is essential for righteous conduct, while its denial is the foundation of corruption and rebellion against divine guidance.

translation: But in fact, his Lord was ever seeing him.
interpretation: This phrase affirms Allah's perpetual and all-encompassing vision and awareness of His servant, meaning that no action, intention, or state—whether public or private, manifest or hidden—escapes His observation. It serves as a powerful reminder of divine omniscience, implying that human accountability is total and that one cannot deceive Allah through outward appearances or secret misdeeds. In context, it often follows warnings against sin or heedlessness, emphasizing that divine justice is rooted in perfect knowledge, so the servant should be ever conscious that they are under the gaze of the All-Seeing.

translation: So I swear by the twilight glow,
interpretation: This verse marks the beginning of a series of profound oaths sworn by Allah upon various signs in His creation, beginning with the twilight glow (the reddening after sunset). The oath serves to emphasize the immense truth and significance of what is about to be mentioned, as the majesty of the things sworn by reflects the certainty and importance of the matter being affirmed. The twilight glow represents a transitional moment between day and night, symbolizing themes of transition, reflection, and the profound wisdom embedded in natural phenomena that point to deeper spiritual realities.

translation: ,and by the night when it gathers [what is within it],
interpretation: This verse uses the imagery of the night as a witness, emphasizing how it 'gathers' or encompasses all things within its darkness. The act of 'gathering' here refers to the night collecting and covering whatever exists upon the earth—people, animals, objects—drawing them into its shadow and stillness. The verse draws attention to the profound, encompassing nature of the night as a sign of divine order, suggesting that just as the night reliably fulfills its function of gathering, so too is the divine promise of accountability and resurrection assured. It serves as a reminder of the natural cycles established by God, calling the listener to recognize the purposeful design in creation and to reflect on the certainty of meeting one's Lord after the 'gathering' of death.

translation: And [by] the moon when it is full (or follows).
interpretation: This verse from Surah Al-Inshiqaq (84:18) serves as one of a series of oaths that Allah swears by various cosmic phenomena to emphasize the certainty of the events described—particularly the realities of the Day of Judgment, human deeds being brought to account, and the ultimate return to Allah. The oath by the moon in its fullness (or as it journeys through its phases, following the sun) is intended to draw attention to the order, precision, and purposeful design within creation. The full moon, in particular, is a sign of completion and brightness, symbolizing clarity and the fulfillment of a cycle. By swearing by it, Allah directs human reflection to the natural world as a testimony to divine power, wisdom, and the inevitable accountability that awaits every soul. It functions rhetorically to underscore that just as the moon completes its cycle according to divine decree, so too will the moral and spiritual order of human life reach its appointed conclusion.

translation: You will surely ride [in successive] layers [of life/events].
interpretation: This verse describes the human condition as a journey through successive stages or states, where one circumstance follows upon another in a continuous progression. The word 'ṭabaq' (layer/level) conveys the idea that existence unfolds in layered experiences—each phase building upon or succeeding the previous one. This can be understood as referring to the multiple stages of life (such as birth, growth, decline, and death), or to the changing circumstances of worldly life where ease follows hardship, success follows failure, or certainty follows doubt. It serves as a profound reminder that life is not static but a dynamic movement through overlapping conditions, calling the reader to recognize the transient and layered nature of worldly existence and to seek meaning beyond its shifting surfaces.

translation: .So why is it that they do not believe?
interpretation: This rhetorical question in Surah Al-Muddathir (74:46) highlights the spiritual obstinacy of those who reject the Quran and Muhammad's message. Rather than seeking an intellectual answer, the question confronts the disbelievers' inner state—exposing that their refusal to believe is not due to a lack of evidence or rational proof, but because of a deliberate turning away from truth. The verse underscores the Quran's view that faith is ultimately a matter of the will and the heart: when people choose denial over reflection, no argument will suffice. It serves as both a rebuke and a lament over the willful blindness that prevents human beings from recognizing divine guidance when it is presented clearly before them.

translation: And when the Qur'an is recited to them, they do not prostrate [i.e., they do not fall down in reverence].
interpretation: This verse is part of a larger passage in Surah Al-Inshiqaq (verses 20-21) that describes the fate of those who reject faith and persist in wrongdoing. The 'sajdah' mentioned here refers not only to the physical act of prostration but more broadly to a state of humble submission, awe, and recognition of divine authority. The inability or refusal to prostrate upon hearing the recitation of the Qur'an reflects a deeper spiritual condition: a hardened heart that is impervious to the truth, guidance, and beauty of the divine word. It suggests an arrogance and self-sufficiency that prevents the person from humbling themselves before God. In contrast to those who are moved to tears and worship when hearing the Qur'an (as described in 17:107), these individuals are so entrenched in denial and disobedience that even the direct recitation of God's speech fails to elicit any response. This is presented as evidence of their deviation and a characteristic of those who will face ultimate punishment, indicating that the Qur'an's transformative power is nullified in hearts already sealed by persistent rejection of the truth.

translation: But those who disbelieve deny [the truth].
interpretation: This statement from Surah Al-Mursalat (77:19) identifies the fundamental spiritual disease of those who reject divine guidance: it is not intellectual confusion but active denial. The Arabic word 'yunkadhibun' (deny/falsify) implies a deliberate rejection of truth that has been clearly presented. The verse suggests that faith and its absence are not merely matters of intellectual assent but reflect the orientation of the heart—those who turn away from Allah actively oppose and dismiss the signs and messages sent to them, preferring to label truth as falsehood. This denial carries weight because it is a conscious choice against clear evidence.

translation: And Allah is most knowing of what they conceal.
interpretation: This phrase, appearing at the close of a verse, serves as a divine declaration emphasizing God's absolute awareness of human beings' hidden intentions, secret thoughts, and concealed deeds. It underscores the theological principle that while individuals may hide their inner states and private actions from one another, nothing remains veiled from Allah's knowledge. This functions both as a warning to those who harbor hypocrisy or evil designs, reminding them that their secrecy offers them no protection from divine judgment, and as a source of comfort to the sincere, assuring them that their unspoken devotion and private struggles are witnessed and known by God. It establishes the limit of human concealment in the face of divine omniscience.

translation: So give them tidings of a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse employs a powerful rhetorical device of irony, where 'tidings' (bashar) typically conveys good news in the Qur'anic lexicon, but here it is paired with 'painful punishment' to underscore the severity of the consequence awaiting those who reject faith. The warning is addressed not to the disbelievers directly but to the Prophet, signifying that the promised punishment is an inevitable divine decree, contrasting sharply with the mercy extended through the call to faith.

translation: Except those who believe and do righteous deeds – for them is an uninterrupted reward.
interpretation: The verse conveys that while much of human effort in this world is marked by ingratitude, loss, or eventual forgetfulness, those who combine sincere faith with consistent good deeds receive from God a reward that is ceaseless and undiminished. The phrase 'أجر غير ممنون' underscores a divine generosity that neither wanes, is cut off, nor is held against the recipient; it is a sustaining recompense tied not to the fleeting value placed on deeds by people, but to God's eternal favor. This places lasting spiritual significance on faith expressed through action, suggesting that true reward transcends the transient measures of worldly life.

translation: By the sky containing great stars (or constellations).
interpretation: This verse is part of a powerful opening section of Surah Al-Burooj (Surah 85), where Allah swears by the heavens and their magnificent features as a prelude to discussing the fate of those who persecuted believers. The phrase "ذات البروج" (containing the zodiac/signs) refers to the majestic constellations and celestial orbits that adorn the sky. The oath by the heavens serves as a solemn witness to the divine justice that follows in the surah—reminding humanity that the same power that governs the cosmos will also hold oppressors accountable for their cruelty, just as it will reward those who remain steadfast in faith.

translation: And the Promised Day.
interpretation: This phrase refers to the Day of Judgment, a definite and guaranteed day appointed by Allah when all of humanity will be gathered to face the ultimate consequences of their earthly lives, making it the inevitable culmination of all worldly events and the day of final accountability.

translation: And a witness and that which is witnessed.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment (or the Day of Gathering) as the witnessed reality, and the witnesses are the prophets, angels, and the ummahs who testify to the truth of Allah's message. It emphasizes that on that Day, every soul will stand before Allah with complete clarity—nothing hidden, no veil between the servant and his deeds. The phrase highlights the certainty of accountability: just as a witness testifies in a courtroom, creation will testify against itself or be testified against, affirming that Allah's justice is perfect and no deed escapes His record.

translation: The companions of the trench were killed/destroyed,
interpretation: This phrase, from Surah Al-Buruj (85:4), refers to a group of believers who were persecuted and killed by a tyrannical ruler who dug trenches (or ditches) and burned them with fire as a test of their faith. The verse condemns the perpetrators of this horrific act and serves as a powerful reminder of the consequences of cruelty, oppression, and the persecution of those who believe in the truth. It highlights the eternal damnation awaiting those who wage war against the faithful and emphasizes the divine justice that ultimately prevails over earthly tyranny.

translation: The fire of [a kindled] fuel,
interpretation: This phrase describes Hell as a fire that requires constant human beings and stones as fuel to keep it blazing, emphasizing its insatiable, ever-burning nature and contrasting it with the ordinary fires of this world that consume their fuel and eventually die out.

translation: When they were sitting over it [i.e., the fire],
interpretation: This phrase is set in a vivid narrative scene. It refers to a group of people who were sitting around a fire or hearth, and the verse uses the image of them being seated as a way to evoke a sense of ease, familiarity, and complacency. The word 'qā'ūd' (قعود) emphasizes their settled posture, suggesting they were not engaged in any urgent action but were simply resting. This setting often serves as a backdrop against which sudden divine intervention or revelation occurs, highlighting the contrast between human routine and the unexpected arrival of God's command or judgment. The verse invites reflection on how moments of ordinary life can be interrupted by profound spiritual events, urging the reader to recognize God's presence and power even in the midst of mundane existence.

translation: And they are witnesses to what they do against the believers.
interpretation: This verse condemns the hostile tribes or groups who not only commit violent or oppressive acts against the Muslim community but also openly witness and celebrate such wrongdoing, bearing collective responsibility for their aggression while refusing to heed the moral lesson found in the fate of earlier peoples who persisted in disbelief.

translation: And they did not blame them except that they believed in Allah, the Almighty, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: This verse refers to the believers during the early persecutions in Makkah who faced rejection and hostility solely for their faith. The opponents had no rational or moral ground for their resentment—hatred arose simply because these individuals embraced the truth and committed to monotheistic belief. It highlights that religious conviction in the face of oppressive social pressure is itself a cause of persecution, and that the divine nature of the truth (Al-'Aziz, Al-Hamid) guarantees its ultimate triumph over human animosity.

translation: He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is, over all things, a Witness.
interpretation: This verse affirms Allah's absolute sovereignty over the entire creation, encompassing both the celestial realms and the earthly domain. By stating that the dominion belongs to Him, it establishes that no authority or power exists independent of His will, and all rule and governance ultimately derive from Him. The concluding declaration that Allah is a Witness over all things emphasizes His omniscient awareness—nothing in the heavens or the earth escapes His observation, knowledge, or judgment. Together, these attributes (sovereignty and witnessing) reinforce the truth that human beings live under the rule of a King who is fully cognizant of every action, intention, and circumstance, making accountability before Him an inevitable reality.

translation: Indeed, those who have tortured the believing men and women and then have not repented, for them is the punishment of Hell, and for them is the punishment of the Burning (al-Ḥarīq).
interpretation: This verse issues one of the most severe warnings in the Qurʾān, establishing a direct link between the persecution of believers and a twofold retribution. The verb *fatana* here carries the sense of subjecting believers to extreme trials, including torture, oppression, and burning, as exemplified historically in the persecution of early Muslims and referenced in other verses (such as 85:10 regarding the People of the Ditch). The verse emphasizes that mere verbal remorse is insufficient; true repentance must manifest in changed actions and sincere turning back from such grave injustice. The mention of two distinct punishments—Hell (*jahannam*) and the Burning (*al-ḥarīq*)—underscores both the magnitude of the crime against innocent human souls and the unalterable nature of divine justice. Spiritually, the verse functions as a moral boundary: harming those who believe, particularly through cruelty or coercion of conscience, places one beyond the pale of mere sin into a category of active enmity against faith itself. The conditional 'then did not repent' (*thumma lam yatūbū*) leaves the door open for redemption only through genuine transformation, indicating that divine mercy, however vast, does not overlook unrepented cruelty toward the oppressed without requiring accountability.

translation: .Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds will have gardens beneath which rivers flow. That is the supreme triumph.
interpretation: This verse establishes a direct causal and conditional relationship between authentic faith (iman) manifested in righteous action and the ultimate, unsurpassed reward of Paradise. The phrase 'gardens beneath which rivers flow' signifies not merely physical gardens but states of spiritual flourishing and perpetual nourishment, where the foundations of existence are sustained by an inexhaustible source. The concluding declaration, 'That is the supreme triumph,' frames salvation not as a passive escape but as the greatest conceivable victory—the definitive triumph over impermanence, suffering, and separation from the Divine. It implies that all other forms of success are provisional, and that true, unassailable victory lies in attaining this eternal state.

translation: Indeed, the grasp of your Lord is severe.
interpretation: This verse appears within a larger passage emphasizing divine omnipotence and moral accountability, following descriptions of human ingratitude and transgression. The phrase uses the metaphor of *batš* (grasp or seizure) to convey the intensity and inescapability of divine retribution. It functions as a warning that God's power to seize wrongdoing is not weak or delayed, but firm and forceful when justice requires it. However, the severity is balanced elsewhere in the Qur'an with divine mercy, suggesting that the harshness of consequence is reserved for those who persist in wrongdoing after having been given ample opportunity for repentance. The verse ultimately underscores the reality of accountability in the afterlife, affirming that no transgression escapes ultimate consequence.

translation: Surely it is He who originates [creation] and brings it back.
interpretation: This phrase affirms God's absolute sovereignty over the cycle of existence. He initiates creation from nothingness—the first 'بداية' (beginning)—and He alone has the power to return all of creation back to Him at the end of time, the 'إعادة' (return). This encompasses both the original act of bringing the universe into being and the eventual resurrection of all beings for the Day of Judgment. The emphasis on 'إنه هو' (surely He is the One) underscores that no one else shares in these divine prerogatives; creation and resurrection are not random cosmic processes but purposeful acts under the complete authority of the One God. This serves as a reminder of human accountability, for the One who gave life can take it and return it, and ultimately every soul will be called to answer for what it did in the fleeting time it was granted.

translation: And He is the Forgiving, the Affectionate (or Loving).
interpretation:
This divine name describes God's relationship with creation through two complementary qualities. *Al-Ghafur* (The Forgiving) refers to God's attribute of consistently forgiving sins and overlooking faults, no matter how great or repeated. *Al-Wadud* (The Affectionate/Loving) describes God's deep love and tenderness toward His servants, actively drawing them to Himself through grace and compassion.

Together, these names reveal that forgiveness in Islam is never cold or mechanical—it flows from genuine love. God's forgiveness is not merely tolerance of wrongdoing, but an expression of His affectionate care for humanity. This creates a profoundly hopeful spiritual reality: repentance is not a desperate plea before an angry judge, but a return to a Lord who is fundamentally predisposed to love and forgive. A believer who turns back to God after sinning is met not with grudging acceptance, but with warm embrace.

The pairing also implies a spiritual dynamic: God loves the servant, and that love motivates forgiveness; the servant recognizes God's love, which inspires repentance and devotion. It is this reciprocal cycle of divine love and human return that forms the heart of the spiritual path in Islam. Some scholars also note that God expresses this *wudd* (affection) by placing love for the believer in the hearts of others, so that the forgiven sinner experiences tangible signs of being welcomed back into the community of faith.

translation: The Lord of the Glorious Throne
interpretation: This phrase, part of a longer verse (Surah Al-Buruj, 85:15), attributes absolute sovereignty and majesty to Allah, who possesses a magnificent throne. The name 'Al-Majeed' combines glory, nobility, and infinite power, emphasizing that all authority in the heavens and earth belongs to Him alone. The throne symbolizes the pinnacle of divine governance, indicating that Allah's rule is not limited by space or time but encompasses all creation. The mention of the throne serves as a reminder of Allah's transcendence and perfection, far above any human conception of power or authority.

translation: Effective/Doer of what He intends
interpretation: This phrase describes God as the One whose will is always accomplished; whatever He purposes or decides comes into being without any obstacle or resistance, since nothing in the heavens or earth can prevent the fulfillment of His command.

translation: , "Had there come to you the story of the armies?"
interpretation: This is the opening of Surah al-Burooj, referencing the well-known trial of the "ditch" (al-ukhdud), where believers were thrown into a blazing trench for refusing to renounce their faith. By framing this as a question, the verse challenges the listener to reflect on the gravity of historical events where oppressive powers mobilized entire armies against those who stood firm in truth. It serves as a rhetorical device to awaken moral awareness, urging the audience to remember the consequences of unchecked tyranny and the ultimate triumph of those who endure persecution with patience and conviction. The question is not merely about past events but a timeless summons to recognize patterns of oppression and to uphold justice against overwhelming odds.

translation: Pharaoh and Thamud
interpretation: This phrase, 'Firʿawn wa Thamud', is commonly found in the Qur'an as a reference to two prominent ancient nations or communities that opposed their prophets and were subsequently destroyed by Allah. The mention of 'Pharaoh' typically refers to the ruler of Egypt who opposed Prophet Moses (Musa), while 'Thamud' refers to the people of Prophet Salih who rejected his message and were struck with a mighty earthquake or a violent thunderbolt due to their persistent transgression. By naming these two together, the Qur'an often sets them as historical archetypes of tyranny, disbelief, and rebellion against divine guidance, serving as a warning to later generations about the consequences of rejecting the truth, persisting in arrogance, and neglecting the signs of Allah. Their inclusion emphasizes that no worldly power or material progress can prevent divine retribution when a society abandons faith and moral responsibility.

translation: But those who disbelieve are in denial.
interpretation: This verse highlights the persistent state of denial of those who reject faith. It emphasizes that their refusal to believe is not merely a passive state but an active rejection, a willful dismissal of truth. This verse serves as a reminder that disbelief is a conscious choice, and those who make it remain trapped in a cycle of denial, despite the clear signs and guidance presented to them.

translation: And Allah surrounds them from behind.
interpretation: This phrase, spoken by the disbelievers of the Quraysh regarding the believers and the Prophet ﷺ, shows their false sense of security. They thought that because they were the majority in control of the land, wealth, and tribal support, the call to Islam would never prevail. Yet this verse delivers a powerful warning: although they could see their forces and resources in front of them, they could not see what was behind them and above them — namely, the encircling power of Allah. It means that no matter how strong the material support of the oppressors may appear, divine power encompasses them from every direction. They were surrounded by Allah's knowledge, will, and decisive authority, even as they plotted to contain the Muslims. Thus the verse is a statement of divine supremacy: worldly power, no matter how vast, cannot escape the encompassing will of God, who will turn the schemes of the arrogant against themselves. It also carries a timeless meaning — that those who feel secure from Allah because of wealth, numbers, or influence are in reality the most exposed, for they cannot perceive the full scope of what surrounds them.

translation: But it is a glorious Quran.
interpretation: This phrase affirms the noble, exalted, and honored status of the Quran. The word 'majid' (مجيد) means glorious, magnificent, or noble, indicating that the Quran is not ordinary speech but a text of supreme honor and value. This verse emphasizes that the Quran is a source of great nobility and prestige, distinguishing it from any mundane or trivial discourse. It underscores the Quran's elevated nature, its timeless significance, and its revered position as a divine revelation meant to guide humanity with wisdom and dignity. The verse serves as a reminder of the Quran's inherent majesty and the respect it commands as a sacred and exalted scripture.

translation: }In a Preserved Tablet
interpretation: This phrase refers to the Qur'an itself or the divine decree, indicating that it is recorded and protected from any alteration or corruption. The 'Preserved Tablet' (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) signifies that what is contained within it is safeguarded by Allah from error, change, or loss. It serves as a reminder that the guidance and truth presented are not subject to human interference, ensuring the integrity and authenticity of the message for all times.

translation: By the sky and the night-comer,
interpretation: This verse from Surah At-Tariq (86:1) employs a powerful and solemn oath, using the celestial realm to emphasize the certainty and gravity of what is to follow. The 'night-comer' (Al-Tariq) is often understood as a striking celestial phenomenon, such as a star or shooting star piercing the darkness of the night. By swearing by the vastness of the sky and this luminous, penetrating light, the verse draws attention to the profound truth about human existence: that every soul is guarded and witnessed, even in the profound darkness of the night or the obscurity of the earth. The oath serves to awaken the listener to the reality that nothing is hidden from divine knowledge, and every individual's deeds, inner states, and ultimate destiny are under constant observation by the All-Knowing Creator.

translation: And what can make you know what is the striking one (al-Tariq)?
interpretation: This rhetorical question is designed to arrest the listener's attention by emphasizing the magnitude and obscurity of 'al-Tariq' before its description is revealed in the subsequent verses. It serves as a Quranic device to underscore human ignorance of certain profound realities, prompting the reader to humbly seek the knowledge that only the Divine possesses.

translation: The piercing star.
interpretation: This refers to a celestial phenomenon — likely a meteor, shooting star, or comet — that cuts through the sky with a luminous trail. In pre-Islamic Arabian thought, such objects were often seen as omens or instruments of fate, but the Qurʾānic context typically strips them of superstitious meaning, redirecting attention to Allah as the sole cause of all events. The piercing, penetrating quality of the star may symbolize the sudden, undeniable clarity with which truth strikes the heart, or the swiftness and precision of divine intervention in worldly affairs. It can also be read as a metaphor for knowledge or guidance that cuts through darkness and confusion with unmistakable brilliance.

translation: .Indeed, [O Muhammad], every soul has a guardian over it (i.e., an angel recording its deeds).
interpretation: The verse states that every soul has a guardian appointed over it—a celestial recorder appointed by God. This guardian angel's role is to observe, document, and preserve every word, deed, and intention of the individual, both good and bad. The purpose of mentioning this is to remind humanity of divine accountability: no action escapes notice, and each person will be confronted with their record on the Day of Judgment. It emphasizes God's omniscience and the moral responsibility each individual bears for their conduct.

translation: So let man consider from what he was created.
interpretation: This verse directs human attention to his own origin as a means of recognizing divine power and resurrection. By reflecting upon his creation, a person is meant to recognize that the One who initiated him from nothing possesses the ability to recreate him, countering any denial of the afterlife.

translation: .He is created from a fluid (gushing forth)
interpretation: .The verse describes the creation of human beings from a fluid that gushes forth, emphasizing the humble and physical origin of humanity. It serves as a reminder that despite the lofty status or abilities humans may attain in life, their origin is rooted in a basic biological process. This can be seen as a call to humility, reminding individuals that no matter their achievements, they share a common and modest beginning with all of humanity, which should encourage modesty, gratitude, and awareness of human frailty

translation: Issuing from between the backbone and the ribs.
interpretation: This phrase describes the origin of human creation, referring to the area between the sacrum (lower backbone) and the ribs. The verse, from Surah At-Tariq, emphasizes the profound nature of human conception and birth, highlighting that Allah creates humans from a specific, concealed place. It serves as a reminder of the miraculous nature of human existence and the power of the Creator, who brings forth life from a region situated between these anatomical structures. This invites reflection on the origins of humanity and the signs of divine power present within the human body itself.

translation: Indeed, He (God) is able to bring him back (to life after death).
interpretation: This verse affirms God's absolute power over resurrection and the return of creation after death. The word "raj'" (return) indicates that bringing the dead back to life is not beyond God's capability—He who created humanity from nothing can certainly recreate them. This statement appears in the context of challenging those who deny the resurrection, emphasizing that the same power that originated life can restore it. It serves as a theological foundation for the certainty of the afterlife, removing any doubt about God's omnipotence to fulfill His promise of resurrection and ultimate judgment.

translation: The Day when the secrets (or intentions) will be tested.
interpretation: This phrase, 'يوم تبلى السرائر' (Yawma tubla al-sarair), translates to 'The Day when the innermost secrets or intentions will be tested' or 'manifested.' The word 'sarair' (سرائر) is the plural of 'sirr' (سر), which refers to what is hidden, secret, or the innermost intentions of the heart. 'Tublā' (تبلى) means to be tested, tried, or examined, but in this context, it carries the meaning of being exposed, laid bare, or manifested.

translation: And so he will have no power [to save himself], nor any helper.
interpretation: This phrase declares that the person who rejects faith and turns away from the message of truth will be left utterly helpless, possessing no inner strength or willpower to save himself from the consequences of his own choices, nor any external ally or intercessor who can rescue him from the outcome he has brought upon himself.

translation: And by the sky which returns [rain],
interpretation: This verse from Surah At-Tariq uses the image of the sky to highlight a profound truth about the nature of existence and divine wisdom. The sky, with its continuous cycles of rain, reflects the principle of cause and effect set by God. Rain falls, nourishes the earth, and then returns in the form of vapor, only to fall again. This constant return mirrors the idea that every action has a consequence, and that nothing is lost in God's creation. It serves as a reminder of the natural order and the sustaining power that governs all things, inviting reflection on the signs present in the universe that point to a deliberate design.

translation: And by the earth that splits (with cracks, bringing forth vegetation),
interpretation: This verse draws attention to the earth’s capacity to fracture and open up, symbolizing a natural process through which life, growth, and renewal emerge. The 'cracks' in the soil are not signs of decay but are channels through which seeds sprout, roots penetrate, and plants break through to the surface. In a broader sense, the verse invites reflection on the idea that what appears on the surface as division or breaking can be a source of new life, productivity, and transformation. The deliberate order and design embedded in such a process point to a purposeful Creator who orchestrates both the structure and the fertility of the earth as part of a sign for those who reflect.

translation: It is indeed a decisive statement,
interpretation: This phrase emphasizes the absolute truth, authority, and conclusive nature of the Qur'an as the speech of Allah. The term 'qawl fṣl' (قول فصل) indicates that it serves as a definitive criterion that distinguishes truth from falsehood, leaving no room for ambiguity or doubt. It underscores the Qur'an's role as a divine decree that judges between matters with ultimate precision, reflecting Allah's perfect will and wisdom without any distortion or alteration.

translation: And it is not in jest.
interpretation: This brief but profound phrase asserts the absolute seriousness and gravity of the matter being addressed, which is the Qur'an itself in the broader context of its surrounding verses (such as in Surah At-Tariq 86:13-14, where this phrase appears). It negates any notion that the Qur'an is trivial play, idle amusement, or meaningless discourse. The statement affirms that the Qur'an is a divine revelation containing ultimate truth, purpose, and consequence—sent to guide humanity, establish moral order, and serve as a criterion for judgment. By emphasizing its non-frivolous nature, it calls for reverence, careful reflection, and sincere engagement with its teachings. The phrase also implicitly warns that approaching the Qur'an with levity, mockery, or indifference is incompatible with its sacred function and will lead to spiritual loss. It underscores that every command, prohibition, promise, and warning within it carries real weight in this life and the hereafter.

translation: ,Indeed, they are planning a scheme,
interpretation: The verse refers to those who are plotting against the truth and the believers. The use of the word 'كيد' (kayd), meaning scheme or plot, indicates a deliberate, covert, and malicious strategy. In the broader context of the Qur'an, this phrase often addresses the opposition faced by Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) from the disbelievers of Quraysh or similar groups who conspired to harm, discredit, or stop the spread of Islam. The interpretation emphasizes that while such schemes may appear threatening, they are ultimately futile against Allah's plan. This serves as a reassurance to believers that divine wisdom and power will prevail over any human plotting, and that those who engage in such schemes will face consequences.

translation: And I will plot a plot [against them].
interpretation: This declaration reflects the resolve and strategic planning of an individual determined to counter what is perceived as opposition or threats, employing cunning and methodical scheming to achieve a decisive advantage.

translation: So leave the disbelievers, give them a little respite.
interpretation: This verse conveys a divine directive of patient forbearance and strategic delay in the face of rejection and hostility from those who refuse faith. On the surface, it appears to command the Prophet and, by extension, the believers, to momentarily step back from confronting the disbelievers, granting them a brief reprieve. However, beneath this outward posture of leniency lies an implicit warning: the respite granted is not a sign of weakness or divine oversight, but rather a temporary allowance within a divine plan. The gentle yet deliberate command to "leave them" suggests that ultimate judgment is inevitable, and the brief reprieve is but a fleeting pause before consequences unfold. The phrase "أَمْهِلْهُمْ رُوَيْدًا" carries a tone of calm assurance, almost a quiet mockery, as though the delay itself is part of the reckoning, allowing the disbelievers to proceed further along a path that will ultimately lead to their own undoing. In essence, the verse teaches that patience in the face of opposition is not passive surrender but an active trust in divine wisdom, which operates on a timescale far beyond human urgency.

translation: Exalt the name of your Lord, the Most High,
interpretation: This opening command establishes the foundational posture of the created toward the Creator: the recognition of divine transcendence through verbal sanctification. The word 'sabbikh' (exalt/glorify) implies an ongoing act of declaring God beyond all imperfection and limitation, while 'al-a'la' (the Most High) affirms His absolute supremacy over all existence. The possessive 'rabb' (Lord) connects transcendence with lordship, suggesting that exaltation is not mere theological abstraction but a response to God's role as sustainer and nurturer of all being. This sets the thematic framework for the surah, which proceeds to contrast divine creation with human moral striving.

translation: Who created and proportioned [all things],
interpretation: This phrase, often rendered as 'Who created and made all things perfect,' emphasizes that God is the originator of creation and the one who brought every creature into existence in a state of balance, proportion, and excellence. The verse affirms divine intentionality in creation: nothing in the universe is random or haphazard, but rather each thing is fashioned according to a precise measure and purpose. This reflects a core Qur'anic theme that the natural order is not accidental but is the product of a wise, designing will, inviting reflection on the underlying harmony and purposefulness of all that exists.

translation: And who has ordained [laws/measure] and guided
interpretation: The verse attributes the act of measuring out (taqdir) and the act of guiding (hidāyah) to God, meaning that all creation is governed by a precise divine order and that ultimate guidance comes only from the One who determines the purpose and path of all that exists. The pairing of 'measuring' with 'guiding' suggests that divine determination is not arbitrary; rather, each created thing is allotted its specific potential and is then led toward the fulfillment of its God-given purpose. The noun in 'والذي' is likely a reference to God, emphasizing His attribute of Omnipotent Wisdom (al-Hakeem) and indicating that the capacity to order creation and lead it to its intended end belongs exclusively to the Divine, who is therefore the only source of genuine guidance for humanity.

translation: And [He is] the one who brings forth the pasture
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's power and benevolence as the Creator who brings forth vegetation and pasture for the benefit of His creation. It highlights a natural process ordained by the Divine will, from which both humans and animals derive sustenance. The mention of pasture can also be read as a sign of the ephemeral nature of worldly life and a reminder that what sprouts from the earth will eventually wither, pointing to the transient character of material existence compared to the eternal nature of the Creator.

translation: And He makes it like stubble, dark and low.
interpretation: After describing the earth as quivering and swelling with growth, the verse depicts a sudden transformation: the lush vegetation that once clothed the land withers into dry, darkened, and worthless refuse. The word ghithā' refers to plant debris swept away by torrential floods—something that appears briefly and then collapses. Aḥwā describes a blackened, parched residue after the vegetation has been struck down and decayed. The verse conveys that whatever worldly flourishing and prosperity exist are temporary; they can be overtaken and reduced to ruin in an instant. This serves as a reminder that the life of the world, despite its apparent strength and permanence, can be upended by divine will, leaving only what endures in the sight of Allah.

translation: We will make you recite, [O Muhammad], and you will not forget,
interpretation: This verse is addressed directly to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and serves as a divine reassurance regarding the preservation of the Qur'an. God promises that He Himself will cause the Prophet to recite the revelation and that he will never forget it. This addresses a natural human concern: the weight and magnitude of receiving a message from God, and the fear that such a profound trust could be lost or forgotten. The verse establishes that the memorization and transmission of the Qur'an is not left to the Prophet's human capacity alone, but is actively guaranteed by God. It also implies a process of gradual revelation and reinforcement, suggesting that divine assistance ensures both the delivery and the lasting retention of the sacred text. This divine guarantee is understood by Muslims to be the foundation of the Qur'an's preservation across generations, as the Prophet's companions memorized and transmitted what they received from him with confidence that it was divinely protected from error.

translation: , except what God wills. Indeed, He knows what is open and what is hidden.
interpretation: This statement occurs within a broader passage emphasizing God's absolute sovereignty and knowledge. The phrase "except what God wills" serves as a divine caveat, affirming that while there are established realities or principles, God's will ultimately supersedes all constraints. The following declaration that God knows "what is open and what is hidden" underscores His omniscience—nothing in creation, whether manifest or concealed, escapes His awareness. Together, these elements convey a profound theological message: human understanding is limited, and ultimate reality rests in the hands of an all-knowing, sovereign deity whose will determines the course of all things beyond what humans can perceive or control. This verse reassures believers of divine wisdom operating beyond human comprehension, encouraging humility, trust, and reliance on God in the face of uncertainty.

translation: And We will make smooth for you the path to ease (the way of goodness and success).
interpretation: This divine promise assures the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) that Allah will facilitate all matters of ease and goodness for him, removing obstacles from the path of righteousness and success. It signifies divine guidance and support in both spiritual and practical affairs, reflecting a broader principle that sincerity and devotion to truth are accompanied by divine facilitation, making the difficult manageable and the complex clear. This verse embodies the concept that aligning one's purpose with the divine will naturally leads to outcomes of simplicity, success, and ultimate ease in navigating life's challenges.

translation: So remind, if the reminder should benefit;
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine instruction to the Prophet Muhammad, and by extension to all believers who carry the message of truth, emphasizing that the primary duty is to convey guidance and wisdom to humanity. It highlights that the responsibility of delivering the message is not contingent upon the listener's response or acceptance; rather, the obligation lies in presenting the truth with clarity and sincerity. The phrase 'if the reminder should benefit' acknowledges human free will, indicating that while divine guidance is universally available and meant for the betterment of all, its transformative effect is realized when hearts are receptive, humble, and open to self-reflection. Those who heed the reminder find spiritual elevation, moral rectification, and inner peace, whereas those who turn away do so at their own loss, having been given the opportunity to embrace truth. Thus, the verse encapsulates the principles of sincere effort without attachment to worldly results, patience in the face of rejection, and trust in the inherent value of truth itself.

translation: He who fears [Allah] will be reminded.
interpretation: The verse teaches that spiritual awareness and divine guidance are not equally distributed among all people; rather, they are granted in proportion to one's consciousness of God. Those who cultivate taqwa—reverent mindfulness of the Divine—open themselves to the benefits of exhortation and wisdom, because their inner disposition makes them receptive to truth. Conversely, heedless hearts, no matter how much advice they receive, remain impervious to it. The Arabic verb yudhakkar (يُذَّكَّرُ) implies being made to remember or take heed, suggesting that fear of Allah activates a latent capacity for reflection. Thus, the verse links ethical preparedness to intellectual and spiritual responsiveness: reverence precedes insight, and humility before God is the precondition for benefiting from His signs.

translation: And the most wretched will avoid it.
interpretation: This phrase refers to those who consciously choose to distance themselves from divine guidance due to their inner corruption and rejection of truth. The 'most wretched' (الأشقى) implies not merely misfortune, but a state of spiritual deprivation resulting from willful disobedience. By avoiding the Qur'an or its message, such a person demonstrates a preference for worldly desires over eternal truth, sealing their own fate through their own choice rather than through divine coercion. This avoidance is both a symptom and a cause of their wretched condition, creating a cycle where turning away from light deepens the darkness within the soul.

translation: Who will enter the Great Fire,
interpretation: This verse describes the ultimate, painful destiny of the disbeliever, emphasizing the severity and permanence of the punishment that awaits those who reject faith, as opposed to a lesser or temporary chastisement. The word 'Great' signifies that the Fire of Hell is the most extreme and horrifying punishment ever conceived, an everlasting torment from which there is no escape or relief.

translation: Then he will neither die therein, nor live.
interpretation: This verse describes a state of existence in the Hereafter that is neither true death nor true life, but rather an intermediate condition of perpetual suffering. The phrase 'then he will neither die therein, nor live' (thumma lā yamūtu fīhā wa lā yaḥyā) applies to the inhabitant of the Fire (Jahannam), as established by its surrounding context in Surah Al-A'la. It depicts a condition worse than death itself, for death would bring an end to suffering, yet the condemned are denied even this mercy. While death would be a release from torment, Allah withholds it so that the punishment is eternal and without cessation. At the same time, this existence is not genuine 'life' in any meaningful sense, because 'life' implies comfort, growth, and the ability to enjoy existence—none of which are available to the dweller of Hellfire. Thus the verse conveys an intensity of suffering that transcends ordinary human comprehension: a state stripped of both the relief that death brings and the dignities that life offers. This portrayal serves as a profound warning, urging reflection upon the gravity of one's ultimate destiny in the Hereafter.

translation: He has succeeded who purifies himself
interpretation: This verse teaches that genuine success and flourishing in life are achieved through inner purification and self-refinement. The Arabic verb 'tazakkā' encompasses more than ritual cleansing; it signifies the purification of the soul from negative traits such as greed, arrogance, and hypocrisy, while cultivating sincerity, generosity, and god-consciousness. In the broader Qur'anic context, this statement emphasizes that material wealth or status alone does not guarantee true success, but rather it is the state of one's heart and character that determines one's ultimate outcome. The verse implicitly contrasts the person who undertakes this spiritual discipline with one who neglects the soul's development, suggesting that human fulfillment comes not from external accumulation but from the conscious effort to elevate one's moral and spiritual condition.

translation: And mentions the name of his Lord and prays.
interpretation: This phrase, drawn from the Qur'an, encapsulates a spiritual discipline that unites remembrance and devotion into a single, continuous act of worship. The verse speaks to the human being who, when engaged in worldly activity or facing the routines of daily life, pauses to invoke the name of his Lord and then proceeds to perform the prayer.
