The one who denies this promise is characterized by arrogance, a love for worldly life, or a refusal to submit to moral accountability. This denial fundamentally contradicts the purpose of human creation, which involves recognizing divine favors and striving for excellence in conduct. It implies a spiritual poverty despite material abundance, as such a person forfeits the highest form of success that transcends worldly attainments.

translation: We will ease him toward hardship.
interpretation: This verse describes a fundamental principle of spiritual gravity: what a person prioritizes in this life becomes the trajectory of their soul in the next. The 'hardship' (al-'usra) here refers not merely to material difficulty, but to a state of spiritual constriction—the narrowing of the heart, the blinding of inner sight, and the painful reckoning that comes when one has lived oriented toward material gains, worldly validation, or self-interest rather than truth, compassion, and remembrance of the Divine. The verse implies that this is not a punitive decree imposed from outside, but an inner consequence: the soul has already been shaped by its choices, and the Hereafter simply reveals what has already been built within. Ease toward hardship is thus the natural fruit of a life spent in spiritual negligence—the path of least resistance leads downward when the heart has been oriented away from the light.

translation: And his wealth will not avail him when he falls (into the abyss of death or destruction).
interpretation: This verse conveys a powerful reminder of the ultimate helplessness of material possessions in the face of death or final reckoning. It emphasizes that no amount of wealth, status, or worldly accumulation can protect a person from the inevitable consequences of their actions or the certainty of their end. The term 'تردى' (taraddā) carries the connotation of falling headlong into ruin, suggesting both physical death and spiritual or moral downfall. The verse challenges the human tendency to equate worldly success with security, affirming that true protection lies only in righteousness and accountability before God. It serves as a sobering reflection on the transient nature of material life and the enduring weight of one's deeds beyond the grave.

translation: Surely upon Us is the guidance
interpretation: This phrase asserts that the responsibility and guarantee for providing guidance to humanity rests entirely with God Himself. It affirms divine sovereignty over the question of direction, suggesting that if people are to find their way, it is not ultimately up to human effort or planning but is a matter that God has taken upon Himself to deliver. This relieves human beings of the burden of worrying whether truth can be known or accessed, since the One who created them has also committed Himself to showing them the way. It establishes a foundation of hope and trust: no matter how lost or confused one may feel, the path to guidance remains available because God Himself has pledged it.

translation: And indeed, to Us belong the Hereafter and the first [life].
interpretation: This verse affirms God’s absolute sovereignty over all realms of existence—both the worldly life (al-ūlā) and the eternal life of the Hereafter (al-ākhira). It emphasizes that both realms belong to God alone, meaning that ultimate ownership, authority, and judgment rest entirely with Him. The verse serves as a reminder that human beings are merely entrusted with the worldly life as a test, while the final and everlasting dominion belongs to God. It also implies that whatever people strive for in this world—wealth, status, power—is transient, since even the first life itself belongs to God. By juxtaposing the two realms, the verse highlights the contrast between the temporary nature of worldly life and the permanence of the Hereafter, urging believers to orient their actions toward what endures. It also reassures that God’s plan encompasses all of creation: He is not merely the Lord of one life but of both, meaning that human deeds, intentions, and accountability extend beyond death into the eternal realm that He alone controls.

translation: So I have warned you of a Blazing Fire.
interpretation: This verse conveys a solemn divine warning of an imminent, intensely burning fire (nar talahha), symbolizing the severe consequences of rejecting faith and righteousness. It emphasizes the prophetic role of conveying timely admonition, urging reflection and repentance before the inevitable arrival of accountability. The vivid imagery of a blazing fire serves to evoke awe and urgency, compelling the listener to heed the warning seriously and seek a path of safety and salvation.

translation: None shall enter it except the most wretched.
interpretation: The Arabic word "lā yaṣlāhā" (لَا يَصْلَاهَا) employs an emphatic negation, meaning not even the most wretched of sinners will be spared from the intense agony of Hellfire. The definite article in "al-ashqā" (الْأَشْقَىٰ) indicates a specific group of people who have completely rejected faith and persisted in wrongdoing. This verse serves as a severe warning that Hellfire is a reality reserved for those who deliberately choose disbelief and rebellion against God, and who refuse to heed divine guidance.

translation: The one who denied and turned away.
interpretation: This phrase describes a person characterized by two reprehensible traits: first, rejecting the truth (whether it be the message of Islam, the existence of Allah, or the Day of Judgment), and second, turning away from obedience and righteousness. It condemns both intellectual denial and practical aversion to faith. The verse serves as a warning that such a person will face consequences for their rejection and abandonment of duty.

translation: And the most righteous will be saved from it [the Fire].
interpretation: This verse from Surah Al-Lail (92:17) emphasizes that salvation from the Hellfire is not merely a matter of faith, but is specifically tied to taqwa—God-consciousness, righteousness, and piety. The word 'al-atqa' (the most righteous) refers to the person who actively avoids sin, purifies their soul, and gives preference to the Hereafter over worldly desires. The passive voice 'yujannabuha' (will be saved/removed from it) suggests a divine guarantee: God Himself will protect the truly righteous from the Fire, indicating that their salvation is an act of divine mercy resulting from their own sincere efforts. It also implies a warning to those who become complacent with mere claims of belief while neglecting righteous deeds.

translation: Who gives his wealth, purifying himself
interpretation: The verse praises those who purify themselves by giving away their wealth, signifying that the act of charity is closely tied to inner purification of the soul, not merely a financial transaction.

translation: And no one has upon Him any favor [that must be] repaid.
interpretation: This phrase from Surah Al-Insan (76:6) emphasizes that no person possesses any claim or right over Allah based on having bestowed favors upon Him. It affirms that Allah, in His infinite majesty and self-sufficiency, is utterly transcendent and beyond any obligation to humanity. Any blessings a person may receive from Allah are not due to any prior generosity on the person's part that created a debt. Rather, this verse underscores the asymmetrical nature of the divine-human relationship: all favor originates from Allah's pure grace and mercy, not from human initiative that could demand reciprocity. This concept serves to humble the believer, removing any basis for spiritual pride or a sense of entitlement before the Divine.

translation: ,But only seeking the face of his Lord, the Most High.
interpretation: This phrase encapsulates the highest motivation and intention for righteous action: the sincere desire to seek the pleasure and approval of Allah alone, without any worldly desires, ego, or ulterior motives. The word 'face' (wajh) here signifies the very essence and being of Allah, the Most High. Therefore, any act of worship, charity, or righteousness performed with this intention transcends being merely a mechanical ritual and becomes a means of drawing closer to the Divine. This intention purifies deeds of any trace of hypocrisy, vanity, or showing off (riya), ensuring that the motivation is purely the love of and submission to Allah. By stating 'the Most High' (al-A'la), it emphasizes Allah's exalted rank and glory, reminding the believer that true greatness lies in striving for His satisfaction, which in turn elevates the spiritual status of the individual.

translation: And he (the Messenger) will surely be pleased (with his followers).
interpretation: This short, broken phrase is part of the conclusion to Surat al-Takathur (Chapter 102), in which Allah describes the intense rivalry and heedlessness of the worldly life that preoccupies people until they enter the grave, where they will realize the truth and consequences of their actions. The verse assures that those who believed and strove in righteousness will attain a state of ultimate satisfaction and delight. For the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, this glad tidings serves as a profound comfort, confirming that his efforts, sacrifices, and the message he delivered were accepted by his Lord, and that those who followed him sincerely will be a source of immense joy for him on the Day of Judgment, when intercession is granted and the rewards are fully realized. It emphasizes the success and pleasure awaiting the believers, contrasting sharply with the regret described earlier in the surah for those who neglected their spiritual duties.

translation: By the morning brightness
interpretation: This opening verse of Surah Ad-Duha establishes a profound principle of divine care by having Allah swear by the daylight that follows the darkest part of the night, symbolizing that periods of hardship and difficulty are always followed by relief and ease. The morning brightness serves as a universal sign of Allah's mercy and the cyclical nature of His mercy, reminding believers that constancy, even in worship or spiritual practice, is not required at the expense of one's well-being and responsibilities, and that Allah's grace continually renews itself with each dawn.

translation: And by the night when it covers with darkness.
interpretation: This verse, part of Surat Adh-Duhaa or its preceding chapter Al-Fajr (though specifically from Surah Al-Inshiqaq or similar Meccan surahs emphasizing natural phenomena as signs), draws attention to the night as a divine sign. The word 'saja' implies the night enveloping or settling over the world in stillness and darkness. The interpretation is that the night serves as a witness to God's power and mercy, providing rest, covering creatures with its veil, and contrasting with the day to balance existence. It invites reflection on the purpose of darkness as part of a purposeful creation, offering tranquility and a period for reflection, renewal, and the acknowledgment of divine wisdom in the alternation of cosmic cycles.

translation: Your Lord has not forsaken you, nor has He detested you.
interpretation: The verse is a profound reassurance and consolation. It explicitly refutes any notion that Allah has abandoned the Prophet Muhammad or turned away from him in displeasure. The negation of both 'forsaking' (وِداع, which implies a complete separation and turning away) and 'detesting' (قلى, which signifies intense dislike or hatred) serves to firmly establish an unbreakable bond of divine love, care, and continued attention between Allah and His Messenger. The use of the present tense ('وَدَّعَ' and 'قَلَى') indicates a continuous state, emphasizing that this divine favor is not a past event but an ongoing, eternal reality. This verse aims to comfort and strengthen the Prophet, assuring him of his elevated status in the sight of Allah, especially in the face of any challenges, oppositions, or periods of apparent delay in revelation that he may have faced. It underscores the foundational principle that divine support for the Prophet is constant and unwavering.

translation: , and the Hereafter is better for you than the first [life]
interpretation: According to the context of the preceding verses, this phrase expresses Allah’s promise to the Prophet ﷺ and all believers that the reward and outcome of the eternal Hereafter will be far superior and more lasting than the blessings and trials of the worldly life. It signifies a divine assurance that whatever hardships or limitations one faces in this temporary world will be replaced by an everlasting, perfect state of success and happiness in the afterlife.

translation: And your Lord is going to give you, and you will be pleased.
interpretation: This verse expresses a divine promise from Allah to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, assuring him of abundant rewards, blessings, and a high station in the Hereafter to such an extent that he will be fully content and pleased. It encompasses the gifts of intercession (al-shafa'ah), the honor bestowed upon him, and his ultimate satisfaction on the Day of Judgment, reflecting Allah's boundless generosity and love for His Prophet.

translation: Did He not find you an orphan and give [you] shelter?
interpretation: This verse is part of a divine passage where God reminds Prophet Muhammad of His grace and care throughout his life. By mentioning his orphanhood, the verse alludes to the Prophet's loss of his father before birth and his mother shortly after, yet God ensured his protection and upbringing by placing him under the care of his grandfather and later his uncle. The verse is meant to console the Prophet and remind him that past hardships were accompanied by divine support, thereby encouraging patience and trust in God's plan.

translation: And He found you lost and guided you.
interpretation: This verse alludes to the Prophet Muhammad being unaware of the divine truth or scripture before revelation, and God guiding him through the Qur'an and prophethood to a clear path. It highlights divine initiative in human guidance: before any seeker can find their way, it is God who first recognizes the lost state and bestows direction, emphasizing that spiritual awareness and purpose are ultimately gifts from God rather than purely human achievements.

translation: And He found you in need and made you [independent] enriched [or sufficient].
interpretation: This verse from Sūrat al-Ḍuḥā (93:8) refers to a period in the Prophet Muhammad's life, before his prophethood, when he experienced material need or poverty. The verse affirms that Allah's grace was already present in that earlier stage: even when the Prophet was without means, divine care was preparing a way toward sufficiency. The word 'aghna' (made independent/enriched) is understood by scholars not merely as the acquisition of wealth, but as a broader state of self-sufficiency and reliance that comes through Allah's favor, which may manifest through lawful livelihood, inner contentment, or the removal of want. The verse thus serves as a reminder that periods of hardship are not signs of divine neglect but are part of a larger pattern of mercy, in which Allah compensates His servants in ways that may not always be material but are always meaningful. It also teaches that true enrichment comes from Allah alone, and that human beings should trust in His provision even when circumstances appear constrained.

translation: As for the orphan, do not oppress [him].
interpretation: This verse is a direct command from the Quran prohibiting the mistreatment, oppression, or humiliation of orphans. It was revealed to address the pre-Islamic Arabian practice of denying orphans their rightful inheritance or treating them unjustly due to their vulnerability. The word 'qahr' (oppress) encompasses various forms of abuse—physical, emotional, financial, or social. The verse establishes a fundamental principle of social justice in Islam: the protection of those who lack the ability to defend themselves. By singling out the orphan, the Quran emphasizes the importance of compassion, kindness, and fair treatment towards vulnerable members of society. It also serves as a reminder to those who are guardians or caretakers of orphans to fulfill their trust responsibly, ensuring the orphan's rights, dignity, and well-being are preserved.

translation: But as for the one who asks, do not repel [him].
interpretation: This verse commands the Prophet Muhammad (and by extension, believers) to be generous and open-handed rather than turning away those who come seeking help, knowledge, or guidance. It emphasizes patience, humility, and compassion, teaching that no one should be denied attention or treated with disdain merely because they are in need or asking questions, even if the request may seem burdensome. The verse reflects a broader Qur'anic ethic of dignity for all people, particularly the vulnerable, and serves as a corrective against any sense of superiority or exclusivity in matters of faith and community life.

translation: And [proclaim] the favor of your Lord.
interpretation: This verse commands the Prophet Muhammad to openly and gratefully proclaim the blessings, gifts, and bounties that Allah has bestowed upon him, such as prophethood, the Qur'an, and guidance; this instruction counters human tendencies toward ingratitude or false modesty by urging continuous, verbal acknowledgment of divine grace as both worship and an invitation for others to recognize Allah's generosity.

translation: Have We not expanded for you, [O Muhammad], your breast?
interpretation: This verse, which opens Surah Ash-Sharh (and is regarded as part of the same revelation as Surah Ad-Duha), signifies Allah's expansive mercy and guidance bestowed upon the Prophet Muhammad. The 'expansion of the breast' symbolizes the opening of the heart to faith, wisdom, and prophethood, allowing him to bear the weight of divine responsibility and convey the message of Islam with clarity and strength. It serves as an assurance of divine support, indicating that just as Allah has granted the Prophet inner peace and capacity for his mission, He will also remove the difficulties he faces, reflecting a broader theme of divine facilitation and comfort in times of trial.

translation: And We have removed from you your burden.
interpretation: This divine assurance signifies that God alleviates the heavy spiritual and moral burdens that weigh upon the human soul, granting relief and ease. While the surface meaning points to the removal of a specific weight or sin, its deeper significance lies in the transformative mercy of the divine, which lightens the path of the believer. It serves as a reminder that human limitations and mistakes are not carried forever; rather, through sincere repentance and divine grace, the past is purified. This concept encourages the soul to move forward with renewed lightness and confidence, trusting that the heavier consequences of past actions need not define one's spiritual trajectory when turned back to God.

translation: Which broke your back [i.e., weighed heavily upon you]?
interpretation: This rhetorical question highlights a past burden or hardship that weighed so heavily upon the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ that it metaphorically 'broke his back,' drawing an analogy to the labor of carrying a heavy load that causes the spine to give way under the strain.

translation: And We have raised high for you your remembrance (i.e., your mention, your name).
interpretation: This verse is a divine assurance to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ that Allah Himself has taken upon Himself the responsibility of glorifying his name throughout the world and elevating his remembrance above all others. It signifies that the Prophet's name is inseparably linked with the declaration of faith (the Shahadah), is mentioned in the adhan (call to prayer), in the sermons, and in the daily prayers of Muslims. This is an honor bestowed directly by Allah, not earned through human effort. It also implies that his message would remain known and preserved, as his name would be invoked alongside the name of Allah by every Muslim until the Day of Judgment.

translation: Indeed, with hardship comes ease.
interpretation: This verse from Surah Ash-Sharh (94:6) conveys a profound divine assurance that no matter how insurmountable a difficulty or trial may appear, it is never permanent or absolute. The Arabic word 'العسر' (difficulty) is articulated in the singular form, whereas 'اليسر' (ease) appears twice in the preceding and following verses (94:5 and 94:6), implying that ease is inherently more powerful, enduring, and abundant than any single hardship. It teaches the believer that suffering is a transient state within a broader tapestry of divine mercy, encouraging perseverance, trust in God (tawakkul), and hope. The verse does not deny the reality of pain or struggle, but it reframes suffering within an eternal perspective where ultimate relief and divine facilitation are guaranteed outcomes for those who remain patient and steadfast. It serves as a spiritual anchor for navigating life's inevitable challenges, reminding the soul that God's wisdom ensures every contraction is followed by an expansion, every darkness by light, and every trial by ultimate ease—whether in this world or the hereafter.

translation: Indeed, with hardship comes ease.
interpretation: This verse is one of the most profound statements of hope and resilience in the Qur'an. It does not merely acknowledge that life contains difficulty, but it establishes a divine principle: no matter how insurmountable a hardship may appear, ease is not only possible but is divinely guaranteed to accompany or follow it. The use of the word 'العسر' (hardship) in the definite singular form emphasizes that whatever specific hardship one faces, the response from Allah is equally certain. The Arabic word 'يسر' (ease) is intentionally general, encompassing relief, facilitation, solutions, and openings that may come from directions the believer cannot foresee. This verse teaches that trials are not permanent states but passages within a broader divine design where ultimate ease belongs to those who maintain trust in Allah, exercise patience (sabr), and persist in righteous striving. It is a divine promise that reassures the believer that Allah's mercy and facilitation are always active, even when circumstances seem overwhelming.

translation: So when you have finished [your duties], then stand up [for worship].
interpretation: This verse commands believers to devote themselves wholeheartedly to the worship of God, especially after completing worldly tasks. It emphasizes that devotion to God should not be confined to specific times but should be a constant priority. After fulfilling necessary worldly responsibilities, one should turn to God with renewed energy and sincerity. The verse also serves as a reminder that life’s ultimate purpose is to serve God, and that worldly engagements are transient, while spiritual commitment is eternal. It encourages a balanced yet God-centered approach to life, where worship becomes the natural conclusion of all endeavors.

translation: And to your Lord, aspire.
interpretation: This verse is a divine command directing the human soul toward a singular, ultimate object of desire: God Himself. The word 'رغب' (rغبة) here encompasses both desire and yearning, suggesting that true aspiration is not the pursuit of worldly gains, status, or fleeting pleasures, but the elevation of the heart toward the Divine. It implies a conscious redirection of the believer's deepest longings-away from the ephemeral attachments of the material world and toward the eternal, absolute reality of God. This aspiration is not merely an emotional state but an active orientation of one's will and purpose. By directing longing solely to God, the verse establishes a principle of spiritual exclusivity: the heart's capacity for deep yearning finds its proper fulfillment only in the Divine. Such orientation brings inner peace, because it anchors the self in something unchanging and infinite, unlike worldly desires which perpetually shift and ultimately disappoint. The verse also subtly critiques the fragmentation of desire that occurs when humans distribute their hopes across multiple sources-careers, relationships, possessions-since none can bear the full weight of the soul's deepest yearning. True contentment, it suggests, arises when desire is purified and unified, focused on the One who is the source of all being. Ultimately, this aspiration to God is both a journey and a destination: it transforms the quality of one's life in this world while drawing the soul toward its ultimate return.

translation: By the fig and the olive,
interpretation: This phrase opens Surah At-Tin by invoking the fig and the olive as witnesses or symbols in an oath, emphasizing their sacred and symbolic importance in divine wisdom, as both fruits hold historical, spiritual, and nutritional significance in the lands of prophecy, connecting to the themes of creation, faith, and human potential that the surah subsequently addresses.

translation: .And (by) the Mount of Sinai (Ṭūr Sīnīn)
interpretation: The mention of Mount Sinai in this oath refers to the location where Allah spoke directly to the Prophet Musa (Moses), symbolizing the giving of the Torah and divine revelation. As part of the opening oaths of Surah At-Tur, it serves as a reminder of the site of profound prophetic experience and divine communication, emphasizing that truth and guidance flow from Allah to humanity through chosen messengers at specific times and places. The reference underscores the sacredness of revelation and the weight of the divine message that came upon the mountain.

translation: And this city of security (Makkah).
interpretation: The verse refers to Makkah as the 'city of security,' a place divinely designated as a sanctuary where violence and conflict are prohibited. This designation emphasizes the sacred status of Makkah in Islam, where even birds and game are protected from harm, and where pilgrims can perform their rites in peace. The verse also serves as a reminder to the audience of the intimate connection between the land and divine revelation, as Makkah is the city where Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was born and received the Qur'an.

translation: We have certainly created man in the best of stature (form).
interpretation: This verse affirms the deliberate excellence with which Allah fashioned humanity, highlighting that the human being is crafted in an optimal and balanced form—both physically and spiritually—reflecting divine wisdom and purpose in creation.

translation: Then We returned him to the lowest of the low.
interpretation: This verse refers to the decline of the human being from the highest spiritual and moral station—where the soul is capable of attaining divine nearness and lofty understanding—down to the depths of degradation when one chooses to reject truth, indulge in heedlessness, and pursue base desires. It serves as a powerful warning that despite the lofty potential bestowed upon humanity (being created in the best stature, as mentioned in the preceding verse), a person can fall to the lowest levels of existence through their own choices. This 'lowest of the low' can be understood as a state of spiritual blindness, moral corruption, and a life dominated by materialism and heedlessness of divine purpose, where the higher faculties of the soul are buried under the weight of worldly attachments and misguidance. The verse underscores human free will and the tragic consequences of misusing it, reminding that the fall is self-inflicted and not a predetermined fate.

translation: Except those who believe and do righteous deeds, for they shall have a reward uninterrupted.
interpretation: The verse presents a profound distinction within the divine economy of mercy and justice, affirming that while the broader context may address human frailty and ingratitude, those who anchor themselves in faith (īmān) and manifest that faith through righteous action (ʿamal ṣāliḥ) occupy a uniquely secure position before God. The phrase ajrun ghayru mamnūn signifies a reward that is neither diminished nor interrupted, pointing to a quality of divine generosity that transcends human transactional logic; it is not a wage that can be withheld, weighed, or found insufficient, but a continuous effusion of grace. This suggests that the believer's reward is rooted not merely in the scale of deeds but in the orientation of the heart and the sincerity of submission, wherein God's favor flows as an unending current rather than a finite compensation.

translation: Then what is it that will cause you to deny [or: contradict] the Judgment after this?
interpretation: This rhetorical question at the end of Surah At-Tin serves as a powerful, piercing challenge to the denier. After having cataloged the perfect and purposeful creation of the human being—placed in the best stature and then reduced to the lowest depths except for those who believe and do righteous deeds—the verse confronts the questioner directly: Given all the clear signs of design, purpose, accountability, and ultimate justice that you have witnessed within your own being and in the world around you, what possible excuse remains for you to still deny the Day of Judgment? It is not an inquiry seeking information, but a rebuke that exposes the absurdity and willful blindness of denying divine recompense when the very fabric of creation testifies to a wise Creator who does not act in vain.

translation: ,,Is not Allah the best of judges?
interpretation: This rhetorical question emphasizes Allah's absolute and supreme authority as the ultimate judge and arbiter of all matters. It affirms that no decree, law, or judgment can surpass His in wisdom, justice, and fairness. The verse invites reflection on the perfection of divine justice, contrasting it with human judgments that are often flawed, biased, or incomplete. It serves as a reminder to place ultimate trust in Allah's decisions, recognizing that His rulings—whether regarding destiny, morality, or the hereafter—are always the most just and beneficial, even if they are not immediately understood by human perception.

translation: ,chapter=96,verse=1,text=Read in the name of your Lord who created,
interpretation: The opening command of the Qur'an establishes knowledge as a sacred act rooted in the recognition of divine creation. By instructing the Prophet ﷺ to begin reading with the name of his Lord, the verse frames all pursuit of knowledge as an act of worship, requiring intentionality, humility, and acknowledgment that creation itself is a sign of God's power and wisdom. Creation here is not merely biological or physical but encompasses everything brought into existence, positioning learning as a means to reflect upon and understand the purpose behind what God has made.

translation: He created man from a clinging substance.
interpretation: This verse describes the origin of human life as beginning with a small, clinging entity, referring to the embryo that attaches to the uterine wall. It emphasizes that human beings, despite their later achievements and complexity, originate from a humble and fragile biological starting point. The verse serves as a reminder of human insignificance in the grand scheme of creation, encouraging humility before God who brought forth life from such a modest beginning. It also subtly invites reflection on the stages of human development as signs of divine power and purposeful design.

translation: Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the boundless generosity and nobility of God, who not only commands His servant to read and acquire knowledge but also frames the act of reading as a divine gift, inviting humanity to share in the boundless generosity of their Creator through learning and understanding.

translation: Who taught by the pen.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that knowledge and learning are gifts from Allah, not merely products of human invention. The mention of the pen (`al-qalam`) highlights the importance of writing as a means of preserving and transmitting knowledge. In a broader sense, it draws attention to the divine origin of writing and literacy, which became foundational to civilization, revelation, and intellectual development. The pen also symbolizes discipline, reflection, and the recording of truth, suggesting that genuine knowledge comes through revelation and careful instruction, not solely through human reasoning or experience.

translation: He taught man what he knew not.
interpretation: This verse expresses the profound nature of divine grace in bestowing knowledge upon humanity. God, in His infinite wisdom and generosity, elevated human beings by teaching them what they could not have discovered on their own. This encompasses all forms of knowledge—intellectual, spiritual, moral, and practical—that enable human beings to understand themselves, the world around them, and their purpose in existence. The verse underscores that true knowledge is ultimately a gift from God rather than a purely human achievement, reminding humanity to approach learning with humility and gratitude. It also implies that the capacity to learn and the means of acquiring knowledge are themselves divine favors, motivating believers to seek knowledge as an act of worship and to use it responsibly in service of righteousness and the betterment of creation.

translation: No! Indeed, mankind transgresses.
interpretation: This verse is a divine rebuke and a definitive negation ('Kalla') that draws attention to a fundamental truth about human nature: the tendency towards transgression and overstepping bounds. The word 'Insaan' (mankind/human being) here refers to the soul in its unrefined state, driven by ego and material desires, or specifically to those who deny the truth out of arrogance. When a human being is granted blessings, wealth, status, or even a taste of independence and self-sufficiency, their nature often inclines towards 'Tughyan'—a state of insolence, rebellion, and exceeding the proper limits set by Allah. This transgression can manifest in various forms: disobeying Allah, oppressing others, feeling self-sufficient and forgetting the Creator, or claiming rights and status that have not been given. It is a warning that human nature, left unchecked, naturally gravitates toward arrogance and excess when it perceives strength or abundance, necessitating constant spiritual vigilance and accountability.

translation: He sees himself as self-sufficient.
interpretation: This fragment describes the moment when the human being sees that he has become independent or wealthy, and as a result, he feels no need for God, for guidance, for prayer, or for the Hereafter. The verse refers to a psychological and spiritual reality: when a person achieves wealth, power, or prestige, he often falls into the illusion that he has achieved self-sufficiency, that he owes nothing to anyone, and that his success is purely the result of his own effort and ability, forgetting God’s grace and bounty. This self-sufficient outlook leads him to arrogance, turning away from God and from moral accountability, and to belittling others.

translation: Indeed, to your Lord is the return.
interpretation: This concise yet profound statement in Surah Al-A'la (87:25) serves as a powerful reminder of the ultimate destination of all human beings. The verse emphasizes that every soul will inevitably return to Allah, the Creator and Sustainer of all things. This return is not merely physical but encompasses one's deeds, intentions, and ultimate accountability. The use of the emphatic particle 'inna' (indeed) underscores the certainty and inevitability of this return. It serves as a motivational call for self-reflection, urging individuals to consider their actions and spiritual state, knowing that they will stand before their Lord. The verse also implies that life in this world is transient, and the true, everlasting life is in the Hereafter, where one will face the consequences of their choices. It encourages believers to live with mindfulness of this eventual return, striving for righteousness and piety in all aspects of life.

translation: Have you seen the one who forbids
interpretation: This verse refers to a specific person, Abu Lahab, and continues in the next verses to describe the condemnation of those who actively stand in opposition to the message of truth, reminding the believer that attempts to suppress or obstruct divine guidance ultimately meet the fate predicted by God, and that such opposition cannot harm the message itself, but only harms those who pursue it.

translation: A servant when he prays.
interpretation: This is an incomplete fragment from a longer Quranic passage (likely from Surah Al-'Alaq 96:10) describing the condition of a servant who actively turns away and grows arrogant from the remembrance of Allah when he prays. It emphasizes a spiritual paradox and a warning: mere ritual performance of prayer is not sufficient if it is accompanied by arrogance, turning away from divine guidance, or neglecting the inner reality of devotion.

translation: Have you seen if he is upon guidance?
interpretation: This rhetorical question challenges those who ridicule the believer's adherence to faith, suggesting that being upon true guidance is far more honorable and beneficial than amassing worldly wealth or status, which the disbelievers often pride themselves in; it implies that the true measure of a person's worth lies in their moral and spiritual orientation, not their material possessions, and that those who reject the Prophet's message will ultimately face regret when they witness the reward of those who were guided.

translation: Or enjoin righteousness?
interpretation: This phrase, from Surah Al-Dhariyat (51:55), refers to urging people to be conscious of Allah, to worship Him alone, and to fulfill the duties He has imposed, while also commanding what is good and forbidding what is evil.

translation: Have you seen the one who denies and turns away?
interpretation: This verse challenges the Prophet Muhammad to reflect on the moral condition of a person who rejects the truth of the Quran and refuses to turn back to Allah. The rhetorical question "أرأيت" (have you seen / do you realize) serves as an attention-grabbing device, urging the Prophet—and by extension, all believers—to recognize and contemplate the spiritual state of those who consciously deny divine guidance and turn away from worship and obedience. It is an implicit rebuke of such arrogance and a call to remain steadfast in conveying the message regardless of the denial encountered.

translation: Does he not know that Allah sees?
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical question from Allah, addressing a warning about human behavior. The word 'يعلم' is in the past tense, meaning 'has not known' or 'does he not realize,' which indicates that the person being addressed is in a state of ignorance or denial of Allah's omniscience. The phrase 'أن الله يرى' emphasizes that Allah is always watching and observing all human actions, whether they be deeds of obedience or sin, performed in private or public. This serves as a powerful warning that no act escapes Allah's sight, making such denial or heedlessness irrational. The verse also implies a spiritual lesson: the person who behaves as if unaware of Allah's watchfulness either forgets the reality of the Day of Judgment or suppresses that knowledge due to arrogance or heedlessness, thus exposing themselves to divine accountability.

translation: ]Nay, if he (Abu Jahl) does not stop, We will seize him by the forelock (the front of the head), lying, sinful forelock.}
interpretation: This verse refers to a specific individual, Abu Jahl, who was a prominent leader of Quraysh and a fierce opponent of the Prophet Muhammad and his message. The verse issues a stern divine warning that if he does not cease his aggressive opposition, denial, and arrogance against the truth, he will be seized and dragged by the forelock—the front part of the head traditionally grasped to humiliate and overpower someone. The description of this forelock as "lying" and "sinful" characterizes his nature as one who habitually rejects truth through lies and persistently commits sins. This serves as a powerful metaphor for divine justice: no matter how powerful or defiant a person may be, the ultimate authority lies with God, who can subdue even the mightiest tyrants. The verse also functions as a reminder that obstinate rejection of truth carries severe consequences, both in this world and the hereafter, and that human arrogance cannot ultimately prevail against divine will.

translation: A lying, sinful forelock (or forehead).
interpretation: This verse describes a specific part of the disbeliever's body—metaphorically the forelock or front of the head—as characterized by lying and sin. In classical Arabic and Qur'anic usage, the 'nasiya' (forelock) often represents the mind, will, or the seat of one's choices and actions. By attributing falsehood and error to this part, the verse suggests that the person's entire capacity for thought and decision-making has been corrupted by rebellion against truth. It is not merely that such a person commits occasional sins, but that their very faculty of judgment is distorted; their intellect has become an instrument of denial and deviation. This serves as a powerful image of how persistent rejection of guidance affects not just behavior but the very ability to perceive and choose truth, indicating a state where the heart and mind are so aligned with falsehood that they actively produce it.

translation: So let him call his assembly (or his companions).
interpretation: This phrase, from Surah Al-Alaq (96:17), is part of a divine challenge issued in the context of warning the Prophet ﷺ (and, by extension, believers) against the arrogance and persecution by the oppressive Quraysh leaders like Abu Jahl, who tried to prevent the spread of the Quran. The word 'nadiyah' (ناديه) refers to a gathering place, council, or close circle of supporters and allies. The verse conveys a tone of resolute confrontation and sarcasm: as if to say, 'Let him summon his entire group and whatever power he possesses to oppose the truth.' It reflects the Quranic principle that falsehood, no matter how organized or powerful it appears, is ultimately helpless against divine truth. It also serves as a test of the opponents' intentions, exposing the futility of their collective efforts when confronted with the message of Allah. The broader passage emphasizes that true success and salvation belong to those who purify themselves, remember the name of their Lord, and pray—contrasting the empty rallying of worldly power with the spiritual discipline required for true victory.

translation: We will soon summon the Zabaniyah (angels of Hell).
interpretation: This verse refers to the angels who are guardians of Hellfire, whom Allah will call to seize and punish the wrongdoers on the Day of Judgment. The mention of summoning them underscores the certainty of divine justice and the terrifying fate awaiting those who reject truth and persist in wrongdoing.

The verse is a directive from Allah to the Prophet Muhammad, commanding him not to heed the denier of the Day of Judgment, but rather to prostrate and draw near to Allah in worship. The prostration is not merely a physical act but an expression of humility and devotion, bringing the believer closer to the Divine. This verse establishes a fundamental principle of spiritual focus: when faced with rejection or opposition, the appropriate response is not argument or compromise, but steadfast worship and drawing nearer to Allah. The act of prostration symbolizes ultimate submission, and through it, the worshipper attains proximity (qurb) to Allah. The verse underscores that true elevation comes through humility before Allah, not through responding to or being distracted by those who reject faith.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree.
interpretation: This opening of Surah Al-Qadr establishes the profound significance and divine origin of the Qur'an itself. The phrase 'We sent it down' is spoken by Allah in the first person plural of majesty, indicating that the descent of the Qur'an is not a human accomplishment but a sacred event initiated by the Divine. By specifying that this revelation occurred during the 'Night of Decree' (Laylat al-Qadr), the verse immediately signals that this particular night possesses immense spiritual weight, setting the stage for the verses that follow to describe its extraordinary value. The entire surah essentially functions as an honor bestowed upon both the night itself and the Book that was revealed within it.

translation: And what can make you know what the Night of Decree is?
interpretation: This rhetorical question emphasizes the profound and awe-inspiring nature of the Night of Decree (Laylat al-Qadr), highlighting that its true reality, immense value, and the full scope of its blessings are beyond human comprehension. It is a night so extraordinary that only Allah truly knows its full significance, and its merits are far greater than any worldly measure could convey.

translation: The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months.
interpretation: This verse establishes the Night of Qadr as a singularly unparalleled period of spiritual opportunity, whose virtue exceeds that of eighty-three years of continuous worship. This profound elevation is not merely quantitative but qualitative—it represents a night upon which divine grace, mercy, and preordained decrees descend so densely that the very atmosphere becomes saturated with angelic presence and benevolent purpose. The believer is thus invited to recognize that spiritual treasures far exceeding lifetimes of ordinary devotion are accessible within a single night of sincere devotion, contemplation, and supplication. This serves as a divine mercy, acknowledging human limitations while providing a concentrated season of grace that accommodates the reality of finite lifetimes, demonstrating that the sacred is not bound to duration alone but to the intensity of divine presence that a given moment can contain.

translation: The angels and the Spirit descend therein by permission of their Lord for every matter.
interpretation: This verse from Surah Al-Qadr (97:4) describes the spiritual atmosphere of the Night of Decree, a night more powerful than a thousand months. The descent of the angels and the Spirit (often understood as Angel Jibreel) signifies a profound outpouring of divine mercy, guidance, and peace. This descent occurs by Allah's command, emphasizing His absolute sovereignty over all creation. The phrase 'for every matter' indicates that the destinies, decrees, and affairs for the entire following year are arranged and settled on this blessed night. It highlights the active engagement of the unseen realm in human affairs by divine will, offering believers an unparalleled opportunity for worship, reflection, and spiritual elevation.

translation: Peace be upon him until the emergence of dawn.
interpretation: This phrase appears in Surah Al-Saffat (37:181) where God sends peace and blessings upon the Prophet Salih and his followers until the coming of the Day of Resurrection, which is metaphorically described as the 'emergence of dawn' (morning light). The imagery of dawn signifies the transition from darkness to light, symbolizing divine clarity, truth prevailing over falsehood, and the ultimate fulfillment of God's promise. It conveys that the righteous are eternally honored and safeguarded by God, while also serving as a reminder that earthly trials are temporary, and divine justice will arrive with certainty like the break of day.

translation: Those who disbelieved from the People of the Book and the polytheists were not going to desist until there came to them clear evidence.
interpretation: This verse affirms that rejection of truth, whether by scriptural communities who distorted their revealed teachings or by those who worshipped false deities alongside God, persists only because the decisive proof has not yet reached them in a manner that compels recognition; once that undeniable evidence arrives—in the form of the Prophet Muhammad and the Qur'an—their excuse for remaining in denial is removed, and they are called to accountability.

translation: A messenger from Allah reciting purified scriptures
interpretation: This phrase emphasizes the divine origin and pure nature of the Prophet's message. The 'purified scriptures' refer to the Qur'an as revelations free from any distortion, falsehood, or human interpolation, presented by a messenger sent directly by God. The verse affirms the authenticity of the prophetic transmission and the sanctity of the revealed text, which stands as a source of guidance untouched by worldly corruption or human caprice.

translation: In it are valuable books.
interpretation: This verse refers to a blessed or elevated setting—such as the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ al-Mahfūẓ) or a place of knowledge—wherein are recorded significant and precious scriptures. It signifies that within this divine source or elevated repository are contained writings of great worth, meaning that the knowledge preserved there is not trivial or corrupt, but rather essential, authoritative, and honored, representing guidance and truth that carry real spiritual and intellectual weight for those who reflect upon them.

translation: And those who were given the Scripture did not divide [into sects] except after clear evidence had come to them.
interpretation: This verse states that the people of the Book (Jews, Christians, and others who received previous scriptures) did not splinter into differing factions and opposing groups until after definitive proof and clear evidence had already reached them from God. The implication is that their division was not born out of ignorance or lack of information—rather, they divided into sects despite having access to truth, suggesting that their schisms arose from motives such as worldly desire, arrogance, partisanship, or deliberate deviation after the truth had been made manifest. This serves as a warning that merely possessing knowledge or scripture is not sufficient to preserve unity; sincere submission to the truth is required to prevent division.

translation: And they were commanded not except to worship Allah, devoting religion to Him alone, upright, and to establish prayer and give zakah. And that is the religion of the upright community.
interpretation: This verse encapsulates the essence of the divine mission given to humanity in Islam: a call to pure, sincere worship of God alone, free from any form of polytheism or idolatry. The command to "worship Allah, devoting religion to Him alone" (mukhlasina lahu al-din) emphasizes the concept of ikhlas (sincerity and purity of intention), which is the foundation of all acts of devotion. The description of the believers as "hanifan" (upright) points to a natural inclination toward the truth, aligning one's life with the fitrah, the innate disposition to recognize and submit to the One God. The mention of establishing prayer (salat) and giving zakah highlights the integration of personal spirituality with social responsibility. Prayer represents the believer's direct connection with God, a constant renewal of faith and dependence on the Divine, while zakah embodies the practical expression of compassion, justice, and communal solidarity. Together, these acts form the dual axis of devotion: nurturing the soul while caring for society. The concluding phrase, "and that is the religion of the upright community" (al-qayyimah), refers to the enduring, straight, and just order of life that has been the consistent call of all prophets. It signifies a religion that is not confined to rituals but encompasses a complete way of life, characterized by moral integrity, balance, and submission to God. The verse thus frames Islam not as a set of arbitrary rituals but as a holistic, purpose-driven way of living that uplifts both the individual and the community.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve from among the People of the Book and the polytheists will be in the fire of Hell, abiding eternally therein. Those are the worst of creation.
interpretation: This verse establishes a severe and categorical warning about the ultimate end of two specific groups: those among the People of the Book (Jews and Christians) who rejected the message of Islam, and the polytheists (those who associate partners with God). By grouping them together, the verse underscores that rejection of the truth, whether by distorting previously revealed scriptures or by polytheism, leads to the same grievous consequence: eternal abode in Hellfire. The phrase 'they are the worst of creation' serves as a profound moral and spiritual judgment, indicating that disbelief fundamentally corrupts one's nature and misorients one's purpose as a human being. Unlike other creation, humans possess the capacity for belief, moral choice, and recognition of the Divine; to squander this potential through willful disbelief and idolatry places one beneath even the instinctive creatures in the cosmic hierarchy. This is not merely a statement of future punishment but a declaration of their degraded spiritual status in this world, as they have exchanged truth for falsehood, thereby becoming the most misguided and morally bankrupt of all beings. The verse calls the reader to reflect deeply on the weight of belief and the gravity of rejecting divine guidance.

translation: Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds - it is they who are the best of creation.
interpretation: The verse draws a sharp boundary in human identity based on a two-fold criterion: faith (iman) and righteous action (amal salih). It does not say 'the best of people' (khayr al-bashar) but 'the best of creation' (khayr al-bariyyah), which is a sweeping ontological claim. The believer who acts rightly is elevated above all other categories of being in the created order, including those who possess worldly power, knowledge, wealth, or lineage. This establishes that ultimate value in existence is not determined by external attributes but by an inward orientation toward the Divine coupled with outward ethical consequence. The pairing of belief and action is non-negotiable in the Qur'anic worldview: belief without action remains incomplete, and action without belief lacks its animating purpose. The phrase 'best of creation' is exclusive in tone - 'ula'ika hum' (they alone are) - leaving no room for a neutral moral category. One is either among this best of creation, or one is not among them. This creates a profound sense of both hope and urgency: hope because the criteria are accessible to anyone, urgency because the bar is not low. It is not ancestry, not nation, not ritual performance alone, but a living synthesis of conviction and conduct that constitutes true excellence in God's creation.

translation: }Their reward with their Lord is gardens of perpetual bliss, with rivers flowing beneath them, where they will remain forever. Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. That is [the reward] for those who fear their Lord.
interpretation: The verse describes the ultimate recompense for the righteous: an eternal, blissful state in gardens of Eden where divine pleasure is mutual—God is pleased with the believer, and the believer finds ultimate satisfaction in God. This reciprocal pleasure (ridā) signifies that salvation is not merely the absence of punishment but the highest spiritual attainment, the realization of complete harmony with the Divine. The closing phrase 'that is for those who fear their Lord' (khashiya) frames reverent awe of God not as mere terror but as the foundational disposition that leads to this perfect state of contentment. The imagery of flowing rivers, eternal residence, and mutual approval together point to a fulfillment that transcends worldly pleasure, rooted in the soul's ultimate return to its Lord.

translation: When the earth is shaken with its [final] shaking,
interpretation: This verse refers to the eschatological event when the earth will undergo a tremendous, final convulsion that will shatter its stability and bring forth all that lies within it. This shaking serves as a divine warning of the Day of Judgment, marking the transition from the worldly life to the realm of ultimate accountability before God.

translation: And the earth will have cast out its burdens (everything within it).
interpretation: This verse from Surah Az-Zalzalah (99:2) describes a profound moment of eschatological transformation. The earth, which has long contained within its depths the physical remains of humanity—buried bodies, treasures hoarded in mines, and the very foundation of human civilization built upon its surface—will expel them. This act signifies not merely a geological upheaval but a disclosure of all that was hidden, preserved, or concealed. On the Day of Judgment, the earth will no longer be a silent keeper of secrets; it will bear witness against or on behalf of those who lived upon it. The 'burdens' (athqāluha) refer to everything the earth carried, including the graves of the dead and the wealth buried within it. This act of expulsion is paired with the earth's testimony in the following verses (99:3-4), where it will declare what was done upon it by its inhabitants. Theologically, this emphasizes divine omniscience and justice: no deed, no matter how deeply buried or hidden, will remain undisclosed. It also underscores the earth's role as a witness in the courtroom of the Last Day, reflecting a Qur'anic theme where elements of creation bear testimony to human actions. The verse evokes a sense of awe and accountability, reminding believers that the physical world itself will participate in the ultimate reckoning, stripping away all veils between action and consequence.

translation: And man says, 'What has happened to it?'
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Qiyamah (75:10), captures the stunned bewilderment of the human being on the Day of Judgment when the earth is violently shaken and convulsed. The question "What has happened to it?" is not a genuine inquiry seeking information, but rather an expression of overwhelming shock and disbelief at the catastrophic transformation of the earth, which had previously been stable and familiar. Throughout worldly life, people often take the earth's steadfastness for granted, assuming it will always remain as it is, and they deny or forget the promised resurrection. So when this day suddenly arrives and the earth is shattered and made ridged, the human being is seized with terror and confusion, his former certainty overturned. The rhetorical question thus exposes the contrast between worldly heedlessness and the helplessness of the soul when confronted with the undeniable reality of the Hereafter.

translation: That Day, it [the earth] will tell its news.
interpretation: This vivid image from the Qur'an portrays the Day of Judgment as a moment of ultimate revelation, when the earth itself will bear witness and disclose every deed—both good and evil—committed upon it. Rather than merely being a passive stage for human activity, the earth is presented as an active, conscious entity that retains knowledge of all events. This could symbolize that nothing in creation is wasted or forgotten; the physical world itself becomes a testament to human choices. The verse challenges the notion that actions can be concealed or that their consequences are limited to this life. It underscores the themes of accountability and the comprehensive nature of divine omniscience—every act, no matter how small or hidden, will be brought to light. For believers, this serves as a powerful motivator for ethical living, knowing that all of creation is a potential witness. For those inclined toward wrongdoing, it offers a stark warning that there is no true anonymity in the moral universe. Ultimately, the verse invites reflection on the relationship between human conduct and the world we inhabit, suggesting that we leave lasting imprints—both physical and spiritual—on the reality around us.

translation: That your Lord has inspired to it (the earth).
interpretation: This phrase refers to God's inspiration or command being revealed to the earth, indicating that the earth will respond to divine instruction by bringing forth its contents and throwing out what lies within it, whether treasures or the bodies of the dead, as part of the Day of Judgment's cosmic upheaval. It emphasizes that even the inanimate earth acts in submission to its Creator's will, signaling a profound transformation during the eschatological event.

translation: That Day, the people will depart separated [into categories] to be shown their deeds.
interpretation: This verse portrays the Day of Judgment as a moment of profound sorting, where individuals are grouped according to the spiritual and moral consequences of their earthly choices. The 'separation into categories' reflects an ultimate accountability, where one's deeds—rather than worldly status, wealth, or appearances—become the defining measure of their eternal state. It underscores the Qur'anic theme that human actions, both seen and hidden, carry weight and will ultimately be revealed in their true form, emphasizing the need for conscious self-evaluation and ethical responsibility in this life, as one's ultimate grouping in the hereafter is determined by the cumulative reality of one's deeds, not by superficial or transient distinctions.

translation: So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it.
interpretation: This Qur'anic statement affirms that no human action, however small or seemingly insignificant, escapes divine notice. The metaphor of an atom—the smallest unit of matter known to the audience of the revelation—emphasizes the absolute precision of divine accounting. Good deeds are not weighed by their external magnitude or by the scale of human perception, but are recorded and presented in their entirety before the individual. This verse also implicitly establishes the complementary truth that evil, too, will be accounted for, framing a moral order in which nothing is lost, forgotten, or wasted. It calls for consistent ethical conduct, regardless of whether the action is publicly observable, socially valued, or considered trivial, since the divine evaluator perceives and rewards even the smallest intention and movement toward goodness.

translation: And whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it.
interpretation: This verse affirms the absolute justice and meticulous accountability of God on the Day of Judgment. The phrase 'مثقال ذرة' (the weight of a speck or an atom) employs a powerful metaphor to emphasize that no deed, however small or hidden from human perception, escapes God's notice. The use of 'شرا' (evil) does not limit the scope to major sins but encompasses all forms of wrongdoing, including intentions and minor transgressions. The verb 'يره' (he will see it) indicates that the individual will inevitably encounter the consequences of their actions, signifying that divine recompense is not arbitrary but perfectly calibrated to each deed. This serves as a profound warning against underestimating sin and underscores the importance of moral integrity, as humans are accountable even for the most minute ethical failures. It also complements verses emphasizing reward for good, presenting a balanced divine moral economy where both virtue and vice are precisely recorded and justly requited.

translation: By the snorting steeds (horses charging into battle),
interpretation: This opening of Surah Al-'Adiyat employs a vivid, sensory oath to draw attention to the powerful reality of war horses surging forward in cavalry charges. The verb ضَبْحًا (ḍabḥan) refers to the distinctive snorting or panting sound horses make as they race into battle—a visceral auditory image. By swearing by this striking phenomenon, Allah underscores that even seemingly mundane natural or worldly occurrences are subject to divine purpose and signification. The oath typically signals that something weighty and serious is about to be affirmed or clarified, often concerning human ingratitude, obliviousness to divine signs, or moral accountability. In classical exegesis, these 'charging steeds' are understood as the warhorses of jihad, whose thundering hooves and snorting breath serve as a metaphor for the energy, force, and impact of decisive action. The wider context of the surah contrasts this outward, kinetic power with the inward spiritual blindness of humans, who remain unmindful of the profound realities—death, resurrection, and ultimate accountability—despite being surrounded by overwhelming signs. The choice of such a dramatic, almost cinematic opening invites the listener to pause and recognize that the forces operating in the world, whether horses or human endeavors, are ultimately under divine command and point toward deeper truths about existence, purpose, and the reckoning that awaits every soul.

translation: By those that charge [i.e., the swift horses] and strike sparks of fire,
interpretation: This verse uses a powerful and evocative image of horses charging into battle, their hooves striking against rocks or the hard ground and producing sparks. It serves as an oath, drawing attention to the magnificent and fearsome nature of warhorses used in jihad, and by extension, to the serious and weighty matter that follows. The vivid imagery is meant to stir the soul, reminding the listener of the power, courage, and sacrifice required in times of conflict, and highlighting the gravity of the subject matter about to be addressed.

translation: And [by] the dawn-breakers that raid at morn,
interpretation: The verse alludes to swift, sudden raids carried out at the break of dawn, a common Arab metaphor for overwhelming, decisive action whose effect is felt before the target can prepare a defense. By swearing an oath by such raids, the Qur'an draws attention to the reality that outcomes—particularly those unfolding in human communities—are not arbitrary; they follow discernible patterns that can be anticipated. The image of the dawn raid suggests the moment when hidden intentions and long-prepared plans are suddenly exposed and executed, implying that what seems sudden to the unaware is often the visible culmination of a deliberate sequence. The deeper meaning points to divine awareness of every movement and intention, and the certainty with which cause gives way to consequence, much like a swift morning strike that overtakes its target without warning.

translation: And stirred up thereby clouds of dust.
interpretation: This vivid image portrays the powerful and far-reaching impact of a single intentional action—how even a small deed can ripple outward, stirring up dust and commotion that affect many. It serves as a metaphor for human influence, reminding the believer that one's choices, whether in word or deed, set in motion consequences that extend far beyond the initial moment, shaping the environment and lives of others in ways both visible and unseen.

translation: And he was taken in between them [a group / in the midst of a gathering].
interpretation: The verse describes a scene where a figure—often understood in context to be the tyrannical Pharaoh or one of his people—becomes surrounded or caught within a gathered crowd. It conveys the idea of being ensnared by a collective force or being the focal point of a gathered multitude, often interpreted as Pharaoh being lured by his people into the sea or a trap as part of his destined downfall, illustrating how the arrogant and oppressive inevitably become ensnared by the very forces they rally, leading to their ultimate demise. This serves as a divine lesson about the consequences of arrogance and the inevitability of divine justice.

translation: Indeed, mankind is ungrateful to his Lord.
interpretation: This verse from Surah Al-Adiyat (100:6) highlights the ingratitude of human beings toward Allah. The word 'kanud' specifically describes someone who acknowledges blessings only in times of hardship, complaining about difficulties while forgetting or denying the countless favors of God. It points to a fundamental flaw in human nature: a tendency to focus on afflictions rather than gratitude. The verse serves as a reminder that despite Allah's continuous mercy and provision, many people respond with denial, impatience, or ingratitude. The use of 'innal-insana' (indeed, mankind) is general, though some scholars note that it may refer to a specific type of person who exhibits extreme ungratefulness, while others understand it as a general characteristic of human beings. The verse calls for self-reflection, urging believers to recognize and appreciate Allah's blessings rather than taking them for granted or responding with complaint and ingratitude.

translation: And indeed, he is, over that, a witness.
interpretation: This verse affirms that the human being himself is a witness over his own deeds, thoughts, and inner states on the Day of Judgment, for one's own soul and conscience will testify to what one actually did and intended, regardless of any outward denial in this world.

translation: And indeed, [man's] love of wealth is intense.
interpretation: This verse highlights the powerful and often overwhelming attachment humans have to material possessions and worldly gain. It acknowledges love of wealth as a deep-seated trait of human nature, one that can drive behavior toward accumulation, greed, and neglect of spiritual responsibilities. The verse serves as a sobering reminder that this intense attachment is a test, and believers are called to recognize it within themselves, cultivate detachment, and prioritize generosity, charity, and accountability to God over the pursuit of riches.

translation: Then will they not know when what is in the graves is brought forth (i.e., resurrected)?
interpretation: The verse poses a rhetorical question to those who deny the resurrection, asking whether they will only come to know the truth when the dead are brought forth from their graves on the Day of Judgment. It implies that their denial is based on ignorance of the reality of the afterlife, and that certainty will be forced upon them when the resurrection actually occurs, leaving no room for doubt. The word 'بُعْثِرَ' (bu'thira) literally means 'to be dug up' or 'to be brought forth in a disarrayed state,' indicating the sudden and overwhelming nature of the resurrection when all hidden secrets and buried deeds will be exposed.

translation: And what is in the breasts will be brought forth
interpretation: This phrase signifies the ultimate unveiling of inner realities—those concealed thoughts, intentions, feelings, and secrets hidden within the human soul. On the Day of Judgment, nothing remains hidden; every concealed belief, hidden motive, suppressed emotion, and unspoken intention will be made manifest and exposed before the Divine. This emphasizes the absolute transparency and accountability that awaits all of creation, where the external deeds are but a reflection of the internal state, and both will be weighed and judged with perfect equity and justice.

translation: Indeed, their Lord, that Day, is [fully] Aware of them.
interpretation: This verse affirms God's perfect and intimate knowledge of His servants on the Day of Judgment. The use of 'their Lord' emphasizes a relationship of ownership and accountability, while 'Aware' (Khabir) denotes deep, comprehensive, and experiential knowledge. It means that no thought, motive, or deed escapes divine notice; every person will be recompensed precisely for what they intended and did. This serves both as a warning to those who acted insincerely, knowing that their hidden intentions are fully exposed, and as a source of comfort for the sincere, who can trust that their struggles and inner goodness are seen and will be justly rewarded.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. The Striking Calamity (al-Qāri'ah).
interpretation: Al-Qāri'ah is one of the именований the Day of Judgment, mentioned in the surah of the same name, and literally means 'the striker, the one that strikes with a blow', referring to the sudden and devastating onset of the Hour that will strike all of creation without warning. Its function in the Qur'anic discourse is to direct the listener's attention immediately to the reality of the Hereafter and to shake any heedlessness or complacency, for the Day will overtake humanity unexpectedly, just as a sudden blow or a crashing calamity overtakes a person without anticipation. By naming the Hour with such a vivid and fear-inducing appellation, the verse establishes the foundational premise upon which the rest of the surah builds: the inevitability, suddenness, and overwhelming nature of the Final Judgment, before which no worldly rank, wealth, or power will avail.

translation: }The Striker
interpretation: Al-Qari'ah is one of the names of the Day of Judgment, and it is derived from the verb qara'a meaning to strike or knock. The verse asks rhetorically "What is al-Qari'ah?" to emphasize the magnitude of this Day and its terrifying events, prompting reflection on its reality as a day of great horror and upheaval.

translation: And what can make you know what the Striking Calamity is?
interpretation: The rhetorical question 'And what can make you know what the Striking Calamity is?' serves as a dramatic device to underscore the terrifying and overwhelming nature of the Day of Judgment. It emphasizes the human inability to fully comprehend the magnitude and terror of this event, highlighting that its reality surpasses human understanding and experience. This verse creates a sense of awe and fear, warning of an event so catastrophic that it defies complete description.

translation: The Day when mankind will be like scattered moths.
interpretation: This vivid image depicts a scene of profound human insignificance and vulnerability before the immense power of divine judgment. The comparison to scattered moths (farash mabthuth) evokes creatures that are fragile, directionless, and easily blown about by winds, suggesting that on the Day of Judgment, all the distinctions people clung to in worldly life—power, status, wealth, and even apparent control—will dissolve into helplessness. The use of 'farash' (moths), rather than butterflies or birds, is particularly significant: moths are creatures drawn heedlessly to light, fluttering chaotically without true orientation. This mirrors how humanity, despite its pursuits and attachments in worldly life, remains unaware of the ultimate reality gathering them. The image also conveys a sense of overwhelming multiplicity and crowding, as moths gather in swarms, which suggests the vastness of the assembly on that Day where entire generations and civilizations will be brought together without regard to earthly hierarchies. Ultimately, the verse invites believers to reflect on the transient nature of worldly power and to cultivate a sense of humility, preparedness, and inward orientation toward what truly endures beyond the fleeting existence of this world.

translation: And the mountains will be like carded wool.
interpretation: This vivid image in Surah Al-Qari'ah (101:5) depicts the radical transformation of the created order on the Day of Judgment. Solid, firmly-rooted mountains—the very symbols of permanence and stability in the earthly realm—will be reduced to something insubstantial and easily scattered, comparable to loose, fluffy wool that has been teased apart. The comparison conveys not only the physical disintegration of the mountains but also the collapse of human reliance upon material strength and earthly security. What appears immovable and eternal will reveal its true fragility before divine power, emphasizing that the ultimate reality transcends the physical structures of this world and that only what is anchored in the eternal truth of God remains unshakeable.

translation: Then as for one whose scales are heavy [with good deeds],
interpretation: This opening phrase of verse 6 of Surah Al-Qari'ah establishes the first of two possible outcomes on the Day of Judgment described in this surah. The phrase 'ثقلت موازينه' (his scales/weighings are heavy) indicates that this person's record of deeds, when placed on the scale of divine justice, outweighs any negative deeds. This metaphorical weighing signifies the comprehensive accountability that will occur before Allah. The term 'thaqulat' denotes a sense of overwhelming weight, suggesting an abundance of righteous actions such as faith, sincere worship, moral integrity, and beneficial conduct. The use of 'ama' (as for) introduces this outcome with a sense of definitive consequence—it is not a matter of chance but the natural result of one's earthly life. This contrasts with the subsequent verse that will describe those whose scales are light, creating a dichotomy that emphasizes human free will and ultimate accountability. The concept of 'mawazin' (scales/weights) is symbolic rather than literal in mainstream Islamic interpretation, representing Allah's perfect and precise justice where every deed, intention, and consequence is measured.

translation: So he will be in a pleasing life.
interpretation: This phrase refers to the ultimate state of the righteous soul that has been granted success by Allah; it denotes a life of absolute contentment, bliss, and satisfaction. This 'pleasing life' (عيشة راضية) encompasses both the highest spiritual fulfillment—being pleased with Allah and having Allah pleased with the individual—and the resulting eternal reward in Paradise, where every longing of the soul is met without any toil, grief, or difficulty. It signifies a state of complete harmony between the servant and their Lord, free from the anxieties, regrets, and dissatisfaction that characterize worldly existence. Ultimately, it describes the perfect, everlasting happiness that awaits those who attain salvation.

translation: But as for one whose scales are light (deeds fall short),
interpretation: This phrase from Surah Al-Qari'ah (101:8) refers to the person whose good deeds are insufficient on the Day of Judgment when weighed against their evil deeds. The 'light scales' signify a failure to attain righteousness sufficient for salvation, resulting in a dire consequence described in the following verse—their abode will be Hawiyah, a place of intense heat and suffering. Theologically, this serves as a profound warning about the seriousness of one's actions and accountability before God, emphasizing that mere faith without righteous works cannot save a soul. It calls believers to reflect deeply on the weight and sincerity of their deeds, recognizing that true success lies in deeds that endure and carry weight in God's sight.

translation: Then his destination will be the Abyss (Hawiyah).
interpretation: This phrase refers to the ultimate end of those who reject faith and indulge in wrongdoing.
